knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unit-level polar convention and requires no convexity, closedness, boundedness, or nonemptiness assumption on the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, its polar set is \mathcal{P}_Q:=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle g,x\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }x\in Q\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a subset Q of Euclidean space is the set of vectors whose inner product with every point of Q is at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal{P}_Q=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:\forall x\in Q,\ \langle g,x\rangle\le1\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Function Convex Maximum Scalarization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is equality of optimal values; it does not assert equality of minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be closed and convex on \(Q\), and suppose their constrained level sets on \(Q\) are bounded. Define \(f(x)=\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\). Then there exists \(\lambda^*\in[0,1]\) such that
\[
\min_{x\in Q} f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\bigl(\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two functions are closed and convex on Q and their constrained level sets are bounded, the minimum value of their pointwise maximum equals the minimum value of a suitable convex combination of them.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ are closed and convex on }Q
\text{The constrained level sets of }f_1\text{ and }f_2\text{ on }Q\text{ are bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda^*\in[0,1]:\quad \min_{x\in Q}f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\{\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Domination Rigidity for Sublinear Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sublinear function dominated globally by a linear function on a subspace must coincide with it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a linear subspace. If \(\sigma_1:U\to\mathbb R\) is linear, \(\sigma_2:U\to\mathbb R\) is sublinear, and
\[\sigma_2(x)\le\sigma_1(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in U,\]
then
\[\sigma_2(x)=\sigma_1(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a linear subspace, a sublinear function dominated everywhere by a linear function must equal that linear function everywhere.
assumptions_latex: U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a linear subspace}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in U,\ \sigma_2(x)=\sigma_1(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Definition of Convexity and Concavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions on a real Hilbert space, allowing both infinite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and define \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,\xi)\in\mathcal H\times\mathbb R\mid f(x)\leq\xi\}\). The function \(f\) is convex when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of \(\mathcal H\times\mathbb R\), and it is concave when \(-f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is convex when its epigraph is convex, and it is concave when its negative is convex.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is convex},\qquad f\text{ is concave}\iff -f\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Characterization of Strong Convexity in an Arbitrary Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if second-order test on the interior of a convex set, retaining continuity on the full domain and allowing $\mu=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex with nonempty interior, let $\|\cdot\|$ be a norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\mu\geq0$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous on $Q$ and twice continuously differentiable on $\operatorname{int}Q$, then $$f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu}^{2}(Q,\|\cdot\|)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle\nabla^2f(x)h,h\rangle\geq\mu\|h\|^2$$ for every $x\in\operatorname{int}Q$ and every $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function continuous on a convex set and twice continuously differentiable on its nonempty interior belongs to the mu-strongly convex class exactly when every interior Hessian quadratic form is bounded below by mu times the squared chosen norm; the characterization includes mu equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu}^{2}(Q,\|\cdot\|)\iff \forall x\in\operatorname{int}Q,\ \forall h\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \langle\nabla^2f(x)h,h\rangle\geq\mu\|h\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Formula for the Closure of a Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x'\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then, with equality in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \[ (\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}f\bigl(x+t(x'-x)\bigr)\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n. \]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Hessian comparison for a standard self-concordant function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of the local Hessian metrics within the open unit Dikin ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f be standard self-concordant, x\in\operatorname{dom}f, and y\in W^0(x;1). Then
\[
\bigl(1-\|y-x\|_x\bigr)^2\nabla^2f(x)\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq\frac{1}{\bigl(1-\|y-x\|_x\bigr)^2}\nabla^2f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard self-concordant function, the Hessian at any point in the open unit Dikin ellipsoid around x is bounded above and below by explicit multiples of the Hessian at x.

igl(1-\|y-x\|_x igr)^2
abla^2f(x)\preccurlyeq
abla^2f(y)\preccurlyeq igl(1-\|y-x\|_x igr)^{-2}
abla^2f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Largest Convex Lipschitz Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and maximality of a whole-space convex extension preserving a prescribed Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}(\mathbb R^n)\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(C\). Then a convex \(L\)-Lipschitz function on \(\mathbb R^n\) agreeing with \(f\) on \(C\) exists. Among all such functions, the pointwise largest is \[f_1(x)=((f+I_C)\mathbin{\dagger}(L\|\cdot\|))(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\{f(y)+L\|x-y\|\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function that is L-Lipschitz on a nonempty convex set has a convex L-Lipschitz extension to the whole space. The largest such extension is the infimum of f(y)+L‖x−y‖ over y in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1(x)=\inf_{y\in C}\{f(y)+L\|x-y\|\}\text{ is the largest convex }L\text{-Lipschitz extension of }f|_C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Convergence Implies Uniform Convergence on Compact Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result requires every function and the pointwise limit to be finite-valued on all of finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex for every \(k\), and suppose that \(f_k(x)\to f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). Then \(f\) is convex and, for every compact set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\sup_{x\in S}|f_k(x)-f(x)|\longrightarrow 0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise limit of finite-valued convex functions on R^n is convex, and the convergence is uniform on every compact subset of R^n.
assumptions_latex: f_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex for every }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex and }\forall S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ compact},\ \sup_{x\in S}|f_k(x)-f(x)|\to0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary extension realizes the lower-semicontinuous hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a proper convex function on a Hilbert space with open domain and continuity throughout that domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathcal H\to]-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}g\) open, and suppose that \(g\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{dom}g\). Define
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
g(x),&x\in\operatorname{dom}g,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{y\to x}g(y),&x\in\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}g),\\
+\infty,&x\notin\overline{\operatorname{dom}g}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f=\breve g\) and \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function continuous on its open domain extends to the boundary by its limiting values and takes positive infinity outside the closed domain. This extension is its lower-semicontinuous hull and is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\breve g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pythagorean inequality for convex projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Squared-distance estimate for any point of the projected set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and set \(p=\pi_Q(x_0)\). Then, for every \(x\in Q\), \[\|x-p\|^2+\|p-x_0\|^2\le \|x-x_0\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For projection p of x0 onto a closed convex set, the squared distance from any feasible point x to p plus the squared projection distance is at most the squared distance from x to x0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Upper Boundedness Implies Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pointwise continuity criterion for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F$ be convex on $V$ and let $u\in V$. If there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $u$ and a finite constant $M$ such that $F(v)\le M$ for every $v\in U$, then $F$ is continuous at $u$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function is bounded above by a finite constant on a neighborhood of a point, then it is continuous at that point.
assumptions_latex: There exist a neighborhood $U$ of $u$ and $M<+\infty$ such that $F(v)\le M$ for every $v\in U$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $F$ is continuous at $u$.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). A function is a map \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional taxonomy collecting four exact representations; it is an organizing definition rather than a claim that every representation is computationally finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal E(f)=\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f,\operatorname{epi}f,(L_f(\alpha))_{\alpha\in\mathbb R},\mathcal S_f\bigr),\quad \operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\},\quad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\},\quad L_f(\alpha)=\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Here \(\mathcal S_f\) denotes any exact set-generated description, such as \(f=g+\delta_C\), a support representation, a gauge representation, or an auxiliary-variable epigraph lift. The four encoding classes are respectively extended-value, epigraphical, level-family, and set-generated encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The encoding profile of \(f\) consists of its effective domain, epigraph, complete family of lower level sets, and any exact representation generated from sets. Extended values encode domain restrictions; the epigraph records every inequality \(f(x)\le t\); the level family records every threshold test \(f(x)\le\alpha\); and a set-generated encoding describes the same function through indicators, support or gauge constructions, or a projected lifted set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E(f)=\left(\{f<+\infty\},\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\},(\{f\le\alpha\})_{\alpha\in\mathbb R},\mathcal S_f\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in L_f(\alpha)\},\] whenever the relevant vertical fibers or level index sets have the standard endpoint property.
special_cases_latex: \[f=g+\delta_C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dom}f=C\cap\operatorname{dom}g.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}L_f(\alpha)\times[\alpha,+\infty)\] after taking the upward closure in the second coordinate.
boundary_notes: The four-way classification is a synthesized taxonomy and was not found as a named definition in the inspected sources.
Incomplete collections of level sets need not determine a function uniquely.

notation.meaning: Closed-threshold lower level set at height alpha; no topological closedness is implied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of the Inequality-Constrained Primal Perturbation Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of the value function induced by componentwise convex inequality perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb E^n\) be convex, let \(f\) be convex on \(\Omega\), and let every component of \(\mathbf g\) be convex on \(\Omega\). Define \(w(\mathbf z)=\inf\{f(\mathbf x):\mathbf g(\mathbf x)\leq\mathbf z,\ \mathbf x\in\Omega\}\). Then \(w\) is convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If Ω is convex and f and every component of g are convex, then the optimal value as a function of the inequality bound is convex.
assumptions_latex: g_i\text{ is convex on }\Omega\text{ for every component }i
w(\mathbf z)=\inf\{f(\mathbf x):\mathbf g(\mathbf x)\leq\mathbf z,\ \mathbf x\in\Omega\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w\text{ is convex on }\operatorname{dom}w

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex conjugate and Legendre–Fenchel transform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to functions that need not themselves be convex and includes the exponential example and biconjugate notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}, its convex conjugate is f^\bullet(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}, where \langle p,x\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i. This is the Legendre\text{--}Fenchel transform, and f^{\bullet\bullet}=(f^\bullet)^\bullet. For f(x)=e^x, f^\bullet(p)=p\log p-p for p>0, equals 0 for p=0, and equals +\infty for p<0. On closed proper convex functions the transform gives a one-to-one correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex conjugate of any extended-real function is the supremum of the affine pairing minus the function. This operation is the Legendre–Fenchel transform; applying it twice gives the biconjugate. The extract also gives the conjugate of the exponential function and identifies the closed proper convex class as the bijective regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\bullet(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x))

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is convex on }(0,\infty)\iff f\text{ is convex on }(0,\infty).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), the following are equivalent: (i) for every \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\), the sublevel set \(V_\gamma=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\leq\gamma\}\) is closed; (ii) \(f\) is lower semicontinuous; and (iii) \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function on R^n is lower semicontinuous exactly when all its scalar sublevel sets are closed, equivalently when its epigraph is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall\gamma\in\mathbb{R},\ \{x:f(x)\leq\gamma\}\text{ is closed}\bigr]\iff f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative and Gâteaux differential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the extended-real boundary behavior of directional derivatives for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:V\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the directional derivative at \(u\) in direction \(v\), when it exists, is \[F'(u;v)=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}\frac{F(u+\lambda v)-F(u)}{\lambda}.\] The function is Gâteaux differentiable at \(u\) if there exists \(u^*\in V^*\) such that \(F'(u;v)=\langle v,u^*\rangle\) for every \(v\in V\); this functional is unique and is denoted \(F'(u)\). If \(F\) is convex, the difference quotient is nondecreasing as a function of \(\lambda>0\), so its limit as \(\lambda\downarrow0\) always exists in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\), possibly as \(\pm\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the right-hand limit of the difference quotient. A Gâteaux differential is the unique continuous linear functional representing all directional derivatives. For a convex function, every such one-sided directional limit exists in the extended reals, although it may be infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(u;v)=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}\frac{F(u+\lambda v)-F(u)}{\lambda};\quad F'(u;v)=\langle v,F'(u)\rangle\ \forall v\in V\text{ in the Gâteaux-differentiable case}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone convex composition rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar outer composition, with monotonicity required only on the image of the inner function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(\psi:\operatorname{dom}\psi\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval containing \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\), and let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and nondecreasing on \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\). Then \(f=\phi\circ\psi\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex scalar function composed with a convex function remains convex when the outer function is nondecreasing on the inner function's image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation by Continuous Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies on a nonempty closed convex domain under nonempty interior or finite-dimensional ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subset E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:G\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex. Assume either \(\operatorname{int}G\ne\varnothing\) or that \(E\) is finite-dimensional. If \[A=\{g:E\to\mathbb R:g\text{ is continuous and affine, and }g\le f\text{ on }G\},\] then, for every \(x\in G\), \[f(x)=\sup_{g\in A}g(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex function on a nonempty closed convex set equals the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine functions lying below it, provided the domain has nonempty interior or the ambient space is finite-dimensional.
assumptions_latex: f:G\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in G,\quad f(x)=\sup\{g(x):g\text{ is continuous affine and }g\le f\text{ on }G\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity of a Pointwise Supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise supremum of an arbitrarily indexed family of closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\Delta$ be an arbitrary index set and define
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y).
\]
If, for every $y\in\Delta$, the function $\phi(\cdot,y)$ is closed and convex on $Q$, then $f$ is closed and convex on
\[
\widehat Q=\left\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of an arbitrarily indexed family of closed convex functions is closed and convex on the subset of the common domain where the supremum is finite.
assumptions_latex: \forall y\in\Delta,\quad \phi(\cdot,y)\text{ is closed and convex on }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex on }\widehat Q=\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Function on Euclidean Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is restricted to scalar, finite-valued functions whose domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} is convex if, for every x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n and every \lambda\in(0,1),\quad f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on all of Euclidean space is convex when its value at every strict convex combination of two points does not exceed the corresponding convex combination of its endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff (\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n)(\forall\lambda\in(0,1))\;f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-value convex function on the real line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by the convexity inequality and equivalent epigraph characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), not identically \(+\infty\), is convex if, for every \(x,x'\in\mathbb R\) and every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \[f\bigl(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x'\bigr)\le \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x').\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^2:f(x)\le r\}\) is a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial extended-real-valued function on the real line is convex when it satisfies the convexity inequality for every pair of points and every weight strictly between zero and one; equivalently, its epigraph is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x,x'\in\mathbb R,\ \forall\alpha\in(0,1):\ f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x')\le\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x')\bigr]\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is a nonempty convex subset of }\mathbb R^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Sublevel and Minimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Under the chapter's standing convention, the function is finite-valued on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), hence continuous. The minimizer set may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex. For every \alpha\in\mathbb{R}, the set Q(\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\} is convex and closed. Moreover, \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x) is convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sublevel set of a finite-valued convex function on Euclidean space is convex and closed. Its possibly empty set of global minimizers is also convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(\alpha)=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ is convex and closed, and }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\text{ is convex and closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Maximum Rule for Closed Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maxima of extended-real closed convex functions, including the exact active-function subdifferential formula at interior-domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $f_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, be closed convex functions. Define $f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)$ and $I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}$. Then $f$ is closed and convex, $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)$, and, for every $x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$, $$\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite pointwise maximum of closed convex functions is closed and convex. Its domain interior is the intersection of the component domain interiors, and at every such interior point its subdifferential is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active component functions.
assumptions_latex: f_i\text{ is closed and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex},\quad \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i),\quad \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right)\ \forall x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extrapolation Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of the domain is needed for the reverse implication; otherwise the quantified extrapolation condition can be vacuous on a nonconvex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex. Then \(f\) is convex if and only if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(\beta\geq0\) such that \(y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[f\bigl(y+\beta(y-x)\bigr)\geq f(y)+\beta\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex domain, a function is convex exactly when extending a secant ray beyond one endpoint gives the corresponding affine lower bound on the function value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff f\bigl(y+\beta(y-x)\bigr)\geq f(y)+\beta\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\text{ for all admissible }x,y,\beta

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph, Epigraph, and Strict Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set representations of a real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\),
\[
\operatorname{gr}f=\{(x,r)\in D\times\mathbb R:r=f(x)\},
\]
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in D\times\mathbb R:r\ge f(x)\},\qquad
\operatorname{epi}^{>}f=\{(x,r)\in D\times\mathbb R:r>f(x)\}.
\]
For each \(x\in D\), the vertical fiber of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is \([f(x),+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph contains points whose second coordinate equals the function value. The epigraph and strict epigraph use, respectively, a non-strict or strict lower bound by the function value. Each epigraph fiber is the ray starting at that value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gr}f=\{(x,r):x\in D,\ r=f(x)\},\quad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):x\in D,\ r\ge f(x)\},\quad \operatorname{epi}^{>}f=\{(x,r):x\in D,\ r>f(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient inequalities characterize convexity and strict convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both equivalences hold on a convex domain for a Gâteaux-differentiable real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset V\) be convex and let \(F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\) be Gâteaux differentiable. Then \(F\) is convex on \(\mathcal A\) if and only if \[F(v)\ge F(u)+\langle F'(u),v-u\rangle\qquad\forall u,v\in\mathcal A.\] Moreover, \(F\) is strictly convex on \(\mathcal A\) if and only if \[F(v)>F(u)+\langle F'(u),v-u\rangle\qquad\forall u,v\in\mathcal A,\ u\ne v.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gâteaux-differentiable function on a convex set is convex exactly when every first-order affine approximation is a global underestimator. It is strictly convex exactly when the inequality is strict between distinct points.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ convex}\iff F(v)\ge F(u)+\langle F'(u),v-u\rangle;\quad F\text{ strictly convex}\iff F(v)>F(u)+\langle F'(u),v-u\rangle\ (u\ne v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite definition and properties; the source's strict-convexity/differentiability equivalence requires the customary essential or domain regularity qualifications in fully general formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), its Fenchel conjugate is \(f^*(s)=\sup_{w\in\mathbb{R}^p}\{w^\top s-f(w)\}\). It is closed and convex, and \(f(w)\geq w^\top s-f^*(s)\). If \(f\) is closed and convex, then \(f=f^{**}\), hence \(f(w)=\sup_s\{w^\top s-f^*(s)\}\); generally \(f^{**}\leq f\) and \(f^{**}\) is the greatest closed convex minorant. For separable \(f(w)=\sum_k f_k(w_k)\), \(f^*(s)=\sum_k f_k^*(s_k)\). If \(a\neq0\) and \(h(w)=f(aw+b)\), then \(h^*(s)=f^*(s/a)-b^\top s/a\). Under the appropriate closed-convex regularity, strong convexity of modulus \(\mu\) corresponds to \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz differentiability of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel conjugate is the supremum of all linear pairings minus the function. It is always closed and convex and supplies affine lower bounds. Closed convex functions equal their biconjugates; otherwise the biconjugate is the greatest closed convex lower bound. Conjugation separates across coordinates and obeys the stated affine-change rule, while strong convexity corresponds to smoothness of the conjugate under standard regularity conditions.
assumptions_latex: a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ for the affine-change rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(s)=\sup_w\{w^\top s-f(w)\},\qquad f^{**}\leq f,\qquad f=f^{**}\text{ if }f\text{ is closed and convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity under Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition restricted to the inverse image of a bounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be bounded, and let \(\phi\) be closed and convex on \(S\). For the affine operator \(\mathcal A(x)=Ax+b:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\mathcal A(x)\in S\}\) and \(f(x)=\phi(\mathcal A(x))\). Then \(f\) is closed and convex on \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a function is closed and convex on a bounded set, then its composition with an affine mapping is closed and convex on the inverse image of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex on }Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epi-limits and compact-local convergence of convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes convexity preservation by epigraphical limits and a convergence equivalence away from the boundary of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraphical upper limit of any sequence of convex functions is convex, and an existing epigraphical limit is convex. For a lower-semicontinuous convex limit function whose domain has nonempty interior, epi-convergence, pointwise convergence on some dense subset, and uniform convergence on every compact set avoiding the boundary of the domain are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(f^\nu:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is convex for every \(\nu\in\mathbb N\).
For the equivalence, \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is convex and lower semicontinuous, and \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Preserved by Partial Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a marginal value function over the projection of a convex feasible set; no attainment assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex and let \(\phi\) be convex with \(\operatorname{dom}\phi\supseteq Q\). Define \(\widehat Q=\{x:\exists y\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\}\) and \(f(x)=\inf_y\{\phi(x,y):(x,y)\in Q\}\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(\widehat Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partially minimizing a convex function over the fibers of a convex set produces a convex marginal function on the projection of that set, without requiring the infimum to be attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex on }\widehat Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Active-Index Subgradients of a Pointwise Supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite pointwise suprema of closed convex functions on a common convex set, with the source's one-sided relative-subdifferential rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Delta$ be any set, let $Q$ be convex, and suppose that $\phi(\cdot,y)$ is closed and convex on $Q$ for every $y\in\Delta$. Define $$f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y),\qquad \widehat Q=\{x\in Q:f(x)<+\infty\},$$ and $I(x)=\{y\in\Delta:\phi(x,y)=f(x)\}$. Then $f$ is closed and convex on $\widehat Q$, and for every $x\in\widehat Q$, $$\partial_{\widehat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{y\in I(x)}\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y)\right).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-valued restriction of a pointwise supremum of closed convex functions on a common convex set is closed and convex. At every point of that restriction, its relative subdifferential contains the convex hull of the relative subdifferentials of the active functions; equality is not asserted.
assumptions_latex: \phi(\cdot,y)\text{ is closed and convex on }Q\ \forall y\in\Delta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex on }\widehat Q,\quad \partial_{\widehat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{y\in I(x)}\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y)\right)\ \forall x\in\widehat Q.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity is equivalent to monotonicity of the differential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The monotonicity inequality is imposed for all pairs in the convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset V\) be convex and let \(F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\) be Gâteaux differentiable. Then \(F\) is convex on \(\mathcal A\) if and only if its differential is monotone on \(\mathcal A\), namely \[\langle u_1-u_2,F'(u_1)-F'(u_2)\rangle\ge0\qquad\forall u_1,u_2\in\mathcal A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gâteaux-differentiable real-valued function on a convex domain is convex exactly when its differential is a monotone mapping.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is convex on }\mathcal A\iff\langle u_1-u_2,F'(u_1)-F'(u_2)\rangle\ge0\quad\forall u_1,u_2\in\mathcal A.

\]
is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithm of the sum of the exponentials of finitely many convex functions is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(x)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{f_i(x)}\right)\text{ is convex.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local compact max-affine representation of a convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-dimensional representation at each point of an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex on an open convex set \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex function on an open convex domain is locally, around each domain point, the maximum of a compact family of affine functions.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is open and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal N\ni\bar x\;\exists S\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\text{ compact}:\quad f(x)=\max_{(y,t)\in S}(y^\top x-t)\quad\forall x\in\mathcal N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Real Representation of Objectives and Constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\overline{\mathbb R}=[-\infty,+\infty]\). An extended-real function is a map \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convention allowing both infinite values; most optimization applications subsequently restrict attention to proper functions with values in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le t\}.\] A real-valued function \(g:C\to\mathbb R\) on \(C\subseteq X\) has the canonical extension \[\widetilde g(x):=\begin{cases}g(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] This extension has \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde g=C\) and encodes minimization over \(C\) as unconstrained minimization of \(\widetilde g\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function may take finite values as well as \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\). Its effective domain is the set where its value is below \(+\infty\), and its epigraph contains exactly the finite-height points lying above its values. A function defined only on \(C\) is extended to the ambient space by assigning \(+\infty\) outside \(C\), thereby encoding the domain restriction without changing the original epigraph over finite heights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in C}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\widetilde g(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}g(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widetilde g(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_X(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
Restricting \(f\) to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), or extending its declared domain by assigning \(+\infty\) elsewhere, leaves its finite-height epigraph unchanged.
special_cases_latex: \[\widetilde g=g+\delta_C\] when \(g\) is already defined on the ambient space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hard feasibility conditions and objective values can be manipulated within one function class.
boundary_notes: The sum \(+\infty+(-\infty)\) is undefined, so arithmetic involving improper functions requires an explicit convention.
Allowing \(-\infty\) is useful for formal completeness but is excluded by properness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-value convex functions and indicator constraint encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines effective domain, convexity, properness, closedness, and convex-set indicators in the extended-value framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^p:f(w)<+\infty\}\). The function is convex when \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and \(f\) restricted to that domain is convex; it is proper when \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\), and closed when every sublevel set \(\{w:f(w)\leq\alpha\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), is closed. For a convex set \(C\), the indicator \(I_C(w)=0\) for \(w\in C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise is convex and encodes the constraint \(w\in C\) by addition to an objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-value function is convex when its finite-valued domain is convex and its restriction there is convex. It is proper when that domain is nonempty and closed when all real sublevel sets are closed. The zero-or-infinity indicator of a convex set is convex and encodes membership as part of an extended-value objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I_C(w)=\begin{cases}0,&w\in C,\\+\infty,&w\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad I_C\text{ is convex.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient and Relative Strata of an Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(D:=\operatorname{dom}f\). The affine hull of \(D\) is \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional domain geometry. Relative interior is used because a nonempty convex domain may be lower-dimensional and have empty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{int}D:=\{x\in D:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq D\},\] \[\operatorname{ri}D:=\{x\in D:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}D\subseteq D\}.\] The ambient boundary and relative boundary are \[\operatorname{bd}D:=\operatorname{cl}D\setminus\operatorname{int}D,\qquad \operatorname{rbd}D:=\operatorname{cl}D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D.\] The domain is full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}D=\mathbb R^n\), and lower-dimensional otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain is stratified into ambient interior, relative interior, and boundary portions. Ambient interior uses neighborhoods in \(\mathbb R^n\), whereas relative interior uses neighborhoods only inside \(\operatorname{aff}D\). Thus a convex domain contained in a proper affine subspace can have no ambient interior while still having a nonempty relative interior. Its relative boundary is the closure of the domain with the relative interior removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{int}D\subseteq\operatorname{ri}D\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}D,\qquad \operatorname{aff}D=\mathbb R^n\Longrightarrow\operatorname{int}D=\operatorname{ri}D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}D\iff x\text{ is interior to }D\text{ in the subspace topology of }\operatorname{aff}D.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is an affine set, then \(\operatorname{ri}D=D\) and \(\operatorname{rbd}D=\varnothing\).
For a nondegenerate line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\), its ambient interior is empty, its relative interior excludes the endpoints, and its relative boundary consists of the endpoints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty convex set in finite dimensions has nonempty relative interior.
Continuity statements for proper convex functions naturally use \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), not necessarily \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
boundary_notes: The closure in the relative-boundary formula is the ambient closure; the resulting set lies in \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
Infinite-dimensional relative-interior notions may be empty and often require quasi-relative interior substitutes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Biconjugate Nonconvexity Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an extended-real measure of the maximum vertical discrepancy between a function and its biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \alpha(f):=\sup_x\bigl(f(x)-f^{**}(x)\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\quad \operatorname{dom}f\text{ nonconvex}\Rightarrow\alpha(f)=+\infty.\quad \alpha(f)<+\infty\text{ measures the failure of convexity, and }\alpha(f)=0\Rightarrow f\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Define alpha(f) as the supremum of f(x) minus its biconjugate f**(x). It is nonnegative and may be infinite; it is infinite whenever the effective domain of f is nonconvex. When finite, it measures departure from convexity, and alpha(f)=0 implies that f is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective domain of an extended-value convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the effective-domain portion of the compound extract; its epigraph, affine-function, and whole-space-convention components belong to separate foundational branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and f:S\to[-\infty,+\infty]. With \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,\mu)\in S\times\mathbb{R}:\mu\geq f(x)\}, the effective domain is \operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{x\in S:f(x)<+\infty\}. If f is convex, then \operatorname{dom}f is convex. Its dimension is called the dimension of f, and f is convex if and only if its restriction to \operatorname{dom}f is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain is the projection of the epigraph onto the argument space, equivalently the set where the function is below positive infinity. For a convex function this domain is convex; its dimension defines the dimension of the function, and restricting the function to this domain does not change convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{x\in S:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad f\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{dom}f\text{ convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary pointwise suprema preserve closed convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An arbitrary nonempty index family, restricted to the points where its supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\Delta\ne\varnothing$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $\phi:Q\times\Delta\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Define
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y),\qquad
\widehat Q=\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\}.
\]
If, for every $y\in\Delta$, the function $x\mapsto\phi(x,y)$ is convex on $Q$ and has a closed epigraph, then $f$ is convex and closed on $\widehat Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of any nonempty family of closed convex functions is closed and convex on the subset of the common domain where the supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x):=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)\text{ is convex and closed on }\widehat Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and its basic consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes extended-value conventions, effective-domain convexity, midpoint convexity, concavity, and optimality notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} is convex if, for all x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n and \lambda\in[0,1], f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y), with the inequality understood to hold when f(x)=+\infty or f(y)=+\infty. Then \operatorname{dom}f=\{x\mid f(x)<+\infty\} is convex. Convexity implies midpoint convexity, and continuous midpoint-convex functions are convex. A function h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\} is concave iff -h is convex. A global minimizer satisfies f(x^*)\leq f(y) for every y; a local minimizer satisfies this in some neighborhood of x^*. For convex f, every local minimizer is global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity is the Jensen inequality for every pair of points and every weight in [0,1], with the stated extended-value convention. Its effective domain is convex. Convexity implies midpoint convexity, whose converse holds under continuity. Concavity is convexity after sign reversal, and every local minimizer of a convex function is global.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex, and every local minimizer of convex }f\text{ is global.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Domain and Effective Domain of a Convex Bifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the joint and parameter domains and states their projection, convexity, and proper-slice properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex bifunction \(F\) with graph function \(\Gamma_F\), the graph domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F=\{(u,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m+n}:\Gamma_F(u,x)<+\infty\}\), and \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:Fu\not\equiv +\infty\}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^m}(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F)\), and this set is convex. If \(F\) is proper, then \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:Fu\text{ is proper}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph domain is the effective domain of the joint graph function. The bifunction domain consists of parameters whose slices are not identically positive infinity. It is the parameter projection of the graph domain and is convex. For a proper bifunction, its elements are exactly the parameters with proper slices.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a convex bifunction from }\mathbb{R}^m\text{ to }\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^m}(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F)\text{ is convex};\qquad F\text{ proper}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{dom}F=\{u:Fu\text{ is proper}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value Dichotomy for a Relatively Open Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued convex functions whose effective domain is relatively open; the second alternative allows positive or negative infinity at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, and suppose \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is relatively open. Then either \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or \(f(x)\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function has a relatively open effective domain, then it either never takes the value negative infinity or has no finite values anywhere. Having full effective domain is a special case of the relative-openness hypothesis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper extended-value convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes properness epigraphically, pointwise, through the effective domain, and as positive-infinity extension from a finite convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty] is proper if and only if \operatorname{epi}f\neq\varnothing and \operatorname{epi}f contains no vertical line. Equivalently, (\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n)\,f(x)<+\infty and (\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n)\,f(x)>-\infty. Equivalently, C=\operatorname{dom}f is nonempty and f|_C is finite; in that case C is convex and f is the extension to \mathbb{R}^n of a finite convex function on C obtained by setting f(x)=+\infty for x\notin C. A convex function that is not proper is improper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex extended-value function is proper exactly when its epigraph is nonempty and contains no vertical line, or equivalently when it is finite somewhere and never equals negative infinity. This is also equivalent to having a nonempty effective domain on which the function is finite, with positive infinity assigned outside that domain. A convex function failing these conditions is improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ proper}\iff\bigl[(\exists x)\,f(x)<+\infty\ \land\ (\forall x)\,f(x)>-\infty\bigr]\iff\bigl[\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\ \land\ f|_{\operatorname{dom}f}\text{ is finite}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Conjugates of Improper Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate behavior under the standard convention allowing improper conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f^*(x^*):=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).\] Under the standard rules \(a-(+\infty)=-\infty\) and \(a-(-\infty)=+\infty\) for finite \(a\), \[f\equiv+\infty\Longrightarrow f^*\equiv-\infty,\qquad (\exists x_0\in X\; f(x_0)=-\infty)\Longrightarrow f^*\equiv+\infty.\]

Fenchel conjugates are permitted to be improper.
Standard subtraction of an infinite extended-real value from a finite pairing value is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undefined Mixed-Infinity Arithmetic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic obstruction to unrestricted pointwise calculus for improper extended-value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In standard extended-real arithmetic, \((+\infty)+(-\infty)\) and \((+\infty)-(+\infty)\) are undefined. A pointwise sum or difference producing either form is therefore not an extended-real-valued function there unless an additional convention is imposed. Convex-calculus formulas involving such operations require compatibility assumptions that exclude these forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite or cancelling infinite values make pointwise arithmetic undefined, so unrestricted convex calculus is unavailable without compatibility assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f^*(x^*):=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).\] Under standard extended-real arithmetic, if \(f\equiv+\infty\), then every term in the supremum is \(-\infty\), so \(f^*\equiv-\infty\). If \(f(x_0)=-\infty\) for some \(x_0\), then the term indexed by \(x_0\) equals \(+\infty\) for every \(x^*\), so \(f^*\equiv+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Improper functions yield degenerate conjugates: identically positive infinity conjugates to negative infinity, while any negative-infinite value forces positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty Subdifferential of the Identically Infinite Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of supporting-subgradient calculus in the empty-domain regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the standard convex subdifferential definition, \[\partial f(x):=\{x^*:\ f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\},\] with \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) whenever \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\). Hence \[f\equiv+\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Real Indicator Encoding of Feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(C\subseteq X\), and \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-oriented indicator convention, assigning positive infinity outside the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real indicator of \(C\) is \[\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] The constrained objective associated with \(g\) and \(C\) is \[F:=g+\delta_C,\qquad F(x)=\begin{cases}g(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] whenever the extended-real sum is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of \(C\) assigns zero to feasible points and \(+\infty\) to infeasible points. Adding it to an objective preserves objective values on \(C\) and excludes points outside \(C\) from finite-valued minimization. Thus a hard set constraint becomes part of an extended-real objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in C}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}(g+\delta_C)(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}g(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(g+\delta_C)(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty).\]
\[\operatorname{dom}(g+\delta_C)=C\cap\operatorname{dom}g.\]
special_cases_latex: \[g\equiv0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname*{argmin}\delta_C=C\] when \(C\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[C\text{ convex}\iff\delta_C\text{ convex}.\]
\[C\ne\varnothing\iff\delta_C\text{ proper}.\]
\[C\text{ closed}\iff\delta_C\text{ closed}.\]
boundary_notes: This is not the zero-one indicator used in probability or combinatorics.
If \(g(x)=-\infty\) outside \(C\), the expression \(g(x)+\delta_C(x)\) requires care because \(-\infty+(+\infty)\) is undefined.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiple Constraints as a Sum of Indicators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family variant of hard feasibility encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(F_1,\ldots,F_m\subseteq X\), with \(m\ge1\), \[\sum_{i=1}^m\iota_{F_i}=\iota_{\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i}.\] Hence, for any objective \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), minimizing \(g\) subject to \(x\in F_i\) for every \(i\) is represented by minimizing \(g+\sum_{i=1}^m\iota_{F_i}\) over \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph and Hypograph of an Extended-Real Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-height epigraphs and hypographs in \(X\times\mathbb R\); infinite heights are encoded through empty or full vertical fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le t\},\qquad \operatorname{hypo}f:=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:t\le f(x)\}.\] For each \(x\in X\), the epigraph fiber is \[\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=\begin{cases}[f(x),+\infty),&f(x)\in\mathbb R,\\\mathbb R,&f(x)=-\infty,\\\varnothing,&f(x)=+\infty.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph is the set of finite-height points on or above the graph of \(f\); the hypograph is the set on or below it. Each epigraph fiber is upward closed. A finite value is its fiber's least height, \(-\infty\) produces a complete vertical line, and \(+\infty\) produces an empty fiber.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\) and \(\inf\mathbb R=-\infty\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{hypo}f=\{(x,t):(x,-t)\in\operatorname{epi}(-f)\}.\]
\[\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_X(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
special_cases_latex: For finite-valued \(f\), the graph is the lower boundary of its epigraph.
\[\operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty).\]
immediate_consequences_latex: The epigraph uniquely determines the extended-real function.
Lower level sets are horizontal slices: \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}=\{x:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\).
boundary_notes: The graph alone does not display the upward-closed set structure used in convex analysis.
The finite-height convention keeps the epigraph in a real vector space rather than adjoining infinite coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph and Hypograph Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph, epigraph, and hypograph and states the exact epigraph characterization of convexity and hypograph characterization of concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), with effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(\operatorname{graph}f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\), \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(x)\leq t\}\), and \(\operatorname{hypo}f=\{(x,t):x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ t\leq f(x)\}\). Then \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\), and \(f\) is concave if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}f\) is a convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph records points at the function value, the epigraph contains points on or above the graph, and the hypograph contains points on or below it. A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is convex, and it is concave exactly when its hypograph is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is convex},\qquad f\text{ is concave}\iff\operatorname{hypo}f\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of Sublevel and Superlevel Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary non-strict level sets, states their convexity under convexity or concavity of the function, and preserves the nonconverse boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), its \(\alpha\)-sublevel set is \(C_\alpha=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). If \(f\) is convex, then \(C_\alpha\) is convex for every \(\alpha\). The converse fails: convexity of every sublevel set does not imply convexity of \(f\); for example, \(f(x)=-e^x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) is not convex but has convex sublevel sets. Dually, if \(f\) is concave, then \(\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(x)\geq\alpha\}\) is convex for every \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sublevel set of a convex function is convex, and every superlevel set of a concave function is convex. Having convex sublevel sets is not sufficient for the function itself to be convex; minus the exponential is a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\forall\alpha,\ \{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ convex},\quad f\text{ concave}\Rightarrow\forall\alpha,\ \{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(x)\geq\alpha\}\text{ convex};\ \text{the first implication is not reversible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Foundational Properties of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex functions on convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A function \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is convex iff \(f(\alpha x+\beta y)\le\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)\) whenever \(x,y\in\Omega\), \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\), and \(\alpha+\beta=1\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex. Consequently, \(f(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f(x_i)\) for every finite convex combination. If \(\Omega\) is open and \(f\) is bounded above on a nonempty open subset of \(\Omega\), then \(f\) is continuous on \(\Omega\). If \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \(\rho_C(x)=\min_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity is equivalent to the two-point convexity inequality and to convexity of the epigraph; it yields Jensen's finite inequality. A convex function on an open convex domain that is locally bounded above on an open subset is continuous, and distance to a nonempty closed convex set is convex.
assumptions_latex: For continuity, \(\Omega\) is open and \(f\) is bounded above on a nonempty open subset
For the distance claim, \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ convex}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ convex}\), Jensen's finite inequality holds, the stated boundedness condition implies continuity, and \(\rho_C\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Convexity, Strict Convexity, and Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for extended-real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper convex if it is not identically \(+\infty\) and \(\varphi(tx+(1-t)y)\le t\varphi(x)+(1-t)\varphi(y)\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). It is strictly convex if equality can occur only when \(x=y\) or \(t\in\{0,1\}\). Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi=\{x:\varphi(x)<+\infty\}\), which is convex and may be open, closed, or neither.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is not everywhere infinite and satisfies the convexity inequality. It is strictly convex when equality is possible only for equal endpoints or an endpoint weight. Its finite-valued domain is convex but need not be open or closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, Strictly Convex, and Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the defining chord inequality and the elementary affine, line-restriction, and continuity properties stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex when \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \(f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\leq \theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)\). It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for \(x\neq y\) and \(0<\theta<1\). It is concave, respectively strictly concave, exactly when \(-f\) is convex, respectively strictly convex. Every affine function is both convex and concave, and every function that is both convex and concave is affine. Moreover, \(f\) is convex if and only if every line restriction \(g(t)=f(x+tv)\) is convex on \(\{t:x+tv\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\). A convex function is continuous on \(\operatorname{relint}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), so discontinuities can occur only on the relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is convex when its domain is convex and its value at every convex combination is at most the corresponding convex combination of its endpoint values. Strict convexity uses strict inequality for distinct endpoints and an interior weight; concavity is convexity after sign reversal. Affine functions are exactly the functions that are both convex and concave. Convexity can be checked on every line restriction, and a convex function is continuous on the relative interior of its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\leq\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y),\quad f\text{ convex}\iff f|_{\text{every intersecting line}}\text{ convex},\quad f\text{ is continuous on }\operatorname{relint}(\operatorname{dom}f).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-real-valued functions, arithmetic conventions, and effective domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records only the arithmetic and order conventions explicitly specified in the extract; operations such as \(\infty+(-\infty)\) are not defined here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-real-valued function is a function \(f:\mathbb E\to[-\infty,\infty]\) defined on all of \(\mathbb E\). For every finite \(a\), \(a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty\) and \(a-\infty=-\infty+a=-\infty\). If \(a>0\), then \(a\infty=\infty a=\infty\) and \(a(-\infty)=(-\infty)a=-\infty\); if \(a<0\), then \(a\infty=\infty a=-\infty\) and \(a(-\infty)=(-\infty)a=\infty\). Moreover, \(0(\pm\infty)=(\pm\infty)0=0\), \(-\infty<a<\infty\) for every finite \(a\), and \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in\mathbb E:f(x)<\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is defined everywhere on the underlying space and may take finite values or either infinity. The stated conventions govern addition of finite values to infinity, multiplication of infinity by positive, negative, or zero scalars, and the ordering of finite and infinite values. Its effective domain consists of the points where its value is strictly below positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\leq t\}.\]

Then \(E_x=[f(x),+\infty)\) when \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), while \(E_x=\varnothing\) otherwise. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Value Epigraphs and Their Vertical Fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the epigraph of an extended-real-valued function and characterizes epigraphical sets, effective domains, infinite values, and properness through vertical fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}},\quad \operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,\alpha)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\alpha\ge f(x)\}. Its projection onto \mathbb{R}^n is \operatorname{dom}f. For each x, \{x\}\times\mathbb{R} misses \operatorname{epi}f iff f(x)=+\infty, and is contained in \operatorname{epi}f iff f(x)=-\infty. A set E\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1} is the epigraph of an extended-real-valued function iff every vertical fiber E\cap(\{x\}\times\mathbb{R}) is either empty or a closed interval unbounded above. The associated function is proper iff E\ne\varnothing and E contains no entire vertical line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph consists of the finite-height points lying on or above the function. Its projection is the effective domain; an empty vertical fiber represents value positive infinity, while a full vertical line represents value negative infinity. Exactly the sets whose vertical fibers are empty or closed upper rays are epigraphs, and the associated function is proper precisely when the set is nonempty and has no full vertical fiber.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,\alpha):\alpha\ge f(x)\},\quad \pi_x(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{dom}f,\quad E\text{ is epigraphical}\iff \forall x,\ E\cap(\{x\}\times\mathbb{R})\text{ is empty or a closed upper ray}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph transformation calculus consists of the identities \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\sup_{i\in I}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\] and, for \(f(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\), \[P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F),\quad P(x,z,t)=(x,t).\] An exact projected epigraph representation occurs when \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper envelope is represented by intersecting all constituent epigraphs. Eliminating auxiliary variables by partial minimization corresponds to projecting a higher-dimensional epigraph. Projection can omit boundary points, so the projected set is always contained in the marginal epigraph and its closure always contains that epigraph; exact equality requires additional attainment or closedness conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i,\qquad P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\inf_zF(\cdot,z))\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x,t)\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\iff(\exists z)\ F(x,z)\le t.\]
Exactness at a finite \(x\) includes the boundary point \((x,f(x))\) precisely when the infimum over \(z\) is attained.
special_cases_latex: For a finite maximum, \(\operatorname{epi}(\max_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i\).
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then it equals \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Intersections preserve convexity and closedness.
If \(F\) is convex, its marginal \(f\) is convex, although closedness may fail without further hypotheses.
boundary_notes: Linear images of closed convex sets need not be closed.
The identity for upper envelopes does not extend to pointwise infima by simply replacing intersection with union.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph and strict epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For proper functions with values in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be not identically \(+\infty\). Its epigraph and strict epigraph are \[\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:r\geq f(x)\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}_{s}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:r>f(x)\}.\] If \(S_r(f):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\leq r\}\), then \[(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff x\in S_r(f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph consists of the points lying on or above a function, while the strict epigraph uses strict inequality. A pair (x,r) belongs to the epigraph exactly when x belongs to the sublevel set at height r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):r\geq f(x)\},\quad \operatorname{epi}_sf=\{(x,r):r>f(x)\},\quad (x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff f(x)\leq r.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph reformulation of a constrained minimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a standard minimization problem with inequality and equality constraints; convexity is unnecessary for the equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le 0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), its epigraph form is \(\min_{x,t}t\) subject to \(f_0(x)\le t\) and the original constraints. A pair \((x^\star,t^\star)\) is optimal for the epigraph form if and only if \(x^\star\) is optimal for the original problem and \(t^\star=f_0(x^\star)\). The lifted objective is linear in \((x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce a scalar t, minimize t, and impose f0(x) ≤ t together with the original constraints. A lifted pair is optimal exactly when its x-component solves the original problem and t equals the attained objective value; the lifted objective is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^\star,t^\star)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x,t}\{t:f_0(x)\le t,\ f_i(x)\le0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\iff x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\ \text{and}\ t^\star=f_0(x^\star).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Hull of a Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical definition and the equivalent perspective-infimum formula, including its stated nondegeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), the positive hull \(\operatorname{pos}f\) is the greatest positively homogeneous function majorized by \(f\), with \[ (\operatorname{pos}f)(x)=\inf\{\alpha\mid (x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{pos}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}. \] Equivalently, its epigraph is the smallest cone of epigraphical type containing \(\operatorname{epi}f\). If \(f\not\equiv+\infty\), then \[ (\operatorname{pos}f)(x)=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}(\lambda\star f)(x),\qquad (\lambda\star f)(x)=\lambda f(\lambda^{-1}x)\ \text{for }\lambda>0. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive hull of an extended-real-valued function is its greatest positively homogeneous minorant. Its value is obtained from the positive hull of the function's epigraph. When the function is not identically positive infinity, it is also the pointwise infimum of its perspective rescalings over nonnegative scales.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\operatorname{pos}f)(x)=\inf\{\alpha:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{pos}(\operatorname{epi}f)\},\quad f\not\equiv+\infty\Rightarrow(\operatorname{pos}f)(x)=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}(\lambda\star f)(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Intersection Can Be Empty Despite Common Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp properness failure for an infinite upper envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(f_n(x)=n\) on a nonempty real vector space \(X\). Every \(f_n\) is finite, proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and all effective domains equal \(X\). Nevertheless,
\[\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}f_n(x)=+\infty\quad(x\in X),\qquad
\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\varnothing.\]
Thus common-domain membership does not ensure properness of an infinite supremum; pointwise boundedness above is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant functions f_n=n are all proper closed convex functions with the same full domain, but their supremum is identically positive infinity and their epigraph intersection is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_n f_n\equiv+\infty\) and \(\bigcap_n\operatorname{epi}f_n=\varnothing\), although \(\operatorname{dom}f_n=X\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Intersection Can Be Empty Despite Common Domains

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and Properness of Epigraph Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological and properness consequences for arbitrary upper envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=\sup_{i\in I}f_i\). If every \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\]
is closed, so \(f\) is lower semicontinuous. Moreover,
\[\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)<+\infty\}.\]
Under the codomain convention \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the supremum \(f\) is proper exactly when this set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary supremum of lower-semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is an intersection of closed sets. Its effective domain consists of points where the family is pointwise bounded above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(f=\sup_i f_i\) is lower semicontinuous; moreover, \(f\) is proper iff \(\{x:\sup_i f_i(x)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness and Properness of Epigraph Intersections

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Intersection of an Upper Envelope
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(I\ne\varnothing\), and each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is defined on the same set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary, possibly infinite upper envelopes in the minimization-oriented extended-real convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(x):=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x),\qquad x\in X.\] Its epigraph intersection representation is \[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] Thus an epigraph intersection is the function encoding of a pointwise upper envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of a family of functions is encoded by the intersection of their epigraphs. A pair \((x,t)\) lies above the supremum exactly when it lies above every constituent function. The identity applies to arbitrary index sets and remains valid when the supremum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff(\forall i\in I)\ f_i(x)\le t\iff(x,t)\in\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}=\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x:f_i(x)\le\alpha\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For two functions, \(\operatorname{epi}(\max\{f_1,f_2\})=\operatorname{epi}f_1\cap\operatorname{epi}f_2\).
The supremum of affine functions is represented by an intersection of halfspaces in one higher dimension.
immediate_consequences_latex: If every \(f_i\) is convex, then \(f\) is convex.
If every epigraph is closed, the intersection epigraph is closed, so \(f\) is closed.
boundary_notes: The effective domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:\sup_i f_i(x)<+\infty\}\), which may be strictly smaller than \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\) for an infinite family.
An empty index set would require a separate convention for its supremum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Functions and Projected Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\), and \(P(x,z,t)=(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional projection correspondence, explicitly distinguishing exact projection, missing boundary points, and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projected epigraph set is \[E:=P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\{(x,t):(\exists z\in\mathbb R^m)\ F(x,z)\le t\}.\] It satisfies \[E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}E.\] The representation is exact when \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\), and closed-exact when additionally \(E\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph image obtained by deleting auxiliary variables contains those thresholds attained by some auxiliary point. The marginal epigraph also contains limiting thresholds arising from unattained infima. Consequently, the projected epigraph may miss its lower boundary, but its closure contains the entire marginal epigraph. Exactness means no such boundary points are missing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), \((x,f(x))\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) if and only if \(\inf_zF(x,z)\) is attained.
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then both inclusions become equalities.
special_cases_latex: When \(m=0\), \(P\) is the identity and exactness is automatic.
If a compactness condition ensures attainment for every finite-valued fiber, the projection contains every lower-boundary point.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\) is convex, then \(f\) is convex.
Closedness of \(F\) alone does not ensure closedness of \(f\), because projection need not preserve closedness.
boundary_notes: The closure inclusion is not a claim that \(\operatorname{epi}f=\operatorname{cl}E\) in every improper case.
Projection preserves convexity but may destroy closedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(g(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\}\), with the infimum of an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Then
\[(A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{(y,t):\exists x,\ Ax=y,\ f(x)\leq t\}\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\]
The inclusion is equality if and only if, for every \(y\) with \(g(y)\in\mathbb{R}\), the problem \(\inf_{Ax=y}f(x)\) attains its infimum. Without attainment, the image can omit boundary points \((y,g(y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear epigraph image lies inside the epigraph of the fiber infimum. Equality holds exactly when every finite fiber minimum is attained.
