knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subsequence compactness of densely bounded saddle functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise boundedness is required only on a dense Cartesian subset, while convergence is uniform on every closed bounded subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \((K_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Suppose there are dense sets \(C'\subseteq C\) and \(D'\subseteq D\) such that \((K_i(u,v))_{i\ge1}\) is bounded for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then some subsequence \((K_{i_j})_{j\ge1}\) converges uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\times D\) to a finite concave-convex function \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of finite saddle functions that is pointwise bounded on a dense Cartesian subset has a subsequence converging locally uniformly, in the closed-bounded-set sense, to a finite saddle function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Local Boundedness and Lipschitz Regularity of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional regularity theorem using the ball and norm notation stated in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then \(f\) is locally bounded and locally Lipschitz continuous at \(x_0\). More precisely, there exist \(\epsilon>0\) and \(L>0\) such that \(B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) and
\[
|f(y)-f(x_0)|\le L\|y-x_0\|_{(1)}\qquad\text{for all }y\in B_1(x_0,\epsilon).
\]
In particular, \(f\) is bounded on \(B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every interior point of the effective domain of a finite-dimensional convex function, the function is locally bounded and locally Lipschitz. On a sufficiently small stated ball, its difference from the value at the center is bounded by a constant times the stated norm distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\epsilon,L>0:\ B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall y\in B_1(x_0,\epsilon),\ |f(y)-f(x_0)|\le L\|y-x_0\|_{(1)},\ \text{and }f\text{ is bounded on }B_1(x_0,\epsilon)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise bounded saddle families are locally uniformly bounded and equi-Lipschitz
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pointwise control set must generate the whole product domain after closure and convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \(\{K_i\}_{i\in I}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Suppose \(C'\subseteq C\), \(D'\subseteq D\), \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}(C'\times D'))\supseteq C\times D\), and \(\{K_i(u,v):i\in I\}\) is bounded for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then for every closed bounded \(S\subseteq C\times D\), there exist finite constants \(M_S,L_S\) such that \(|K_i(x)|\le M_S\) and \(|K_i(x)-K_i(y)|\le L_S\|x-y\|\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(x,y\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a family of finite saddle functions is pointwise bounded on a subset whose closed convex hull covers the product domain, then the family is uniformly bounded and equi-Lipschitz on every closed bounded subset of that domain.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\text{ and }D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are relatively open and convex}
\{K_i\}_{i\in I}\text{ is a family of finite concave-convex functions on }C\times D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall S\subseteq C\times D\text{ closed and bounded},\;\exists M_S,L_S<\infty\;\forall i\in I:\;\sup_{x\in S}|K_i(x)|\le M_S,\quad |K_i(x)-K_i(y)|\le L_S\|x-y\|\;\forall x,y\in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Local Lipschitz Regularity of a Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional extended-real-valued convex functions; the assertions apply only within the ordinary interior of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is convex, then $f$ is continuous on $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$. For every compact interval $[a,b]\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$, there exists $L\ge 0$ such that $|f(x)-f(x')|\le L|x-x'|$ for all $x,x'\in[a,b]$. Consequently, the difference quotients $(f(x)-f(x'))/(x-x')$, with $x\ne x'$, are bounded on every bounded interval contained in $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function on the real line is continuous and locally Lipschitz on the interior of its effective domain, and its difference quotients are locally bounded there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists L\ge0\;\forall x,x'\in[a,b],\quad |f(x)-f(x')|\le L|x-x'|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Limits at Finite Domain Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary regularity of one-dimensional extended-real-valued convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be convex with $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\ne\varnothing$. If $a\in\mathbb R$ is the left endpoint of $\operatorname{dom}f$, then $f(a+):=\lim_{x\downarrow a}f(x)$ exists in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $f(a)\ge f(a+)$. If $b\in\mathbb R$ is the right endpoint, then $f(b-):=\lim_{x\uparrow b}f(x)$ exists in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $f(b)\ge f(b-)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every finite endpoint of the domain of a convex function with nonempty domain interior, the inward one-sided limit exists, and the endpoint value cannot be smaller than that limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow f(a+)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\ f(a)\ge f(a+);\qquad b\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow f(b-)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\ f(b)\ge f(b-)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity and Boundedness of Convex Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bounded-subgradient condition always implies Lipschitz continuity on the specified set; openness of the set is required for the stated converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(X\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and fix \(L\). Define \(\mathrm{(i)}\) by \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\), and \(\mathrm{(ii)}\) by \(\|g\|_*\le L\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Then \(\mathrm{(ii)}\Rightarrow\mathrm{(i)}\). If \(X\) is open, then \(\mathrm{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(ii)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on a subset of the interior of its domain, uniform boundedness by L of every subgradient on the set implies that the function is L-Lipschitz there. If the set is open, the Lipschitz and bounded-subgradient conditions are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x\in X\;\forall g\in\partial f(x),\ \|g\|_*\le L\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[\forall x,y\in X,\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\bigr],\quad\text{and if }X\text{ is open, the two conditions are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint continuity of parameterized saddle functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity in the parameter may be imposed everywhere or only for primal-variable pairs in a dense Cartesian subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, let \(T\) be a locally compact topological space, and let \(K:C\times D\times T\to\mathbb{R}\). Assume that \(u\mapsto K(u,v,t)\) is concave for every \((v,t)\), \(v\mapsto K(u,v,t)\) is convex for every \((u,t)\), and either (i) \(t\mapsto K(u,v,t)\) is continuous for every \((u,v)\in C\times D\), or (ii) there are dense sets \(C'\subseteq C\) and \(D'\subseteq D\) for which this parameter map is continuous for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then \(K\) is jointly continuous on \(C\times D\times T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued parameterized saddle function is jointly continuous when its parameter sections are continuous; it is enough to require this continuity for variable pairs in a dense Cartesian subset.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\text{ and }D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are relatively open and convex}
T\text{ is a locally compact topological space}
\forall v,t,\;K(\cdot,v,t)\text{ is concave},\quad \forall u,t,\;K(u,\cdot,t)\text{ is convex}
\bigl[\forall(u,v)\in C\times D,\;K(u,v,\cdot)\in C(T)\bigr]\;\text{or}\;\bigl[\exists C'\subseteq C,D'\subseteq D\text{ dense}:\forall(u,v)\in C'\times D',\;K(u,v,\cdot)\in C(T)\bigr]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\in C(C\times D\times T).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best sampled value bounded by the pointwise continuity modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an arbitrary real-valued function on a set when the infimum is attained; no convexity or algorithmic assumptions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\), let \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\in Q\), and suppose \(x^*\in Q\) attains \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)\). Define \(f_k^*:=\min_{0\le i\le k}f(x_i)\), \(v_k^*:=\min_{0\le i\le k}\|x_i-x^*\|\), and \(\omega_f(x^*;t):=\sup\{|f(x)-f(x^*)|:x\in Q,\ \|x-x^*\|\le t\}\). Then \[f_k^*-f^*\le \omega_f(x^*;v_k^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many sampled points, the gap between the best sampled value and the attained minimum is at most the pointwise modulus of continuity evaluated at the distance of the closest sample to the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_k^*-f^*\le \omega_f(x^*;v_k^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Relative to a Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuity along a subset without imposing continuity under approaches from outside it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a function on \(\mathbb R^n\) and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). The function \(f\) is continuous relative to \(S\) if and only if its restriction \(f|_S\) is continuous; equivalently, for every \(x\in S\), \(\lim_{S\ni y\to x}f(y)=f(x)\). No condition is imposed on approaches to \(x\) from outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is continuous relative to a subset S when its restriction to S is continuous. Thus its values must approach f(x) as points approach x along S, but approaches from outside S need not satisfy this condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is continuous relative to }S\iff f|_S\text{ is continuous}\iff \forall x\in S,\ \lim_{S\ni y\to x}f(y)=f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense-set convergence determines a finite saddle-function limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hypothesis requires a finite pointwise limit on a dense Cartesian subset of the relatively open product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \((K_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Then this limit exists and is finite for every \((u,v)\in C\times D\); the function \(K(u,v)=\lim_{i\to\infty}K_i(u,v)\) is concave-convex; and \(K_i\to K\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\times D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise, interior, and compactly contained convex regularity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a real Hilbert space. For finite-dimensional relative statements, work in \(A=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxonomy of increasingly uniform local regularity regimes for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Three local convex regularity regimes are distinguished. Pointwise regularity at \(x\) means that \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), equivalently locally Lipschitz or locally upper bounded there. Interior regularity means \[f\text{ is locally Lipschitz at every }x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f.\] In finite dimensions, intrinsic interior regularity replaces the interior by \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and uses the relative topology of \(A\). Compactly contained regularity means that for every nonempty compact \(K\subset\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists \(L_K<+\infty\) satisfying \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\qquad(\forall x,y\in K).\] The constant may depend on \(K\); no global Lipschitz bound is part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local convex regularity has three useful scales. Pointwise regularity means continuity at one point, equivalently local Lipschitz continuity or local upper boundedness there. Interior regularity means local Lipschitz continuity at every interior point. In finite dimensions, the intrinsic version uses the relative interior and its affine-hull topology. Compactly contained regularity strengthens this to one Lipschitz constant on each compact subset of the relative interior, while allowing the constant to change from one compact set to another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise, interior, and compactly contained regularity are defined by continuity at one point, local Lipschitz continuity throughout the intrinsic interior, and a uniform Lipschitz constant on each compact intrinsic-interior subset, respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Pointwise regularity at \(x\) is equivalent to boundedness above on some neighborhood of \(x\).
Compactly contained regularity is local Lipschitz regularity made uniform over each fixed compact subset.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then interior regularity holds on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
Every proper convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) has compactly contained regularity on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: On each admissible compact \(K\), \(f\) is uniformly continuous.
Regularity constants can deteriorate as compact sets approach the relative boundary.
boundary_notes: Compact subsets touching the relative boundary are not covered.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, relative-interior statements require additional care because the relevant interior may be empty and finite-dimensional compactness arguments fail.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant associated with compact set \(K\)
compact containment in the relative interior

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential definitions for finite-valued functions on Euclidean space, together with two continuity implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is upper semicontinuous at $x$ if every sequence $x_k\to x$ satisfies $\limsup_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\le f(x)$, and lower semicontinuous at $x$ if every such sequence satisfies $f(x)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)$. It is continuous at $x$ if it is both upper and lower semicontinuous there. Every locally Lipschitz function is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper semicontinuity prevents limiting values along convergent sequences from exceeding the value at the limit, while lower semicontinuity prevents them from falling below it. Having both properties is equivalent to continuity, and local Lipschitz continuity implies continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{usc}_x(f)\land\operatorname{lsc}_x(f)\iff f\text{ is continuous at }x,\qquad f\text{ locally Lipschitz}\implies f\text{ continuous}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Semicontinuity at a Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise definitions for a real-valued functional on a normed space, with an equivalent upper-limsup characterization and the continuity consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), where \(X\) is a normed space, and let \(x_0\in X\). The functional \(f\) is upper semicontinuous at \(x_0\) if \(\forall\varepsilon>0\,\exists\delta>0\) such that \(\|x-x_0\|<\delta\) implies \(f(x)-f(x_0)<\varepsilon\). It is lower semicontinuous at \(x_0\) if \(-f\) is upper semicontinuous there. Equivalently, upper semicontinuity means \(\limsup_{x\to x_0}f(x)\le f(x_0)\). If \(f\) is both upper and lower semicontinuous at \(x_0\), then it is continuous at \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued functional is upper semicontinuous at a point when nearby values cannot exceed its value there by any fixed positive amount; it is lower semicontinuous when its negative is upper semicontinuous. Upper semicontinuity is equivalently characterized by the limiting upper value being at most the value at the point. Both forms of semicontinuity imply continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }x_0\iff \limsup_{x\to x_0}f(x)\le f(x_0),\quad f\text{ is lower semicontinuous at }x_0\iff -f\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }x_0;\quad \mathrm{usc}+\mathrm{lsc}\Rightarrow\mathrm{continuous}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-value failure regimes for convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}D=\overline D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D\). Limits are taken with \(y\to x\) and \(y\in\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic-boundary taxonomy based on the interior lower limit and the assigned boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the intrinsic interior lower limit at \(x\) by \[\ell_f(x)=\liminf_{\substack{y\to x\\y\in\operatorname{ri}D}}f(y)\in[-\infty,+\infty].\] Boundary behavior is classified as follows. It is regular finite when \(x\in D\), \(\ell_f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(f(x)=\ell_f(x)\). It is a finite upward jump when \(x\in D\), \(\ell_f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(f(x)>\ell_f(x)\). It is excluded-boundary divergence when \(x\notin D\), so \(f(x)=+\infty\), with either finite approach value \(\ell_f(x)<+\infty\) or divergent approach \(\ell_f(x)=+\infty\). Finally, it is included divergent behavior when \(x\in D\) and \(f(x)=\ell_f(x)=+\infty\), which is impossible under the effective-domain convention and is therefore represented instead by exclusion from \(D\). Lower semicontinuity at \(x\) is exactly \(f(x)\leq\ell_f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-boundary point, compare the assigned function value with the lower limiting values approached from the relative interior. A regular finite boundary point has a finite matching limit. A finite upward jump has a boundary value strictly above a finite interior limit. If the boundary point is outside the effective domain, its value is positive infinity; the interior values may either remain finitely bounded along some approaches or diverge to positive infinity. Lower semicontinuity is precisely the requirement that the assigned value not exceed the intrinsic lower limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((f(x),\ell_f(x))\) classifies regular finite, upward-jump, finite-approach excluded, and divergent excluded boundary behavior; lower semicontinuity at \(x\) is \(f(x)\leq\ell_f(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A finite upward jump is characterized by \(x\in D\) and \(f(x)>\liminf_{y\to x,\,y\in\operatorname{ri}D}f(y)\).
A closed convex function excludes any boundary point whose finite assigned value would exceed the interior lower limit.
special_cases_latex: For a univariate convex function at an endpoint \(a\), the one-sided limit \(f(a+)\) exists in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(f(a)\geq f(a+)\).
The indicator of a closed convex set has regular finite value \(0\) at included boundary points and value \(+\infty\) outside the set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity guarantees interior continuity but does not prevent boundary jumps.
Closing a convex function lowers an upward-jump boundary value to the corresponding lower-semicontinuous envelope value.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy uses \(\liminf\); a full limit need not exist at a multidimensional boundary point.
The inequality direction \(f(x)\geq\ell_f(x)\) is specific to the one-dimensional endpoint result and is not asserted universally in higher dimensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex and finite at \(x_0\). (i) If \(\partial f(x_0)
eq\varnothing\), then \(f'(x_0;h)>-\infty\) for every \(h\in X\). (ii) If \(f\) is bounded above on a neighborhood of some \( ar x\in X\) and \(f'(x_0;h)>-\infty\) for every \(h\in X\), then \(\partial f(x_0)

The function is continuous at \(x_0\) relative to its domain when \[\lim_{\substack{x\to x_0\\x\in D}}f(x)=f(x_0).\] Equivalently, \(f(x_k)\to f(x_0)\) for every sequence \(x_k\in D\) converging to \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite boundary continuity means convergence to the finite boundary value along every sequence in the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative continuity at \(x_0\) is equivalent to convergence along every domain sequence approaching \(x_0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Continuous Convex Extension from the Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous finite extension to the boundary of a locally simplicial convex set under bounded-on-bounded upper control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and locally simplicial. Let \(f:\operatorname{ri}C\to\mathbb R\) be convex and bounded above on every bounded subset of \(\operatorname{ri}C\). Then there exists a unique finite convex function \(\bar f:C\to\mathbb R\), continuous relative to \(C\), such that \(\bar f|_{\operatorname{ri}C}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If C is a locally simplicial convex set and a finite convex function on its relative interior is bounded above on every bounded subset there, then the function has exactly one extension to a finite convex function continuous on all of C.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex and locally simplicial}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\bar f:C\to\mathbb R:\ \bar f\text{ is finite, convex, and continuous relative to }C,\quad \bar f|_{\operatorname{ri}C}=f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise limsup bounds become locally uniform upper bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is one-sided and uniform only on closed bounded subsets lying inside the relatively open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). If \(\limsup_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\), then for every closed bounded \(S\subset C\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(i_0\) such that \(f_i(x)\le f(x)+\varepsilon\) for all \(i\ge i_0\) and all \(x\in S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense pointwise convergence of convex functions is locally uniform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves finiteness of the dense-set limits and the relative openness of the common domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). Suppose there is \(C'\subset C\) with \(\operatorname{cl}C'\supset C\) such that \(\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\in\mathbb R\) exists for every \(x\in C'\). Then \(\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\) exists for every \(x\in C\); the function \(f(x)=\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\) is finite and convex on \(C\); and \(f_i\to f\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If finite convex functions on a relatively open convex set converge to finite values on a dense subset, their pointwise limit extends to the entire set, is finite and convex, and the convergence is uniform on every closed bounded subset.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional and coordinate-partial criteria for saddle differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization at a finite point of a concave-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K be concave in u\in\mathbb{R}^m and convex in v\in\mathbb{R}^n, with K(u,v) finite. Then K is differentiable at (u,v) if and only if K is finite on a neighborhood of (u,v) and the directional-derivative mapping (u',v')\mapsto K'(u,v;u',v') is linear on \mathbb{R}^{m+n}. In particular, K is differentiable at (u,v) if all m+n two-sided coordinate partial derivatives at (u,v) exist and are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite saddle function is differentiable at a point exactly when it is locally finite and its directional derivative is linear in the direction. Existence and finiteness of all two-sided coordinate partial derivatives is sufficient.
assumptions_latex: K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is concave in }u\text{ and convex in }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v)\iff\bigl[K\text{ is finite on a neighborhood of }(u,v)\text{ and }K'(u,v;\cdot,\cdot)\text{ is linear}\bigr];\quad\bigl[\text{all }m+n\text{ finite two-sided coordinate partial derivatives exist}\bigr]\Rightarrow K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate parameter continuity and convexity imply joint continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the full hypothesis and the dense-set weakening of parameter continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be relatively open and convex, let \(T\) be locally compact, and let \(f:C\times T\to\mathbb R\). If \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex on \(C\) for every \(t\in T\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is continuous on \(T\) for every \(x\in C\), then \(f\) is jointly continuous on \(C\times T\). It suffices that there exist \(C'\subset C\) with \(\operatorname{cl}C'\supset C\) such that \(f(x,\cdot)\) is continuous on \(T\) for every \(x\in C'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on a relatively open convex set times a locally compact parameter space is jointly continuous when it is convex in the first variable and continuous in the parameter. Parameter continuity need only be verified on a subset dense in the convex domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and block decomposition of saddle-function directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional differentiability at points of an open convex region on which the saddle function is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be concave in its first argument and convex in its second, and let C\times D be an open convex set on which K is finite. For every (u,v)\in C\times D, the directional derivative K'(u,v;u',v') exists and is finite for every (u',v')\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n. As a function of (u',v'), it is positively homogeneous, concave in u', and convex in v', and satisfies K'(u,v;u',v')=K'(u,v;u',0)+K'(u,v;0,v').
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every point of an open convex region where a concave-convex saddle function is finite, all directional derivatives exist and are finite. The derivative is positively homogeneous and concave-convex in the direction, and it equals the sum of its first-block and second-block directional derivatives.
assumptions_latex: K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is concave in }u\text{ and convex in }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall (u',v')\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n,\quad K'(u,v;u',v')\in\mathbb{R},\quad K'(u,v;u',v')=K'(u,v;u',0)+K'(u,v;0,v'),\text{ and }K'(u,v;\cdot,\cdot)\text{ is positively homogeneous and concave-convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise-bounded convex sequences have locally uniformly convergent subsequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise boundedness may be imposed on the whole domain or only on a dense subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). Suppose either that \((f_i(x))_{i\ge1}\) is bounded for every \(x\in C\), or that there is a dense subset \(C'\subset C\) for which it is bounded at every \(x\in C'\). Then there exist indices \(i_1<i_2<\cdots\) and a finite convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f_{i_j}\to f\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sequence of finite convex functions that is pointwise bounded on its relatively open convex domain—or merely on a dense subset—has a subsequence converging uniformly on each closed bounded subset to a finite convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Boundary Discontinuity Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and sequential witness at a finite effective-domain boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x_0\in D\cap\operatorname{rbd}D\), with \(f(x_0)\in\mathbb R\). A finite boundary discontinuity occurs when \(f\) is not continuous at \(x_0\) relative to \(D\). Equivalently, there are \(x_k\in D\), \(x_k\to x_0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[|f(x_k)-f(x_0)|\ge\varepsilon\] for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite boundary discontinuity is failure of relative continuity at a boundary point where the function has a finite value; a domain sequence witnesses the failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative discontinuity is equivalent to a domain sequence whose values remain separated from \(f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Discontinuity Criterion

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper convex function can be finite yet discontinuous at a boundary point when lower semicontinuity there is absent.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit one-dimensional example is directly checkable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional finite jump at the boundary caused by nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
+\infty,&x<0,\\
1,&x=0,\\
0,&x>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is proper and convex, and \(f(0)=1\) is finite. Nevertheless, for every sequence \(x_k>0\) with \(x_k\to0\), one has \(f(x_k)=0\not\to f(0)\). Thus \(f\) is discontinuous at the boundary point \(0\) relative to its effective domain and is not lower semicontinuous there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function equal to zero on positive numbers and one at zero has a finite jump discontinuity at the boundary of its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Discontinuity

children.title: Boundary Blow-Up
children.top_down_role: Divergent function behavior along approaches to the domain boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Blow-Up Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential divergence at an excluded finite relative-domain boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{rbd}D\setminus D\). Boundary blow-up at \(\bar x\) means \[x_k\in\operatorname{ri}D,\quad x_k\to\bar x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x_k)\to+\infty.\] Equivalently, the extension already assigning \(f(\bar x)=+\infty\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(D\cup\{\bar x\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary blow-up means universal divergence to positive infinity along relative-interior approaches to an excluded boundary point; equivalently, the positive-infinity extension is lower semicontinuous there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every relative-interior sequence approaching \(\bar x\) has values tending to \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Blow-Up Regime

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closed proper convex function may diverge to \(+\infty\) as a finite-dimensional domain boundary is approached from its interior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic barrier blow-up at an excluded boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
-\log x,&x>0,\\
+\infty,&x\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}f=(0,+\infty)\). At the boundary point \(0\),
\[
\lim_{\substack{x\downarrow0\\x\in\operatorname{dom}f}}f(x)=+\infty.
\]
Hence interior continuity and local Lipschitz regularity do not yield finite control up to the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative logarithm is closed and convex on the positive half-line but diverges to positive infinity at the boundary zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Blow-Up

children.title: Directional Boundary Dependence
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior that varies across admissible approach directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Boundary Dependence Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique approach behavior at a finite effective-domain boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in D\cap\operatorname{rbd}D\), with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\). Boundary behavior is directionally dependent at \(\bar x\) if there are sequences \(x_k,y_k\in\operatorname{ri}D\), both converging to \(\bar x\), for which the extended limits of \(f(x_k)\) and \(f(y_k)\) exist and are unequal. Consequently, no unique relative-interior boundary limit exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional boundary dependence occurs when two admissible interior approaches to the same finite boundary point produce different extended limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unequal limits along two relative-interior sequences preclude a unique boundary limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Boundary Dependence Criterion

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Even for a closed proper convex function finite at a boundary point, limits along interior approaches can depend on the approach path.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic perspective exhibiting path-dependent limits at a finite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f(x,y)=y^2/x\) when \(x>0\), \(f(0,0)=0\), and \(f(x,y)=+\infty\) otherwise. This quadratic perspective is proper, closed, and convex. As \((x,y)\to(0,0)\) through \(x>0\), the path \(y=0\) gives \(f(x,0)=0\), the path \(y=\sqrt{x}\) gives \(f(x,\sqrt{x})=1\), and the path \(y=x^{1/4}\) gives \(f(x,x^{1/4})=x^{-1/2}\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed quadratic perspective is finite at the origin but approaches zero, one, or infinity along different interior paths to that boundary point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic geometry of a closed proper convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Fix \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex analysis; the definition records both the recession function and the recession cone of the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic function geometry of \(f\) is the pair \(\mathcal G_\infty(f)=(f^\infty,\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f))\), where \[f^\infty(d):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}\in(-\infty,+\infty]\] and \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f):=\{(d,\beta)\in E\times\mathbb R:(x,r)+t(d,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f\ \text{for every }(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f, t\ge0\}.\] The limit is independent of \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and the defining geometric identity is \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=\{(d,\beta):f^\infty(d)\le\beta\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a finite-dimensional space, its asymptotic geometry consists of its recession function and the recession cone of its epigraph. The recession value in direction \(d\) is the limiting growth rate \(\lim_{t\to\infty}[f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)]/t\), independent of the chosen base point in the effective domain. A pair \((d,\beta)\) is a recession direction of the epigraph exactly when translating every epigraph point by every nonnegative multiple of \((d,\beta)\) remains in the epigraph. Equivalently, this cone is the epigraph of \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal G_\infty(f)=(f^\infty,\operatorname{epi}f^\infty),\qquad \operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.\]
\[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\]
special_cases_latex: For an affine function \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\), one has \(f^\infty(d)=\langle a,d\rangle\).
For an indicator \(f=\iota_C\) of a nonempty closed convex set, \(f^\infty=\iota_{\operatorname{rec}C}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(f^\infty\) is lower semicontinuous, convex, and positively homogeneous.
The directions satisfying \(f^\infty(d)\le0\) are precisely the common recession directions of all nonempty sublevel sets of \(f\).
boundary_notes: The base-point limit formula need not define the appropriate horizon object for an arbitrary nonconvex function.
Infinite-dimensional variants require an explicitly selected topology and may involve noncompact bounded sublevel sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Function of a Monotone Convex Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The undefined symbol c in the displayed definition is interpreted as φ, consistently with all hypotheses and the stated recession formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let r:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be convex and nondecreasing, with \operatorname{dom}r=(-\infty,\eta) for some \eta\in[0,+\infty] and r_\infty(1)=+\infty. Let \varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be closed, proper, and convex, with \varphi(\mathbb{R}^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}r\ne\varnothing. Define g(x)=r(\varphi(x)) for x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi and g(x)=+\infty otherwise. Then g is closed, proper, and convex, and
\[
g_\infty(d)=\begin{cases}r_\infty(\varphi_\infty(d)),&d\in\operatorname{dom}(\varphi_\infty),\\+\infty,&d\notin\operatorname{dom}(\varphi_\infty).\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondecreasing convex outer function satisfying the stated domain and recession assumptions preserves closed proper convexity under composition with φ, and the recession function of the composition is obtained by composing the two recession functions on the domain of φ's recession function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is closed, proper, and convex, and }g_\infty(d)=r_\infty(\varphi_\infty(d))\text{ on }\operatorname{dom}(\varphi_\infty),\text{ with }g_\infty(d)=+\infty\text{ otherwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent criteria for orthant-bounded quadratic functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes boundedness for every positive scaling of the quadratic term and for unit scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(z\geq0\Rightarrow z^{\mathrm T}Mz\geq0\), and \(z\geq0,\ z^{\mathrm T}Mz=0\Rightarrow q^{\mathrm T}z\geq0\); (b) for every \(\sigma>0\), \(f_\sigma(z)=z^{\mathrm T}(q+\sigma Mz)\) is bounded below on \(z\geq0\); (c) \(f(z)=z^{\mathrm T}(q+Mz)\) is bounded below on \(z\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic function is bounded below on the nonnegative orthant exactly when its quadratic form is nonnegative there and its linear term is nonnegative along every nonnegative zero-curvature direction. Equivalently, boundedness holds for every positive scaling of the quadratic term, and it suffices that it hold at unit scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&[\forall z\geq0,\ z^{\mathrm T}Mz\geq0\ \text{ and }\ (z^{\mathrm T}Mz=0\Rightarrow q^{\mathrm T}z\geq0)]\\&\iff[\forall\sigma>0,\ \inf_{z\geq0}z^{\mathrm T}(q+\sigma Mz)>-\infty]\\&\iff[\inf_{z\geq0}z^{\mathrm T}(q+Mz)>-\infty].\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded nonempty solution set at one parameter enforces bounded solution sets at all parameters and regularity of the marginal value.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the recession function of \(f\) is defined by
\[
(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},\qquad d\in X.
\]
For every \(d\in X\), the limit exists in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), equals \(\sup_{t>0}(f(x+td)-f(x))/t\), and is independent of the selected \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function records the limiting slope of a closed proper convex function along each direction; the slope equals the supremum of the difference quotients and is independent of the chosen domain point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Sublinear Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic structure of the recession function in the closed proper convex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then \(\operatorname{rec}f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear. Thus
\[(\operatorname{rec}f)(0)=0,\qquad (\operatorname{rec}f)(\lambda d)=\lambda(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\quad(\lambda\geq0),\]
and
\[(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_1+d_2)\leq(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_1)+(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function of a closed proper convex function is a proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, positively homogeneous, and subadditive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph-Recession Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation and global directional-growth inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in H\) and \(s\in\mathbb R\),
\[(d,s)\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\iff(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\leq s.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f),\]
and, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\geq0\),
\[f(x+td)\leq f(x)+t(\operatorname{rec}f)(d).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the recession function is the recession cone of the original epigraph, and recession values bound global directional growth.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f)=\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment under common-recession conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an arbitrary finite or infinite family of consistent closed proper convex inequalities and includes a more general condition involving a finite polyhedral subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0\) and \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) be closed proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(I\) is arbitrary, and suppose \(F:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\in I\}\neq\varnothing\). The infimum of \(f_0\) over \(F\) is attained if there is no direction of recession common to \(f_0\) and every \(f_i\). More generally, it is attained if there exists a finite \(I_0\subseteq I\) such that each \(f_i\), \(i\in I_0\), is polyhedral and every recession direction common to \(f_0\) and all \(f_i\) is a direction along which \(f_0\) and every \(f_i\), \(i\in I\setminus I_0\), are constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent, possibly infinite system of closed proper convex inequalities, the convex objective attains its constrained infimum when the functions have no common recession direction. More generally, attainment holds when finitely many constraint functions are polyhedral and every common recession direction leaves the objective and every remaining constraint function constant.
assumptions_latex: f_0,f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are closed proper convex for every }i\in I
I\text{ is an arbitrary finite or infinite index set}
\text{Either no recession direction is common to }f_0\text{ and all }f_i,\text{ or the stated finite-polyhedral-subfamily condition holds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f_0(x)\neq\varnothing

\[f^{0+}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f} igl(f(x+y)-f(x) igr).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representations and calculus of recession functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity, ray-limit formulas, lower-boundedness consequence, and sum and linear-precomposition calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(y\in\mathcal H\). Then \(\operatorname{rec}f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \[(\operatorname{rec}f)(y)=\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}=\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)}{\alpha}=\sup_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] If \(\inf_{z\in\mathcal H}f(z)>-\infty\), then \(\operatorname{rec}f\geq0\). If \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{rec}(f+g)=\operatorname{rec}f+\operatorname{rec}g\). If \(\mathcal K\) is a real Hilbert space, \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ran}L\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{rec}(g\circ L)=(\operatorname{rec}g)\circ L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function remains in that class and is given by equivalent ray-limit and supremum formulas. It is nonnegative when the function is bounded below, distributes over sums with intersecting domains, and commutes with bounded linear precomposition when the operator range meets the outer function's domain.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the composition rule: }\mathcal K\text{ is a real Hilbert space},\ g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K),\ L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K),\ \operatorname{ran}L\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H),\quad(\operatorname{rec}f)(y)=\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}=\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)}{\alpha}=\sup_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha};\quad\inf f>-\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{rec}f\geq0;\quad\operatorname{rec}(f+g)=\operatorname{rec}f+\operatorname{rec}g;\quad\operatorname{rec}(g\circ L)=(\operatorname{rec}g)\circ L.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Set Recession Cone and Constancy Space of a Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common recession geometry of nonempty level sets, propagation of compactness, and characterization of directions along which a convex function is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex, and let \(V_\gamma=\{x:f(x)\leq\gamma\}\). All nonempty level sets have the same recession cone, denoted \(R_f\), and \[R_f=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:(d,0)\in R_{\operatorname{epi}f}\}.\] If one nonempty level set is compact, then every nonempty level set is compact. Moreover, \[L_f=R_f\cap(-R_f),\] and \[d\in L_f\iff f(x+\alpha d)=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f\text{ and every }\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All nonempty level sets of a closed proper convex function share the recession cone formed by the horizontal directions of the epigraph recession cone. Compactness of one nonempty level set implies compactness of all nonempty level sets. The bidirectional recession directions are exactly the directions along which the function is constant on every full line through its domain.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{V_\gamma}=R_f=\{d:(d,0)\in R_{\operatorname{epi}f}\}\text{ for every nonempty }V_\gamma;\quad V_{\gamma_0}\text{ compact}\Rightarrow V_\gamma\text{ compact for every nonempty }V_\gamma;\quad d\in L_f\iff(\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R})\ f(x+\alpha d)=f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calculus Rules for Recession Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States separate recession-function rules for positive sums, pointwise suprema, affine precomposition, and qualified linear image functions, preserving the failure boundary for the image rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following rules hold under their respective assumptions. If \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are closed proper convex functions, \(t_j>0\), and some \(x_0\) is finite for every \(f_j\), then \[ \left(\sum_{j=1}^m t_jf_j\right)'_\infty=\sum_{j=1}^m t_j(f_j)'_\infty. \] If \(\{f_j\}_{j\in J}\) is a family of closed proper convex functions and \(\sup_{j\in J}f_j(x_0)<+\infty\) for some \(x_0\), then \[ \left(\sup_{j\in J}f_j\right)'_\infty=\sup_{j\in J}(f_j)'_\infty. \] If \(A(x)=A_0x+a\), \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}(\mathbb R^m)\), and \(A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), then \[ (f\circ A)'_\infty=f'_\infty\circ A_0. \] For a linear image function \((Ag)(d)=\inf\{g(z):Az=d\}\), the formula \[ (Ag)'_\infty(d)=\inf_{Az=d}g'_\infty(z) \] requires an additional qualification ensuring that the image function is proper convex and the defining infimum is attained. A sufficient kernel-coercivity condition supplied by the source is \(g'_\infty(z)>0\) for every \(z\in\ker A\setminus\{0\}\), with the required attainment control. The image formula is not asserted without such a qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession functions commute with finite positive sums, suitably finite pointwise suprema, and affine precomposition under the stated assumptions. A corresponding rule for linear infimal images requires an additional kernel-coercivity and attainment qualification and is not unconditional.
assumptions_latex: f_j\text{ are closed proper convex},\quad t_j>0,\quad\exists x_0\ \forall j:\ f_j(x_0)<+\infty\text{ for the sum rule}
f_j\text{ are closed proper convex},\quad\exists x_0:\sup_{j\in J}f_j(x_0)<+\infty\text{ for the supremum rule}
g'_\infty(z)>0\quad\forall z\in\ker A\setminus\{0\},\text{ together with the required properness and attainment, for the image rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\sum_jt_jf_j\right)'_\infty=\sum_jt_j(f_j)'_\infty,\quad \left(\sup_jf_j\right)'_\infty=\sup_j(f_j)'_\infty,\quad(f\circ A)'_\infty=f'_\infty\circ A_0,\quad(Ag)'_\infty(d)=\inf_{Az=d}g'_\infty(z)\text{ under the stated image qualification}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-Function Characterization of Global Uniform Continuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity Along a Recession Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes directions along which a proper convex function is globally nonincreasing, including the additional propagation property under closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper convex function and let \(y\) be a vector. If, for some \(x\), \(\liminf_{\lambda\to+\infty}f(x+\lambda y)<+\infty\), then \(\lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\) is nonincreasing on \(\mathbb R\). This monotonicity holds for every \(x\) if and only if \(f^{0+}(y)\leq0\). If \(f\) is closed, monotonicity for one \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) implies monotonicity for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, finite asymptotic liminf along a line forces the function to be nonincreasing along that entire line. Global nonincrease in direction y is equivalent to the recession value in direction y being nonpositive. For a closed function, nonincrease from one domain point propagates to every base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial, recession, and horizon variants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). No convexity is imposed unless stated separately.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A variant family separating base-point radial growth, global recession inequalities, and lower-semicontinuous horizon growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the radial lower asymptotic slope, the global recession majorant, and the horizon function by \[f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0}(d):=\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t},\] \[f^{\mathrm{rec}}(d):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ t>0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},\] and \[f^{\mathrm{hor}}(d):=\liminf_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\ d'\to d}}\frac{f(x_0+td')-f(x_0)}{t}.\] The asymptotic variant family is \(\mathcal V_\infty(f;x_0):=(f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0},f^{\mathrm{rec}},f^{\mathrm{hor}})\). These objects are kept distinct for a general proper function. If \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, all three are independent of \(x_0\) and coincide with the closed convex recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic variant family distinguishes three constructions. The radial slope measures lower limiting growth along one ray from a selected base point. The global recession majorant takes the supremum of all difference quotients over every feasible base point and positive step. The horizon function additionally permits perturbations of the direction before taking the lower limit, thereby encoding lower-semicontinuous asymptotic behavior. For a general proper function these variants can differ and the radial object can depend on its base point. For a lower-semicontinuous convex function they coincide with the ordinary recession function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal V_\infty(f;x_0)=(f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0},f^{\mathrm{rec}},f^{\mathrm{hor}}),\qquad f\in\Gamma_0(E)\Longrightarrow f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0}=f^{\mathrm{rec}}=f^{\mathrm{hor}}=f^\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{\mathrm{rec}}(d)=\inf\{\beta\in\mathbb R:f(x+td)\le f(x)+t\beta\ \text{for all }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\ge0\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a positively homogeneous lower-semicontinuous convex function \(p\), all variants equal \(p\).
For an indicator \(\iota_C\), the convex-case common value is \(0\) on \(\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Coincidence of the three variants is a structural regularity furnished by closed convexity, not part of their general definition.
The perturbed-direction lower limit distinguishes horizon behavior from growth observed along a single fixed ray.
boundary_notes: Conventions for horizon functions vary with homogenization and base-point normalization; the convention must be matched to a source.
Without convexity, no equality among the three constructions is asserted.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: organizes commonly used radial, recession, and horizon constructions.
The exact horizon convention and the claimed convex-case coincidence require an inspected authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Horizon Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-regularized horizon construction for a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define
\[
f^\infty(d)=\liminf_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\d'\to d}}\frac{f(td')}{t}
=\liminf_{\substack{\lambda\downarrow0\\d'\to d}}\lambda f(d'/\lambda).
\]
The function \(f^\infty\) is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous in the sense that
\[
f^\infty(\mu d)=\mu f^\infty(d)\qquad(\mu>0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variational horizon function is the lower-regularized linear-scale growth of a proper function; it is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty(d)=\liminf_{t\to+\infty,\,d'\to d}f(td')/t\), equivalently \(\liminf_{\lambda\downarrow0,\,d'\to d}\lambda f(d'/\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity and Representations of Horizon Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General lower-semicontinuity and homogeneity, followed by the stronger convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(f^\infty\) is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous. If \(f\not\equiv+\infty\), then for every \(w\), \[f^\infty(w)=\liminf_{\lambda\searrow0,\,x\to w}\lambda f(\lambda^{-1}x)=\lim_{\delta\searrow0}\inf_{\substack{0<\lambda<\delta\\x\in B(w,\delta)}}\lambda f(\lambda^{-1}x).\] If \(f\) is convex, then \(f^\infty\) is sublinear. If, moreover, \(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, then for every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(w\), \[f^\infty(w)=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}=\sup_{\tau>0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every horizon function is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous and admits a small-scale liminf formula unless the original function is identically positive infinity. For a convex function it is sublinear; for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function it equals the limiting and supremal asymptotic slope along every ray from any domain point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty\text{ is lsc and positively homogeneous; under convexity it is sublinear, and under proper lsc convexity it equals the asymptotic ray slope.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Convex Horizon–Recession Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between the variational horizon function and convex recession growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^\infty(d)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)
=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}
=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.
\]
The common value is independent of \(x_0\), and
\[

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Open-Half-Line Boundary Information Is Lost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonclosed convex example under the variational horizon convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=(0,+\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(f=\delta_C\). Then \(f\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous, and
\[
f^\infty(d)=
\begin{cases}
0,&d\geq0,\\
+\infty,&d<0
\end{cases}
=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(d).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{cl}f=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\), one also has
\[
f^\infty=(\operatorname{cl}f)^\infty.
\]
Thus the horizon construction does not retain whether the finite boundary point belonged to the original domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercivity, level-boundedness, and inf-compactness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((E,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), write \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in E:f(x)\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definitions apply in normed spaces; compact-level conclusions are topology-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is coercive when \[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists R>0\ \forall x\in E:\ \|x\|\ge R\Longrightarrow f(x)>M,\] equivalently \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to+\infty\). It is level-bounded when \(L_\alpha(f)\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). It is inf-compact in a topology \(\tau\) when every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is \(\tau\)-compact. The coercivity-level-boundedness interface is the implication chain \[\text{inf-compactness}\Longrightarrow\text{level-boundedness}\Longleftrightarrow\text{coercivity},\] where the first implication presumes that compact sets are bounded. In finite-dimensional spaces, lower semicontinuity makes every sublevel closed, so coercivity is equivalent to inf-compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function is coercive if its values eventually exceed every real threshold outside a sufficiently large norm ball. It is level-bounded if every real sublevel set is bounded. It is inf-compact in a chosen topology if every sublevel is compact in that topology. Coercivity and level-boundedness are equivalent directly from these quantifiers. Compact sublevels imply bounded sublevels whenever compact sets are bounded. In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity closes the sublevels and bounded closed sets are compact, so a lower-semicontinuous coercive function is inf-compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ coercive}\Longleftrightarrow(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\ L_\alpha(f)\text{ bounded}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ coercive}\Longleftrightarrow\inf_{\|x\|\ge R}f(x)\longrightarrow+\infty\quad(R\to+\infty).\]
\[f\text{ level-bounded}\Longleftrightarrow\text{every sequence }(x_n)\text{ with }\sup_n f(x_n)<+\infty\text{ is bounded}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(f\) is lower semicontinuous, coercivity is equivalent to compactness of all sublevel sets.
If additionally \(\inf f<+\infty\), any nonempty compact sublevel below a finite comparison value yields attainment of \(\inf f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every minimizing sequence of a level-bounded function with finite infimum is bounded.
Lower semicontinuity and finite-dimensional coercivity provide the compactness mechanism used in existence arguments.
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional normed spaces, closed bounded sublevels need not be norm compact.
Coercivity alone does not assert lower semicontinuity or attainment.

notation.meaning: The closed-value sublevel set at height \(\alpha\).
The topology in which inf-compactness is evaluated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cones and Compactness of Convex Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the common recession cone of all nonempty sublevel sets and characterizes compact sublevels by strict positivity of the recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(S_r(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\le r\}\). For every \(r\in\mathbb R\) with \(S_r(f)\ne\varnothing\), \[ [S_r(f)]_\infty=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:f'_\infty(d)\le0\}. \] Moreover, the following are equivalent: (i) some sublevel set is nonempty and compact; (ii) every sublevel set is compact; and (iii) \(f'_\infty(d)>0\) for every \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All nonempty sublevel sets of a convex function have the same recession cone, namely the directions where its recession function is nonpositive. A nonempty compact sublevel exists exactly when every sublevel is compact, equivalently when recession growth is strictly positive in every nonzero direction.
assumptions_latex: r\in\mathbb R\text{ and }S_r(f)\ne\varnothing\text{ for the recession-cone identity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [S_r(f)]_\infty=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:f'_\infty(d)\le0\},\qquad (\exists r:\varnothing\ne S_r(f)\text{ compact})\iff(\forall r:S_r(f)\text{ compact})\iff(\forall d\ne0:f'_\infty(d)>0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Characterizations of Minima and Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four conjugacy correspondences for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then (i) \(\inf f=-f^*(0)\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\partial f^*(0)\); (ii) \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\) if and only if \(f^*\) is differentiable at \(0\), in which case \(\nabla f^*(0)=\bar x\); (iii) \(f\) is level-coercive (level-bounded) if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\); and (iv) \(f\) is coercive if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, the conjugate's value and subdifferential at zero give the infimum and minimizers. A unique minimizer is equivalent to differentiability of the conjugate at zero. Level-boundedness is equivalent to zero lying in the interior of the conjugate domain, while coercivity is equivalent to that domain being all of Euclidean space.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf f=-f^*(0),\quad\operatorname{argmin}f=\partial f^*(0);\quad \operatorname{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\iff\bigl(f^*\text{ is differentiable at }0\text{ and }\nabla f^*(0)=\bar x\bigr);\quad f\text{ is level-bounded}\iff0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*);\quad f\text{ is coercive}\iff\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb{R}^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero- and One-Coercivity of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two convex-function growth regimes, states attainment under closedness, and records their specialization to positive-semidefinite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(f\) is \(0\)-coercive when the equivalent compact-sublevel conditions hold; equivalently, \(f(x)\to+\infty\) whenever \(\|x\|\to+\infty\). If \(f\) is closed and \(0\)-coercive, it attains its minimum on \(\mathbb R^n\). It is \(1\)-coercive when \(f'_\infty=I_{\{0\}}\), equivalently, \[ \frac{f(x)}{\|x\|}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }\|x\|\to+\infty. \] For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle Qx,x\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c\), where \(Q=Q^\top\succeq0\), \[ f'_\infty(d)=\begin{cases}\langle b,d\rangle,&d\in\ker Q,\\+\infty,&d\notin\ker Q,\end{cases} \] and \(0\)-coercivity, \(1\)-coercivity, and \(Q\succ0\) are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-coercivity means that the function tends to infinity whenever the argument escapes to infinity; for convex functions this is equivalent to compact sublevel sets. Closed zero-coercive convex functions attain a minimum. One-coercivity means superlinear growth. For a positive-semidefinite convex quadratic, both coercivity notions are equivalent to positive definiteness of the quadratic term.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is closed for the minimum-attainment conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\text{-coercive}\iff f(x)\to+\infty\text{ as }\|x\|\to\infty;\quad 1\text{-coercive}\iff f'_\infty=I_{\{0\}}\iff f(x)/\|x\|\to+\infty;\quad f\text{ quadratic}:\ 0\text{-coercive}\iff1\text{-coercive}\iff Q\succ0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercivity Need Not Give Attainment on a Nonreflexive Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp ambient-space boundary for the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a nonreflexive Banach space and choose \(\ell\in X^*\) with \(\|\ell\|=1\) that does not attain its norm on the closed unit ball. Define
\[
f(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x).
\]
Then \(f\) is finite, continuous, convex, and coercive, but
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=-\frac12,
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-nonattaining functional on a nonreflexive Banach space yields a continuous convex coercive function whose infimum is not attained.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\in X^*\), \(\|\ell\|=1\), does not attain its norm on the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x)\) is coercive and convex but has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Need Not Give Attainment on a Nonreflexive Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reflexive-Space Direct-Method Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional attainment under weak compactness and weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive. Then
\[
\min_{x\in X}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is weakly compact; if \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a reflexive Banach space, a proper weakly lower-semicontinuous coercive function attains a finite minimum and has a weakly compact minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min f\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and weakly compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded. Then
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing,
\]
and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous level-bounded function on finite-dimensional space attains a finite minimum and has a nonempty compact minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min f\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\inf f=\min f\in\mathbb{R}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that
\[
f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)>-\infty.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{argmin}f=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)=f(\bar x)\}
\]
is nonempty and compact. In particular, proper lower semicontinuity supplies closed sublevel sets, while level-boundedness makes a nonempty sublevel set containing a minimizing sequence compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous level-bounded function on finite-dimensional space attains a finite minimum, and its set of minimizers is nonempty and compact.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Coercive Attainment on a Nonreflexive Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp ambient-space boundary for the direct-method attainment theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\ell\in X^*\) satisfy \(\|\ell\|=1\) without attaining its norm on the closed unit ball. Define
\[
f(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x).
\]
Then \(f\) is finite, continuous, convex, and coercive, but
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=-\frac12
\]
is not attained. Such a functional exists on every nonreflexive Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonreflexive Banach space, a norm-nonattaining functional produces a continuous convex coercive function whose infimum is not attained.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\in X^*\), \(\|\ell\|=1\), does not attain its norm on the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x)\) is coercive and convex, but \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Coercive Attainment on a Nonreflexive Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reflexive-Space Attainment from Weak Lower Semicontinuity and Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional direct-method variant of the attainment consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive. Then
\[
\min_{x\in X}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is weakly compact; if \(f\) is convex, it is also convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a reflexive Banach space, a proper weakly lower-semicontinuous coercive function attains a finite minimum, and its minimizer set is weakly compact.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and weakly compact, and \(\min f\in\mathbb{R}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descending, flat, and lineality directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy is based on the sign and two-sided vanishing of the recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the descending, nonascending, flat, and asymptotic-lineality direction sets by \[D_-(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)<0\},\qquad D_{\le0}(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\},\] \[D_0(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)=0\},\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)=f^\infty(-d)=0\}.\] A nonzero member of \(D_-(f)\) is an asymptotically descending direction; a nonzero member of \(D_0(f)\) is an asymptotically flat direction; and a nonzero member of \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)\) is a two-sided flat or asymptotic-lineality direction. For every nonempty sublevel \(L_\alpha(f)\), \[\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=D_{\le0}(f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sign of the recession function separates asymptotic directions into descending directions, where the asymptotic slope is negative; nonascending directions, where it is nonpositive; and flat directions, where it vanishes. A two-sided flat direction is one on which the recession function vanishes in both orientations. The nonascending cone is exactly the recession cone of every nonempty sublevel set. Thus nonzero nonascending directions characterize unbounded rays that can remain inside a sublevel, while two-sided flat directions isolate asymptotic invariance along complete lines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_-(f)\subseteq D_{\le0}(f),\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)=D_0(f)\cap(-D_0(f)),\qquad \operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=D_{\le0}(f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in D_{\le0}(f)\Longleftrightarrow f(x+td)\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\ge0.\]
\[d\in\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)\Longleftrightarrow f(x+td)=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\in\mathbb R.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\), \(D_{\le0}(f)=\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)=\operatorname{lin}C\).
If \(D_{\le0}(f)=\{0\}\), every nonempty sublevel is bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero direction in \(D_{\le0}(f)\) forces every nonempty sublevel to be unbounded.
A direction in \(D_-(f)\) is incompatible with existence of a finite global minimum.
boundary_notes: A one-sided zero recession value does not imply invariance in the opposite direction.
Flatness of \(f^\infty\) is asymptotic and does not by itself imply multiple minimizers unless the corresponding ray or line meets the solution set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sign taxonomy induced by the recession function.
The asserted common recession cone of sublevels and the two-sided invariance formulation require source verification.

children.title: Recession Lineality
children.top_down_role: Bidirectional recession structure associated with invariant asymptotic geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(f)=\{d:(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(-d)=0\}\) is a vector subspace, and \(f(x+td)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Recession Function p. 164

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession lineality space of \(f\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(f)=\{d\in X\mid(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=0\text{ and }(\operatorname{rec}f)(-d)=0\}.
\]
It is a vector subspace of \(X\). Every \(d\in\operatorname{lin}(f)\) is a two-sided invariant direction:
\[
f(x+td)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R},
\]
with equality understood in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession lineality consists of directions with zero recession slope in both signs; it is a subspace along which the function is translation invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession Lineality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate-Domain Characterization of Recession Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then
\[
\operatorname{lin}(f)=(\operatorname{span}\operatorname{dom}f^*)^\perp
=\{d\in X:\langle d,u\rangle=0\text{ for every }u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.
\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{lin}(f)\neq\{0\}\) exactly when \(\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\) is not dense in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession lineality is the orthogonal complement of the span of the conjugate domain, and it is nontrivial exactly when that span is not dense.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(f)=(\operatorname{span}\operatorname{dom}f^*)^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Domain Characterization of Recession Lineality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constancy Space of a Closed Proper Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional recession directions and the resulting translation invariance of a convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\), its constancy space is the lineality space of its recession cone: \[L_f:=R_f\cap(-R_f).\] Moreover, \[d\in L_f\iff f(x+\alpha d)=f(x)\quad\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constancy space is the lineality space of the function's recession cone. It consists exactly of directions along which the function is invariant under every real translation from every point of its domain.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_f=R_f\cap(-R_f),\qquad d\in L_f\iff(\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R})\ f(x+\alpha d)=f(x).
