knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel conjugate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal and dual spaces paired canonically; the metric operator determines the displayed Euclidean norm but is not needed in the conjugate formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mathbb{E} be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let B:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{E}^* be self-adjoint and positive definite, and set \|x\|=\langle Bx,x\rangle^{1/2}. For a proper convex function f:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}, its Fenchel conjugate f_*:\mathbb{E}^*\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} is defined by
\[
f_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\},\qquad s\in\mathbb{E}^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on a finite-dimensional real vector space, the Fenchel conjugate at a dual vector is the supremum, over all primal vectors, of the dual pairing minus the function value.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb{E}\text{ is a finite-dimensional real vector space}
B:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{E}^*\text{ is self-adjoint and positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\},\quad s\in\mathbb{E}^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Foundational convex-analysis definitions and correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compact consolidation of the independently meaningful definitions and claims in the extracted section.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended-real vectors, [a,b]=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i\le x_i\le b_i\} and (a,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i<x_i<b_i\}, with the usual conventions for infinite endpoints, and \operatorname{dom}f=\{x:-\infty<f(x)<+\infty\}. A function f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\} is convex when f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y) for x,y\in\mathbb R^n and 0\le\lambda\le1; it is proper when \operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing and strictly convex when the inequality is strict for x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f and 0<\lambda<1. Concavity is convexity of -h. A set is convex exactly when it contains all finite convex combinations of its points; its convex hull is the set of such combinations, its closed convex hull is the smallest closed convex superset, and a finite set has closed convex hull. A set S is convex iff its indicator \delta_S is convex, and f is convex iff \operatorname{epi}f is convex. For convex f, \arg\min f is convex, pointwise suprema of convex functions are convex, and finite suprema of affine functions on polyhedral effective domains characterize polyhedral convex functions. Sums of convex functions are convex, and f_1\square f_2 is convex provided it never equals -\infty; for indicators these operations represent intersection and Minkowski sum. The subdifferential is \partial f(x)=\{p:f(y)-f(x)\ge\langle p,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\}, with p\in\partial f(x) iff x\in\arg\min_y(f(y)-\langle p,y\rangle); it is convex, is nonempty for convex f at x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f), and equals \{\nabla f(x)\} when f is convex and differentiable at x. For convex f the one-sided directional derivative f'(x;d) exists for every d and is convex in d; if f is polyhedral convex, some \varepsilon>0 independent of x satisfies f'(x;d)=f(x+d)-f(x) whenever x\in\operatorname{dom}f and \|d\|_1\le\varepsilon. For nonempty \operatorname{dom}f, f^\bullet(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\} is convex; for nonempty \operatorname{dom}h, h^\circ(p)=\inf_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-h(x)\} and h^\circ(p)=-(-h)^\bullet(-p).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extract defines the elementary objects of convex analysis and records their principal set–function correspondences, closure and polyhedral representations, convexity-preserving operations, subgradient and directional-derivative properties, and convex and concave conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated definitions, equivalences, representations, and convexity properties hold under their respective displayed hypotheses.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compound proposition for functions on open convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathcal D	o\mathbb R, where \mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n is open and convex. Then: (a) f is convex iff \operatorname{epi}f is convex. (b) Every level set of a convex f is convex, all such level sets have the same recession cone, and boundedness of one implies boundedness of all. (c) A convex f is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable on \mathcal D; d\mapsto f'(x;d) is convex and globally Lipschitz with the local modulus at x, and f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x;y-x). (d) f'(x;v)+f'(x;-v)\ge0 and f'(x;x-y)-f'(y;x-y)\ge0. (f) f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in\partial f(x)}a^	op d, and (x,d)\mapsto f'(x;d) is jointly upper semicontinuous. (g) If f\in C^1(\mathcal D), convexity is equivalent both to f(y)\ge f(x)+
abla f(x)^	op(y-x) and to monotonicity of 
abla f. (h) If f\in C^1(\mathcal D), strong convexity is equivalent to the existence of c>0 with (
abla f(x)-

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite function on an open convex domain, convexity is equivalent to convexity of the epigraph and entails convex level sets, local Lipschitz continuity, directional differentiability, supporting subgradients, and maximal monotonicity of the subdifferential. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper extended-value convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The codomain excludes \(-\infty\), and the function is required not to be identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), not identically \(+\infty\), is convex if, for all \(x,x'\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \[f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x')\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x'),\] with the inequality interpreted in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). These functions form \(\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R^n\). Equivalently, a real-valued convex function on a nonempty convex set \(C\) becomes such a function by setting \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-value convex function maps Euclidean space into the real numbers together with positive infinity, is not everywhere positive infinity, and satisfies the convexity inequality in that extended ordered set. A real-valued convex function on a convex domain has an equivalent representation obtained by assigning positive infinity outside its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R^n\iff f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x')\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x')\text{ for all admissible }x,x',\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and active-index subgradients of a pointwise supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-supremum rule stated with the source's relative subdifferentials on the original and effective domains; the subgradient conclusion is only an inclusion and does not assert attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Delta\ne\varnothing\), let \(Q\) be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional real vector space, and suppose that \(\phi(\cdot,y):Q\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is closed and convex for every \(y\in\Delta\). Define
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y),\qquad \widehat Q=\{x\in Q:f(x)<+\infty\},
\]
and \(I(x)=\{y\in\Delta:\phi(x,y)=f(x)\}\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(\widehat Q\) and is closed there as an extended-real-valued function. Moreover, for every \(x\in\widehat Q\),
\[
\partial_{\widehat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{Conv}\bigl\{\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y):y\in I(x)\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty family of closed convex extended-real functions on a common convex set, their pointwise supremum is convex and closed on its finite effective domain. At each point of that domain, the relative subdifferential of the supremum contains the convex hull of the relative subdifferentials of the active members. This is only an inclusion; the statement does not assert that an active index exists.
assumptions_latex: Q\ne\varnothing\text{ is convex in a finite-dimensional real vector space}
\phi(\cdot,y):Q\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is closed and convex for every }y\in\Delta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex and closed on }\widehat Q,\qquad \partial_{\widehat Q}f(x)\supseteq\operatorname{Conv}\bigl\{\partial_{Q,x}\phi(x,y):y\in I(x)\bigr\}\quad\forall x\in\widehat Q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derives a first-order Taylor upper bound from Hölder continuity of the gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be convex in a finite-dimensional normed space with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), and let \(f:Q	o\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable. If, for some \(v\in(0,1]\) and \(G_v\in[0,+\infty]\), \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_*\le G_v\|x-y\|^v\) for all \(x,y\in Q\), then for every \(x,y\in Q\) with \([x,y]\subseteq Q\), \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac{G_v}{1+v}\|y-x\|^{1+v}.\]

\(Q\subset\mathbb E\) is convex and \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable.
\(v\in(0,1]\), \(G_v\in[0,+\infty]\), and \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le G_v\|x-y\|^v\) for all \(x,y\in Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex if, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).\] Consequently, for every finite family \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\in\mathbb R^n\) and weights \(\lambda_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), \(f(\sum_i\lambda_i x^i)\le\sum_i\lambda_i f(x^i)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Strict Convexity, and Concavity of Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued functions on convex subsets of finite-dimensional real spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is convex if \(f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). A convex function \(f\) is strictly convex if the inequality is strict for all distinct \(x,y\in C\) and all \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). The function \(f\) is concave if \(-f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on a convex domain is convex when it satisfies the two-point convexity inequality, strictly convex when that inequality is strict for distinct points and an interior mixing weight, and concave when its negative is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned} f\text{ convex}&\iff \forall x,y\in C\;\forall\alpha\in[0,1],\ f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\\ f\text{ strictly convex}&\iff \forall x\neq y\in C\;\forall\alpha\in(0,1),\ f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)<\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\\ f\text{ concave}&\iff -f\text{ is convex}. \end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of a Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The epigraphical characterization is retained as stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\operatorname{con}f\) is the greatest convex function majorized by \(f\): \[\operatorname{con}f=\sup\{g\mid g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}},\ g\text{ convex},\ g\leq f\},\] pointwise. Equivalently as stated, its epigraph is obtained by the epigraphical closure of \(\operatorname{con}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). Furthermore, \(f=\operatorname{con}f\) exactly when \(f\) is convex, and \(\operatorname{con}\delta_C=\delta_{\operatorname{con}C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of an extended-real-valued function is its greatest convex minorant, equivalently the pointwise supremum of all convex functions below it. The operation fixes exactly convex functions and sends a set indicator to the indicator of the set's convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{con}f=\sup\{g\mid g\text{ convex},\ g\leq f\};\quad f=\operatorname{con}f\iff f\text{ is convex};\quad \operatorname{con}\delta_C=\delta_{\operatorname{con}C}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subset E\) be convex and let \(\{f_\omega\}_{\omega\in\Omega}\) be convex functions on \(G\). If \(x\mapsto\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}f_\omega(x)\) is defined on \(G\), then it is convex. Moreover, if \(\alpha_\omega\ge0\) and only finitely many \(\alpha_\omega\) are nonzero, then \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\alpha_\omega f_\omega\) is convex on \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of convex functions on a common convex domain is convex whenever it is defined there. Any finite nonnegative linear combination of such functions is also convex.
assumptions_latex: f_\omega:G\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex for every }\omega\in\Omega
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{\omega\in\Omega}f_\omega\text{ and }\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\alpha_\omega f_\omega\text{ are convex on }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Rule for Monotone Convex Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate convex outer composition, including convexity and the interior-point subdifferential formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\psi$ be convex, and let $\varphi$ be a univariate convex function that is nondecreasing on
\[
\operatorname{Im}\psi=\{\psi(x):x\in\operatorname{dom}\psi\}.
\]
Then $f=\varphi\circ\psi$ is convex. Moreover, for every $x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\psi)$,
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{Conv}\!\left\{\lambda\,\partial\psi(x):\lambda\in\partial\varphi(\psi(x))\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a convex function with a univariate convex outer function that is nondecreasing on the inner function's image preserves convexity; at interior domain points, the composite subdifferential is the convex hull of the scaled inner subdifferentials generated by outer subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\varphi\circ\psi\text{ is convex, and }\partial f(x)=\operatorname{Conv}\{\lambda\partial\psi(x):\lambda\in\partial\varphi(\psi(x))\}\text{ for every }x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\psi).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, strict convexity, and strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued functions on nonempty convex subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if, for every \(x,x'\in C\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \[f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x')\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x').\] It is strictly convex if this inequality is strict whenever \(x\neq x'\). It is strongly convex with modulus \(c>0\) if, for every such \(x,x',\alpha\), \[f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)x')\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(x')-\frac c2\alpha(1-\alpha)\lVert x-x'\rVert^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a nonempty convex set is convex when its value at every nontrivial convex combination is at most the corresponding convex combination of its values. Strict convexity requires strict inequality for distinct points. Strong convexity with modulus c>0 additionally subtracts (c/2)α(1−α) times the squared distance between the points.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex, strictly convex, or strongly convex according to the corresponding inequality above.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Polyhedral Convexity, Conjugacy, and Domain Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bundled foundational definitions and properties for locally polyhedral extended-real functions on a finite-dimensional coordinate space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and nonempty. For \(f:\mathbb R^V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\), and \(g\) is concave when \(-g\) is convex. A convex function \(f\) is locally polyhedral when its restriction to every bounded box meeting \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is polyhedral; a convex set \(P\) is locally polyhedral when its intersection with every bounded box meeting \(P\) is a polyhedron. Moreover, \(f\) is locally polyhedral iff \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,\alpha):x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \alpha\ge f(x)\}\) is locally polyhedral. Define \(f^\bullet(p)=\sup_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\}\) and, for concave \(g\), \(g^\circ(p)=\inf_x\{\langle p,x\rangle-g(x)\}\). For locally polyhedral convex \(f\), \((f^\bullet)^\bullet=f\), although \(f^\bullet\) need not be locally polyhedral; if \(f\) is polyhedral, then \(f^\bullet\) is polyhedral. If \(f_0(x)=f(x-z)+\langle q,x\rangle+\beta\), then \(f_0^\bullet(p)=f^\bullet(p-q)+\langle p,z\rangle-\langle q,z\rangle-\beta\). A linearity domain is a set \(P=\operatorname{argmin}(f-p)\); on it \(f(x)=\langle p,x\rangle+\beta\), and only finitely many maximal linearity domains meet any bounded box. The function is domain-integral when every linearity domain is an integral polyhedron, in which case the supremum defining \(f^\bullet\) may be restricted to \(\mathbb Z^V\); it is co-domain-integral when \(f^\bullet\) is domain-integral. The concave notions are defined analogously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally polyhedral convex function is polyhedral on every bounded box meeting its effective domain, equivalently its epigraph is locally polyhedral. The extract defines convex and concave conjugates, records biconjugacy and the affine-translation rule, defines linearity domains, and characterizes domain-integrality by the ability to restrict conjugate maximization to integer points; co-domain-integrality means integrality of the conjugate's linearity domains.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is locally polyhedral for the biconjugacy and linearity-domain assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is locally polyhedral}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is locally polyhedral},\quad (f^\bullet)^\bullet=f,\quad f_0^\bullet(p)=f^\bullet(p-q)+\langle p,z\rangle-\langle q,z\rangle-\beta,\quad f\text{ domain-integral}\Rightarrow f^\bullet(p)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb Z^V}(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)).

\langle Ax,u\rangle=\langle x,A^*u\rangle

\|A\|_{1,2}:=\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}\|Ax\|_{

\mathbb E_1}^*,

\|A\|_{1,2}=\|A^*\|_{2,1}.

\mathbb E_1}^*\leq \|A\|_{1,2}\|u\|_{

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, concave, and strictly convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for real-valued functions on a convex domain, including restriction of a globally defined function to a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is convex if \(f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). It is concave if \(-f\) is convex, and strictly convex if the displayed inequality is strict whenever \(x\neq y\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), convexity over \(C\) means that the same inequality holds for all such \(x,y,\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex domain, a function is convex when its value at every interpolation does not exceed the corresponding interpolation of its endpoint values. Concavity means convexity of the negative, and strict convexity requires a strict inequality for distinct endpoints and an interior interpolation parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ convex}\iff \forall x,y\in C\;\forall\alpha\in[0,1],\ f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\quad f\text{ concave}\iff -f\text{ convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-Value Convexity and Closedness Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional family that remains convex for arbitrary nonnegative boundary values and is closed exactly when every boundary value vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\mid x^2+y^2=1\}, let \phi:S\to\mathbb{R} satisfy \phi\ge 0, and define f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} by f(x,y)=0 if x^2+y^2<1, f(x,y)=\phi(x,y) if x^2+y^2=1, and f(x,y)=+\infty if x^2+y^2>1. Then f is convex, \operatorname{dom}f=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\mid x^2+y^2\le 1\}, and f is closed, equivalently lower semicontinuous, if and only if \phi\equiv 0 on S.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set the function equal to zero inside the Euclidean unit disk, to arbitrary nonnegative values on its boundary, and to positive infinity outside. The function is convex and has the closed unit disk as its domain. It is closed, equivalently lower semicontinuous, exactly when every boundary value is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex},\quad \operatorname{dom}f=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2\mid x^2+y^2\le 1\},\quad f\text{ is closed/lower semicontinuous}\iff \phi\equiv 0\text{ on }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel–Young equality at a subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inner product identifies the finite-dimensional space with its dual for the concluding conjugate-subgradient statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mathbb{E} be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let f:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be proper and convex, and define
\[
f_*(g)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle g,y\rangle-f(y)\}.
\]
For every x\in\mathbb{E} and g\in\partial f(x),
\[
f(x)+f_*(g)=\langle g,x\rangle,
\]
and, in particular,
\[
x\in\partial f_*(g).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever g is a subgradient of a proper convex function at x, the Fenchel–Young inequality holds with equality, and x is a subgradient of the conjugate at g.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb{E}\text{ is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)+f_*(g)=\langle g,x\rangle\quad\text{and}\quad x\in\partial f_*(g)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biconvex sets, functions, and optimization problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two-block biconvexity and records its relation to joint convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal A\times\mathcal B\), define \(\mathcal C_\alpha=\{\beta\in\mathcal B:(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal C\}\) and \(\mathcal C_\beta=\{\alpha\in\mathcal A:(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal C\}\). The set \(\mathcal C\) is biconvex when every \(\mathcal C_\alpha\) and every \(\mathcal C_\beta\) is convex. A function \(f:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R\) is biconvex when each restriction \(\alpha\mapsto f(\alpha,\beta)\) on \(\mathcal C_\beta\) and \(\beta\mapsto f(\alpha,\beta)\) on \(\mathcal C_\alpha\) is convex. A biconvex optimization problem is \(\min_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal C}f(\alpha,\beta)\) with both \(\mathcal C\) and \(f\) biconvex. Joint convexity implies biconvexity, but not conversely; for example, \(f(\alpha,\beta)=(1-\alpha\beta)^2\) on \([-2,2]^2\) is biconvex but not jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is biconvex if every section obtained by fixing either variable block is convex. A function on such a set is biconvex if it is convex in either block while the other is fixed. Biconvex optimization minimizes such a function over such a set. Joint convexity is sufficient but not necessary for biconvexity; the squared bilinear-residual example demonstrates the strict distinction.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m\text{ and }\mathcal B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ are nonempty convex sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C\text{ and }f\text{ are biconvex exactly under the stated sectionwise convexity conditions, and joint convexity }\Rightarrow\text{ biconvexity, while the converse fails.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Foundational metric convex atoms
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\); and let \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family groups the elementary Euclidean convex atoms used to build affine-quadratic, homogeneous, and residual models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathfrak M_n:=\left\{x\mapsto\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha\right\}\cup\{\text{proper closed sublinear }h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\}\cup\{x\mapsto d_C(x)\},\] where \(d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\). Every member is convex; the displayed quadratic members are finite and continuous, and each distance member is finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The foundational metric family consists of positive-semidefinite affine quadratics, proper closed sublinear functions such as norms and support functions, and Euclidean distance functions to nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak M_n=\mathfrak M_n^{\mathrm{aq}}\cup\mathfrak M_n^{\mathrm{ph}}\cup\mathfrak M_n^{\mathrm{dist}}\subset\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A quadratic member is convex exactly when \(Q\succeq0\).
A proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear member has the representation \(h=\sigma_D\) for a unique nonempty closed convex set \(D\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(Q=0\) gives affine functions.
Taking \(C=\{b\}\) gives \(d_C(x)=\|x-b\|\).
Every norm is a finite sublinear member.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine precomposition yields residual functions such as \(x\mapsto d_C(Ax-b)\).
Nonnegative sums of compatible members remain convex.
boundary_notes: The union notation defines a modeling family, not a closure under every convexity-preserving operation.
Distance to a nonconvex set is generally not convex, so convexity of \(C\) is essential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Cone to a Strictly Feasible Convex Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the supporting-vector and subgradient orientations stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be convex, x^*\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f), Q=\{x:f(x)\le0\}, and \inf_x f(x)<0. Define Q^*(x^*)=\{c:\langle c,x-x^*\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in Q\}. If f(x^*)=0, then Q^*(x^*)=\{\lambda s:\lambda\ge0,\ s\in\partial f(x^*)\}; if f(x^*)<0, then Q^*(x^*)=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility, the supporting cone of a convex zero-sublevel set at a boundary point is the nonnegative cone generated by the point's subgradients; at a strict interior point it is the zero cone, using the extract's sign conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minima and Solution Sets of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality, convexity of the minimizer set, and uniqueness under strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex. Every local minimizer of \(f\) is a global minimizer, and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\), if nonempty, is convex. If, in addition, \(f\) is proper and strictly convex, then \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) contains at most one point and hence is a singleton whenever it is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex extended-real-valued function, every local minimum is global and the set of minimizers is convex. If the function is also proper and strictly convex, it has at most one minimizer.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is proper and strictly convex for the uniqueness conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{locargmin}f\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}f,\quad \operatorname{argmin}f\text{ is convex, and under proper strict convexity }|\operatorname{argmin}f|\le1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Jensen Inequality Characterizes Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued functions on Euclidean space and arbitrary finite convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex if and only if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and every \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\in[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), \[f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on Euclidean space is convex exactly when Jensen's inequality holds for every finite convex combination of points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i)\text{ for every finite convex combination}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, Strictly Convex, and Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex if, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).\] It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever \(x\ne y\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\). The function \(f\) is (strictly) concave exactly when \(-f\) is (strictly) convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on Euclidean space is convex when its value at every line-segment combination does not exceed the corresponding combination of endpoint values. It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct endpoints and an interior weight. It is concave or strictly concave when its negative is convex or strictly convex, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff (\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n)(\forall\lambda\in[0,1])\;f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y),\quad f\text{ is (strictly) concave}\iff -f\text{ is (strictly) convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost differentiability–almost strict convexity conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes boundary-sensitive differentiability and strict convexity through Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Call \(g\) almost differentiable when \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\), \(g\) is differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}g)\), and \(\partial g(x)=\varnothing\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\setminus\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}g)\). Call \(g\) almost strictly convex when it is strictly convex on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial g\). Then \[f\text{ is almost differentiable}\iff f^*\text{ is almost strictly convex},\qquad f^*\text{ is almost differentiable}\iff f\text{ is almost strictly convex}.\] In particular, an almost strictly convex function is strictly convex on \(\operatorname{rint}(\operatorname{dom}g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the function is almost differentiable exactly when its Fenchel conjugate is almost strictly convex, and conversely the conjugate is almost differentiable exactly when the original function is almost strictly convex. Almost differentiability includes an empty subdifferential at every domain point outside the nonempty interior; almost strict convexity means strict convexity on every convex subset of the subdifferential domain.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ almost differentiable}\iff f^*\text{ almost strictly convex},\quad f^*\text{ almost differentiable}\iff f\text{ almost strictly convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex affine-quadratic functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-valued Euclidean affine-quadratic family. Extended-valued quadratic functions on restricted affine domains are not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-quadratic curvature family is \[\mathfrak Q_n:=\left\{q_{Q,a,\alpha}:x\mapsto\tfrac12x^\top Qx+a^\top x+\alpha\ \middle|\ Q\succeq0\right\}.\] The affine term controls tilt and offset, while \(Q\) controls curvature. The member is affine exactly when \(Q=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex affine-quadratic function is a quadratic polynomial whose symmetric curvature matrix is positive semidefinite. Its linear and constant terms do not affect convexity, and zero curvature yields the affine subfamily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q_{Q,a,\alpha}(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+a^\top x+\alpha\text{ is convex on }\mathbb R^n\Longleftrightarrow Q\succeq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[z^\top Qz\ge0\quad\forall z\in\mathbb R^n.\]
If \(Q=B^\top B\), then \[q_{Q,a,\alpha}(x)=\tfrac12\|Bx\|^2+a^\top x+\alpha.\]
special_cases_latex: \(Q=0\) gives an affine function.
\(Q\succ0\) gives a strictly convex quadratic with unique unconstrained minimizer \(-Q^{-1}a\).
\(Q=\lambda I\), \(a=0\), gives the scaled squared Euclidean norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The gradient is \(\nabla q(x)=Qx+a\) and the Hessian is the constant matrix \(Q\).
The perspective of the homogeneous quadratic part produces a quadratic-over-linear function.
boundary_notes: An indefinite \(Q\) yields a nonconvex quadratic on \(\mathbb R^n\).
Positive semidefiniteness does not imply strict convexity when \(Q\) has a nontrivial nullspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(a:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is affine if there exist a linear functional \(\ell:X\to\mathbb{R}\) and a scalar \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
a(x)=\ell(x)+\beta\qquad(x\in X).
\]
Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in X\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
a(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)=\lambda a(x)+(1-\lambda)a(y).
\]
Every affine function is both convex and concave because the defining equality implies both corresponding Jensen inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function is a linear functional plus a constant, equivalently a function preserving every affine combination; it is both convex and concave.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic minimization over the entire vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a(x)=\ell(x)+\beta\) on a real vector space \(X\). If \(\ell=0\), then \(a\equiv\beta\), every point minimizes \(a\), and \(\inf_Xa=\beta\). If \(\ell\ne0\), then \(a\) is unbounded above and below, so \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Xa=\varnothing\) and \(\inf_Xa=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function has a global minimizer exactly when its linear part vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Xa=X\) if \(\ell=0\); otherwise it is empty and \(\inf_Xa=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential segments and affine conjugate segments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two implications relating a line segment in a subdifferential value to affinity of the conjugate on that segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(x,u_0,u_1\in\mathcal H\). Then
\[
[u_0,u_1]\subset\partial f(x)\;\Longrightarrow\; f^*\text{ is affine on }[u_0,u_1].
\]
Conversely, if \(f^*\) is affine on \([u_0,u_1]\) and \(x\in\partial f^*(]u_0,u_1[)\), then
\[
[u_0,u_1]\subset\partial f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an entire segment lies in the subdifferential of f at x, then the conjugate is affine on that segment. Conversely, if the conjugate is affine on the segment and x belongs to the image of its subdifferential over the open segment, then the whole closed segment lies in the subdifferential of f at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [u_0,u_1]\subset\partial f(x)\Rightarrow f^*\text{ affine on }[u_0,u_1],\quad \bigl(f^*\text{ affine on }[u_0,u_1]\ \wedge\ x\in\partial f^*(]u_0,u_1[)\bigr)\Rightarrow [u_0,u_1]\subset\partial f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Conjugate and Affine-Minorant Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the conjugate of a closed convex function and identifies its epigraph with the parameters of its affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a closed convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\). Its conjugate is \[f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle x,x^*\rangle-f(x)\}=-\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x)-\langle x,x^*\rangle\}.\] Moreover, for \(h_{x^*,\mu^*}(x)=\langle x,x^*\rangle-\mu^*\), \[h_{x^*,\mu^*}\le f\text{ pointwise}\iff \mu^*\ge f^*(x^*),\] so the set of pairs \((x^*,\mu^*)\) defining affine minorants of \(f\) is \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel conjugate is the supremum of the affine perturbations obtained by subtracting the function. A slope-intercept pair defines an affine minorant of the function exactly when it lies in the epigraph of the conjugate.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a closed convex function on }\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(\langle x,x^*\rangle-f(x)),\qquad \{(x^*,\mu^*)\mid \langle x,x^*\rangle-\mu^*\le f(x)\ \forall x\}=\operatorname{epi}f^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Functions and Restricted Superposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterizations and coordinate reconstruction of scalar-valued affine functions on finite-dimensional real coordinate spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is affine if and only if there exist $a\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)=a^Tx+b$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Equivalently, for every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\alpha+\beta=1$, one has $f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)$. In this representation, $b=f(0)$ and $a_i=f(e_i)-f(0)$, so $f(x)=f(0)+\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\bigl(f(e_i)-f(0)\bigr)$. Consequently, any violation of the restricted-superposition identity proves that $f$ is not affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-valued function is affine exactly when it is a linear functional plus a constant, equivalently when it preserves every two-point affine combination. Its coefficients are determined by its values at zero and at the standard basis vectors. A violation of restricted superposition certifies non-affineness.
assumptions_latex: e_1,\ldots,e_n\text{ is the standard basis of }\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is affine}\iff \exists a\in\mathbb{R}^n,\,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ f(x)=a^Tx+b\iff \forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\;\forall\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R},\ \alpha+\beta=1:\ f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y),\quad b=f(0),\ a_i=f(e_i)-f(0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Affine Minorant at a Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine support with slope restricted to the direction space of the affine hull of the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb{R}^n\). For every \(x_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists \(s\in\operatorname{par}(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f))\) such that \[f(x)\ge f(x_0)+\langle s,x-x_0\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every relative-interior point of its domain, a convex function has a global affine minorant that agrees with the function at that point; its slope can be chosen in the direction subspace parallel to the affine hull of the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s\in\operatorname{par}(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f))\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ f(x)\ge f(x_0)+\langle s,x-x_0\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Φ-Conjugates, Φ-Biconjugates, and Φ-Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines generalized conjugacy symmetrically for functions on either side of an arbitrary coupling, together with the induced envelope classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X,Y\neq\varnothing and \Phi:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}. For f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}, define f^{\Phi}(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\Phi(x,y)-f(x)\} and f^{\Phi\Phi}(x):=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\Phi(x,y)-f^{\Phi}(y)\}. For g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}, define g^{\Phi}(x):=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\Phi(x,y)-g(y)\} and g^{\Phi\Phi}(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\Phi(x,y)-g^{\Phi}(x)\}. A \Phi-envelope on X is any pointwise supremum of functions \Phi(\cdot,y)+\alpha, with y\in Y and constants \alpha; \Phi-envelopes on Y are defined analogously using \Phi(x,\cdot)+\alpha. If X=Y and \Phi is not symmetric, the two envelope classes on that space may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a coupling Φ on two nonempty sets, the Φ-conjugate is obtained by subtracting the function from the coupling and taking a supremum over its domain; applying the construction from the opposite side gives the Φ-biconjugate. Φ-envelope functions are pointwise suprema of coupling sections plus constants. When both sets coincide but Φ is asymmetric, the two orientations can produce different envelope classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\Phi}(y)=\sup_{x\in X}(\Phi(x,y)-f(x)),\quad f^{\Phi\Phi}(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}(\Phi(x,y)-f^{\Phi}(y)),\quad g^{\Phi}(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}(\Phi(x,y)-g(y)),\quad g^{\Phi\Phi}(y)=\sup_{x\in X}(\Phi(x,y)-g^{\Phi}(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact continuous affine minorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally convex spaces and extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a locally convex space with continuous dual \(V^*\), and let \(F:V\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). A continuous affine function \(\ell\le F\) is exact at \(u\in V\) when \(\ell(u)=F(u)\). Necessarily \(F(u)<+\infty\), and for some \(u^*\in V^*\), \[\ell(v)=\langle v-u,u^*\rangle+F(u)=\langle v,u^*\rangle+F(u)-\langle u,u^*\rangle.\] Its constant term is maximal among affine minorants with slope \(u^*\), and \[F(u)-\langle u,u^*\rangle=-F^*(u^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous affine minorant of F is exact at u if it equals F there. Exactness forces F(u) to be finite; the minorant has a continuous-dual slope u* and its maximal constant term equals minus the conjugate value at u*.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a locally convex space with continuous dual }V^*.
u\in V,\quad \ell\text{ is continuous affine},\quad \ell(v)\le F(v)\ \forall v\in V,\quad \ell(u)=F(u).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(u)\in\mathbb R,\quad \ell(v)=\langle v-u,u^*\rangle+F(u)\text{ for some }u^*\in V^*,\quad F(u)-\langle u,u^*\rangle=-F^*(u^*).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gamma-Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Gamma-regularization both as an affine-minorant supremum and as a greatest Gamma-class minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: G(x):=\sup\{a(x):a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\le F\}.\quad\text{Equivalently, }G\in\Gamma(V),\ G\le F,\text{ and }(H\in\Gamma(V),\ H\le F)\Rightarrow H\le G.\text{ Such }G\text{ is the }\Gamma\text{-regularization of }F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gamma-regularization of F is the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine functions below F. Equivalently, it is the largest minorant of F belonging to Gamma(V).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G=\sup\{a:a\text{ continuous affine},\ a\le F\}\iff G=\max\{H\in\Gamma(V):H\le F\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine maps and their affine-combination characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued affine maps, including unique parameter recovery from zero and standard-basis evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m is affine if and only if it has the form f(x)=Ax+b for some A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and b\in\mathbb{R}^m. Equivalently, for all x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n and \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R} satisfying \alpha+\beta=1,\quad f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y). The pair (A,b) is unique, with b=f(0) and A=[\,f(e_1)-f(0)\ \cdots\ f(e_n)-f(0)\,]. The map is linear if and only if b=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued map is affine exactly when it has the form Ax+b, equivalently when it preserves two-point affine combinations. Its matrix and offset are unique and recoverable from its values at zero and the standard basis. It is linear exactly when the offset is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is affine}\iff\exists A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^m\ \forall x,\ f(x)=Ax+b\iff\forall x,y,\alpha,\beta\ (\alpha+\beta=1\Rightarrow f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y));\quad (A,b)\text{ is unique}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+b^\top x+c,
\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The function \(q\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \(Q\) is positive semidefinite, meaning
\[
d^\top Qd\geq0\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Equivalently, its constant Hessian satisfies \(\nabla^2q(x)=Q\succeq0\). It is strictly convex if \(Q\succ0\); positive semidefiniteness alone permits flat directions and therefore need not imply strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic function with symmetric Hessian is convex exactly when its quadratic coefficient matrix is positive semidefinite, and strictly convex when it is positive definite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Definite Quadratic Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate quadratics; singular Hessians belong to the sibling boundary leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\succ0\) and \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+b^{\mathsf T}x+c\), then with \(x_\star=-Q^{-1}b\), \[q(x)=q(x_\star)+\tfrac12(x-x_\star)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_\star),\qquad \min q=c-\tfrac12b^{\mathsf T}Q^{-1}b.\] Thus \(x_\star\) is the unique minimizer and the unique solution of \(Qx+b=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic completes the square around its unique stationary minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}q=\{-Q^{-1}b\}\) and \(\min q=c-\tfrac12b^{\mathsf T}Q^{-1}b\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Quadratic Minimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Curvature Constants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean curvature constants for a convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(Q\succeq0\), \(\nabla q(x)=Qx+b\). The sharp global Euclidean gradient-Lipschitz constant is \(L=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\). If \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)>0\), then \(q\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and \(\mu\) is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme Hessian eigenvalues give the sharp smoothness and strong-convexity constants.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\) and, when positive, \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\) are the sharp global curvature constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Curvature Constants

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong convexity on a convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition with the zero-curvature boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex. A function \(f\) is strongly convex on \(Q\) with parameter \(\mu>0\) if, for every \(x,y\in Q\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \[f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}\alpha(1-\alpha)\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\] The class is denoted \(\mathcal S_\mu^0(Q)\). Setting \(\mu=0\) recovers ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex set is strongly convex with parameter μ>0 when every chord lies above the function by at least the quadratic curvature term (μ/2)α(1−α)‖x−y‖². This class is denoted S^0_μ(Q); the boundary case μ=0 is ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}\alpha(1-\alpha)\lVert x-y\rVert^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate variational representation of a strictly convex quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization of the Fenchel-conjugate definition to an affine-quadratic function with positive-definite Hessian; the extract does not assert the resulting closed-form formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), \(b,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), and
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c.
\]
Then the conjugate of \(f\) at \(y\) is defined by
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^*(y)
&=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{y^Tx-f(x)\}\\
&=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{y^Tx-\tfrac12x^TAx-b^Tx-c\right\}\\
&=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{-\tfrac12x^TAx-(b-y)^Tx-c\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine-quadratic function with positive-definite Hessian, its conjugate at y is the attained maximum of yᵀx minus the quadratic, equivalently the maximum of −xᵀAx/2−(b−y)ᵀx−c.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(y)=\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{-\frac12x^TAx-(b-y)^Tx-c\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Programs and Directional Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and optimality properties for minimizing a continuous, directionally differentiable function over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in S} f(x)\), where \(S\) is closed and \(f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\) is continuous on an open set \(\mathcal O\supseteq S\). The problem is a convex program when \(S\) and \(f\) are convex; then its nonempty optimal-solution set is convex. If \(S\) is convex and \(f\) is directionally differentiable, every local minimizer \(\bar x\in S\) satisfies \(f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)\ge 0\) for all \(x\in S\). A feasible point satisfying this condition is directionally stationary. If additionally \(f\) is convex on \(S\), the condition is sufficient for \(\bar x\) to be a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex program minimizes a convex function over a convex feasible set, and its nonempty solution set is convex. For a directionally differentiable objective on a convex feasible set, every local minimizer is directionally stationary. Under convexity of the objective, directional stationarity is also sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is convex for the stationarity assertions}
f\text{ is directionally differentiable for the directional condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ local minimizer}\Rightarrow f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)\ge0\ \forall x\in S;\quad f\text{ convex on }S\Rightarrow\bigl[f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)\ge0\ \forall x\in S\bigr]\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ global minimizer}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order characterizations of differentiable convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes ordinary, strict, and strong convexity on a convex subset of an open differentiability domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be differentiable on an open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(C\subset\Omega\) be convex. Then: (i) \(f\) is convex on \(C\) iff \(f(x)\ge f(x_0)+\langle
abla f(x_0),x-x_0angle\) for all \(x_0,x\in C\); (ii) \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\) iff this inequality is strict whenever \(x
e x_0\); (iii) \(f\) is strongly convex with modulus \(c\) on \(C\) iff \(f(x)\ge f(x_0)+\langle
abla f(x_0),x-x_0angle+	frac{c}{2}\|x-x_0\|^2\) for all \(x_0,x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable function on an open set, convexity on a convex subset is equivalent to every tangent affine function being a global underestimator there. Strict convexity corresponds to strict inequality at distinct points, and strong convexity of modulus c corresponds to adding the quadratic term (c/2) times the squared distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ convex/strictly convex/strongly convex of modulus }c\iff\text{ the corresponding first-order inequality holds on }C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order criteria for convexity and strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive definiteness is stated only as a sufficient condition for strict convexity, while the convex and strongly convex criteria are equivalences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be twice differentiable on an open convex set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). Then: (i) \(f\) is convex on \(\Omega\) iff \(
abla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\); (ii) if \(
abla^2f(x)\succ0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\), then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(\Omega\); (iii) \(f\) is strongly convex with modulus \(c\) on \(\Omega\) iff \(\langle
abla^2f(x)d,dangle\ge c\|d\|^2\) for every \(x\in\Omega\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable function on an open convex set is convex exactly when every Hessian is positive semidefinite. Positive definiteness everywhere implies strict convexity. Strong convexity of modulus c is equivalent to every Hessian being uniformly bounded below by c times the identity.

\(f	ext{ convex}\iff
abla^2f\succeq0;\quad 
abla^2f\succ0\Rightarrow f	ext{ strictly convex};\quad f	ext{ is }c	ext{-strongly convex}\iff
abla^2f\succeq cI	ext{ on }\Omega.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(b\in\operatorname{range}Q\), then the stationary equation \(Qx+b=0\) is solvable and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}q(x)=-Q^\dagger b+\ker Q,
\qquad
\min q=c-\tfrac12b^\top Q^\dagger b.
\]
The minimizer is nonunique because every null direction of \(Q\) is flat. If \(b\notin\operatorname{range}Q\), then there exists \(d\in\ker Q\) with \(b^\top d\neq0\); choosing the sign of \(d\) gives \(q(x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular convex quadratic has minimizers precisely when its linear term lies in the Hessian range; otherwise a null direction makes it unbounded below.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper closed sublinear functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be extended-real-valued with \(0\in\operatorname{dom}h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family consists of convex degree-one positive-homogeneous functions, equivalently proper closed sublinear functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathfrak H_n:=\{h:h(\lambda x)=\lambda h(x)\ \forall x,\lambda>0,\quad h(x+y)\le h(x)+h(y)\ \forall x,y,\quad h\text{ proper and lsc}\}.\] Equivalently, \(h\in\mathfrak H_n\) exactly when \(h=\sigma_D\) for a unique nonempty closed convex set \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-homogeneous convex family consists of proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear functions. Such a function scales linearly under positive dilation, is subadditive, and is exactly the support function of a unique nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h\in\mathfrak H_n\Longleftrightarrow h\text{ is proper, lsc, positively homogeneous, and subadditive}\Longleftrightarrow h=\sigma_D\text{ for a unique nonempty closed convex }D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}h\text{ is a closed convex cone}.\]
\[D=\{v:\langle v,x\rangle\le h(x)\ \forall x\},\qquad h(x)=\sup_{v\in D}\langle v,x\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: Every norm and seminorm is sublinear; a norm is finite and symmetric.
Every linear function is sublinear, with a singleton representing set \(D\).
Indicators of closed convex cones are extended-valued sublinear functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), \(\partial h(x)=\operatorname{argmax}_{v\in D}\langle v,x\rangle\).
The conjugate of \(h=\sigma_D\) is \(h^*=\iota_D\).
boundary_notes: Positive homogeneity alone does not imply convexity; subadditivity supplies the missing condition.
The value at \(\lambda=0\) is governed by properness and lower semicontinuity rather than by the displayed scaling rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Approximation of the Euclidean Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit smoothable-function construction for the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=\|x\|_2\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(\mu>0\), define \[h_\mu(x)=\sqrt{\|x\|_2^2+\mu^2}-\mu.\] Then \(h\) is \((1,1)\)-smoothable and \(h_\mu\) is a \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximation of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive mu, subtracting mu from the square root of the squared Euclidean norm plus mu squared gives a 1/mu-smooth approximation of the Euclidean norm with parameters (1,1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h(x)=\|x\|_2\text{ is }(1,1)\text{-smoothable, with }h_\mu(x)=\sqrt{\|x\|_2^2+\mu^2}-\mu.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity, Subadditivity, and Sublinearity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines positive homogeneity, subadditivity, and their conjunction for real-valued functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is positively homogeneous if $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\lambda\ge 0$. It is subadditive if $f(x+y)\le f(x)+f(y)$ for every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$. It is sublinear if it is both positively homogeneous and subadditive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive homogeneity means nonnegative scaling of the argument scales the function value by the same factor. Subadditivity bounds the value at a sum by the sum of the values. A function satisfying both properties is sublinear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is sublinear}\iff\left[f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\lambda\ge0\right]\land\left[f(x+y)\le f(x)+f(y)\ \forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\right].

Let \(f\) be a nonnegative convex function satisfying \(f(0)=0\). Then \(f^{\circ}\) is nonnegative, closed, and convex, with \(f^{\circ}(0)=0\), and

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative as the Support Function of the Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The symbol ∂₂ denotes the subdifferential with respect to the direction argument of p↦f′(x₀;p).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then, for the function \(p\mapsto f'(x_0;p)\), \[\partial_2 f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0),\] and, for every \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), \[f'(x_0;p)=\max\{\langle g,p\rangle:g\in\partial f(x_0)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of the domain of a convex function, the subdifferential at zero of the directional-derivative function equals the original subdifferential. The directional derivative is consequently the support function of that subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_2 f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0)\quad\text{and}\quad f'(x_0;p)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x_0)}\langle g,p\rangle\quad\forall p\in\mathbb R^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity of Degree p
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for an extended-real-valued function on an explicitly specified conic domain, including nonnegative scaling factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p\ge0 and let f:\operatorname{dom}f\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}, where \operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n. The function f is positively homogeneous of degree p if \operatorname{dom}f is a cone—so x\in\operatorname{dom}f and \tau\ge0 imply \tau x\in\operatorname{dom}f—and f(\tau x)=\tau^p f(x) for every x\in\operatorname{dom}f and every \tau\ge0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is positively homogeneous of degree p at least zero when its domain is closed under nonnegative scaling and scaling an argument by any nonnegative factor scales the function value by that factor raised to p.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is positively homogeneous of degree }p\iff\bigl[(x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \tau\ge0\Rightarrow\tau x\in\operatorname{dom}f)\ \land\ (f(\tau x)=\tau^pf(x)\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall\tau\ge0)\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Sublinearity of Convex Directional Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded theorem for a convex extended-real-valued function at a finite base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty] be convex and let f(x)\in\mathbb{R}. For every y\in\mathbb{R}^n, the quotient q_y(\lambda):=\frac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda} is nondecreasing in \lambda>0. Consequently, f'(x;y) exists as an extended-real limit and f'(x;y)=\inf_{\lambda>0}q_y(\lambda). Moreover, y\mapsto f'(x;y) is convex and positively homogeneous, f'(x;0)=0, and -f'(x;-y)\leq f'(x;y) for every y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite point of a convex function, the forward difference quotient in each direction is nondecreasing as a function of the positive step. Its limit at zero therefore exists and equals the infimum over all positive steps. The resulting directional-derivative function is convex and positively homogeneous, vanishes at zero, and satisfies the stated inequality between opposite directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\mapsto\frac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda}\text{ is nondecreasing on }(0,\infty),\quad f'(x;y)=\inf_{\lambda>0}\frac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda};\quad f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is convex and positively homogeneous},\ f'(x;0)=0,\ -f'(x;-y)\leq f'(x;y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinear and superlinear envelope representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation theorem for bounded positively homogeneous functions on finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be positively homogeneous of degree one and satisfy \(\sup_{\|g\|\le1}h(g)<\infty\). If \(h\) is upper semicontinuous, there is a family of sublinear functions \(\{p_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\) such that \(h(g)=\inf_{\lambda\in\Lambda}p_\lambda(g)\) for every \(g\in\mathbb R^n\). If \(h\) is lower semicontinuous, there is a family of superlinear functions \(\{q_\lambda\}_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\) such that \(h(g)=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}q_\lambda(g)\) for every \(g\in\mathbb R^n\). The index set \(\Lambda\) may be chosen independently of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-semicontinuous, degree-one positively homogeneous function bounded above on the unit ball is the pointwise infimum of sublinear functions. Under lower semicontinuity it is the pointwise supremum of superlinear functions. A common index set can be used for all such functions.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is positively homogeneous of degree one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\text{ u.s.c.}\Rightarrow h=\inf_{\lambda\in\Lambda}p_\lambda\text{ with each }p_\lambda\text{ sublinear};\quad h\text{ l.s.c.}\Rightarrow h=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}q_\lambda\text{ with each }q_\lambda\text{ superlinear}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional stationarity is equivalent to global minimality under positive homogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a nonnegative B-differentiable function on a closed convex cone and does not assume convexity of the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a closed convex cone, and let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+$ be B-differentiable and positively homogeneous of degree $p\ge 1$ on an open set containing $X$. For every $\bar x\in X$, $\bar x$ is d-stationary for $f$ on $X$ if and only if $\bar x$ is a global minimizer of $f$ on $X$. Every such point satisfies $f(\bar x)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative B-differentiable function that is positively homogeneous of degree at least one on a neighborhood of a closed convex cone, directional stationarity on the cone is equivalent to global minimality, and every such point has objective value zero.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
f\text{ is B-differentiable on an open set containing }X
f\text{ is positively homogeneous of degree }p\ge 1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is d-stationary on }X\iff\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad f(\bar x)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative Structure of a Sublinear Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of the directional derivative at a core-domain point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $p:\mathbf E\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be sublinear and $\bar x\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom}p)$. Define $q(d)=p'(\bar x;d)$. Then $$q(\lambda\bar x)=\lambda p(\bar x)\quad\forall\lambda\in\mathbb R,$$ $$q(d)\leq p(d)\quad\forall d\in\mathbf E,$$ and $$\operatorname{lin}q\supseteq\operatorname{lin}p+\operatorname{span}\{\bar x\}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a core-domain point of a sublinear function, the directional derivative agrees linearly with the function along the line generated by that point, is dominated pointwise by the original function, and has lineality containing the original lineality plus that line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(\lambda\bar x)=\lambda p(\bar x)\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R,\qquad q\leq p,\qquad \operatorname{lin}q\supseteq\operatorname{lin}p+\operatorname{span}\{\bar x\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perspective representation of a convex sublevel cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional perspective homogenization under interior-domain and nonempty strict-sublevel assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous and convex, and let a\in\mathbb{R}. Assume H(0)>a, 0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}H), and \{z:H(z)<a\}\neq\varnothing. Define \mathcal H^\circ=\{z:\exists\beta>0,\ H(\beta^{-1}z)\le a\}, \mathcal H=\operatorname{cl}\mathcal H^\circ, and G(z)=\inf_{\beta>0}\beta\bigl(H(\beta^{-1}z)-a\bigr). Then G is convex, \mathcal H=\{z:G(z)\le0\}, and \mathcal H is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated domain and sublevel assumptions, the infimum of the perspective expression is convex. Its zero sublevel set equals the closure of the radial homogenization of the level-a sublevel set, and that closure is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is convex},\qquad \mathcal H=\{z:G(z)\le0\},\qquad \mathcal H\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(\|\cdot\|:X\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is a norm when, for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\|x\|=0\iff x=0,
\qquad
\|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\,\|x\|,
\qquad
\|x+y\|\leq\|x\|+\|y\|.
\]
These conditions make every norm finite-valued, convex, and positively homogeneous. Conversely, a finite-valued sublinear function that is positive definite and symmetric, meaning \(p(x)=p(-x)\), satisfies absolute homogeneity and is a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive; equivalently, it is a symmetric positive-definite finite sublinear function.
knowledge_statements.title: Norm Families

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Finite-Dimensional ℓp Norm Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coordinate-norm family and its sharp exponent boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^n\), \[\|x\|_p=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad \|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|\] are norms. If \(n\ge2\) and \(0<p<1\), the power formula is not a norm because \(\|e_1+e_2\|_p=2^{1/p}>2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate ℓp formula defines a norm for p at least one; below one it violates the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\cdot\|_p\text{ is a norm for }1\le p\le\infty,\text{ while the power formula is not a norm for }0<p<1.
knowledge_statements.title: The Finite-Dimensional ℓp Norm Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse Triangle Inequality and Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic metric regularity shared by every norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every norm and all \(x,y\), \[\bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le\|x-y\|.\] Consequently the norm function is 1-Lipschitz in its induced metric and continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every norm satisfies the reverse triangle inequality and is 1-Lipschitz in its own metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl|\|x\|-\|y\|\bigr|\le\|x-y\|\quad\forall x,y\in X.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Triangle Inequality and Continuity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) is a norm, its unit ball is convex, absorbing, and balanced, and \(p\) is its Minkowski functional; conversely, suitable balanced convex generators produce seminorms or norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm can be represented as the Minkowski functional of its balanced convex unit ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropy prox geometry on probability simplices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic properties of normalized negative entropy relative to the \ell_1 norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \Delta_n and \Delta_m, define d_1(x)=\ln n+\sum_{i=1}^n x^{(i)}\ln x^{(i)} and d_2(y)=\ln m+\sum_{j=1}^m y^{(j)}\ln y^{(j)}, with 0\ln0=0. Then d_1 and d_2 are 1-strongly convex with respect to \|\cdot\|_1; at x_0=\bar e_n/n and y_0=\bar e_m/m they equal zero; and \max_{x\in\Delta_n}d_1(x)=\ln n and \max_{y\in\Delta_m}d_2(y)=\ln m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized negative entropy on a probability simplex is 1-strongly convex in the l1 norm, vanishes at the uniform distribution, and has maximum log of the simplex dimension.
assumptions_latex: d_1(x)=\ln n+\sum_i x^{(i)}\ln x^{(i)},\quad d_2(y)=\ln m+\sum_j y^{(j)}\ln y^{(j)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_1,d_2\text{ are 1-strongly convex w.r.t. }\|\cdot\|_1;\quad d_1(\bar e_n/n)=d_2(\bar e_m/m)=0;\quad \max_{\Delta_n}d_1=\ln n,\ \max_{\Delta_m}d_2=\ln m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Norm Criterion and Dual Formula for a Submodular-Induced Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The function f is the continuous convex extension associated with F in the source. The displayed dual formula applies when the equivalent norm conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be submodular and non-decreasing with \(F(\varnothing)=0\), and define \(\Omega_\infty(w)=f(|w|)\). Then \(\Omega_\infty\) is a norm if and only if \(F(\{k\})>0\) for every \(k\in V\). Under these equivalent conditions, \[\Omega_\infty^*(s)=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq V}\frac{|s|(A)}{F(A)}=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq V}\frac{\|s_A\|_1}{F(A)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The submodular-induced penalty is a norm exactly when the normalized, non-decreasing submodular function is strictly positive on every singleton. When this holds, its dual norm is the maximum over nonempty subsets of the restricted l1 norm divided by the set-function value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega_\infty\text{ is a norm}\iff\forall k\in V,\ F(\{k\})>0;\quad \text{when this holds, }\Omega_\infty^*(s)=\max_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq V}\frac{\|s_A\|_1}{F(A)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Young Functions, Orlicz Spaces, and the Luxemburg Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Young function, its Orlicz space of random variables, and the Luxemburg norm, including completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive convex function \(\psi\) satisfying \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\psi(x)=\infty\) is a Young function. Its Orlicz space is \(L_\psi=\{X:\mathbb E\psi(|X|/c)<\infty\text{ for some }c>0\}\). The Luxemburg norm is \(\|X\|_\psi=\inf\{c>0:\mathbb E\psi(|X|/c)\le 1\}\), and \((L_\psi,\|\cdot\|_\psi)\) is a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Young function is positive and convex, vanishes at zero, and tends to infinity. Its Orlicz space consists of random variables satisfying the stated rescaled integrability condition. The Luxemburg formula defines a norm under which the space is complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\psi=\{X:\exists c>0,\ \mathbb E\psi(|X|/c)<\infty\},\qquad \|X\|_\psi=\inf\{c>0:\mathbb E\psi(|X|/c)\le1\},\quad (L_\psi,\|\cdot\|_\psi)\text{ is Banach}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex relaxation and dual representation of the submodular-support norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The penalty coefficients are written as 1/q and 1/r, resolving the extract's apparent OCR substitutions 1/g and 1/p; the displayed dual formula is otherwise preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F$ be nondecreasing and satisfy $F(\{k\})>0$ for every $k\in V$. The tightest convex, positively homogeneous lower bound of
\[
w\longmapsto \frac1q\lVert w\rVert_q^q+\frac1rF(\operatorname{Supp}(w))
\]
is a norm $\Omega_q$, whose dual norm satisfies, for every $s\in\mathbb R^p$,
\[
\Omega_q^*(s)=\sup_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq V}\frac{\lVert s_A\rVert_r}{F(A)^{1/r}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondecreasing set function that is positive on every singleton, the tightest convex homogeneous lower bound of the q-power penalty plus the support-set penalty is a norm. Its dual norm is the supremum, over all nonempty subsets, of the restricted r-norm divided by the corresponding set-function value to the power 1/r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega_q^*(s)=\sup_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq V}\frac{\lVert s_A\rVert_r}{F(A)^{1/r}}\quad\forall s\in\mathbb R^p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asphericity condition and coefficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed strict inequality for the coefficient is preserved; it excludes the boundary case \(\gamma_0=\gamma_1\), despite the preceding weak inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Positive scalars }\gamma_0\le\gamma_1\text{ satisfy the asphericity condition for }f\text{ relative to }\|\cdot\|\text{ if }B_{\|\cdot\|^*}(\gamma_0)\subseteq\partial f(0)\subseteq B_{\|\cdot\|^*}(\gamma_1),\quad B_{\|\cdot\|^*}(\gamma):=\{g\in\mathbb E^*:\|g\|^*\le\gamma\}.\text{ The asphericity coefficient is }\alpha:=\gamma_0/\gamma_1<1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function f and a chosen norm, positive radii gamma_0 at most gamma_1 satisfy the asphericity condition when the subdifferential of f at zero contains the dual-norm ball of radius gamma_0 and is contained in the dual-norm ball of radius gamma_1. The asphericity coefficient is gamma_0/gamma_1, stipulated to be less than one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty-function approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines separable convex residual-penalty fitting and identifies finite-p norm approximation as a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbf{R}^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbf{R}^m, r=Ax-b, and let \phi:\mathbf{R}\to\mathbf{R} be convex. The penalty-function approximation problem is \min_x\sum_{i=1}^m\phi(r_i), and it is a convex optimization problem. For 1\le p<\infty, minimizing \|r\|_p is equivalent to minimizing \sum_{i=1}^m|r_i|^p, corresponding to \phi(u)=|u|^p. Symmetry, nonnegativity, and \phi(0)=0 are common additional properties but are not required for the convexity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty-function approximation applies the same convex scalar penalty to every component of an affine residual and minimizes their sum, producing a convex problem. Finite-p norm fitting is the special case using the pth power of absolute value. Symmetry, nonnegativity, and zero penalty at zero are optional rather than assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m\phi((Ax-b)_i)\text{ is convex};\qquad 1\le p<\infty\implies \operatorname*{argmin}_x\|Ax-b\|_p=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\sum_{i=1}^m|(Ax-b)_i|^p.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness of the Half-Squared ℓp Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative smoothness of a canonical norm-generated convex function for finite p at least two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in[2,\infty)\) and define \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_p^2=\tfrac12\left(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p\right)^{2/p}\). Then \(f\) is \((p-1)\)-smooth with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_p\); in particular, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), \[f(y)\leq f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\frac{p-1}{2}\|x-y\|_p^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every finite p at least two, one half of the squared ℓp norm is (p−1)-smooth relative to the ℓp norm and satisfies the corresponding global quadratic upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is }(p-1)\text{-smooth with respect to }\|\cdot\|_p\), and \(\forall x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ f(y)\leq f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\tfrac{p-1}{2}\|x-y\|_p^2.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Characterization of the Euclidean Operator Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The induced norm of a real matrix when both its domain and codomain carry Euclidean norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), equip \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathbb R^m\) with Euclidean norms and define
\[
\|A\|_{1,2}:=\max_{x\ne0}\frac{\|Ax\|_2^*}{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}}=\max_{\|x\|_{\mathbb E_1}=1}\|Ax\|_2^*,
\]
where \(\|\cdot\|_2^*=\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb E_2}\). Then
\[
\|A\|_{1,2}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(A^TA)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real matrix acting between Euclidean spaces, the induced operator norm equals the square root of the largest eigenvalue of A transpose A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Positivity of a Norm-Augmented Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The subgradient bound is uniform over every point and every subgradient; L may equal zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq E be convex in a finite-dimensional normed space (E,\|\cdot\|), with dual norm \|\cdot\|_*. Let \phi:Q\to\mathbb{R} be convex. Suppose that some L\ge 0 satisfies \|g_x\|_*\le L for every x\in Q and every g_x\in\partial\phi(x). Then \[f(x):=\max\{\phi(x),L\|x\|\}\] is strictly positive on Q in the source's specified sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every subgradient of a convex function on Q has dual norm at most L, then the maximum of that function and L times the ambient norm is strictly positive on Q; the statement also permits L equal to zero.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is finite-dimensional and normed by }\|\cdot\|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x):=\max\{\phi(x),L\|x\|\}\text{ is strictly positive on }Q.
