knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational representation of the submodular-support norm expression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed starred notation $\Omega_q^*$ is preserved exactly from the extract, although its title refers to $\Omega_q$; this discrepancy requires span-level verification before canonical normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $F$ be a nondecreasing submodular function satisfying $F(\{k\})>0$ for every $k\in V$, and let $f$ denote the function appearing in the variational formulation. For every $w\in\mathbb R^p$,
\[
\Omega_q^*(w)=\inf_{\eta\ge 0}\left\{\frac1q\sum_{k\in V}\frac{|w_k|^q}{\eta_k^{q-1}}+\frac1r f(\eta)\right\}.
\]
Here $|w_k|^q/\eta_k^{q-1}$ is defined to be $0$ when $w_k=0$, and $+\infty$ when $w_k\ne0$ and $\eta_k=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondecreasing submodular function positive on every singleton, the extracted starred norm expression equals an infimum over nonnegative eta of a weighted coordinatewise q-power term plus one over r times f(eta). A zero numerator contributes zero, while a nonzero numerator with zero eta contributes positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, convex, absorbing, and contain \(0\). The Minkowski gauge of \(C\) is
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},
\qquad x\in X.
\]
The function \(\gamma_C:X\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is finite and sublinear; explicitly,
\[
\gamma_C(x+y)\leq\gamma_C(x)+\gamma_C(y)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gamma_C(\alpha x)=\alpha\gamma_C(x)
\]
for all \(x,y\in X\) and all \(\alpha\geq0\). Moreover,
\[
\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C
\subseteq\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}.
\]
If \(C\) is closed in the Hilbert-space topology, then
\[
C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski gauge of a convex absorbing set containing the origin is a finite sublinear function. Its open unit sublevel set lies in the original set, the original set lies in its closed unit sublevel set, and a closed original set equals that closed unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definiteness and Coercivity of Finite-Dimensional Gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex absorbing sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space; symmetry is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be closed, convex, absorbing, and contain \(0\). Then \[\gamma_C(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{rec}C.\] Hence \(\gamma_C\) is positive definite iff \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(C\) is bounded. In this case there are \(0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty\) with \[\alpha\|x\|_2\le\gamma_C(x)\le\beta\|x\|_2,\] so \(\gamma_C\) is coercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional gauge is positive definite and coercive exactly when its unit set is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive definiteness of \(\gamma_C\), boundedness of \(C\), and \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\) are equivalent and imply two-sided norm bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness and Coercivity of Finite-Dimensional Gauges

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge generated by a closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-generated gauges, their domains and canonical unit sublevel sets, the converse functional characterization, and the norm specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), define \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}\). Then \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\mathbb R_+C\), and \(\gamma_C\) is convex, nonnegative, and positively homogeneous. Conversely, every convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous function \(\gamma\) is the gauge of \(\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\). Moreover, \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=\operatorname{hull}(C\cup\{0\})\), the canonical closed convex generator containing the origin. A gauge is a norm exactly when it has full domain, vanishes only at zero, and is even; equivalently, its canonical unit set contains zero in its interior, is compact, and is centrally symmetric. General gauges may be asymmetric or extended-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex set is the least nonnegative scaling needed to contain a point. Its domain is the cone generated by the set, and it is convex, nonnegative, and positively homogeneous. These properties characterize gauges through their unit sublevel sets. Norms are the finite, definite, even gauges; general gauges may be asymmetric or infinite in some directions.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is closed and convex}
\gamma:\mathbb R^d\to[0,+\infty]\text{ is convex, nonnegative, and positively homogeneous for the converse}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\quad \operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\mathbb R_+C,\quad \{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=\operatorname{hull}(C\cup\{0\}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex distance-residual losses
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear; let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\); and let \(\rho:[0,+\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional family covers distances, norm residuals, and convex monotone penalties of such residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[L_{A,b,C,\rho}(x):=\rho\bigl(d_C(Ax-b)\bigr),\qquad d_C(y):=\inf_{c\in C}\|y-c\|.\] The metric residual loss family is the collection of all such \(L_{A,b,C,\rho}\). Every member is convex; it is finite whenever \(\rho\) is finite on \([0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric residual loss applies a convex nondecreasing scalar penalty to the Euclidean distance between an affine residual and a nonempty closed convex target set. This includes plain distance, norm residuals, and powers or robust convex penalties of distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak R:=\{x\mapsto\rho(d_C(Ax-b)):C\ne\varnothing\text{ closed convex},\ \rho\text{ proper lsc convex nondecreasing}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\rho(t)=t\), \[L_{A,b,C,\rho}(x)=d_C(Ax-b).\]
special_cases_latex: \(\rho(t)=t^2\) gives squared-distance residual loss.
\(A=I\), \(b=0\), and \(C\) a closed convex feasibility set gives the distance-to-feasibility loss.
A singleton target \(C=\{c\}\) gives \(\rho(\|Ax-b-c\|)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The zero set of the unpenalized distance residual is \(\{x:Ax-b\in C\}\).
If \(C\) is nonempty closed convex, the projection defining the nearest point is single-valued.
boundary_notes: Distance to a nonconvex set need not be convex and may have multiple nearest points.
If \(\rho\) is convex but decreasing on part of its domain, the composition need not be convex.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance to the target set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metrics and Minkowski Metrics on \(\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an arbitrary metric, gives the discrete metric as a non-algebraic example, and adds the two compatibility axioms defining a Minkowski metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\rho:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a metric if, for all \(x,y,z\in\mathbb R^n\), (i) \(\rho(x,y)>0\) when \(x\ne y\) and \(\rho(x,x)=0\); (ii) \(\rho(x,y)=\rho(y,x)\); and (iii) \(\rho(x,z)\le \rho(x,y)+\rho(y,z)\). The discrete function \(\rho(x,y)=0\) for \(x=y\) and \(\rho(x,y)=1\) otherwise is a metric. A metric is a Minkowski metric if additionally \(\rho(x+z,y+z)=\rho(x,y)\) for all \(x,y,z\) and \(\rho\bigl(x,(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y\bigr)=\lambda\rho(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric is a positive-definite, symmetric distance satisfying the triangle inequality. The discrete metric shows that a metric need not respect vector-space operations. A Minkowski metric additionally is translation invariant and scales linearly along every line segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\text{ is a metric under (i)--(iii), and is a Minkowski metric when the translation and line-segment axioms also hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of Convex-Set Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance to a nonempty closed convex set in a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). Then \[\partial d_C(x)=\begin{cases}\left\{\dfrac{x-P_Cx}{\|x-P_Cx\|}\right\},&x\notin C,\\N_C(x)\cap\{u:\|u\|\le1\},&x\in C.\end{cases}\] In particular, \(d_C\) is Fréchet differentiable on \(H\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the set, distance has the normalized projection residual as its gradient; on the set its subgradients are unit normal vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inside/outside formula holds for \(\partial d_C(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal-Convolution Representation of Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance to an arbitrary nonempty subset of a normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a nonempty subset of a normed space \(X\), let \(\delta_A\) be its indicator, and let \(q(x)=\|x\|\). Then
\[
d_A(x)=(\delta_A\mathbin{\square}q)(x)=\inf_{z\in X}\{\delta_A(z)+\|x-z\|\}=\inf_{a\in A}\|x-a\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a set is the infimal convolution of its indicator with the norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_A=\delta_A\mathbin{\square}\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution Representation of Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Offset-Set Representation of Distance Sublevels

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(B=\{u\in H:\|u\|\leq1\}\). For every \(r\geq0\),
\[
\{x\in H:d_C(x)\leq r\}=C+rB.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative sublevel set of distance to a closed convex set is its closed metric offset.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:d_C(x)\leq r\}=C+rB\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Characterization of the Metric Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-point certificate for a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\). For \(x\in H\) and \(p\in C\),
\[
p=P_Cx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle x-p,c-p\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }c\in C.
\]
Equivalently, \(x-p\in N_C(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is the projection of x exactly when its residual is normal to the set there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=P_Cx\) if and only if \(\langle x-p,c-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(c\in C\).

convex normal cone to C at p

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The distance-to-set function is
\[
d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\|x-P_Cx\|,
\]
where the projection \(P_Cx\) exists uniquely. It satisfies \(d_C(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in C\), and
\[
|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\leq \|x-y\|
\]
for all \(x,y\in H\). Convexity of \(C\) implies convexity of \(d_C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A residual loss generated by \(\phi\) is the extended-real-valued function
\[
L(x)=\phi(r(x))=\phi(Ax-b).
\]
It is convex and satisfies
\[
L(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq \lambda L(x)+(1-\lambda)L(y)
\]
for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). If \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), and each \(\phi_i:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex, then \(x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)\) is a separable residual loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a convex penalty to an affine residual produces a convex loss, including sums of scalar convex residual penalties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Loss Subgradient Chain Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine-composition rule under a continuity qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x)=\phi(Ax-b)\), where \(\phi\) is proper convex and continuous at \(Ax-b\). Then \[\partial L(x)=A^{\mathsf T}\partial\phi(Ax-b).\] Consequently, \(x\) minimizes \(L\) iff some \(u\in\partial\phi(Ax-b)\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}u=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualified residual-loss subgradients are pullbacks of penalty subgradients, yielding exact stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
\(\phi\) is proper convex and continuous at \(Ax-b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\phi\circ(A\cdot-b))(x)=A^{\mathsf T}\partial\phi(Ax-b)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-Squares Residual Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical smooth quadratic member of the residual-loss family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x)=\tfrac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2\), \[\nabla L(x)=A^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b),\qquad \nabla^2L(x)=A^{\mathsf T}A.\] Its minimizers solve \(A^{\mathsf T}Ax=A^{\mathsf T}b\), and it is strictly convex exactly when \(A\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least squares has gradient, Hessian, normal equations, and strict-convexity boundary determined by A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}L=\{x:A^{\mathsf T}Ax=A^{\mathsf T}b\}\), and strict convexity holds iff \(\ker A=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Residual Loss

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Huber loss is defined for \(t\in\mathbb R\) by
\[
h_\delta(t)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12t^2,&|t|\leq\delta,\\
\delta|t|-\tfrac12\delta^2,&|t|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
It is convex and continuously differentiable, with
\[
h_\delta'(t)=
\begin{cases}
t,&|t|\leq\delta,\\
\delta\operatorname{sign}(t),&|t|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
The loss is quadratic near zero, linear in the tails, and has slope bounded in magnitude by \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Huber loss joins a quadratic center to linear tails and is convex, continuously differentiable, and bounded in slope.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Convex Losses

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Losses Cannot Redescend Nontrivially
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between convex bounded-influence and nonconvex redescending losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\rho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex and \[\lim_{t\to-\infty}\rho'(t)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\rho'(t)=0,\] then \(\rho\) is constant. Thus a nonconstant differentiable convex loss cannot have influence that redescends to zero in both tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant differentiable convex loss cannot have a score returning to zero in both tails.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two-sided redescending derivative implies that \(\rho\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Losses Cannot Redescend Nontrivially

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Influence and Lipschitz Convex Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite scalar convex losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite convex \(\rho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(M\ge0\), the following are equivalent: \[|\rho(s)-\rho(t)|\le M|s-t|\quad(s,t\in\mathbb R),\] and \[\partial\rho(t)\subseteq[-M,M]\quad(t\in\mathbb R).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite scalar convex loss has uniformly bounded subgradients exactly when it is globally Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is finite and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz iff every subgradient has magnitude at most \(M\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Influence and Lipschitz Convex Losses

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Huber Loss as a Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representation of the seeded Huber loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta>0\), \[h_\delta(t)=\min_{u\in\mathbb R}\left\{\delta|u|+\tfrac12(t-u)^2\right\}.\] The unique minimizer is \(u_\star=\operatorname{sign}(t)(|t|-\delta)_+\), and \(h_\delta'(t)=t-u_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber loss is the Moreau envelope of scaled absolute value, with soft thresholding as auxiliary minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_\delta(t)=\min_u\{\delta|u|+\tfrac12(t-u)^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Huber Loss as a Moreau Envelope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral convex functions with finitely many affine pieces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set, and let \(\ell_i(x)=a_i^\top x+b_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), be finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the proper finite-dimensional polyhedral convex family. It includes extended-valued domain restrictions through a polyhedral indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(x):=\max_{1\le i\le p}\ell_i(x)+\iota_D(x)=\begin{cases}\max_i(a_i^\top x+b_i),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] The finite-piece epigraph family consists exactly of proper convex piecewise-linear functions, equivalently proper functions whose epigraphs are polyhedral convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-piece epigraph function is the maximum of finitely many affine functions on a polyhedral effective domain and is positive infinity outside that domain. These functions are exactly the proper convex piecewise-linear functions and exactly the proper functions with polyhedral epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is proper, convex, and piecewise linear}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is polyhedral}\Longleftrightarrow f=\max_{1\le i\le p}\ell_i+\iota_D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):x\in D,\ r\ge a_i^\top x+b_i\ \forall i\}.\]
A finite half-space description of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) separates into vertical inequalities defining \(D\) and nonvertical inequalities defining the affine pieces.
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb R^n\), then \(f\) is a finite maximum of affine functions.
If \(p=1\), the function is affine on \(D\) and infinite outside.
The absolute value \(|t|=\max\{t,-t\}\) is a scalar member.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite maxima of members remain polyhedral convex.
The conjugate of a proper polyhedral convex function is polyhedral convex.
boundary_notes: A general piecewise-quadratic function is not part of this finite affine-piece family.
An infinite supremum of affine functions can be closed and convex without having a polyhedral epigraph.

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of the polyhedral domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A max-affine function has the representation
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\}.
\]
It is convex and finite everywhere, and its epigraph is the polyhedron
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):t\geq a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\ \text{for every }i\}.
\]
With \(I(x)=\{i:f(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\}\), its subdifferential is \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A max-affine function is the maximum of finitely many affine functions; its epigraph is polyhedral and its active slopes determine its subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Max-Affine Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative and Differentiability of a Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local geometry of an everywhere-finite maximum of finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)\) and \(I(x)=\{i:f(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\}\). For every direction \(d\), \[f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}a_i^{\mathsf T}d.\] Moreover, \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if and only if all active slopes coincide; then \(\nabla f(x)\) is their common value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the maximum of the active slopes applied to the direction, and differentiability occurs exactly when all active slopes agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}a_i^{\mathsf T}d\), and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\iff a_i=a_j\) for all \(i,j\in I(x)\).

notation.meaning: one-sided directional derivative of f at x along d

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Derivative and Differentiability of a Max-Affine Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Lipschitz Bound for Max-Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean Lipschitz regularity determined by the finitely many component slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_i(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)\), \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n),\quad L=\max_i\|a_i\|.\] Thus every finite max-affine function is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite max-affine function is globally Lipschitz, with the largest component-slope norm as a valid constant.
assumptions_latex: The domain carries the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le(\max_i\|a_i\|)\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz Bound for Max-Affine Functions

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex piecewise-linear exactly when it is a finite maximum of linear forms.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex piecewise-linear if there exist \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}a_i^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
Equivalently, \(f\) is finite, convex, polyhedral, and positively homogeneous. Its domains of linearity are the polyhedral cones on which a fixed subset of the linear forms is active, and its epigraph is a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex piecewise-linear function is a maximum of finitely many linear forms and is therefore polyhedral and positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Convex Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Slope Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima of linear forms under this leaf's homogeneous convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_i a_i^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=f(x)\}\), \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.\] Hence \(x\) minimizes \(f\) iff \(0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\), and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) iff all active slopes coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential is the convex hull of active slopes, giving exact optimality and differentiability tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Slope Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper piecewise-linear convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\ge1\). Extended-real values encode the domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the definition permits a polyhedral effective domain and finitely many affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise-linear convex, equivalently polyhedral convex, when
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
Thus its finite-valued restriction is the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine functions on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real function on Euclidean space is piecewise-linear convex when its domain is a nonempty polyhedron and, on that domain, it is the maximum of finitely many affine functions; it equals positive infinity outside the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\max_i(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i)+\delta_C(x),\qquad C\text{ polyhedral}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is piecewise-linear convex if and only if its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):r\ge f(x)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set containing no vertical line.
The representation may be written as \(f=h+\delta_C\), where \(h=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}\cdot+\beta_i)\) and \(\delta_C\) is the convex indicator of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(f\) is finite everywhere and is exactly a finite maximum of affine functions.
The functions \(x\mapsto\|x\|_1\) and \(x\mapsto\|x\|_\infty\) are finite-valued piecewise-linear convex functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper piecewise-linear convex function is closed and convex.
Each sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is polyhedral.
boundary_notes: This finite-piece definition is specific to finite-dimensional spaces.
A general continuous piecewise-linear function need not be convex; convexity is encoded here by the finite-maximum representation.
The term does not include piecewise linear–quadratic functions unless their quadratic terms vanish.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator: zero on C and positive infinity outside C.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex piecewise linear–quadratic when \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\), the domain is polyhedral, and
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\quad\text{for }x\in P_i,

with coincident formulas on overlaps, while \(f(x)=+\infty\) outside its domain. The assembled extended-real function must be convex; in particular, each quadratic restriction is convex along its region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel-conjugacy closure for proper lower-semicontinuous convex piecewise linear–quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and piecewise linear–quadratic, then its Fenchel conjugate \(f^*\) has the same properties and is piecewise linear–quadratic. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise-Affine Proximal Map and PLQ Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PLQ-specific regularization structure for a proper closed convex PLQ function in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and PLQ, and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}\] is single-valued, nonexpansive, and piecewise affine. The Moreau envelope \[e_\lambda f(x)=\min_y\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}\] is finite, continuously differentiable, and PLQ, with \[\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex PLQ function has a piecewise-affine proximal mapping and a continuously differentiable PLQ Moreau envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and PLQ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is nonexpansive and piecewise affine, while \(e_\lambda f\) is continuously differentiable PLQ with \(\nabla e_\lambda f=\lambda^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Proximal Map and PLQ Moreau Envelope

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise linear–quadratic if and only if its subdifferential is piecewise polyhedral, meaning that \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,v):v\in\partial f(x)\}\] is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function is PLQ exactly when its subdifferential graph is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is PLQ}\iff\operatorname{gph}\partial f\text{ is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Characterization of Convex PLQ Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph structure of the convex subdifferential for finite-dimensional PLQ functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential graph of a closed convex PLQ function is a finite union of polyhedral convex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and PLQ.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Plus-composite-affine and squared plus-composite-affine functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary convex piecewise-linear and piecewise-quadratic functions used in PLQ representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A plus-composite-affine function has the form \(p(x)=\max\{a^\top x+\alpha,0\}\), where \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). Such functions are convex but are not closed under subtraction. If \(\mathcal F\) consists of squares of affine functions and squares of plus-composite-affine functions, then every \(g\in\mathcal F\) is nonnegative, convex, and differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A plus-composite-affine function is the positive part of an affine function, also called a ReLU. These functions are convex but are not closed under subtraction. Squares of affine functions and squares of such ReLU functions are nonnegative, convex, and differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(x)=\max\{a^\top x+\alpha,0\},\qquad g\in\mathcal F\Longrightarrow g(x)\geq0\text{ and }g\text{ is convex and differentiable}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a Finite Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded representation for the convex piecewise-linear subclass of piecewise linear–quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge 1\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and define
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{a_i^Tx+b_i\},\qquad I(x)=\{i:f(x)=a_i^Tx+b_i\}.
\]
Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}
=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex piecewise-linear function expressed as the maximum of finitely many affine functions, the subdifferential at any point is the convex hull of the slopes of the active affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Temperature-scaled entropy and log-partition pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\ge1\), \(\Delta_n=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i p_i=1\}\), and \(\tau>0\). Adopt \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar-valued entropic family on the probability simplex and its full-domain Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-domain entropic pair at temperature \(\tau\) consists of the extended negative entropy
\[H_\tau(p)=\begin{cases}\tau\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\log p_i,&p\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&p\notin\Delta_n,\end{cases}\]
and its log-partition conjugate
\[L_\tau(y)=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{y_i/\tau}\right),\qquad y\in\mathbb R^n.\]
The family is \(\mathcal E_n=\{(H_\tau,L_\tau):\tau>0\}\), with \(L_\tau=H_\tau^*\) and \(H_\tau=L_\tau^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each positive temperature, the log-domain entropic family pairs negative Shannon entropy on the probability simplex with the temperature-scaled log-sum-exp function on all of Euclidean space. The two functions are Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E_n=\{(H_\tau,L_\tau):\tau>0,\ L_\tau=H_\tau^*,\ H_\tau=L_\tau^*\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L_\tau(y)=\sup_{p\in\Delta_n}\left\{\langle p,y\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\]
The gradient coordinates are the Gibbs probabilities \(\nabla_iL_\tau(y)=e^{y_i/\tau}/\sum_j e^{y_j/\tau}\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\tau=1\), \(L_1(y)=\log\sum_i e^{y_i}\) and \(H_1(p)=\sum_i p_i\log p_i+\delta_{\Delta_n}(p)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(H_\tau\) and \(L_\tau\) are proper closed convex functions.
Translation along the all-ones direction satisfies \(L_\tau(y+c\mathbf1)=L_\tau(y)+c\).

The sign convention is negative entropy, which is convex; Shannon entropy itself is its negative and is concave.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-sum-exp soft maximum of affine scores
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m\ge1\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(\tau>0\). Define affine scores \(s_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth convex aggregation of affine functions on Euclidean space, with positive smoothing temperature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exponential soft-max aggregation generated by \((s_i)_{i=1}^m\) at temperature \(\tau\) is
\[\operatorname{smax}_\tau(s_1(x),\ldots,s_m(x))=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{s_i(x)/\tau}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
Its normalized exponential weights are
\[w_i(x)=\frac{e^{s_i(x)/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^m e^{s_j(x)/\tau}},\qquad w(x)\in\Delta_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given finitely many affine scores and a positive temperature, their exponential soft maximum is the temperature times the logarithm of the sum of their exponentials after temperature scaling. Its associated weights are the normalized exponentials of those scores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_\tau(x)=\tau\log\sum_{i=1}^m\exp\!\left((a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)/\tau\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F_\tau(x)=\sup_{p\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_i p_i s_i(x)-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\]
\[\nabla F_\tau(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i(x)a_i.\]
special_cases_latex: For coordinate scores \(s_i(x)=x_i\), this becomes \(\tau\log\sum_i e^{x_i/\tau}\).
For \(m=1\), the aggregation equals the sole affine score.
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\max_i s_i(x)\le F_\tau(x)\le\max_i s_i(x)+\tau\log m.\]
\(F_\tau\) is finite, smooth, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: The parameter must satisfy \(\tau>0\); the hard maximum is obtained only as the limiting case \(\tau\downarrow0\).
Replacing affine scores by arbitrary functions preserves convexity only under additional hypotheses, such as convexity of every score.

notation.meaning: Normalized exponential weight of score i.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(x)=\exp(a^{\mathsf T}x+b)\). The function is positive and smooth on \(\mathbb R^n\), with
\[
\nabla f(x)=f(x)a,
\qquad
\nabla^2f(x)=f(x)aa^{\mathsf T}\succeq0.
\]
It is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(x,d\in\mathbb R^n\), the restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+td)\) is strictly convex when \(a^{\mathsf T}d\neq0\) and constant when \(a^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential of an affine form is smooth and convex; along a line it is strictly convex unless the direction is orthogonal to the affine slope, in which case it is constant.

children.title: Log-Sum-Exp Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Smooth logarithmic aggregation of exponential terms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The temperature-scaled log-sum-exp is a smooth convex approximation of \(\max_i z_i\) with additive error at most \(\tau\log m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional temperature-scaled log-sum-exp aggregation.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-sum-exp aggregator is
\[
L_\tau(z)=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{z_i/\tau}\right).
\]
It is finite, smooth, and convex on \(\mathbb R^m\). For \(M=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i\),
\[
M\leq L_\tau(z)\leq M+\tau\log m.
\]
Consequently, \(L_\tau(z)\to\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\), with an error bound uniform over \(z\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temperature-scaled log-sum-exp smoothly approximates the maximum, with error between zero and temperature times the logarithm of the number of terms.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum-Exp Aggregation

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shift-Stable Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact normalization for evaluating finite log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M=\max_i z_i\), \[L_\tau(z)=M+\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{(z_i-M)/\tau}\right).\] Every normalized exponent is nonpositive and at least one is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the largest coordinate gives an exact overflow-resistant evaluation of log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\tau(z)=M+\tau\log\sum_i e^{(z_i-M)/\tau}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Shift-Stable Evaluation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropic Variational Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temperature-scaled log-sum-exp over the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\Delta_m=\{p\geq0:\sum_i p_i=1\}\) and \(0\log0=0\), \[L_\tau(z)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\left\{\langle p,z\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\] The unique maximizer is \(p_i=e^{z_i/\tau}/\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}\); equivalently, \(L_\tau=(\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i+\delta_{\Delta_m})^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is the conjugate of scaled negative entropy on the simplex, with soft-max as its unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\tau(z)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\{\langle p,z\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Variational Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Log-Sum-Exp Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative weighted finite log-sum-exp aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(w_i\geq0\) and not all \(w_i\) vanish, then \[\tau\log\sum_i w_i e^{z_i/\tau}=\tau\log\sum_{i:w_i>0}\exp\!\left(\frac{z_i+\tau\log w_i}{\tau}\right).\] Thus positive weights are affine coordinate offsets, while zero weights delete terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted log-sum-exp reduces to ordinary log-sum-exp after offsetting coordinates by temperature times log weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted log-sum-exp is ordinary log-sum-exp over the positive-weight indices after the offsets \(z_i\mapsto z_i+\tau\log w_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Log-Sum-Exp Reduction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Sum-Exp–Simplex Entropy Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugate of log-sum-exp, including its simplex effective domain and boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(g(x)=\log(\sum_{j=1}^n e^{x_j})\), and let \(\Delta_n=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n y_i=1\}\). With \(0\log0=0\), for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[g^*(y)=\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\log y_i,&y\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&y\notin\Delta_n.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of log-sum-exp is negative entropy on the probability simplex, using the standard boundary convention, and is infinite outside the simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^*(y)=\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\log y_i,&y\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&y\notin\Delta_n.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The soft-max vector is the gradient of log-sum-exp, and its covariance-form Jacobian is positive semidefinite with nullspace containing \(\mathbf1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L_\tau(z)=\tau\log\bigl(\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}\bigr)\), define
\[
p_i(z)=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}.
\]
Then \(p(z)\) lies in the relative interior of the probability simplex and
\[
\nabla L_\tau(z)=p(z),
\qquad
\nabla^2L_\tau(z)=\tau^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\succeq0.
\]
Moreover, \(p(z+c\mathbf1)=p(z)\), and the Hessian annihilates \(\mathbf1\), expressing translation invariance along the all-ones direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft-max is the simplex-valued gradient of log-sum-exp; its Hessian is a scaled categorical covariance and ignores common shifts of all coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Euclidean Curvature Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean smoothness of temperature-scaled log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\), \[0\preceq\nabla^2L_\tau(z)\preceq\frac1{2\tau}I.\] Hence soft-max is globally \(1/(2\tau)\)-Lipschitz in Euclidean norm. For \(m\geq2\), the constant is the sharp supremum, approached when probability is split equally between two coordinates and tends to zero on the others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The soft-max Jacobian has operator norm at most one over twice the temperature, and the bound is globally sharp.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Soft-Max Quotient Parametrization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soft-max coordinates on the relative interior of the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Soft-max is constant exactly on cosets \(z+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\) and induces a bijection \[\mathbb R^m/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\longrightarrow\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m.\] For \(p\in\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\), all representing logits satisfy \(z_i=\tau\log p_i+c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modulo a common shift, logits correspond bijectively to strictly positive probability vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Soft-max induces a bijection from \(\mathbb R^m/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\) onto \(\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-Temperature Concentration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration of soft-max around a unique maximizing coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(i_*\) uniquely maximizes \(z_i\), and let \(\delta=z_{i_*}-\max_{j\ne i_*}z_j>0\). Then
\[
1-p_{i_*}(z)\leq (m-1)e^{-\delta/\tau}.
\]
Consequently \(p(z)\to e_{i_*}\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\), at an exponential rate controlled by the logit gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a unique largest logit, soft-max concentrates exponentially fast on its index as temperature decreases.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq2\), \(\tau>0\), and \(z\) has a unique maximizing coordinate with gap \(\delta>0\).

notation.meaning: gap between the largest and second-largest coordinates

children.title: Logarithmic Barrier Atom Family
children.top_down_role: Boundary-divergent convex functions on positive and matrix domains.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar and positive-definite logarithmic barrier atoms
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\ge1\). Write \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) for the positive orthant and \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) for the cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar and spectral barrier atoms with extended-real domain enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The logarithmic barrier atom family contains the scalar atom
\[\ell(t)=\begin{cases}-\log t,&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\le0,\end{cases}\]
its positive-orthant sum \(B_+(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\) for \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and the matrix atom
\[B_{\det}(X)=\begin{cases}-\log\det X,&X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\\+\infty,&X\notin\mathbb S_{++}^n.\end{cases}\]
Both extended-real barriers diverge when an interior sequence approaches the corresponding domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic logarithmic barrier is negative logarithm on the positive ray and positive infinity elsewhere. Summing this atom gives the positive-orthant barrier, while applying it spectrally gives negative log determinant on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_+(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i,\qquad B_{\det}(X)=-\log\det X=-\sum_i\log\lambda_i(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(B_{\det}(X)=B_+(\lambda(X))\).
For positive affine slacks \(s_i(x)>0\), a weighted scalar barrier has the form \(-\sum_i\mu_i\log s_i(x)\) with \(\mu_i>0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the matrix and scalar atoms coincide.
For a diagonal positive-definite matrix \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(-\log\det X=-\sum_i\log x_i\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The scalar, orthant, and log-determinant atoms are proper closed convex functions.
If \(x^k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) approaches a point with a zero coordinate, then \(B_+(x^k)\to+\infty\); analogously, \(\lambda_{\min}(X^k)\downarrow0\) implies \(B_{\det}(X^k)\to+\infty\).
boundary_notes: The atom is finite only in the strict interior of its positive domain.
General self-concordant barriers are a larger class and need not be logarithmic sums or log determinants.

notation.meaning: Cone of symmetric positive-definite n by n matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The scalar negative-log atom is the extended-real function
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
-\log x,&x>0,\\
+\infty,&x\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
On \((0,+\infty)\), it is smooth and strictly convex, with
\[
f'(x)=-x^{-1},
\qquad
f''(x)=x^{-2}>0.
\]
It satisfies \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-real negative logarithm is smooth and strictly convex on the positive half-line and diverges to positive infinity at zero.

children.title: Log-Determinant Barrier Atoms
children.top_down_role: Barrier atoms on positive-definite matrix domains.

assumptions_latex: \(n\geq1\), and \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) is the cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The atom \(F(X)=-\log\det X\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and diverges to \(+\infty\) as \(X\) approaches a singular positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-determinant barrier on the symmetric positive-definite cone.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-determinant barrier atom is
\[
F(X)=
\begin{cases}
-\log\det X,&X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\\
+\infty,&X\notin\mathbb S_{++}^n.
\end{cases}
\]
For every \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and symmetric \(H\), its first and second directional derivatives are
\[
DF(X)[H]=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}H),
\qquad
D^2F(X)[H,H]=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}HX^{-1}H).
\]
The second derivative is positive for every nonzero symmetric \(H\), so \(F\) is strictly convex. Moreover, \(F(X_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(X_k\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) converges to a singular matrix in \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log-determinant is strictly convex on the positive-definite cone and diverges as a positive-definite matrix converges to a singular positive-semidefinite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Barrier Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Conjugate of Negative Log-Determinant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-inner-product conjugate on real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), \[F^*(Y)=\begin{cases}-n-\log\det(-Y),&Y\in\mathbb S_{--}^n,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] For \(Y\prec0\), the unique maximizing matrix is \(X=-Y^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate is a shifted negative log-determinant on the negative-definite cone, with optimizer given by inversion.
assumptions_latex: The trace inner product is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*(Y)=-n-\log\det(-Y)\) for \(Y\prec0\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Conjugate of Negative Log-Determinant

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Congruence and Logarithmic Homogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation laws for negative log-determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\succ0\), invertible \(A\), and \(t>0\), \[F(AXA^{\mathsf T})=F(X)-2\log|\det A|,\qquad F(tX)=F(X)-n\log t.\] Thus orthogonal conjugation leaves \(F\) invariant and \(F\) is logarithmically homogeneous with parameter \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log-determinant is orthogonally invariant and logarithmically homogeneous, with an exact congruence transformation law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(AXA^{\mathsf T})=F(X)-2\log|\det A|\) and \(F(tX)=F(X)-n\log t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Congruence and Logarithmic Homogeneity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Calculus of the Log-Determinant Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records convexity and the first three differential formulas for the negative log-determinant on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F:\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{S}_+^n)\to\mathbb{R}$ be $F(X)=-\ln\det X$. Then $F$ is convex and continuously differentiable, $\nabla F(X)=-X^{-1}$, and for every $X\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{S}_+^n)$ and $\Delta\in\mathbb{S}^n$, $\langle\nabla^2F(X)\Delta,\Delta\rangle_F=\|X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}\|_F^2=\langle X^{-1}\Delta X^{-1},\Delta\rangle_F=\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^2)$ and $D^3F(X)[\Delta,\Delta,\Delta]=-2\langle I_n,[X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3\rangle_F=-2\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative log-determinant is convex on the positive-definite cone, has gradient minus the matrix inverse, has a Hessian quadratic form equal to the squared Frobenius norm of the symmetrically scaled direction, and has the stated cubic trace formula for its third directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is convex and continuously differentiable},\quad \nabla F(X)=-X^{-1},\quad \langle\nabla^2F(X)\Delta,\Delta\rangle_F=\|X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}\|_F^2=\langle X^{-1}\Delta X^{-1},\Delta\rangle_F=\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^2),\quad D^3F(X)[\Delta,\Delta,\Delta]=-2\langle I_n,[X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3\rangle_F=-2\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\) has domain-boundary blowup if, for every sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\subset C\) converging to a boundary point \(\bar x\in\partial C\), one has \[\lim_{k\to\infty}F(x_k)=+\infty.\] Equivalently, the extension \(\bar F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), defined by \(\bar F=F\) on \(C\) and \(\bar F=+\infty\) outside \(C\), cannot be approached with bounded values from within \(C\) at any finite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex barrier blows up at its domain boundary when every interior sequence approaching any boundary point has function values tending to positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite boundary divergence versus escape along unbounded sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Boundary blowup controls approaches to finite points of \(\partial C\), not escape to infinity. For \(F(x)=-\log x\) on \(C=(0,+\infty)\), \(F(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\), whereas \(F(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary divergence does not imply coercivity or boundedness below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Domain-boundary blowup does not imply coercivity or a finite lower bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Csiszár and Kullback–Leibler entropic divergences
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(N\ge1\), \(x=(x_i)\), \(y=(y_i)\in\mathbb R^N\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex with an effective domain containing \(\mathbb R_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional positive-vector divergences; the primary definition uses a strictly positive reference vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Csiszár entropic divergence generated by \(\phi\) is
\[D_\phi(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\phi(x_i/y_i),&y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N,\\+\infty,&y\notin\mathbb R_{++}^N.\end{cases}\]
For \(\phi(t)=t\log t\) on \(t>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, this becomes the Kullback–Leibler divergence
\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\]
when \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entropic divergence is obtained by summing the perspective terms of a convex scalar generator. Choosing the generator t log t yields the Kullback–Leibler divergence between strictly positive vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_\phi(x,y)=\sum_i y_i\phi(x_i/y_i),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(x,y\in\Delta_N\cap\mathbb R_{++}^N\), then \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\) is the Bregman divergence of \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\).
Each summand \(y_i\phi(x_i/y_i)\) is the perspective of \(\phi\).
special_cases_latex: For \(x=y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|x)=0\).
On the probability simplex, the definition is the usual discrete relative entropy.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(D_\phi\) is jointly convex in \((x,y)\) under the stated perspective convention.
For positive probability vectors, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\ge0\).
boundary_notes: The displayed source convention assigns positive infinity unless both arguments of the KL specialization are strictly positive.
The divergence is generally asymmetric: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y\|x)\).
This is not a metric and does not generally satisfy the triangle inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropy function and asymptotic slope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropy generators for φ-divergences, including the superlinear-growth boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is an entropy function if it is lower semicontinuous and convex, \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\subseteq[0,+\infty)\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\cap(0,+\infty)\neq\varnothing\). Its asymptotic slope is \(\varphi'_{\infty}=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\varphi(x)/x\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). If \(\varphi'_{\infty}=+\infty\), then \(\varphi\) is called superlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entropy function is a lower-semicontinuous convex extended-real function whose domain lies in the nonnegative half-line and contains a positive point. Its asymptotic slope is the limit of φ(x)/x at positive infinity; it is called superlinear when this slope is infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi\text{ is an entropy function}\iff \varphi\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex},\ \operatorname{dom}\varphi\subseteq[0,+\infty),\ \operatorname{dom}\varphi\cap(0,+\infty)\neq\varnothing;\quad \varphi'_{\infty}=+\infty\Rightarrow\varphi\text{ is superlinear}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: φ-divergence of measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the singular component, the infinite-value boundary, the superlinear case, and the common-support discrete formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi\) be an entropy function and write the Lebesgue decomposition of \(\alpha\) relative to \(\beta\) as \(\alpha=(d\alpha/d\beta)\beta+\alpha^\perp\). Define
\[
\mathcal D_\varphi(\alpha\mid\beta)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal X}\varphi\!\left(\frac{d\alpha}{d\beta}\right)d\beta+\varphi'_\infty\alpha^\perp(\mathcal X),&\alpha,\beta\geq0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
If \(\varphi'_\infty=+\infty\), then \(\mathcal D_\varphi(\alpha\mid\beta)=+\infty\) whenever \(\alpha\not\ll\beta\). For \(\alpha=\sum_i a_i\delta_{x_i}\) and \(\beta=\sum_i b_i\delta_{x_i}\) on the same \(n\) points,
\[
\mathbf D_\varphi(\mathbf a\mid\mathbf b)=\sum_{i:b_i\ne0}b_i\varphi(a_i/b_i)+\varphi'_\infty\sum_{i:b_i=0}a_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The φ-divergence integrates the entropy generator against the absolutely continuous density and charges singular mass at the generator's asymptotic slope; it is infinite for non-nonnegative inputs. For a superlinear generator it is infinite unless α is absolutely continuous with respect to β. On a common finite support, it is the weighted coordinate sum plus the corresponding zero-denominator mass term.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal M(\mathcal X)\) and \(\alpha=(d\alpha/d\beta)\beta+\alpha^\perp\) is the Lebesgue decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D_\varphi(\alpha\mid\beta)=\int\varphi(d\alpha/d\beta)\,d\beta+\varphi'_\infty\alpha^\perp(\mathcal X)\) for nonnegative \(\alpha,\beta\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise, with the stated discrete specialization.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the extended scalar negative-entropy atom by \[h(t)=\begin{cases}t\log t,&t>0,\\0,&t=0,\\+\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\] The separable negative-entropy function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \[H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n h(x_i).\] Its effective domain is \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\); on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), it equals \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\). The boundary value uses the continuous convention \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is the separable convex function summing each coordinate times its logarithm, continuously extended by zero at zero and by infinity on negative coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Finite Subgradient at a Zero Coordinate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order boundary singularity of the lower-semicontinuous entropy extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed entropy atom \(h(t)=t\log t\) for \(t>0\), \(h(0)=0\), and \(h(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\), one has \(\partial h(0)=\varnothing\). Consequently, if \(H(x)=\sum_i h(x_i)\), then \(\partial H(x)=\varnothing\) whenever some \(x_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is finite at zero, but its slope tends to negative infinity, so no finite subgradient exists at a zero coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is the lower-semicontinuous extension of \(t\log t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial h(0)=\varnothing,\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\mathbb R_{++}^n\Longrightarrow\partial H(x)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: No Finite Subgradient at a Zero Coordinate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Differential Geometry of Negative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient, Hessian, and strict convexity of separable negative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[\nabla H(x)_i=1+\log x_i,\qquad \nabla^2H(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(x_1^{-1},\ldots,x_n^{-1})\succ0.\] The closed extended function is strictly convex on \(\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy has logarithmic gradient, positive diagonal Hessian, and is strictly convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla H(x)=\mathbf1+\log x,\qquad \nabla^2H(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(1/x_i)\succ0.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Differential Geometry of Negative Entropy

children.title: Relative-Entropy Functions
children.top_down_role: Convex divergence-like functions comparing positive arguments.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n d(x_i,y_i)\) is a jointly convex, nonnegative extended-real function, and \(D(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\) on its finite domain.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), define \[d(a,b)=\begin{cases}a\log(a/b)-a+b,&a>0,\ b>0,\\b,&a=0,\ b\geq0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] For \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the generalized relative-entropy function is \[D(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n d(x_i,y_i).\] It is the lower-semicontinuous perspective extension of negative entropy, is jointly convex, and satisfies \(D(x,y)\geq0\), with equality precisely when \(x=y\) wherever it is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized relative entropy sums scalar perspective terms, includes their lower-semicontinuous boundary values, and is jointly convex and nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Derivatives of Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order structure on strictly positive arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[\nabla_xD(x,y)_i=\log\frac{x_i}{y_i},\qquad \nabla_yD(x,y)_i=1-\frac{x_i}{y_i}.\] The Hessian is block diagonal by coordinates, with blocks \[\begin{pmatrix}1/x_i&-1/y_i\\-1/y_i&x_i/y_i^2\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\] whose null direction is \((x_i,y_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative entropy has explicit interior gradients and positive-semidefinite rank-one coordinate Hessian blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
abla_xD=\log(x/y),\qquad
abla_yD=\mathbf1-x/y,\qquad
abla^2D\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Derivatives of Relative Entropy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity and Failure of Joint Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-scaling ray structure of generalized relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda\ge0\) and every \((x,y)\) in the effective domain, \[D(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda D(x,y).\] Thus \(D\) is affine along common positive-scaling rays and is not jointly strictly convex on any convex set containing two distinct points of such a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized relative entropy is jointly one-homogeneous and therefore cannot be jointly strictly convex along common-scaling rays.
assumptions_latex: \((x,y)\) lies in the effective domain of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda D(x,y)\quad(\lambda\ge0).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Failure of Joint Strict Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Sum Inequality for Generalized Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate lower bound with the closed support convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfy \(x_i>0\Rightarrow y_i>0\), and set \(s=\sum_i x_i\), \(t=\sum_i y_i\). Then \[\sum_i x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}\ge s\log\frac{s}{t},\qquad D(x,y)\ge d(s,t),\] with the closed zero conventions. If \(s,t>0\), equality holds exactly when \(x_i/y_i=s/t\) for every index with \(x_i+y_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-sum inequality bounds coordinatewise relative entropy by the relative entropy of the total masses, with equality for proportional vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(x,y)\ge d\!\left(\sum_i x_i,\sum_i y_i\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum Inequality for Generalized Relative Entropy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eigenvalue and singular-value spectral functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^n\) be the real symmetric matrices and let \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be rectangular matrices. Write \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb R^n\) for ordered eigenvalues and \(\sigma(Y)\in\mathbb R^r\), \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), for ordered singular values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional orthogonally invariant extended-real matrix functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spectral matrix function is a proper function obtained by applying a proper vector function to a matrix spectrum. On symmetric matrices it has the form
\[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)),\qquad X\in\mathbb S^n.\]
On rectangular matrices it has the form
\[G(Y)=\psi(\sigma(Y)),\qquad Y\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.\]
The symmetric spectral subclass requires \(\varphi\) to be permutation invariant and \(\psi\) to be invariant under permutations and sign changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral matrix calculus constructs proper matrix functions by applying a vector function to the ordered eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix or to the ordered singular values of a rectangular matrix. Orthogonal invariance corresponds to permutation symmetry, or absolute permutation symmetry, of the associated vector function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F=\varphi\circ\lambda\quad\text{or}\quad G=\psi\circ\sigma.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Permutation invariance of \(\varphi\) gives \(F(UXU^{\mathsf T})=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(U\).
Absolute permutation invariance of \(\psi\) gives \(G(UYV^{\mathsf T})=G(Y)\) for compatible orthogonal \(U,V\).
special_cases_latex: \(\varphi(z)=\max_i z_i\) yields \(F(X)=\lambda_{\max}(X)\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_p\) yields the Schatten \(p\)-norm \(\|Y\|_{S_p}\).
\(\varphi(z)=-\sum_i\log z_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) yields \(-\log\det X\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If the associated symmetric vector function is proper, closed, and convex, then its spectral lift is proper, closed, and convex.
The matrix function depends only on the spectrum, not on the chosen eigenvectors or singular vectors.
boundary_notes: For nonsymmetric square matrices, arbitrary eigenvalue compositions are not covered.
Permutation symmetry alone suffices for eigenvalues; singular-value constructions require absolute permutation symmetry when the associated function is defined on all of \(\mathbb R^r\).

notation.meaning: Ordered eigenvalue vector of a symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trace-power spectral function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the kth spectral power sum on the space of real symmetric matrices; no convexity claim is made.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(k\ge1\), define \(\pi_k:S_n\to\mathbb R\) by \[\pi_k(X):=\langle X^k,I_n\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(X^k)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\lambda^{(i)}(X)\bigr)^k,\qquad X\in S_n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive integer k, the trace-power function on real symmetric matrices is the trace of X^k, equivalently the sum of the kth powers of the eigenvalues of X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_k(X)=\langle X^k,I_n\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(X^k)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\lambda^{(i)}(X)\bigr)^k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytic trace spectral function and its domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of a spectral matrix function induced by a scalar power series.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(\tau)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_k\tau^k\) have radius of convergence \(R>0\), with \(a_k\ge 0\) for every \(k\ge 2\). For \(X\in S_n\), define \(F(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda^{(i)}(X))\), where \(\lambda^{(1)}(X)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda^{(n)}(X)\). Then \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{X\in S_n:\lambda^{(1)}(X)<R,\ \lambda^{(n)}(X)>-R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar power series of radius R, with nonnegative coefficients from degree two onward, defines a spectral function by summing over the eigenvalues. Its domain consists of the symmetric matrices whose eigenvalues all lie strictly between -R and R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(X):=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda^{(i)}(X)),\qquad \operatorname{dom}F=\{X\in S_n:\lambda^{(1)}(X)<R,\ \lambda^{(n)}(X)>-R\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational spectral quantities for complex square matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectrum is the set of all eigenvalues of a complex square matrix. The spectral radius is the largest absolute value of an eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma(A)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }A\},\qquad \rho(A)=\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\lambda|\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eigenvalue Bounds for a Symmetric Additive Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided bounds for every ordered eigenvalue of the sum of two real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A,B\in\mathbb{S}^n, and arrange their eigenvalues nondecreasingly. Then, for every k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, \lambda_k(A)+\lambda_{\min}(B)\le\lambda_k(A+B)\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_{\max}(B).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a symmetric matrix B changes each ordered eigenvalue of A by an amount between the smallest and largest eigenvalues of B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k(A)+\lambda_{\min}(B)\le\lambda_k(A+B)\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_{\max}(B).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eigenvalues of nonnegative integer powers of a positive-semidefinite matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The positive-semidefinite hypothesis preserves the nonincreasing eigenvalue ordering after componentwise powering. The case k=0 is included as stated, using the standard zero-power convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in S_n\) satisfy \(X\succeq0\), and let \(k\in\mathbb Z\) with \(k\ge0\). If \(\lambda(X)=(\lambda^{(1)}(X),\ldots,\lambda^{(n)}(X))\) is the nonincreasingly ordered eigenvalue vector and \(\lambda(X)^k\) denotes componentwise powering, then \(\lambda(X^k)=\lambda(X)^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix and a nonnegative integer k, the ordered eigenvalues of the matrix power X^k equal the componentwise kth powers of the ordered eigenvalues of X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(X^k)=\lambda(X)^k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral theorem and extremal quadratic-form bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric matrices, including singular and repeated-eigenvalue cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric. Then all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, and \(A\) has \(n\) mutually orthogonal, real, nonzero eigenvectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). If \(\underline\lambda\) and \(\overline\lambda\) are respectively its smallest and largest eigenvalues, then \(\underline\lambda\,x^{\mathsf T}x\le x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le \overline\lambda\,x^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthogonal basis of real eigenvectors. Its quadratic form lies between its smallest and largest eigenvalues times the squared Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{spec}(A)\subseteq\mathbb R,\quad \exists\,x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\text{ mutually orthogonal eigenvectors},\quad \forall x\in\mathbb R^n:\ \underline\lambda\,x^{\mathsf T}x\le x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le\overline\lambda\,x^{\mathsf T}x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Real and complex Gaussian matrix-norm product bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both field-dependent constants stated in the proposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(L\in\mathbb C^{p\times n}\), \(R\in\mathbb C^{q\times n}\), and \(\chi\sim\mathcal N_{\mathbb C}^n\) is standard, then
\[\mathbb E\big[\|L\chi\|_2\|R\chi\|_2\big]\ge \frac\pi4\|L\|_2\|R\|_2.\]
If \(L\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(R\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), and \(\xi\sim\mathcal N_{\mathbb R}^n\) is standard, then
\[\mathbb E\big[\|L\xi\|_2\|R\xi\|_2\big]\ge \frac2\pi\|L\|_2\|R\|_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected product of the Euclidean norms of two linear images of the same standard Gaussian vector is at least pi over four times the product of the matrix 2-norms in the complex case, and at least two over pi times that product in the real case.

L\in\mathbb R^{p\times n},\ R\in\mathbb R^{q\times n},\ \xi\sim\mathcal N_{\mathbb R}^n\text{ standard, in the real case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real orthogonal eigendecomposition of a finite-dimensional symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric. Then all eigenvalues of \(A\) are real, and there exist \(n\) mutually orthogonal, real, nonzero eigenvectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). If they are normalized so that \(\|x_i\|_2=1\), then \[A=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i x_i^{\mathsf T},\] where \(\lambda_i\) is the eigenvalue corresponding to \(x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real symmetric n-by-n matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthogonal basis of real eigenvectors. With unit eigenvectors, the matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues times the corresponding rank-one orthogonal projectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R},\quad x_i^{\mathsf T}x_j=0\ (i\ne j),\quad A=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i x_i^{\mathsf T}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate-Sign Invariance and Absolute-Value Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded equivalence; \(|x|\) denotes componentwise absolute value, and convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(D_i\) be diagonal with every diagonal entry equal to \(1\) except \((D_i)_{ii}=-1\), and set \(\mathcal A=\{D_1,\ldots,D_n\}\). For a proper \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\), the following are equivalent: \[f\text{ is symmetric with respect to }\mathcal A;\qquad f(x)=f(|x|)\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n;\qquad \exists g:\mathbb R_+^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\ \text{such that }f(x)=g(|x|)\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Such an \(f\) is called absolutely symmetric in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function is invariant under each single-coordinate sign flip exactly when its value depends only on the componentwise absolute value of its argument; equivalently, it factors through the absolute-value map to the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ symmetric with respect to }\mathcal A\iff (\forall x)\;f(x)=f(|x|)\iff \exists g:\mathbb R_+^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\;(\forall x)\;f(x)=g(|x|)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submodularity properties of principal-submatrix spectral traces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the spectral set-function construction, two sufficient families, and the failure of scalar concavity alone to guarantee submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} be positive semidefinite, with rows and columns indexed by V, and let h:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}. For A\subseteq V, define F(A)=\operatorname{tr}h(Q_{AA}), where h is applied eigenvaluewise. If Q is diagonal, this construction reduces to a function of a modular set function. Concavity of h alone does not imply submodularity of F; the family h(\lambda)=\lambda/(\lambda+1) admits counterexamples. For h(\lambda)=\log(\lambda+t), t\ge 0, the resulting set function is submodular wherever the spectral trace is well-defined (with the t=0 singular case requiring an extended-value interpretation). For h(\lambda)=\lambda^\rho, \rho\in(0,1], F is nondecreasing and submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a scalar function eigenvaluewise to every principal submatrix and taking its trace defines a spectral set function. Diagonal matrices recover functions of modular set functions. Scalar concavity alone is insufficient for submodularity, with the ratio lambda/(lambda+1) providing counterexamples. Logarithmic shifts yield submodular functions where defined, and powers with exponent in (0,1] yield nondecreasing submodular functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h(\lambda)=\log(\lambda+t),\ t\ge0\Rightarrow F\text{ is submodular wherever well-defined};\qquad h(\lambda)=\lambda^\rho,\ \rho\in(0,1]\Rightarrow F\text{ is nondecreasing and submodular};\qquad h\text{ concave alone}\not\Rightarrow F\text{ submodular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cauchy interlacing for a principal submatrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue bounds for every principal submatrix of a real symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, and let $A_r$ be any principal submatrix of order $r\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. With the eigenvalues of each matrix ordered nondecreasingly, for every $k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $$\lambda_k(A)\leq \lambda_k(A_r)\leq \lambda_{n+k-r}(A).$$ In particular, $\lambda_{\min}(A)\leq\lambda_{\min}(A_r)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every order-r principal submatrix of a real symmetric n-by-n matrix, its kth smallest eigenvalue lies between the kth and the (n+k-r)th eigenvalues of the full matrix. In particular, the principal submatrix's smallest eigenvalue is no smaller than that of the full matrix.

\text{The eigenvalues of }A\text{ and }A_r\text{ are ordered nondecreasingly}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k(A)\leq\lambda_k(A_r)\leq\lambda_{n+k-r}(A),\quad\text{and in particular }\lambda_{\min}(A)\leq\lambda_{\min}(A_r).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary Eigenvalue Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue identities for triangular, similar, shifted, powered, inverted, and transposed square matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\). (a) If \(A\) is triangular, its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries. (b) If \(S\) is nonsingular and \(B=SAS^{-1}\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have the same eigenvalues. (c) If \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(A\), then those of \(cI+A\) are \(c+\lambda_1,\ldots,c+\lambda_n\). (d) For every positive integer \(k\), the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda_1^k,\ldots,\lambda_n^k\). (e) If \(A\) is nonsingular, the eigenvalues of \(A^{-1}\) are \(\lambda_1^{-1},\ldots,\lambda_n^{-1}\). (f) The eigenvalues of \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\) coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triangular matrix has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues. Similarity and transposition preserve eigenvalues; scalar shifts, positive integer powers, and inversion respectively shift, power, and reciprocate the eigenvalues, with inversion requiring nonsingularity.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is nonsingular in the similarity assertion}
k\in\mathbb{N},\ k\ge 1\text{ in the power assertion}
A\text{ is nonsingular in the inverse assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{spec}(A)=\operatorname{diag}(A)\text{ if }A\text{ is triangular};\quad \operatorname{spec}(SAS^{-1})=\operatorname{spec}(A);\quad \operatorname{spec}(cI+A)=c+\operatorname{spec}(A);\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^k)=\{\lambda^k:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)\};\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^{-1})=\{\lambda^{-1}:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)\};\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{spec}(A).
