knowledge_statements.statement_title: Thin SVD and PCA variance characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the thin singular value decomposition with its principal-component interpretation for centered matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(m\ge n\), a thin singular value decomposition is \(Z=UDV^{T}\), where \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfies \(U^{T}U=I_n\), \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfies \(V^{T}V=I_n\), and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) with \(d_1\ge\cdots\ge d_n\ge0\). If the singular values are distinct, the singular-vector pairs are unique up to simultaneous columnwise sign changes. If the columns of \(Z\) are centered, then \(s_j=Zv_j\) are its principal components: \(v_1\) maximizes the sample variance of \(Zv\) over \(\|v\|_2=1\), and successively \(v_j\) maximizes it subject to \(Zv\) being uncorrelated with \(s_1,\ldots,s_{j-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real m-by-n matrix with m at least n has a thin SVD with orthonormal left and right singular vectors and ordered nonnegative singular values. Distinct singular values determine the corresponding singular-vector pairs up to simultaneous sign changes. For a column-centered matrix, the right singular vectors give principal-component loading directions: the first maximizes sample variance, and each later component maximizes variance subject to being uncorrelated with the earlier components.
assumptions_latex: \text{Distinctness of }d_1,\ldots,d_n\text{ for the stated uniqueness conclusion}
\text{Column centering of }Z\text{ for the PCA conclusions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z=UDV^{T},\quad s_j=Zv_j;\qquad v_1\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\|v\|_2=1}\operatorname{Var}(Zv),\ \text{with successive analogous maxima under uncorrelatedness constraints}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ky Fan trace variational formulas and spectral-sum curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representations and curvature of sums of the smallest or largest eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $\lambda_1(A)\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n(A)$. For every $r\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)=\min_{\substack{U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\\ U^\top U=I_r}}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU),$$ and $$\sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)=\max_{\substack{U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\\ U^\top U=I_r}}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU).$$ Consequently, the sum of the $r$ smallest eigenvalues is concave in $A$, whereas the sum of the $r$ largest eigenvalues is convex in $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric matrix, the sum of its r smallest eigenvalues is the minimum compressed trace over matrices with r orthonormal columns, while the sum of its r largest eigenvalues is the corresponding maximum. Hence the smallest-eigenvalue sum is concave and the largest-eigenvalue sum is convex as functions of the matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)=\min_{U^\top U=I_r}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU),\quad \sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)=\max_{U^\top U=I_r}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU);\quad A\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)\text{ is concave, and }A\mapsto\sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Courant–Fischer Minimax and Rayleigh–Ritz Formulas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational characterizations of the ordered eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix, including convexity and concavity of its extreme-eigenvalue functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{S}^n have eigenvalues \lambda_1(A)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(A). For every k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, \lambda_k(A)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}. In particular, \lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}x^\top Ax and \lambda_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}x^\top Ax. Consequently, A\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(A) is convex and A\mapsto\lambda_{\min}(A) is concave on \mathbb{S}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each ordered eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix has equivalent min–max and max–min Rayleigh-quotient characterizations. The largest eigenvalue is convex as a function of the matrix, while the smallest eigenvalue is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k(A)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x},\quad \lambda_{\max}\text{ is convex and }\lambda_{\min}\text{ is concave on }\mathbb{S}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Capped Water-Filling Solution under Trace and Peak-Eigenvalue Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form spectral optimizer for the stated positive-semidefinite log-determinant problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let R_H=V_H\Lambda_HV_H^H\in\mathbb S_+^{n_T}, let r_{R_H}=\operatorname{rank}(R_H), and suppose P_T\le P^{\mathrm{peak}}r_{R_H}. Then
\[
\max_{Q\succeq0}\ \log\det(I+R_HQ)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \operatorname{Tr}(Q)\le P_T,\ \lambda_{\max}(Q)\le P^{\mathrm{peak}}
\]
has the unique solution
\[
Q^\star=V_{H,1}\left[\mu I_{r_{R_H}}-\Lambda_{H,1}^{-1}\right]_{0}^{P^{\mathrm{peak}}}V_{H,1}^H,
\]
where V_{H,1} contains the eigenvectors associated with the positive eigenvalues collected in \Lambda_{H,1}, and \mu>0 satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\left[\mu I_{r_{R_H}}-\Lambda_{H,1}^{-1}\right]_{0}^{P^{\mathrm{peak}}}\right)=P_T.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite log-determinant problem with a total trace budget and a peak eigenvalue bound has a unique optimizer. It allocates power on the positive-eigenvalue subspace by water-filling and clips every allocation between zero and the peak bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,Q^\star=V_{H,1}\left[\mu I_{r_{R_H}}-\Lambda_{H,1}^{-1}\right]_{0}^{P^{\mathrm{peak}}}V_{H,1}^H,\quad \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\left[\mu I_{r_{R_H}}-\Lambda_{H,1}^{-1}\right]_{0}^{P^{\mathrm{peak}}}\right)=P_T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Functions and Spectral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines permutation-invariant vector functions and their spectral lifts to symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let [x] be the nonincreasing rearrangement of x\in\mathbb R^n. A function f on \mathbb R^n is symmetric if f(x)=f([x]) for every x\in\mathbb R^n, equivalently, if coordinate permutations leave its value unchanged. If \lambda(X) denotes the ordered eigenvalue vector of X\in\mathbb S^n and f is symmetric, then X\mapsto f(\lambda(X)) is called a spectral function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian bound for analytic trace spectral functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded curvature bound for a spectral function generated by a real power series.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kt^k\) be a real power series with radius of convergence \(R\in(0,\infty]\), and let \(F(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda^{(i)}(X))\) on \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{X\in S_n:|\lambda^{(i)}(X)|<R\ \forall i\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary definitions and properties of real square matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded compound statement of elementary matrix terminology and properties. The source defines definiteness through quadratic forms without initially requiring symmetry; its later spectral characterization explicitly requires symmetry. Its nonstandard “bounded matrix” definition is retained only as source-specific terminology and is not endorsed as canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, symmetry means A=A^T. Positive and negative definiteness mean x^TAx>0 and x^TAx<0, respectively, for every nonzero x\in\mathbb{R}^n; positive and negative semidefiniteness replace the strict inequalities by \geq0 and \leq0. The source calls A indefinite when it is neither positive nor negative semidefinite. If A is positive definite, then its principal submatrices are positive definite, A_{ii}>0 for every i, A is nonsingular, and A^{-1} is positive definite; sums of positive-definite matrices are positive definite. An inverse satisfies AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I. An eigenpair satisfies Ax=\lambda x with x\neq0. If A is symmetric, its eigenvalues are real and A is positive definite if and only if every eigenvalue is positive. The trace is \operatorname{tr}A=\sum_{i=1}^nA_{ii}, equals the sum of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity, and satisfies \operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}A+\operatorname{tr}B. The extract additionally calls a matrix bounded when its eigenvalues lie in a compact interval excluding zero; as written, this terminology presupposes a real spectrum and is nonstandard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Defines symmetry, quadratic-form definiteness and semidefiniteness, indefiniteness, inverses, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and trace for real square matrices, and states elementary properties of positive-definite matrices and symmetric spectra. It also contains a nonstandard definition of a bounded matrix whose stated interval condition is meaningful only for real eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: A=A^T\text{ for the real-spectrum and eigenvalue characterization of positive definiteness}
A\text{ and }B\text{ are positive definite for the sum property}
\text{Eigenvalues in the trace formula are counted with algebraic multiplicity}
\sigma(A)\subset\mathbb{R}\text{ for the source-specific compact-interval definition of boundedness}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A=A^T\iff A_{ij}=A_{ji}\ (\forall i,j);\quad A\succ0\iff x^TAx>0\ (\forall x\neq0);\quad A\succeq0\iff x^TAx\geq0\ (\forall x);\quad A\prec0\iff x^TAx<0\ (\forall x\neq0);\quad A\preceq0\iff x^TAx\leq0\ (\forall x);\quad A\succ0\Rightarrow(A_{II}\succ0,\ A_{ii}>0,\ A\text{ nonsingular},\ A^{-1}\succ0);\quad A\succ0\land B\succ0\Rightarrow A+B\succ0;\quad A=A^T\Rightarrow[\sigma(A)\subset\mathbb{R}\land(A\succ0\iff\lambda>0\ \forall\lambda\in\sigma(A))];\quad \operatorname{tr}A=\sum_iA_{ii}=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(A),\quad \operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}A+\operatorname{tr}B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eigenvalues under standard matrix transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary spectral identities for a square real matrix, with nonsingularity imposed where inversion is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\), counted with algebraic multiplicity. (a) If \(T\) is nonsingular and \(B=TAT^{-1}\), then \(A\) and \(B\) have the same eigenvalues. (b) For every scalar \(c\), the eigenvalues of \(cI+A\) are \(c+\lambda_1,\ldots,c+\lambda_n\). (c) For every integer \(k\ge 1\), the eigenvalues of \(A^k\) are \(\lambda_1^k,\ldots,\lambda_n^k\). (d) If \(A\) is nonsingular, the eigenvalues of \(A^{-1}\) are \(\lambda_1^{-1},\ldots,\lambda_n^{-1}\). (e) The eigenvalues of \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\) coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Similarity preserves eigenvalues; adding a scalar multiple of the identity shifts them; taking a positive integer power raises them to that power; inversion reciprocates them when the matrix is nonsingular; and transposition preserves them.
assumptions_latex: \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\text{ are the eigenvalues of }A\text{ counted with algebraic multiplicity}
T\text{ is nonsingular in the similarity claim}
k\in\mathbb Z,\ k\ge 1\text{ in the power claim}
A\text{ is nonsingular in the inverse claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{spec}(TAT^{-1})=\operatorname{spec}(A),\quad \operatorname{spec}(cI+A)=\{c+\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^n,\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^k)=\{\lambda_i^k\}_{i=1}^n,\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^{-1})=\{\lambda_i^{-1}\}_{i=1}^n,\quad \operatorname{spec}(A^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{spec}(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ky Fan k-Norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Ky Fan norms of real rectangular matrices through an absolutely permutation-symmetric vector generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\) and \(1\leq k\leq r\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^r\), order the components so that \(|x_{\langle1\rangle}|\geq\cdots\geq|x_{\langle r\rangle}|\), and define \(f_k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k|x_{\langle i\rangle}|\). For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the Ky Fan \(k\)-norm is \[\|X\|_{\langle k\rangle}=f_k(\sigma(X))=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X).\] In particular, \(\|\cdot\|_{\langle1\rangle}\) is the spectral, or Schatten-\(\infty\), norm, and \(\|\cdot\|_{\langle r\rangle}\) is the trace, or Schatten-\(1\), norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Ky Fan k-norm of a real matrix is the sum of its k largest singular values. Its endpoint cases are the spectral norm for k=1 and the trace norm when k equals the number of singular values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|X\|_{\langle k\rangle}=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X),\qquad \|X\|_{\langle1\rangle}=\|X\|_{S_\infty},\qquad \|X\|_{\langle r\rangle}=\|X\|_{S_1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fan Trace Inequality and Equality Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric matrices; the eigenvalue vectors use the common ordering implicit in the spectral map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^n\), \[\operatorname{Tr}(XY)\leq \langle\lambda(X),\lambda(Y)\rangle.\] Equality holds if and only if there exists \(V\in\mathbb O^n\) such that \[X=V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(X))V^T,\qquad Y=V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(Y))V^T.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two real symmetric matrices, their trace product is at most the inner product of their ordered eigenvalue vectors. Equality holds exactly when one orthogonal matrix diagonalizes both matrices with their eigenvalues in the prescribed common order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Tr}(XY)\leq\langle\lambda(X),\lambda(Y)\rangle,\quad\text{with equality iff }\exists V\in\mathbb O^n:\ X=V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(X))V^T,\ Y=V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda(Y))V^T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Largest-Eigenvalue Support Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), \[\lambda_{\max}(X)=\max_{\|u\|_2=1}u^{\mathsf T}Xu=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(PX):P\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}P=1\}.\] Hence \(\lambda_{\max}\) is finite, convex, orthogonally invariant, and semidefinite-order monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest eigenvalue is the support function of trace-one positive-semidefinite matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}(X)=\max_{P\succeq0,\operatorname{tr}P=1}\operatorname{tr}(PX)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Spectral-Function Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric-matrix spectral functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and permutation invariant. Then \(F(X)=f(\lambda(X))\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and orthogonally invariant on \(\mathbb S^n\). Conversely, every proper lower-semicontinuous convex orthogonally invariant \(F\) has this form with the symmetric generator \(f(x)=F(\operatorname{Diag}x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed proper convex orthogonally invariant functions on symmetric matrices correspond exactly to closed proper symmetric convex functions of eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) uses the Frobenius inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f\circ\lambda\) gives a bijective correspondence between symmetric closed proper convex generators and orthogonally invariant closed proper convex matrix functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each Ky Fan sum of the largest k eigenvalues has a semidefinite support representation and is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)=\max_{0\preceq P\preceq I,\operatorname{tr}P=k}\operatorname{tr}(PX)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex spectral functions of symmetric matrices
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\lambda:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^n\) list eigenvalues in nonincreasing order. Let \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric matrices and extended-real orthogonally invariant convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The eigenvalue-based convex function generated by \(\varphi\) is
\[F:\mathbb S^n\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)).\]
Permutation invariance means \(\varphi(Pz)=\varphi(z)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\). The resulting \(F\) is a proper closed convex function and is invariant under orthogonal similarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex eigenvalue-based matrix function is formed by composing the ordered eigenvalue map on symmetric matrices with a proper closed convex permutation-invariant vector function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)),\qquad F(UXU^{\mathsf T})=F(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper orthogonally invariant \(F\) has this representation with \(\varphi(z)=F(\operatorname{diag}z)\), which is permutation invariant.
Closedness and convexity of \(F=\varphi\circ\lambda\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its proper permutation-symmetric associated function \(\varphi\).
special_cases_latex: \(\varphi(z)=\max_i z_i\) gives the maximum-eigenvalue function.
\(\varphi(z)=\sum_i z_i\) gives \(\operatorname{tr}X\).
\(\varphi(z)=\|z\|_p\) gives the corresponding symmetric-matrix Schatten norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain is \(\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda(X)\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\}\).
The value is independent of the ordering convention because \(\varphi\) is permutation invariant.
boundary_notes: The requirement that \(X\) be symmetric is essential for a real ordered eigenvalue vector.
Without permutation invariance, the composition can depend on the arbitrary ordering convention and need not describe an orthogonally invariant function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex spectral functions of rectangular matrices
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), and let \(\sigma:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R_+^r\) list singular values nonincreasingly. Let \(\psi:\mathbb R^r\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and absolutely permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real rectangular matrices and extended-real unitarily invariant convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-value-based convex function generated by \(\psi\) is
\[G:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X)).\]
Absolute permutation invariance means \(\psi(PDz)=\psi(z)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\) and every diagonal sign matrix \(D\). The resulting \(G\) is proper, closed, convex, and invariant under left and right orthogonal transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex singular-value-based function is the composition of the singular-value vector of a rectangular matrix with a proper closed convex vector function invariant under coordinate permutations and sign changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X)),\qquad G(UXV^{\mathsf T})=G(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper orthogonally invariant rectangular-matrix function has an absolutely permutation-symmetric associated vector function.
Closedness and convexity of \(G=\psi\circ\sigma\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its proper absolutely permutation-symmetric associated function.
special_cases_latex: \(\psi(z)=\|z\|_1\) gives the nuclear norm \(\|X\|_*\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_\infty\) gives the operator norm \(\sigma_1(X)\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_2\) gives the Frobenius norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain is \(\{X:\sigma(X)\in\operatorname{dom}\psi\}\).
Every Schatten \(p\)-norm with \(1\le p\le\infty\) belongs to this family.
boundary_notes: Singular values are nonnegative, but absolute symmetry provides the canonical extension of the associated function to all of \(\mathbb R^r\).
Functions depending on singular vectors as well as singular values are outside this family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-convex interpretation of matrix-order convexity on an interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous function \(h:I\to\mathbb{R}\) is matrix-order convex on an interval \(I\) if, for every \(n\geq1\), all \(A,B\in\mathbb{S}^n\) with spectra contained in \(I\), and every \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[h(\theta A+(1-\theta)B)\preceq\theta h(A)+(1-\theta)h(B).\] Here \(h(A)\) is defined by spectral functional calculus and \(C\preceq D\) means that \(D-C\) is positive semidefinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar and Hessian characterizations of matrix convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects scalarization, second-order, block-Hessian sufficient, and largest-eigenvalue consequences of semidefinite-order convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathcal S^p\). (i) The map \(G\) is matrix convex if and only if \(x\mapsto z^TG(x)z\) is convex for every \(z\in\mathbb R^p\). (ii) If every entry \(g_{ij}\) is twice continuously differentiable, matrix convexity is equivalent to \[\sum_{i,j=1}^p z_i z_j\nabla^2 g_{ij}(x)\succeq0\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and }z\in\mathbb R^p.\] (iii) If \(G\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(H(x)=[\nabla^2g_{ij}(x)]_{i,j=1}^p\succeq0\) for every \(x\), then \(G\) is matrix convex. (iv) If \(G\) is matrix convex, then \(x\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(G(x))\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-matrix-valued map is matrix convex exactly when every quadratic scalarization is convex. For twice continuously differentiable entries, this is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of every scalarized Hessian. Positive semidefiniteness of the full block Hessian is sufficient for matrix convexity, and matrix convexity implies convexity of the largest-eigenvalue function.
assumptions_latex: \text{Parts (ii) and (iii) assume the stated twice-continuous differentiability}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is matrix convex}\iff\forall z\in\mathbb R^p,\ z^TG(\cdot)z\text{ is convex};\quad G\text{ matrix convex}\Rightarrow\lambda_{\max}(G(\cdot))\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions and polars of invariant matrix domains reduce exactly to those of their symmetric eigenvalue sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariant Convex Domain Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally invariant convex subsets of real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and permutation invariant, then \[D_C=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}\] is convex and orthogonally invariant. Conversely, if \(D\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) is convex and orthogonally invariant, then \(C_D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\operatorname{Diag}(x)\in D\}\) is convex and permutation invariant and \(D=D_{C_D}\). The ordered section \(\lambda(D)\) lies in the Weyl chamber and need not itself be permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariant convex matrix domains correspond exactly to permutation-invariant convex diagonal sets; ordered eigenvalue sections must not be confused with those symmetric sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\mapsto D_C\) and \(D\mapsto C_D\) give inverse correspondences between permutation-invariant convex vector sets and orthogonally invariant convex symmetric-matrix sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C\) is convex, then \(D\) is convex and invariant under orthogonal conjugation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue representation of orthogonally invariant convex matrix domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and invariant under coordinate permutations. Its spectral lift is \[D=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}.\] Then \(D\) is convex and orthogonally invariant: \(QXQ^{\mathsf T}\in D\) whenever \(X\in D\) and \(Q\) is orthogonal. Conversely, every orthogonally invariant convex set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{S}^n\) is determined by the permutation-invariant convex set \(C=\{\lambda(X):X\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permutation-invariant convex eigenvalue sets lift exactly to orthogonally invariant convex domains of symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Determinant lower bound under a skew-symmetric perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real square matrices whose symmetric part is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y,S,C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(Y=S+C\), \(S^{\mathsf T}=S\succ0\), and \(C^{\mathsf T}=-C\). Then
\[
\lvert\det Y\rvert\geq \det S.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a real square matrix is the sum of a positive-definite symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix, then the absolute value of its determinant is at least the determinant of its symmetric part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lvert\det(Y)\rvert\geq\det(S)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison-rule framework for convexity variants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to I\), where \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval. For each \(t\in(0,1)\), let \(M_t:I\times I\to I\) be a prescribed two-point aggregator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomic scalar framework covering the principal Jensen, level-set, and multiplicative convexity variants represented by descendant nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to an aggregator family \(M=(M_t)_{0<t<1}\), a function \(f\) is \(M\)-convex when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le M_t(f(x),f(y))\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C,\ t\in(0,1).\]
The canonical convexity variants arise from \(M_t(u,v)=tu+(1-t)v\) (ordinary convexity), \(M_t(u,v)=\max\{u,v\}\) (quasiconvexity), and, for positive-valued functions, \(M_t(u,v)=u^tv^{1-t}\) (log-convexity). Strict variants replace the inequality by a strict one for distinct endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar convexity variant can be specified by choosing the two-point comparison used on the right side of a Jensen-type inequality. Arithmetic averaging gives ordinary convexity, the maximum gives quasiconvexity, and geometric averaging gives log-convexity for positive functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le M_t(f(x),f(y)),\qquad x,y\in C,\ 0<t<1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(M_t(u,v)=\max\{u,v\}\), the condition is equivalent to convexity of every sublevel set of \(f\).
For positive \(f\) and \(M_t(u,v)=u^tv^{1-t}\), the condition is equivalent to convexity of \(\log f\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing arithmetic means recovers the usual convex-function class.
Choosing maximum aggregation retains convex minimizer and sublevel-set geometry without requiring a convex epigraph.
immediate_consequences_latex: Ordinary convexity implies quasiconvexity because \(tu+(1-t)v\le\max\{u,v\}\).
Log-convexity implies ordinary convexity for positive functions.
boundary_notes: This record formalizes a taxonomic umbrella rather than asserting that every named generalized-convexity notion is generated by a scalar aggregator.
Cone-ordered vector-valued convexity requires replacing the scalar inequality by an order relation and is not included in the displayed scalar definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict, uniform, and strong convexity regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Let \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative and quantitative convexity regimes on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly convex when, for every \(x\ne y\),
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)<tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
It is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\), where \(\phi\) is increasing and vanishes only at zero, when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)+t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
It is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when the latter holds with \(\phi(r)=\mu r^2/2\) for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity requires a strict Jensen inequality between distinct domain points. Uniform convexity adds a positive distance-dependent deficit, and strong convexity is the quadratic-modulus specialization with a positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{strong convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{uniform convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{strict convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{convexity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(x\mapsto f(x)-\frac\mu2\|x\|^2\) is convex.
Strict convexity is equivalent to the absence of equality in the convex Jensen inequality at every interior point of every nondegenerate domain segment.
special_cases_latex: On a Hilbert space, \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2\) is strongly convex with parameter \(2\) under this normalization.
Affine functions are convex but are not strictly convex on any domain containing a nondegenerate segment.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly convex function has at most one minimizer on any convex subset of its domain.
A positive uniform modulus rules out affine behavior on every nondegenerate segment.
boundary_notes: The reverse implications in the displayed hierarchy generally fail.
Positive-definite Hessians are sufficient in smooth finite-dimensional settings but are not part of the general definition.
Strict convexity depends on the effective domain; vacuous cases can occur when the domain contains no distinct points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient second-order criterion and its sharp nonconverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and \(f\in C^2(C)\). If \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) for every \(x\in C\), then \(f\) is strictly convex. The converse fails: \(f(x)=x^4\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb R\), although \(f''(0)=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract does not state a parameter range for \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous function \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \((2+\kappa)\)-convex if there exists \(K>0\) such that, for every \(v,w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\frac{L(v)+L(w)}{2}-L\!\left(\frac{v+w}{2}\right)\ge K\lvert v-w\rvert^{2+\kappa}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Dimensional Derivative Tests for Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equivalences for convexity and strict convexity from the merely sufficient positive-second-derivative condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let O\subset\mathbb R be an open interval and let f:O\to\mathbb R be differentiable. The following are each equivalent to convexity of f on O: (i) f' is nondecreasing; (ii) f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x)(y-x) for all x,y\in O; and, if f is twice differentiable, (iii) f''(x)\ge0 for every x\in O. Strict convexity is equivalent to f' being strictly increasing, and also equivalent to f(y)>f(x)+f'(x)(y-x) for all distinct x,y\in O. If f is twice differentiable, f''(x)>0 for every x\in O is sufficient, but not necessary, for strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable function on an open real interval, convexity is equivalent to a nondecreasing derivative or to every tangent line lying below the graph; under twice differentiability it is also equivalent to a nonnegative second derivative. Strict convexity is equivalent to a strictly increasing derivative or strict tangent inequality. An everywhere positive second derivative is sufficient but not necessary for strict convexity.
assumptions_latex: O\subset\mathbb R\text{ is an open interval}
f\text{ is twice differentiable for the assertions involving }f''
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ convex}\iff f'\text{ nondecreasing}\iff (\forall x,y\in O)\ f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x)(y-x)\iff f''\ge0;\quad f\text{ strictly convex}\iff f'\text{ strictly increasing}\iff \text{strict tangent inequalities},\quad f''>0\Rightarrow f\text{ strictly convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant-Slope Characterization of Convexity on an Interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the strict-convexity analogue and monotonicity of fixed-base difference quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subset\mathbb R be an interval and f:C\to\mathbb R. Then f is convex on C if and only if, for every x_0<y<x_1 in C, \[\frac{f(y)-f(x_0)}{y-x_0}\le \frac{f(x_1)-f(x_0)}{x_1-x_0}\le \frac{f(x_1)-f(y)}{x_1-y}.\] Consequently, for every x\in C, \Delta_x(y):=(f(y)-f(x))/(y-x) is nondecreasing in y\in C\setminus\{x\}. Strict convexity is equivalent to the corresponding strict inequalities, in which case \Delta_x is strictly increasing on C\setminus\{x\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on an interval is convex exactly when the secant slopes determined by every ordered triple increase from left to right. Equivalently, each fixed-base difference quotient is nondecreasing. Replacing the inequalities by strict inequalities characterizes strict convexity and makes each fixed-base quotient strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \frac{f(y)-f(x_0)}{y-x_0}\le\frac{f(x_1)-f(x_0)}{x_1-x_0}\le\frac{f(x_1)-f(y)}{x_1-y};\quad \Delta_x\text{ is nondecreasing, with strict analogues characterizing strict convexity}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux differentiability characterized by strict convexity of the conjugate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence under equality of the primal subdifferential domain and the interior of the primal effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\). Then \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\) if and only if \(f^*\) is strictly convex on every nonempty convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*\). When these equivalent conditions hold, \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*=\nabla f(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppose the subdifferential of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function is defined exactly on the interior of its effective domain. The function is Gâteaux differentiable there exactly when its conjugate is strictly convex on every nonempty convex subset of the conjugate subdifferential domain. Under these equivalent conditions, that domain equals the image of the primal interior under the gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\iff f^*\text{ is strictly convex on every nonempty convex }C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*;\) moreover, under these conditions, \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*=\nabla f(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual equivalence of Gâteaux differentiability and strict convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric conjugacy equivalences under interior-domain identities for both primal and conjugate subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*=\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\). Then: (i) \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\) if and only if \(f^*\) is strictly convex on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\); and (ii) \(f\) is strictly convex on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\) if and only if \(f^*\) is Gâteaux differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the subdifferential domains of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and its conjugate equal the interiors of their respective effective domains, primal Gâteaux differentiability is equivalent to conjugate strict convexity, and primal strict convexity is equivalent to conjugate Gâteaux differentiability, on those interiors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\iff f^*\text{ is strictly convex on }\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*,\) and \(f\text{ is strictly convex on }\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\iff f^*\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order characterization of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence for differentiable convexity and a one-way sufficient condition for strict convexity on a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable over \(C\). Then \(f\) is convex over \(C\) if and only if \(f(z)\geq f(x)+(z-x)^\top\nabla f(x)\) for all \(x,z\in C\). If this inequality is strict for every \(x,z\in C\) with \(x\neq z\), then \(f\) is strictly convex over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function on a convex set is convex exactly when every first-order affine approximation is a global underestimator on that set. If the underestimation is strict at every distinct pair, the function is strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex on }C\iff \forall x,z\in C,\ f(z)\geq f(x)+(z-x)^\top\nabla f(x);\quad [x\neq z\Rightarrow >]\Rightarrow f\text{ strictly convex on }C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly Convex Lower-Semicontinuous Extension from Positive Second Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs an extended-real strictly convex function on the closure of an open interval by radial boundary limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have effective domain \(D=\operatorname{dom}h\), where \(D\) is a nonempty open interval. Suppose \(h\) is twice differentiable on \(D\) and \(h''(x)>0\) for every \(x\in D\). Fix \(y\in D\), and define
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
h(x),&x\in D,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}h((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y),&x\in\operatorname{bdry}D,\\
+\infty,&x\notin\overline D.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\), \(f|_D=h|_D\), \(D\subset\operatorname{dom}f\subset\overline D\), and \(f\) is strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an extended-real function has a nonempty open interval as its effective domain, is twice differentiable there, and has positive second derivative everywhere, then retaining its interior values, assigning radial limits at boundary points, and assigning positive infinity outside the closed interval produces a proper lower-semicontinuous strictly convex function. It agrees with the original function on the interval, and its effective domain lies between the interval and its closure.
assumptions_latex: D=\operatorname{dom}h\text{ is a nonempty open interval}
f\text{ is defined by the stated interior, radial-boundary-limit, and exterior clauses}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R),\quad f|_D=h|_D,\quad D\subset\operatorname{dom}f\subset\overline D,\quad f\text{ is strictly convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat segments witnessing failure of strict convexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex. For \(x,y\in C\), write \([x,y]=\{tx+(1-t)y:0\le t\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued convex functions on a convex domain; the object records equality segments rather than a topological boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The facial-flatness set of \(f\) is
\[\operatorname{Flat}(f)=\left\{(x,y,t):x,y\in C,\ x\ne y,\ 0<t<1,\ f(tx+(1-t)y)=tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\right\}.\]
A nonempty \(\operatorname{Flat}(f)\) is a certificate that strict convexity fails. Equivalently, the graph of \(f\) contains a nondegenerate line segment, or the lower boundary of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) contains a nontrivial flat segment joining \((x,f(x))\) and \((y,f(y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The facial-flatness set consists of distinct domain endpoints and an interior interpolation parameter at which the convex Jensen inequality is an equality. Its nonemptiness is exactly the failure of strict convexity and identifies a flat segment on the lower epigraph boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is strictly convex on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Flat}(f)=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex \(f\), equality at one interior point of \([x,y]\) identifies affine behavior along the corresponding graph segment.
The points \((x,f(x))\) and \((y,f(y))\) belong to a common nontrivial lower flat portion of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: Every affine function on a domain containing a nondegenerate segment has a nonempty facial-flatness set.
A polyhedral convex function usually has flat regions on cells where one affine piece is active.
immediate_consequences_latex: If two distinct minimizers exist, their entire connecting segment consists of minimizers and supplies facial flatness.
A strictly convex function cannot have a nontrivial segment contained in one finite level set at its minimum value.
boundary_notes: The word “boundary” here refers to the transition from strict Jensen inequality to equality, not to the topological boundary of the effective domain.
Domain geometry alone may make strictness vacuous when the domain contains no nondegenerate segment.
Essential strict convexity uses a different localization through the conjugate subdifferential domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local, global, and strict minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an arbitrary real-valued objective restricted to a feasible subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(x^\star\in\Omega\). The point \(x^\star\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(\Omega\) if \(\exists\varepsilon>0\) such that \(f(x)\ge f(x^\star)\) for every \(x\in\Omega\setminus\{x^\star\}\) satisfying \(\|x-x^\star\|<\varepsilon\). It is a global minimizer if \(f(x)\ge f(x^\star)\) for every \(x\in\Omega\setminus\{x^\star\}\). Replacing \(\ge\) by \(>\) defines strict local and strict global minimizers, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is a local minimizer when no distinct sufficiently close feasible point has a smaller objective value, and it is a global minimizer when no distinct feasible point anywhere in the set has a smaller value. Requiring every compared value to be strictly larger gives the corresponding strict notions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}x^\star\text{ local min}&\iff \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall x\in\Omega\setminus\{x^\star\}:\ \|x-x^\star\|<\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(x)\ge f(x^\star),\\x^\star\text{ global min}&\iff \forall x\in\Omega\setminus\{x^\star\}:\ f(x)\ge f(x^\star),\end{aligned}\quad\text{with strict variants obtained by replacing \(\ge\) with \(>\).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global, constrained, unique, and local minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational minimizer definitions for a proper extended-real-valued function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to]-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. A point \(x\in\mathcal H\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) when \(f(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathcal H}f(y)=\min f(\mathcal H)\in\mathbb R\), and \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{x\in\mathcal H\mid f(x)=\inf f(\mathcal H)\}\). If this set is a singleton, \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal H}f(x)\) denotes its unique element. For \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{Argmin}_{C}f=\operatorname{Argmin}(f+\iota_C)\). A point \(x\) is a local minimizer when there exists \(\rho>0\) such that \(x\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{B(x;\rho)}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimizer attains the finite infimum of a proper extended-real-valued function, and Argmin denotes the set of all such points; lowercase argmin denotes the unique point when this set is a singleton. Minimization over a set C is minimization of the function plus the indicator of C, provided C meets the effective domain. A local minimizer minimizes the function on some positive-radius ball centered at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\), \(\operatorname{argmin}f\), \(\operatorname{Argmin}_{C}f\), and local minimizers are defined as above.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvex function via the max-Jensen inequality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar extended-real quasiconvexity on a convex domain; no continuity or ordinary convexity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\). Thus values at interior points of a segment cannot exceed the larger endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex domain is quasiconvex when its value at every interior convex combination of two points is at most the maximum of its two endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x,y\in C\ \forall t\in(0,1):\quad f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the sublevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is convex.
Every restriction of \(f\) to a line segment is a one-dimensional quasiconvex function.
special_cases_latex: Every convex function is quasiconvex.
Every monotone real-valued function on an interval is quasiconvex, even when it is not convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimizer set \(\operatorname{argmin}_C f\), when nonempty, is convex.
Quasiconvexity is preserved under increasing scalar reparameterizations and pointwise suprema under the standard domain conditions.
boundary_notes: Quasiconvexity does not require a convex epigraph.
A sum of quasiconvex functions need not be quasiconvex.
Quasiconvexity is distinct from quasiconcavity; satisfying both gives quasilinearity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implications between cone quasiconvexity and differentiable cone quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two implication regimes under distinct directional-variation assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a subset of a real linear space \(X\), let \(C\subset\widehat C\) be nonempty subsets of a real linear space \(Y\), assume \(C\cup\{0_Y\}\) is a cone, and let \(f:S\to Y\) and \(\bar x\in S\). (a) If \(f\) is \((-C)\)-quasiconvex at \(\bar x\) and has a directional variation at \(\bar x\) with respect to \(\widehat C\) and \(Y\setminus C\), then \(f\) is differentiably \(C\)-quasiconvex at \(\bar x\). (b) If \(f\) is differentiably \(C\)-quasiconvex at \(\bar x\) and has a directional variation at \(\bar x\) with respect to \(C\), then \(f\) is \((-C)\)-quasiconvex at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-cone quasiconvexity implies differentiable cone quasiconvexity under the first directional-variation hypothesis; the reverse implication holds under directional variation with respect to the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&[f\text{ is }(-C)\text{-quasiconvex and has directional variation w.r.t. }\widehat C\text{ and }Y\setminus C]\Rightarrow[f\text{ is differentiably }C\text{-quasiconvex}],\\&[f\text{ is differentiably }C\text{-quasiconvex and has directional variation w.r.t. }C]\Rightarrow[f\text{ is }(-C)\text{-quasiconvex}].\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line-restriction and continuous one-dimensional characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the general line test with the monotonicity characterization for continuous functions of one real variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if its restriction to every affine line intersecting \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is quasiconvex on the induced one-dimensional domain. Moreover, a continuous \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex if and only if it is nondecreasing, is nonincreasing, or there exists \(c\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(f\) is nonincreasing for \(t\leq c\) and nondecreasing for \(t\geq c\). Any global minimizer of \(f\) can be chosen as \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconvexity can be checked by restricting a function to every affine line. A continuous real function is quasiconvex exactly when it is monotone or decreases up to a point and then increases; any global minimizer can serve as the turning point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff f|_L\text{ is quasiconvex for every affine line }L\text{ meeting }\operatorname{dom}f;\quad f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\text{ continuous and quasiconvex}\iff f\text{ is monotone or valley-shaped as specified}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard quasiconvex optimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes equivalent convex replacement of quasiconvex constraints and level-set reduction to convex problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A standard quasiconvex optimization problem has the form \(\min_x f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(Ax=b\), where \(f_0\) is quasiconvex and the constraint functions \(f_i\) are convex. A quasiconvex constraint may be replaced by a convex constraint function having the same zero-sublevel set. Because the objective's sublevel sets are convex, solving the quasiconvex problem can be reduced to a sequence of convex level-feasibility problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex optimization problem minimizes a quasiconvex objective subject to convex inequalities and affine equalities. Quasiconvex constraints may be represented by convex functions with the same zero-sublevel set, and objective level tests reduce the problem to a sequence of convex feasibility problems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}f_0(x)\text{ admits reduction through convex sublevel-feasibility problems }\{x\in X\mid f_0(x)\le t\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise generalized convexity implies differential cone-quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vector optimization under the componentwise order with inequality and equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m,\ g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k,\ h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p, and let S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\le 0\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}. Fix \bar{x}\in S and define I(\bar{x})=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:g_i(\bar{x})=0\}. Assume \mathbb{R}^m is ordered componentwise, f,g,h have partial derivatives at \bar{x}, every f_j is pseudoconvex at \bar{x}, and h_j,-h_j and every g_i with i\in I(\bar{x}) are quasiconvex at \bar{x}. Then (f,g,h) is differentiably C-quasiconvex at \bar{x}, where C=(-\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{R}_+^m))\times\bigl(-\mathbb{R}_+^k+\operatorname{cone}\{g(\bar{x})\}-\operatorname{cone}\{g(\bar{x})\}\bigr)\times\{0_{\mathbb{R}^p}\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the componentwise order, pseudoconvex objective components and quasiconvex active inequality and signed equality components make the combined objective-constraint map differentiably cone-quasiconvex at the feasible point for the stated product set C.
assumptions_latex: h_j,-h_j\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\text{ and }g_i\ (i\in I(\bar{x}))\text{ are quasiconvex at }\bar{x}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f,g,h)\text{ is differentiably }C\text{-quasiconvex at }\bar{x},\quad C=(-\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{R}_+^m))\times\bigl(-\mathbb{R}_+^k+\operatorname{cone}\{g(\bar{x})\}-\operatorname{cone}\{g(\bar{x})\}\bigr)\times\{0_{\mathbb{R}^p}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvex, quasiconcave, and quasilinear functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set definitions and their immediate relationships for real-valued functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(S_\alpha=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). The function \(f\) is quasiconvex iff \(\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(S_\alpha\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), are convex. It is quasiconcave iff \(-f\) is quasiconvex, equivalently iff every superlevel set \(\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)\geq\alpha\}\) is convex. It is quasilinear iff it is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave; then its domain and every level set \(\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)=\alpha\}\) are convex. Every convex function is quasiconvex, but the converse is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasiconvex when its domain and every sublevel set are convex. It is quasiconcave when every superlevel set is convex and quasilinear when it is both. Quasilinear functions have convex domains and level sets. Convexity implies quasiconvexity, but not conversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ quasiconvex}\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ and all }S_\alpha\text{ are convex};\quad f\text{ quasiconcave}\iff -f\text{ is quasiconvex};\quad f\text{ quasilinear}\Rightarrow \operatorname{dom}f\text{ and every }\{f=\alpha\}\text{ are convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvex local-global failure and strict first-order sufficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The gradient condition is sufficient but not necessary and differs essentially from the convex criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quasiconvex optimization problem may have a local minimizer that is not globally optimal, even for unconstrained minimization of a quasiconvex function on \(\mathbb R\). Let \(X\) be its feasible set and let the quasiconvex objective \(f_0\) be differentiable. If \(x\in X\) and \(
abla f_0(x)^T(y-x)>0\) for every \(y\in X\setminus\{x\}\), then \(x\) is globally optimal. This condition is sufficient but not necessary; an optimal point need not satisfy it. Unlike the convex nonstrict criterion, the strict inequality cannot hold with \(
abla f_0(x)=0\) when \(X\setminus\{x\}
e\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local optimality need not imply global optimality in quasiconvex minimization. For a differentiable quasiconvex objective, however, a feasible point is globally optimal if its gradient has strictly positive inner product with every nonzero feasible displacement. This test is sufficient only, may fail at an optimizer, and in a nontrivial feasible set requires a nonzero gradient.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\arg\min_{z\in X}f_0(z),\quad\text{but the displayed condition is not necessary; local optimality alone need not imply global optimality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiable First-Order Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable test for quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if \[f(y)\le f(x)\Longrightarrow \nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\le0\qquad(x,y\in C).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff[f(y)\le f(x)\Rightarrow\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\le0].\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-sublevel-set characterization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space, let \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and define \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The level-set encoding of scalar quasiconvexity, including empty and full sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is level-set quasiconvex when
\[L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\]
is convex for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The sublevel family is nested: if \(\alpha\le\beta\), then \(L_\alpha(f)\subseteq L_\beta(f)\). Empty sublevel sets and \(C\) itself count as convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is level-set quasiconvex when every one of its real sublevel sets is convex. These sublevel sets form a nested family as the threshold increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R:\quad L_\alpha(f)\text{ is convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition is equivalent to \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is closed as well as convex.
special_cases_latex: For an indicator \(\delta_D\) on \(C\), level-set quasiconvexity is equivalent to convexity of \(D\).
A monotone function on a real interval has interval sublevel sets and is therefore level-set quasiconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Feasibility regions of inequalities \(f(x)\le\alpha\) are convex at every threshold.
The minimum-level set is convex whenever a minimum is attained.
boundary_notes: Convexity of one selected sublevel set does not establish quasiconvexity; every real threshold is quantified.
Convex sublevel sets do not imply convexity of the epigraph or the ordinary Jensen inequality.

notation.meaning: Alpha-sublevel set of f relative to C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation of Quasiconvex Sublevel Sets by Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, nesting compatibility, nonuniqueness, and canonical indicator and distance constructions for a level-parameterized convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be quasiconvex and define \(S_t=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\le t\}\) for \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). For every \(t\), there exists a convex extended-real-valued function \(\phi_t\) such that \[f(x)\le t\iff \phi_t(x)\le0.\] A universal choice is \(\phi_t=\delta_{S_t}\), where \(\delta_{S_t}(x)=0\) for \(x\in S_t\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Every representing family satisfies \(\phi_t(x)\le0\Rightarrow\phi_s(x)\le0\) whenever \(s\ge t\); the stronger condition \(\phi_s(x)\le\phi_t(x)\) for \(s\ge t\) is sufficient. If \(S_t\) is closed, then \(\phi_t(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S_t)\) is another valid choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each sublevel set of a quasiconvex function can be represented as the zero-sublevel set of a convex extended-real-valued function. Its indicator function always supplies such a representation. Represented zero-sublevel sets must remain nested as the level increases, while pointwise nonincrease of the representing functions is a sufficient stronger condition. For closed sublevel sets, distance to the sublevel set gives another representation, demonstrating nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall t\in\mathbb{R}\ \exists\text{ convex }\phi_t:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ such that }f(x)\le t\iff\phi_t(x)\le0;\quad \phi_t=\delta_{S_t}\text{ always works, and if }S_t\text{ is closed then }\phi_t=\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,S_t)\text{ also works}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and uniform quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global strict and uniform quasiconvexity on the effective domain of a proper scalar function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex when, for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and all \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
It is uniformly quasiconvex with modulus \(\phi\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)+t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity replaces the quasiconvex max inequality by a strict inequality between distinct endpoints. Uniform quasiconvexity strengthens it by a positive deficit controlled by the endpoint distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{uniform quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{strict quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{quasiconvexity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict quasiconvexity says every open segment between distinct domain points lies strictly below the larger endpoint value.
Uniform quasiconvexity quantifies this decrease through \(t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\).
special_cases_latex: Every strictly convex function is strictly quasiconvex.
A strictly monotone proper function on an interval is strictly quasiconvex, although it need not be strictly convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly quasiconvex function has at most one global minimizer.
Uniform quasiconvexity excludes nontrivial constant segments in the effective domain.
boundary_notes: Strict quasiconvexity is weaker than strict convexity.
Strict convexity of every sublevel set is not, without qualifications, interchangeable with the displayed strict max inequality.
The local-on-\(C\) versions quantify only over endpoints in a specified subset \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and Uniform Quasiconvexity, Globally and on a Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-real-valued functions on a Hilbert space, including global and subset-restricted strengthened quasiconvexity; extraction-grounded evidence without verified full-text span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(\varnothing\neq C\subset\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at \(0\). For \(z_\alpha=\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\): (i) \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex if \(f(z_\alpha)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); (ii) \(f\) is uniformly quasiconvex with modulus \(\phi\) if \(f(z_\alpha)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); (iii) and (iv) strict and uniform quasiconvexity on \(C\) are defined by the respective conditions with \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity imposes a strict segment maximum inequality for distinct points. Uniform quasiconvexity strengthens the non-strict inequality by a modulus term. The corresponding notions on a nonempty subset restrict the endpoint quantifiers to that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{aligned}f\text{ strictly quasiconvex}&\iff(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in(0,1))\,[x\neq y\Rightarrow f(z_\alpha)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}],\\f\text{ uniformly quasiconvex with modulus }\phi&\iff(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in(0,1))\;f(z_\alpha)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\},\end{aligned}\) with the corresponding definitions on \(C\) obtained by restricting \(x,y\) to \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Sublevel Convergence of Quasiconvex Minimizing Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conclusions for a fixed minimizing sequence: existence and optimality of weak cluster points, weak convergence under strict quasiconvexity, and strong convergence under uniform quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and quasiconvex, and let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be a minimizing sequence of \(f\). Suppose that there exists \(\xi\in(\inf f(\mathcal H),+\infty)\) such that \(C=\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\xi}f\) is bounded. Then: (i) \((x_n)\) has a weak sequential cluster point, and every such point minimizes \(f\); (ii) if \(f+\iota_C\) is strictly quasiconvex, then \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\); (iii) if \(f+\iota_C\) is uniformly quasiconvex, then \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x\) and \(x_n\to x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sublevel above the infimum guarantees weak cluster points of a minimizing sequence, all of which are minimizers. Strict quasiconvexity on that sublevel gives uniqueness and weak convergence, while uniform quasiconvexity gives uniqueness and strong convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and quasiconvex.
\((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a minimizing sequence of \(f\).
There exists \(\xi\in(\inf f(\mathcal H),+\infty)\) such that \(C=\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\xi}f\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence has a weak sequential cluster point and every such point lies in \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\); under strict quasiconvexity, \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{x\}\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\); under uniform quasiconvexity, \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{x\}\) and \(x_n\to x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly convex, then for distinct \(x,y\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)<(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\},\] so \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity implies strict quasiconvexity, but the converse fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity Implies Strict Quasiconvexity

children.title: Semistrict Quasiconvexity
children.top_down_role: Semistrict quasiconvex regimes between ordinary or strict variants.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex precisely when unequal endpoint values imply strict decrease from the larger value at every interior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unequal-endpoint convention; some sources call this semistrict quasiconvexity.

source_refs.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on \(C\) if, whenever \(x,y\in C\), \(f(x)<f(y)\), and \(t\in(0,1)\), one has \[f((1-t)x+ty)<f(y).\] Equivalently, whenever \(f(x)\neq f(y)\), every interior point of \([x,y]\) has value strictly below \(\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\). No strict inequality is imposed when the endpoint values are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistrict quasiconvexity enforces strict improvement from the worse endpoint only when the two endpoint values differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Quasiconvexity

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistrictness Alone Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology-sensitive boundary for the seed's unequal-endpoint-only convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\ne0\). It satisfies the unequal-endpoint semistrict condition but is not quasiconvex because \(f(-1)=f(1)=0<f(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the unequal-endpoint-only definition, semistrict quasiconvexity does not imply ordinary quasiconvexity.
assumptions_latex: Semistrictness uses the packet's unequal-endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex but not quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrictness Alone Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness Implication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between the two strictness regimes under the packet's conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every strictly quasiconvex function is semistrictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity implies semistrict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Implication

children.title: Minimizer-Set Consequences
children.top_down_role: Minimizer geometry associated with strengthened quasiconvexity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
The finite minimum \(m=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex; if \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, this set is a singleton.

notation.meaning: Set of global minimizers of f on C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convexity of the attained minimizer set from uniqueness under strict quasiconvexity.

source_refs.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) be finite and let \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). If \(f\) is quasiconvex, then \(M\) is convex. If \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, then \(M\) contains exactly one point. Semistrict quasiconvexity alone does not imply uniqueness of an attained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attained minimizer set of a quasiconvex function is convex. Strict quasiconvexity makes it a singleton, whereas semistrict quasiconvexity alone need not imply uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer-Set Consequences

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistrictness Does Not Give Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness for the seed's nonuniqueness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On any nontrivial convex set \(C\), a constant function \(f\equiv c\) is semistrictly quasiconvex under the unequal-endpoint convention, while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_C f=C\) is not a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant function is semistrictly quasiconvex but has every feasible point as a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex and }\operatorname*{argmin}_C f=C.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrictness Does Not Give Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistrict Local Minima Are Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global consequence of the unequal-endpoint semistrict condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be semistrictly quasiconvex. Every local minimizer of \(f\) relative to \(C\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a semistrictly quasiconvex function, a local minimum cannot be nonglobal.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Local Minima Are Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of a Minimizer of a Strictly Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: At-most-one-minimizer consequence of strict convexity for an extended-real-valued function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and strictly convex. Then \(f\) has at most one minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper strictly convex function on a Hilbert space has at most one minimizer; existence is not asserted.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{card}(\operatorname{Argmin}f)\le 1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of a Constrained Quasiconvex Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two alternative sufficient-condition regimes for at-most-one minimizer over a convex subset of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex, and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Suppose either (i) \(f+\iota_C\) is strictly quasiconvex, or (ii) \(f\) is convex, \(\operatorname{int}C\cap\operatorname{Argmin}f=\varnothing\), and \(C\) is strictly convex in the sense that \(x,y\in C\) and \(x\neq y\) imply \((x+y)/2\in\operatorname{int}C\). Then \(f\) has at most one minimizer over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex function has at most one minimizer over a convex feasible set meeting its domain if either the extended objective is strictly quasiconvex, or the objective is convex, no global minimizer lies in the feasible set's interior, and the feasible set is strictly convex.
assumptions_latex: Either \(f+\iota_C\) is strictly quasiconvex, or \(f\) is convex, \(\operatorname{int}C\cap\operatorname{Argmin}f=\varnothing\), and \((\forall x,y\in C)[x\neq y\Rightarrow (x+y)/2\in\operatorname{int}C]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{card}(\operatorname{Argmin}_{x\in C}f(x))\le 1\).

children.title: Quasiconvex Preservation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Level-set and monotonicity-based preservation mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure system generated by quasiconvexity-preserving operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Let \(\mathcal F\) be a collection of quasiconvex extended-real functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar quasiconvexity under pointwise supremum, monotone composition, affine precomposition, and partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quasiconvex preservation closure \(\operatorname{Qcl}(\mathcal F)\) is the smallest class containing \(\mathcal F\) and closed under the following well-defined operations: pointwise suprema \(x\mapsto\sup_i f_i(x)\); compositions \(h\circ f\) with nondecreasing \(h\); affine precomposition \(x\mapsto f(Ax+b)\); and partial minimization
\[g(x)=\inf_{y\in D}F(x,y),\]
where \(D\) is convex and \(F\) is jointly quasiconvex in \((x,y)\). Every member produced by these rules is quasiconvex on its induced convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex preservation calculus is the smallest function class generated from given quasiconvex functions by pointwise suprema, nondecreasing scalar compositions, affine precomposition, and partial minimization over a convex auxiliary set under joint quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_i,F\text{ quasiconvex}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sup_i f_i,\ h\circ f,\ f\circ(A\cdot+b),\ \inf_{y\in D}F(\cdot,y)\text{ are quasiconvex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a supremum, \(L_\alpha(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_iL_\alpha(f_i)\).
For partial minimization, the sublevel set is the projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates of the corresponding joint sublevel set, with closure issues handled by the exact induced-domain convention.
special_cases_latex: A finite maximum of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex.
Truncation \(x\mapsto\min\{f(x),\eta\}\) is quasiconvex for quasiconvex \(f\).
Every nonnegative weighted maximum of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Many quasiconvex models can be verified entirely through convexity of induced sublevel sets.
Increasing reparameterizations preserve minimizers and quasiconvexity.
boundary_notes: Arbitrary sums and pointwise infima of quasiconvex functions are not general preservation rules.
For partial minimization, joint quasiconvexity is required; separate quasiconvexity is insufficient.
A decreasing outer function generally converts quasiconvexity toward quasiconcavity rather than preserving it.

notation.meaning: Quasiconvex closure generated by the listed operations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Maximum Preservation of Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of quasiconvex functions under finite pointwise maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quasiconvex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then the pointwise maximum \[f(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\] is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise maximum of finitely many quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f:=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\text{ is quasiconvex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvexity Preservation under Composition and Change of Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation rules for monotone scalar postcomposition and affine or positive-denominator linear-fractional precomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quasiconvex and let \(h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be nondecreasing. Then \(h\circ g\) is quasiconvex. If \(f\) is quasiconvex and the dimensions are compatible, then \(x\mapsto f(Ax+b)\) is quasiconvex on its natural domain. Moreover, \(x\mapsto f\!\left((Ax+b)/(c^Tx+d)\right)\) is quasiconvex on \(D=\{x\mid c^Tx+d>0,\ (Ax+b)/(c^Tx+d)\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondecreasing scalar function composed after a quasiconvex function preserves quasiconvexity. Affine precomposition also preserves quasiconvexity, as does linear-fractional precomposition on the domain where the denominator is positive and the transformed point belongs to the original function's domain.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is quasiconvex and }A,b,c,d\text{ have compatible dimensions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\circ g,\quad x\mapsto f(Ax+b),\quad\text{and}\quad x\mapsto f\!\left(\frac{Ax+b}{c^Tx+d}\right)\bigg|_D\ \text{are quasiconvex}.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).

If \(\phi\) is strictly increasing, composition also preserves strict quasiconvexity and semistrict quasiconvexity under the stated segment definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition with a nondecreasing scalar function preserves quasiconvexity; strict increase also preserves the stated strict and semistrict regimes.
