knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure for Decreasing Outer Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that arbitrary scalar outer composition does not preserve quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(\phi(s)=-s\). Then \(f\) is quasiconvex, but \((\phi\circ f)(x)=-x^2\) is not quasiconvex because \[\{x:-x^2\le-a\}=(-\infty,-\sqrt a]\cup[\sqrt a,\infty)\] is nonconvex for every \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing outer function can convert a quasiconvex function into a nonquasiconvex one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex but }\phi\circ f\text{ is not quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Failure for Decreasing Outer Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat Outer Maps Lose Strictness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes nondecreasing from strictly increasing outer transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(\mathbb R\), but the constant nondecreasing map \(\phi(s)=0\) makes \(\phi\circ f\) constant and therefore not strictly quasiconvex on any nontrivial interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flat portions of a nondecreasing outer map can destroy strict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex but }\phi\circ f\text{ is not}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Outer Maps Lose Strictness

children.title: Affine Precomposition
children.top_down_role: Quasiconvexity preservation under affine changes of variables.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(W\) are real vector spaces, and \(C\subseteq W\) is convex.
\(A:V\to W\) is linear, \(b\in W\), \(T:V\to W\) is defined by \(T(x)=Ax+b\), and \(D=T^{-1}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\) is quasiconvex on the convex set \(D\).

notation.meaning: Affine precomposition map from V to W
Natural inverse-image domain of the composition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to affine maps between real vector spaces on the natural inverse-image domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be real vector spaces, let \(C\subseteq W\) be convex, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex. For a linear map \(A:V\to W\) and \(b\in W\), define \(T(x)=Ax+b\) and \(D=T^{-1}(C)\). Then \(D\) is convex and \(f\circ T\) is quasiconvex on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing a quasiconvex function with an affine map preserves quasiconvexity on the map's convex natural inverse-image domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Precomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness and Injectivity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine-map condition for preserving strict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be strictly quasiconvex and \(T\) affine on a convex set \(D\). Then \(f\circ T\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(D\) if and only if \(T|_D\) is injective. Indeed, if \(T(x)=T(y)\) for distinct \(x,y\in D\), the composite is constant on \([x,y]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition preserves strict quasiconvexity exactly when the affine map is injective on the domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\text{ is strictly quasiconvex on }D\iff T|_D\text{ is injective}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness and Injectivity Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistrict Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine pullback variant for the unequal-endpoint semistrict regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\) and \(T\) is affine, then \(f\circ T\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on the convex set \(D\). No injectivity assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any affine precomposition preserves semistrict quasiconvexity; injectivity is needed only for the strict regime.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex on }D.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Affine Precomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-Image Level Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set mechanism underlying affine pullback preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g=f\circ T\), where \(T(x)=Ax+b\), one has \[\{x\in D:g(x)\le\alpha\}=T^{-1}(\{z\in C:f(z)\le\alpha\})\] for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sublevel of an affine composite is the affine inverse image of the corresponding outer sublevel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha(g)=T^{-1}(L_\alpha(f))\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Level Sets

children.title: Supremum Preservation
children.top_down_role: Common-level-set mechanisms supporting supremum constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be nonempty and let \(f_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex for every \(i\in I\). Then the pointwise supremum \(g:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), defined by \(g(x)=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), is quasiconvex. No finiteness of \(I\), continuity, or attainment of the supremum is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of any nonempty family of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex, without continuity or attainment assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Supremum Preservation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Infimum Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that upper-envelope preservation does not extend to lower envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine functions \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) are quasiconvex, but \(h(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=-|x|\) is not quasiconvex because \[\{x:h(x)\le-1\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\] is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise minima of quasiconvex functions need not be quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_1,f_2\text{ are quasiconvex but }h\text{ is not}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Infimum Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Suprema May Lose Strictness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between finite maxima and arbitrary suprema in the strict regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-1,1]\), let \(f_n(x)=(x^2-1)/n\) for \(n\ge1\). Every \(f_n\) is strictly convex and hence strictly quasiconvex, but \(\sup_{n\ge1}f_n(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\), so the supremum is not strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary supremum of strictly quasiconvex functions can lose strictness even though it remains quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\text{ is strictly quasiconvex for every }n,\text{ but }\sup_n f_n\equiv0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Suprema May Lose Strictness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Maxima Preserve Strict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictness variant for finite upper envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are strictly quasiconvex on a convex set \(C\), then \(g=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite pointwise maximum of strictly quasiconvex functions remains strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maxima Preserve Strict Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-convexity, log-concavity, and reciprocal duality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive scalar functions on convex Euclidean domains; zero-valued log-concave extensions are excluded from the reciprocal statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is log-convex when \(\log f\) is convex, equivalently
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^t f(y)^{1-t}\]
for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). It is log-concave when \(\log f\) is concave, equivalently the displayed inequality is reversed. Reciprocal duality is
\[f\text{ is log-convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1/f\text{ is log-concave}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-convex or log-concave according as its logarithm is convex or concave. Equivalently, its value at a convex combination lies below or above the weighted geometric mean of its endpoint values. Taking the reciprocal exchanges the two classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\log f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow-\log f=\log(1/f)\text{ concave}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is log-convex if and only if \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^tf(y)^{1-t}\).
\(f\) is log-concave if and only if \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\ge f(x)^tf(y)^{1-t}\).
special_cases_latex: Every exponential-affine function \(f(x)=e^{a^{\mathsf T}x+b}\) is both log-convex and log-concave.
On \(\mathbb R_{++}\), \(x\mapsto x^p\) is log-convex for \(p\le0\) and log-concave for \(p\ge0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every positive log-convex function is convex and quasiconvex.
Every positive log-concave function is quasiconcave.
Products and positive powers of log-convex functions remain log-convex whenever their domains are compatible.
boundary_notes: Strict positivity is required for the ordinary logarithm and reciprocal duality.
A nonnegative function that vanishes may be treated as extended log-concave by setting \(\log0=-\infty\), but its reciprocal is then not finite.
Log-concavity does not generally imply ordinary concavity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended Log-Concavity and Positive Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard zero-valued extension of the seed's positive-valued convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:C\to[0,\infty)\), adopt \(\log0=-\infty\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-concave and log-convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions, direct characterization, reciprocal correspondence, and basic curvature implications for log-concave and log-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). When \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the function \(f\) is log-concave if \(\log f\) is concave and log-convex if \(\log f\) is convex. Zero values may be admitted for log-concavity by setting \(\log 0=-\infty\) and requiring the resulting extended-value function \(\log f\) to be concave. If \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and \(f>0\) on its domain, then \(f\) is log-concave if and only if \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\geq f(x)^\theta f(y)^{1-\theta}\] for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and all \(\theta\in[0,1]\). For positive \(f\), log-convexity of \(f\) is equivalent to log-concavity of \(1/f\). Every log-convex function is convex and quasiconvex; every nonnegative concave function is log-concave; and every log-concave function is quasiconcave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-concave or log-convex when its logarithm is concave or convex, respectively. Log-concavity can include zero values by defining log zero as negative infinity. For a positive function on a convex domain, log-concavity is equivalent to its value at each convex combination being at least the corresponding weighted geometric mean. Reciprocation exchanges positive log-convex and log-concave functions. Log-convex functions are convex and quasiconvex, nonnegative concave functions are log-concave, and log-concave functions are quasiconcave.
assumptions_latex: f(x)>0\quad\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}f\quad\text{for the ordinary logarithmic definitions and reciprocal equivalence}
\operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }f>0\text{ on }\operatorname{dom}f\quad\text{for the weighted-geometric-mean characterization}
\log 0=-\infty\quad\text{when zero values are admitted in the extended-value definition of log-concavity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is log-concave}\iff f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\geq f(x)^\theta f(y)^{1-\theta}\quad\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall\theta\in[0,1];\qquad f\text{ is log-convex}\iff 1/f\text{ is log-concave};\qquad f\text{ log-convex}\Rightarrow f\text{ convex and quasiconvex};\qquad f\text{ nonnegative and concave}\Rightarrow f\text{ log-concave};\qquad f\text{ log-concave}\Rightarrow f\text{ quasiconcave}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Functions are nonnegative and are interpreted using extended logarithms when zero values are admitted. All displayed integrals are assumed finite on their effective domains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional log-convex and log-concave functions under pointwise multiplication, positive scaling, summation, integration, marginalization, and convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The log-domain preservation calculus consists of the following closure rules. If \(f_i:C\to(0,+\infty)\) are log-convex and \(a_i>0\), then \(\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\) and \(\sum_i f_i\) are log-convex. If \(f_i:C\to[0,+\infty)\) are log-concave and \(a_i>0\), then \(\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\) is log-concave. If \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to[0,+\infty)\) is jointly log-concave and \(g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^m}F(x,y)\,dy\) is finite and positive, then \(g\) is log-concave. Hence marginals of log-concave densities and convolutions \((f*g)(x)=\int f(x-y)g(y)\,dy\) are log-concave. If \(F(x,y)\) is log-convex in \(x\) for every \(y\) and its integral is finite, then \(x\mapsto\int F(x,y)\,dy\) is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The calculus records operations that preserve convexity or concavity after taking logarithms. Positive weighted products preserve both log-convexity and log-concavity; finite sums preserve log-convexity but generally not log-concavity. Integration preserves log-convexity when the integrand is log-convex in the retained variable. Joint log-concavity is preserved by integrating out variables, which includes marginalization and convolution.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and every product, sum, or integral is defined on its stated effective domain.
For the marginal rule, \(F\) is jointly log-concave and \(0<\int F(x,y)\,dy<+\infty\) at the points under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated products, sums, parameter integrals, marginals, and convolutions remain in their indicated logarithmic-curvature classes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For positive \(h\), log-convexity means \(\log h\) is convex, while log-concavity means \(\log h\) is concave.
The marginal rule is the functional form of the Prékopa preservation principle.
special_cases_latex: If \(p(x,y)\) is a log-concave probability density, then \(p_X(x)=\int p(x,y)\,dy\) is log-concave.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are log-concave, then their convolution \(f*g\) is log-concave.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Laplace transform \(z\mapsto\int p(x)e^{-z^Tx}\,dx\) of a nonnegative function is log-convex on its finite domain.
Positive scaling does not alter log-convexity or log-concavity.
boundary_notes: A sum of log-concave functions need not be log-concave.
For log-concave integration, separate log-concavity in each variable is not a substitute for joint log-concavity.

notation.meaning: A marginal density obtained by integrating out other coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal and Power Class Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power transformations of strictly positive logarithmic curvature classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to(0,\infty)\). A positive power \(f^\alpha\), \(\alpha>0\), preserves whether \(f\) is log-concave or log-convex. A negative power reverses the class: if \(\alpha<0\), then a log-concave \(f\) gives a log-convex \(f^\alpha\), and a log-convex \(f\) gives a log-concave \(f^\alpha\). In particular, reciprocation exchanges the two classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive powers preserve logarithmic curvature, while negative powers and reciprocals exchange log-concavity and log-convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive powers preserve the class and negative powers reverse it.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal and Power Class Exchange

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijections between additive and strictly positive multiplicative curvature descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u:C\to\mathbb R\), \(e^u\) is log-concave exactly when \(u\) is concave, and \(e^u\) is log-convex exactly when \(u\) is convex. Conversely, every strictly positive log-concave or log-convex function has the respective representation \(f=e^u\) with \(u=\log f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponentiation converts concave functions to positive log-concave functions and convex functions to positive log-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is concave iff \(e^u\) is log-concave, and convex iff \(e^u\) is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Parameterizations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal Class Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation exchanging the two positive logarithmic curvature classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to(0,\infty)\), then \[f\text{ is log-concave}\Longleftrightarrow f^{-1}\text{ is log-convex},\qquad f\text{ is log-convex}\Longleftrightarrow f^{-1}\text{ is log-concave}.\] More generally, a positive power preserves the logarithmic curvature sign, whereas a negative power reverses it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocals and negative powers exchange log-concavity with log-convexity; positive powers preserve the class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), \(f^\alpha\) retains the class; for \(\alpha<0\), it belongs to the opposite class.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Class Exchange

children.title: Preservation Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Addition and Maximum Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of two common pointwise aggregation operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(f(x)=e^x\) and \(g(x)=e^{-x}\) are log-affine, hence log-concave. Their sum \(h(x)=e^x+e^{-x}\) is not log-concave because \(h(0)=2<h(-1)^{1/2}h(1)^{1/2}=e+e^{-1}\). Their maximum is \(\max\{f,g\}=e^{|x|}\), whose logarithm \(|x|\) is not concave. Thus neither pointwise addition nor pointwise maximum generally preserves log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two log-affine functions have a sum and maximum that both fail log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise sums and maxima do not generally preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.title: Addition and Maximum Failures

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-Power Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp sign boundary for nonnegative-power preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=e^{-x^2}\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R\), but its reciprocal \(f(x)^{-1}=e^{x^2}\) is not log-concave. Thus negative powers do not generally preserve log-concavity; they reverse logarithmic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocating a Gaussian-shaped log-concave function produces a log-convex, non-log-concave function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negative powers do not universally preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Power Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Log-Concavity Is Essential for Marginals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slice-wise log-concavity in the integrated variable does not suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) and \(F(x,y)=\mathbf1_A(x)e^{-y^2}\). For every fixed \(x\), the function \(y\mapsto F(x,y)\) is log-concave, but \[g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x,y)\,dy=\sqrt\pi\,\mathbf1_A(x)\] is not log-concave because its positive support is disconnected. Thus log-concavity only in the integrated variable cannot replace joint log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slice-wise log-concavity in the eliminated variable can produce a marginal with disconnected support; Prékopa requires joint log-concavity.
assumptions_latex: Log-concavity permits the identically zero slice under the extended-log convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Log-concavity in the integrated variable separately is insufficient for marginal preservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Log-Concavity Is Essential for Marginals

assumptions_latex: Log-concavity is interpreted for functions taking values in \([0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum of two log-concave functions need not be log-concave.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity relative to a cone-induced order
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone, and define \(u\preccurlyeq_K v\) by \(v-u\in K\). Let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vector-valued convexity under the partial order induced by a closed, convex, pointed, solid cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is \(K\)-convex on \(C\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preccurlyeq_K \theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y),\] equivalently, \(\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y)-F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\in K\). It is strictly \(K\)-convex if the difference belongs to \(\operatorname{int}K\) whenever \(x\ne y\) and \(0<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping is cone-ordered convex when its value at every convex combination is below the corresponding convex combination of its endpoint values in the partial order induced by the cone. Strict cone convexity requires the order difference to lie in the cone interior for distinct endpoints and an interior mixing weight.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preccurlyeq_K\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(w^TF\) is an ordinary convex function for every \(w\in K^*\).
If \(F\) is differentiable on an open convex domain, \(K\)-convexity is equivalent to \(F(y)\succcurlyeq_K F(x)+DF(x)(y-x)\) for all \(x,y\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), \(K\)-convexity is componentwise convexity.
For \(K=\mathbb S_+^m\), the definition gives matrix convexity under the Loewner order.
For \(m=1\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+\), it reduces to ordinary scalar convexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every restriction of a \(K\)-convex mapping to a line segment is \(K\)-convex.
Nonnegative dual-cone scalarizations provide scalar convex certificates.
boundary_notes: The induced order is generally partial rather than total.
Strict \(K\)-convexity requires \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\); alternative relative-interior conventions are outside this definition.

notation.meaning: Cone order defined by membership of the difference in \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and order inversion of the inverse-matrix mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix inversion on the open convex cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices, ordered by the Loewner order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{sym}}^{n\times n}\) be the open convex set of positive-definite matrices and let \(J:P\to P\) be given by \(J(A)=A^{-1}\). For all \(A_0,A_1\in P\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\),
\[
J((1-\lambda)A_0+\lambda A_1)\preccurlyeq(1-\lambda)J(A_0)+\lambda J(A_1).
\]
Moreover,
\[
A_0\preccurlyeq A_1\iff A_0^{-1}\succcurlyeq A_1^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive-definite cone, matrix inversion is convex in the Loewner order and reverses that order: the inverse of a convex combination is bounded above by the corresponding convex combination of inverses, and A0 is below A1 exactly when its inverse is above the inverse of A1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J((1-\lambda)A_0+\lambda A_1)\preccurlyeq(1-\lambda)J(A_0)+\lambda J(A_1),\qquad A_0\preccurlyeq A_1\iff A_0^{-1}\succcurlyeq A_1^{-1}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity with Respect to a Proper Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weak and strict order-preserving and order-reversing scalar functions under a proper-cone order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a proper cone. A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(K\)-nondecreasing if \(x\preccurlyeq_K y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)\), and \(K\)-increasing if \(x\preccurlyeq_K y\) and \(x\neq y\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)\). It is \(K\)-nonincreasing if \(x\preccurlyeq_K y\Rightarrow f(x)\geq f(y)\), and \(K\)-decreasing if \(x\preccurlyeq_K y\) and \(x\neq y\Rightarrow f(x)>f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the order induced by a proper cone K, a scalar function is K-nondecreasing when it preserves the weak order and K-increasing when comparable distinct points give a strict increase. K-nonincreasing and K-decreasing reverse the corresponding scalar inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}x\preccurlyeq_Ky&\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)&&\text{for }K\text{-nondecreasing},\\x\preccurlyeq_Ky,\ x\neq y&\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)&&\text{for }K\text{-increasing},\\x\preccurlyeq_Ky&\Rightarrow f(x)\geq f(y)&&\text{for }K\text{-nonincreasing},\\x\preccurlyeq_Ky,\ x\neq y&\Rightarrow f(x)>f(y)&&\text{for }K\text{-decreasing}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory's Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-hull representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). For every \(y\in\operatorname{conv}(X)\), there exist an integer \(m\le n+1\), points \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in X\), and scalars \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(y=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of a subset of n-dimensional Euclidean space is a convex combination of at most n plus one points of that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists m\le n+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in X,\ \exists\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\ \land\ y=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Ordered Convexity and Strict Cone-Ordered Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vector-valued convexity relative to the generalized inequality induced by a proper cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a proper cone. A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(K\)-convex if, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preccurlyeq_K\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).\] It is strictly \(K\)-convex if \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\prec_K\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)\] whenever \(x\neq y\) and \(0<\theta<1\). For \(m=1\) and \(K=\mathbb{R}_+\), these notions reduce to ordinary convexity and strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued function is K-convex when its value at every convex combination is below the corresponding combination of its values in the order induced by K. Strict K-convexity requires strict order for distinct endpoints and an interior mixing parameter. The scalar nonnegative-cone case is ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)&\preccurlyeq_K\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)&&\forall x,y,\ \theta\in[0,1],\\f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)&\prec_K\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)&&\forall x\neq y,\ \theta\in(0,1)\text{ in the strict case}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Conditions for Cone-Order Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes weak cone-order monotonicity and gives a sufficient, non-necessary strict gradient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a proper cone and let \(f\) be differentiable on a convex domain. Then \(f\) is \(K\)-nondecreasing if and only if \(
abla f(x)\in K^*\), equivalently \(
abla f(x)\succcurlyeq_{K^*}0\), for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(
abla f(x)\succ_{K^*}0\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \(f\) is \(K\)-increasing; the converse of this strict implication need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex domain, a differentiable scalar function is nondecreasing in the order induced by K exactly when every gradient lies in the dual cone. A gradient strictly positive in the dual-cone order everywhere is sufficient for strict K-increase, but strict K-increase does not imply that gradient condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Characterization of Differentiable Cone-Ordered Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes differentiable weak and strict cone-ordered convexity through Jacobian affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a proper cone and let \(f:\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[f(y)\succcurlyeq_K f(x)+Df(x)(y-x).\] On a convex domain, \(f\) is strictly \(K\)-convex if and only if \[f(y)\succ_K f(x)+Df(x)(y-x)\] for every distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable vector-valued function is K-convex exactly when its domain is convex and every first-order affine approximation lies below the function in the K-order. On a convex domain, strict K-convexity is characterized by strict K-order domination for every distinct pair of domain points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}f\text{ is }K\text{-convex}&\iff\left[\operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)\ f(y)\succcurlyeq_K f(x)+Df(x)(y-x)\right],\\f\text{ is strictly }K\text{-convex}&\iff\left[\operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }(\forall x\neq y\in\operatorname{dom}f)\ f(y)\succ_K f(x)+Df(x)(y-x)\right].\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Cone Scalarization Characterization of Cone-Ordered Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes weak and strict cone-ordered convexity through nonnegative dual-cone scalarizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a proper cone and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Then \(f\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(x\mapsto w^Tf(x)\) is convex for every \(w\in K^*\). Moreover, \(f\) is strictly \(K\)-convex if and only if \(x\mapsto w^Tf(x)\) is strictly convex for every nonzero \(w\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued function is K-convex exactly when every scalarization by a dual-cone vector is convex. Strict K-convexity is equivalent to strict convexity of every scalarization by a nonzero dual-cone vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\iff(\forall w\in K^*)\ w^Tf\text{ is convex};\qquad f\text{ is strictly }K\text{-convex}\iff(\forall w\in K^*\setminus\{0\})\ w^Tf\text{ is strictly convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-cone scalarization family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone with dual \(K^*\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear scalarization of finite-dimensional cone-ordered mappings; the definition concerns convexity certification, not completeness of weighted-sum optimization for every Pareto point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scalarization interface of \((F,K)\) is the family \[\mathcal S_K(F)=\{\varphi_w:C\to\mathbb R\mid \varphi_w(x)=\langle w,F(x)\rangle,\ w\in K^*\}.\] The family is a complete linear certificate for cone convexity: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if every \(\varphi_w\) with \(w\in K^*\) is convex. For strict \(K\)-convexity, every nonzero \(w\in K^*\) yields a strictly convex scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalarization interface pairs a vector-valued mapping with every nonnegative linear functional from the dual cone. Cone convexity is exactly equivalent to ordinary convexity of all these scalar functions. Thus order-valued Jensen inequalities can be checked through a separating family of scalar inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a proper cone and \(K^*=\{w:\langle w,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\iff(\forall w\in K^*)\;x\mapsto\langle w,F(x)\rangle\text{ is convex}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), cone convexity is equivalent to \(\langle w,F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\rangle\le\theta\langle w,F(x)\rangle+(1-\theta)\langle w,F(y)\rangle\) for all \(w\in K^*\).
For matrix-valued \(F\) and \(K=\mathbb S_+^m\), rank-one scalarizations are \(x\mapsto z^TF(x)z\).
special_cases_latex: When \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), coordinate vectors in \(K^*\) recover the component functions of \(F\).
For a vector optimization objective, a weight \(w\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) produces the weighted-sum objective \(x\mapsto\langle w,F(x)\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A single scalarization can disprove \(K\)-convexity if it is nonconvex.
The full dual-cone family separates any Jensen residual lying outside \(K\).
boundary_notes: Using only one weight generally does not certify \(K\)-convexity.
Weighted-sum scalarization need not generate every Pareto point in a nonconvex vector optimization problem.

notation.meaning: Family of dual-cone linear scalarizations of \(F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Scalarization Does Not Detect Cone-Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of testing vector convexity with one positive scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb{R}\), \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^2\), and \(F(x)=(x^2,-x^2)\). For \(s(y)=y_1+y_2\), \((s\circ F)(x)=0\) is convex. Nevertheless, \(F\) is not \(K\)-convex: the chord residual at \(-1,1\) and \(t=\tfrac12\) is \((1,-1)\notin K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single positive scalarization can be convex even though the vector mapping is not cone-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of one positive scalarization does not imply \(K\)-convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Totality Boundary for Cone Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of when cone comparability extends to every pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cone-induced relation \(u\preceq_Kv\iff v-u\in K\), every pair of vectors in \(Y\) is comparable if and only if \[K\cup(-K)=Y.\] Thus a pointed cone may define a partial order without defining a total order; for example, \(\mathbb{R}_+^2\cup(-\mathbb{R}_+^2)\neq\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone order is total exactly when the cone or its negative contains every vector; pointedness alone does not ensure comparability.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a cone in a real vector space \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\preceq_K\) is total if and only if \(K\cup(-K)=Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incomparable vectors (1,0) and (0,1) have the same value under coordinate summation, so that scalarization loses their order information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparability, minimum, and minimality in cone orders
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone, let \(u\preccurlyeq_Kv\iff v-u\in K\), and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic boundary between scalar intuition and incompletely ordered vector codomains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two points \(u,v\in\mathbb R^m\) are \(K\)-comparable if \(u\preccurlyeq_Kv\) or \(v\preccurlyeq_Ku\); otherwise they are incomparable. A point \(u\in S\) is a minimum element if \((\forall v\in S)\ u\preccurlyeq_Kv\), equivalently \(S\subseteq u+K\). It is a minimal element if \((v\in S\text{ and }v\preccurlyeq_Ku)\Rightarrow v=u\), equivalently \((u-K)\cap S=\{u\}\). The comparability boundary is the set of pairs \((u,v)\in S^2\) with \(v-u\notin K\cup(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone orders generally leave some pairs incomparable. A minimum is below every point and, if it exists, is unique. A minimal point merely has no distinct feasible point below it, so a set may have many minimal points. The comparability boundary consists precisely of pairs whose difference belongs to neither the cone nor its negative.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and solid.
\(S\) is an arbitrary subset of the ordered vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\text{ is minimum}\iff S\subseteq u+K\), whereas \(u\text{ is minimal}\iff(u-K)\cap S=\{u\}\); incomparable pairs satisfy \(v-u\notin K\cup(-K)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Comparability of \(u,v\) is equivalent to \(v-u\in K\cup(-K)\).
Minimality excludes strict improvement in the cone order but does not require comparison with every element of \(S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+\), the order is total and minimum and minimal element coincide.
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\) with \(m>1\), componentwise tradeoffs commonly produce incomparable points.
immediate_consequences_latex: A set has at most one minimum element because the cone order is antisymmetric.
Distinct minimal elements must be mutually incomparable.
boundary_notes: Scalar notions such as \(\min S\) cannot be transferred unchanged to a partial order.
Minimality is weaker than weak Pareto minimality conventions based on \(\operatorname{int}K\); those conventions are not identified here.

notation.meaning: Set \(\{u-k:k\in K\}\) of points no greater than \(u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower- and upper-curvature regularity classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\) be a convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable where an upper-curvature condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute Hilbert-space curvature classes described by a lower modulus and an upper quadratic model; relative-curvature variants require a separate reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an increasing function \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) vanishing only at \(0\) and a constant \(L\ge0\), define \(\mathcal C_{\phi,L}(D)\) to consist of functions satisfying, for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in(0,1)\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)+\theta(1-\theta)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le \theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y),\] and, whenever \(f\) is differentiable on \(D\), \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2.\] The first inequality gives quantitative lower curvature; the second gives quantitative upper curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantitative curvature class fixes a modulus that measures the Jensen deficit from below and a constant controlling the quadratic Taylor remainder from above. Uniform convexity corresponds to a general positive modulus, strong convexity to a quadratic modulus, and gradient smoothness to the quadratic upper model.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is increasing and vanishes only at \(0\).
The upper model is imposed only where \(f\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal C_{\phi,L}(D)\) means that \(f\) has lower curvature modulus \(\phi\) and upper quadratic-curvature constant \(L\) on \(D\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong convexity with parameter \(\mu>0\) is obtained from \(\phi(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\).
For convex differentiable functions on the whole Hilbert space, the upper quadratic model is equivalent to \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f\).
special_cases_latex: \(\phi=0\) formally recovers ordinary convexity, though it is not a uniform-convexity modulus under the stated positivity convention.
If both \(\phi(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\) and the upper model hold, then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth.
immediate_consequences_latex: The parameters are monotone: a valid upper constant remains valid when enlarged, and a valid lower modulus remains valid when decreased.
Quadratic lower and upper control bound the curvature scale between \(\mu\) and \(L\).
boundary_notes: The constants and moduli depend on the chosen norm.
Self-concordance and relative smoothness are distinct nonuniform curvature models and are not implied by this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz-gradient smoothness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\mathbb E,\|\cdot\|)\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), let \(D\subseteq\mathbb E\) be convex, and let \(f\) be differentiable on an open set containing \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-order smoothness on a convex set, with arbitrary primal and dual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\ge0\), the function \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth on \(D\) if \[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|\qquad(\forall x,y\in D).\] The least admissible \(L\), when attained or interpreted as an infimum, is the gradient Lipschitz modulus of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is gradient-smooth on a convex set when its gradient is globally Lipschitz there, measured from the primal norm to its dual norm. The smoothness parameter is the uniform upper bound on how rapidly the gradient can change per unit displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at every point of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x,y\in D)\;\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(f\) is convex and differentiable on the whole Hilbert space, \(L\)-smoothness is equivalent to \(f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Taylor Formula with Segment Remainder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general multivariable-calculus theorem for twice continuously differentiable real-valued functions on an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(x\in U\) and \(r>0\) satisfy \(B(x,r)\subseteq U\). Then, for every \(y\in B(x,r)\), there exists \(\xi\in[x,y]\) such that \[f(y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\frac12(y-x)^T\nabla^2f(\xi)(y-x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function, each point y in a ball contained in the open domain admits a second-order Taylor formula about x, with the Hessian evaluated at some point on the segment from x to y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\xi\in[x,y]\) such that \(f(y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\tfrac12(y-x)^T\nabla^2f(\xi)(y-x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Characterization of L-Smoothness in ℓp Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global second-order characterization using the operator norm from the primal ℓp norm to its dual ℓq norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(L\geq0\), let \(p\in[1,\infty]\), and let \(q\in[1,\infty]\) satisfy \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\) if \[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C).\] The regime is global when \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), restricted when the inequality is asserted only on a specified proper subset \(C\), and local when every point has a neighborhood on which the inequality holds with some finite, possibly neighborhood-dependent constant. Global Lipschitzness implies restricted and local Lipschitzness, but neither converse holds without additional uniformity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient smoothness may hold globally, only on a specified domain, or locally with constants that need not be uniform.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact quadratic-majorant characterization of smooth convexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, and let \(L>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convex Hilbert-space regime; the converse from a one-sided quadratic model can fail without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The smooth quadratic upper-bound property with constant \(L\) is \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\qquad(\forall x,y\in\mathcal H).\] For convex differentiable \(f\), this property is equivalent to \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f\), and also to convexity of \(Lq-f\), where \(q(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex function admits, at every base point, a tangent quadratic majorant with curvature L. In the global Hilbert-space convex setting, existence of all these majorants is exactly equivalent to an L-Lipschitz gradient. It is also equivalent to convexity of the complementary quadratic function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable on all of \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz}\iff(\forall x,y)\ f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\iff Lq-f\text{ is convex}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The quadratic majorant at \(x\) is \(q_x(y)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\), and the condition is \(f\le q_x\) for every \(x\).
The equivalent Jensen form is \(f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\ge\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)-\frac L2\theta(1-\theta)\|x-y\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: For \(L=0\), the global differentiable case reduces to affine functions, but the stated equivalence is parameterized by \(L>0\).
For a convex quadratic with Hessian \(A\), the property holds exactly when \(A\preccurlyeq LI\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each model is value- and gradient-matching at its base point.
The inequality supplies a uniform upper bound on the first-order Taylor remainder.
boundary_notes: For a nonconvex function, the descent-lemma inequality can hold with a smaller constant than the gradient Lipschitz modulus.
A local model on a proper subset is not automatically a global smoothness certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Smooth Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The reciprocal-\(L\) formulas require \(L>0\). The restricted-set clause asserts only inequalities (2.1.9), (2.1.12), and (2.1.14), not all six equivalences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be dual to \(\|\cdot\|\), and let \(L>0\). Membership \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|)\) is equivalent to each of the following conditions holding for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) and, where present, all \(\alpha\in[0,1]\):
\[
0\le f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\le\frac L2\|x-y\|^2;
\]
\[
f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac1{2L}\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*^2\le f(y);
\]
\[
\frac1L\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*^2\le\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle;
\]
\[
0\le\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\le L\|x-y\|^2;
\]
\[
\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\ge f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2L}\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*^2;
\]
\[
0\le\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)-f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\le\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)L}{2}\|x-y\|^2.
\]
Moreover, if \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(Q)\), then the first and fourth inequalities hold for all \(x,y\in Q\), and the sixth holds for all \(x,y\in Q\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convex L-smoothness is equivalently characterized by each of six Taylor-remainder, cocoercivity, gradient-monotonicity, and interpolation inequalities. On a subset Q, the extract additionally guarantees only the two-sided Taylor bound, the two-sided gradient inner-product bound, and the two-sided Jensen-gap bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n,\|\cdot\|)\iff\text{each one of the six universal conditions};\quad f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(Q)\Rightarrow\text{conditions 1, 4, and 6 hold on }Q

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-Lipschitz gradient bounds the first-order Taylor remainder above by one half L times the squared displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a base point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[q_x(y)=f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] The family \((q_x)_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\) is an \(L\)-quadratic upper-model family for \(f\) when \[f(y)\leq q_x(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Every model is first-order exact at its base point: \(q_x(x)=f(x)\) and \(
abla q_x(x)=
abla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic upper model adds an L-curvature quadratic to the first-order Taylor model and globally majorizes the function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L>0\), the model \[q_x(y)=f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac L2\|y-x\|^2\] has the unique minimizer \[y_x=x-L^{-1}
abla f(x)\] and minimum \[q_x(y_x)=f(x)- rac1{2L}\|
abla f(x)\|^2.\] If \(f(y)\le q_x(y)\) for every \(y\), then \[f(y_x)\le f(x)- rac1{2L}\|
abla f(x)\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the quadratic upper model gives the gradient step and a one-step decrease certificate.
assumptions_latex: The final inequality additionally assumes that \(q_x\) majorizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min q_x=\{x-L^{-1}\nabla f(x)\}\), and majorization implies \(f(y_x)\le f(x)-(2L)^{-1}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\).

Let \(L>0\) and \[q_x(y)=f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] Then \(q_x\) has the unique minimizer \[y_x=x- rac1L
abla f(x),\] and \[\min_y q_x(y)=f(x)- rac{1}{2L}\|
abla f(x)\|^2.\] If \(q_x\) majorizes \(f\), this gives \[f(y_x)\le f(x)- rac{1}{2L}\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional-gradient iteration with adaptive or fixed step size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General conditional-gradient method whose canonical home is A05; the listed A02 curvature node is only a legitimate cross-index for the quadratic-model step rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $s_0\in K$. For each $t\geq 1$, choose $\bar s_{t-1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{s\in K}\langle\nabla\Psi^*(s_{t-1}),s\rangle$ and set $s_t=(1-\rho_t)s_{t-1}+\rho_t\bar s_{t-1}$ with $\rho_t\in[0,1]$. The step may be selected by line search on $[s_{t-1},\bar s_{t-1}]$, by maximizing the stated smoothness-based quadratic lower model, or by the fixed schedule $\rho_t=2/(t+1)$. For $d_t=\bar s_{t-1}-s_{t-1}$ and $\|d_t\|_2>0$, the quadratic-model choice is $\rho_t=\min\{1,\mu\langle d_t,\nabla\Psi^*(s_{t-1})\rangle/\|d_t\|_2^2\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a point in K, maximize the current linearization over K and take a convex-combination step toward the maximizer. The step can use line search, a smoothness-based quadratic model, or the fixed schedule 2/(t+1); the displayed quadratic formula requires a nonzero search direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_t=(1-\rho_t)s_{t-1}+\rho_t\bar s_{t-1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature-Complement Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent global formulation of Euclidean convex smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable and \(L>0\). Then \[\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f)\le L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\mapsto\frac L2\|x\|^2-f(x)\text{ is convex}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex differentiable function is L-smooth exactly when its complement in the L-curvature quadratic is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f)\le L\iff (L/2)\|\cdot\|^2-f\text{ is convex}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of the Curvature Complement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent global formulation of Euclidean convex smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable and let \(L>0\). Then \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz if and only if \[x\longmapsto \frac{L}{2}\|x\|^2-f(x)\] is convex. Equivalently, for all \(x,y\), \[f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\le\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex differentiable function is L-smooth exactly when subtracting it from the L-curvature quadratic leaves a convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f)\le L\iff (L/2)\|\cdot\|^2-f\text{ is convex}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian eigenvalue characterization of L-smooth convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean characterization for twice continuously differentiable convex functions on all of R^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and convex, and let \(L\ge 0\). Then \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_2\) if and only if \(\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(x))\le L\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable convex function on R^n has an L-Lipschitz gradient in the Euclidean norm exactly when the largest eigenvalue of its Hessian is at most L at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }L\text{-smooth with respect to }\|\cdot\|_2\iff \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 f(x))\le L

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed Hessian Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-continuously-differentiable characterization without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex and \(f\in C^2(C)\). Then \(
abla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(C\) if and only if \[\|
abla^2f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L\quad(x\in C),\] equivalently \(-LI\preceq
abla^2f(x)\preceq LI\). Moreover, \[\operatorname{Lip}(
abla f;C)=\sup_{x\in C}\|
abla^2f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}},\] with either side possibly infinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral upper curvature bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Euclidean norms and the Loewner order on symmetric matrices are used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global twice-continuously-differentiable finite-dimensional Euclidean regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hessian upper-curvature regime with constant \(L\ge0\) is \[
abla^2f(x)\preccurlyeq LI\qquad( orall x\in\mathbb R^n).\] If \(f\) is convex, then \(0\preccurlyeq
abla^2f(x)\preccurlyeq LI\) for every \(x\), and this condition is equivalent to \(L\)-smoothness in the Euclidean norm. Equivalently, \(\lambda_{\max}(
abla^2f(x))\le L\) for all \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable function has Hessian upper curvature L when every directional second derivative is at most L times the squared direction norm. For convex functions the Hessian is also positive semidefinite, and the spectral upper bound is exactly equivalent to an L-Lipschitz gradient.
assumptions_latex: For the smoothness equivalence, \(f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ convex and }L\text{-smooth}\iff(\forall x)\ 0\preccurlyeq\nabla^2f(x)\preccurlyeq LI\iff(\forall x)\ \lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2f(x))\le L.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x,d\in\mathbb R^n\), \(d^T\nabla^2f(x)d\le L\|d\|_2^2\).
The induced spectral norm satisfies \(\|\nabla^2f(x)\|_2\le L\) when the Hessian is positive semidefinite.
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic \(f(x)=\frac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c\), the condition is \(A\preccurlyeq LI\).
When \(L=0\) and \(f\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\), \(f\) is affine.
immediate_consequences_latex: All eigenvalues of the Hessian of a convex \(L\)-smooth function lie in \([0,L]\).
The first-order Taylor remainder is bounded above by \(\frac L2\|y-x\|_2^2\).
boundary_notes: The spectral statement uses the Euclidean norm; other norms require the corresponding induced Hessian norm.
Pointwise twice differentiability without continuity may require a more careful formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Baillon–Haddad equivalence family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable, and let \(L>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Hilbert-space convex-gradient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Baillon–Haddad family is the equivalence between \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity and \(1/L\)-cocoercivity of the gradient: \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge rac1L\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|^2\] for all \(x,y\in\mathcal H\). Under scaling, \(L^{-1}
abla f\) is firmly nonexpansive; for \(L=1\), nonexpansiveness and firm nonexpansiveness coincide for gradients of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For gradients of convex functions, Lipschitz continuity automatically strengthens to cocoercivity with the reciprocal constant, and the two properties are equivalent. After dividing by L, the gradient is firmly nonexpansive, a property stronger than ordinary nonexpansiveness for general operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz}\iff\nabla f\text{ is }L^{-1}\text{-cocoercive}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(L^{-1}\nabla f\) is firmly nonexpansive.
\(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and monotone with the sharpened inner-product bound shown above.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the gradient satisfies
\[
\langle \nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle
\ge \frac{1}{L}\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2^2.
\]
Thus convexity together with \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity of the gradient strengthens ordinary monotonicity of \(\nabla f\) to \(1/L\)-cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient of an L-smooth convex function on Euclidean space is 1/L-cocoercive: its directional increase controls the squared change of the gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Cocoercivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Essential for Cocoercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive cocoercivity for a smooth nonconvex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=-	frac{L}{2}\|x\|_2^2\), the gradient \(
abla f(x)=-Lx\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, but \[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle=-L\|x-y\|_2^2<0\] whenever \(x
eq y\). Hence it is not \( eta\)-cocoercive for any \( eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothness without convexity is insufficient: a concave quadratic has a Lipschitz but anti-monotone gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz but not \(\beta\)-cocoercive for any \(\beta>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Reciprocal Smoothness Constant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of the Baillon–Haddad constant over the smooth convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=	frac{L}{2}\|x\|_2^2\), equality holds in \[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle= rac1L\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2^2\] for every \(x,y\). Therefore no constant larger than \(1/L\) is uniformly valid over all convex functions with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal constant 1/L is optimal, as witnessed by the isotropic quadratic of curvature L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The uniform Baillon--Haddad constant \(1/L\) is sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Reciprocal Smoothness Constant

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Convex Cocoercivity Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint displacement and gradient-change bound for strongly convex smooth gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\geq rac{\mu L}{\mu+L}\|x-y\|_2^2+ rac1{\mu+L}\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex smooth gradient simultaneously controls squared displacement and squared gradient change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\Delta\nabla f,\Delta x\rangle\geq\frac{\mu L}{\mu+L}\|\Delta x\|_2^2+\frac1{\mu+L}\|\Delta\nabla f\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Cocoercivity Refinement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman Form of Gradient Cocoercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided strengthened first-order inequality for smooth convex gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f(x)-f(y)-\langle
abla f(y),x-yangle\geq rac1{2L}\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2^2.\] Its symmetrized form is the \(1/L\)-cocoercivity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each Bregman remainder of a smooth convex function controls half the squared gradient change; its symmetric form is Baillon–Haddad cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(x,y)\geq\frac1{2L}\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2^2\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Form of Gradient Cocoercivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cocoercive gradient operator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(f\) be differentiable on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator property of a gradient on a Hilbert-space domain; no convexity is built into the bare definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \( eta>0\), the gradient \(
abla f:D	o\mathcal H\) is \( eta\)-cocoercive if \[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge eta\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|^2\qquad( orall x,y\in D).\] The largest admissible \( eta\), interpreted as a supremum, is the cocoercivity modulus of the gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient is beta-cocoercive when its change has at least beta times its squared norm as alignment with the displacement. This quantitatively combines monotonicity and Lipschitz control in one inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(( orall x,y\in D)\;\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge eta\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|^2.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\beta\nabla f\) is firmly nonexpansive.
For every \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\), \(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\nabla f\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth on the whole Hilbert space, then \(\nabla f\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive.
A firmly nonexpansive gradient is \(1\)-cocoercive.
immediate_consequences_latex: A cocoercive gradient is monotone.
A \(\beta\)-cocoercive gradient is \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz unless it is constant, with the same inequality valid in the constant case.
boundary_notes: Monotonicity alone does not imply cocoercivity.
The definition uses a Hilbert inner product and is not transferred verbatim to arbitrary Banach spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Averaged forward-gradient fixed-point map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable on a real Hilbert space, assume \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L>0\), and choose \(0<\gamma<2/L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained smooth convex minimization represented as a fixed-point problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the forward-gradient mapping \[T_\gamma=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma
abla f.\] Since \(
abla f\) is \(1/L\)-cocoercive, \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=\gamma L/2\in(0,1)\). Its fixed-point set is \[\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\{x:
abla f(x)=0\}=\operatorname{Argmin}f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient fixed-point interface replaces smooth convex minimization by finding a fixed point of the forward-gradient map. For steps below two over L, the map is averaged and therefore nonexpansive. Its fixed points are exactly the stationary points, which equal the global minimizers of a differentiable convex function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\gamma=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\nabla f\text{ is }(\gamma L/2)\text{-averaged and }\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\operatorname{Argmin}f.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a nonexpansive \(R\) such that \(T_\gamma=(1-\gamma L/2)\operatorname{Id}+(\gamma L/2)R\).
The fixed-point equation \(x=T_\gamma x\) is equivalent to \(\nabla f(x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\gamma=1/L\), \(T_\gamma\) is firmly nonexpansive.
At \(\gamma=2/L\), the averagedness parameter reaches \(1\); the open-step regime stated here excludes that boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every fixed point is a global minimizer of \(f\).
The mapping is nonexpansive for every \(0<\gamma<2/L\).
boundary_notes: If \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\varnothing\), the fixed-point set is empty.
The identity with minimizers uses unconstrained convex differentiable optimization; constrained problems require a projection or proximal operator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint Gradient Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition. As stated, it presupposes that the argmax defines a selection in Q_2; the supplied assumptions alone do not guarantee existence or uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q_2\subseteq\mathbb E_2, let \phi:Q_2\to\mathbb R be differentiable, and let L_2(\phi)>0. The adjoint gradient mapping V:Q_2\to Q_2 is defined, for u\in Q_2, by V(u)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in Q_2}\left\{\langle\nabla\phi(u),v-u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\frac{L_2(\phi)}{2}\|v-u\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point u, the adjoint gradient mapping selects a point v in Q2 maximizing the linearized increase of phi minus a quadratic displacement penalty with coefficient L2(phi).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(u)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{v\in Q_2}\left\{\langle\nabla\phi(u),v-u\rangle_{\mathbb E_2}-\frac12L_2(\phi)\|v-u\|_{\mathbb E_2}^2\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-gradient point and gradient mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The base point may lie outside Q. The definition requires the displayed strongly convex subproblem to have a unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), and a set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), whenever the minimizer exists uniquely, define
\[
x_Q(\bar x;\gamma):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\left\{f(\bar x)+\langle f'(\bar x),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{\gamma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\right\},
\qquad g_Q(\bar x;\gamma):=\gamma\bigl(\bar x-x_Q(\bar x;\gamma)\bigr).
\]
The mapping \(g_Q\) is the gradient mapping of \(f\) on \(Q\). If \(Q=\mathbb R^n\), then
\[
x_Q(\bar x;\gamma)=\bar x-\frac1\gamma f'(\bar x),\qquad g_Q(\bar x;\gamma)=f'(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected-gradient point minimizes the affine model of the objective plus a quadratic regularizer, and the gradient mapping is the scaled displacement to that point. On the whole space these reduce to the ordinary gradient step and gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_Q(\bar x;\gamma)=\gamma(\bar x-x_Q(\bar x;\gamma)),\qquad Q=\mathbb R^n\implies x_Q(\bar x;\gamma)=\bar x-\gamma^{-1}f'(\bar x),\quad g_Q(\bar x;\gamma)=f'(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(T_\gamma x=x-\gamma\nabla f(x)\). Then, for all \(x,y\in H\),
\[
\|T_\gamma x-T_\gamma y\|^2
\le \|x-y\|^2-\gamma\left(\frac{2}{L}-\gamma\right)
\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|^2
\le \|x-y\|^2.
\]
Consequently, every gradient step with \(\gamma\in[0,2/L]\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every stepsize between zero and 2/L, subtracting the scaled gradient defines a nonexpansive map.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Points of Gradient-Step Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate supplied by every positive-stepsize gradient map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable and let \(\gamma>0\). For \(T_\gamma=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\nabla f\),
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}=\operatorname*{argmin}f.
\]
Thus a point is a fixed point of the gradient map exactly when it globally minimizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive stepsize, the fixed points of a convex gradient-step map are exactly the global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\nabla f)=\operatorname*{argmin}f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Points of Gradient-Step Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Upper Stepsize for Nonexpansiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of gradient-map nonexpansiveness beyond 2/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), where \(L>0\). Then
\[
T_\gamma x=(1-\gamma L)x.
\]
If \(\gamma>2/L\), its Lipschitz constant is \(|1-\gamma L|>1\), so \(T_\gamma\) is expansive. Consequently the upper bound \(2/L\) is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a one-dimensional quadratic, every stepsize above 2/L makes the gradient map expansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(T_\gamma)=|1-\gamma L|>1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Upper Stepsize for Nonexpansiveness

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha=\gamma L/2\in(0,1)\). There exists a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\) such that
\[
T_\gamma=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha R.
\]
Equivalently, one may take
\[
R=\operatorname{Id}-\frac{2}{L}\nabla f,
\]
which is nonexpansive by gradient cocoercivity. Hence \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with the explicit parameter \(\alpha=\gamma L/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient step with stepsize strictly below 2/L is averaged, with averaging parameter gamma L/2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Stepsize Boundary for Averaged Gradient Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of strict averagedness at the endpoint gamma=2/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=\tfrac L2x^2\), where \(L>0\). At \(\gamma=2/L\),
\[
T_\gamma=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma\nabla f=-\operatorname{Id}.
\]
The map \(-\operatorname{Id}\) is nonexpansive but is not \(\alpha\)-averaged for any \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Hence \(0<\gamma<2/L\) is sharp for strict averagedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the endpoint 2/L, a quadratic objective yields minus the identity, which is nonexpansive but not strictly averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\gamma=-\operatorname{Id}\) is not \(\alpha\)-averaged for any \(0<\alpha<1\).

The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\langle Ax-Ay,x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|Ax-Ay\|^2

and

\|(x-2\beta Ax)-(y-2\beta Ay)\|\le\|x-y\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cocoercivity–Averagedness Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hilbert-space correspondence between cocoercivity and averaged forward maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\to H\), \(\beta>0\), and \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). Then \(A\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if and only if
\[
T_\gamma=\operatorname{Id}-\gamma A
\]
is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=\gamma/(2\beta)\). Equivalently,
\[
T_\gamma=(1-\alpha)\operatorname{Id}+\alpha(\operatorname{Id}-2\beta A),
\]
and \(\operatorname{Id}-2\beta A\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Beta-cocoercivity is equivalent to averagedness of every interior-stepsize forward map with parameter gamma divided by 2 beta.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive if and only if \(\operatorname{Id}-\gamma A\) is \(\gamma/(2\beta)\)-averaged.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong convexity with quadratic modulus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued Hilbert-space definition with curvature measured by the Hilbert norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)-\frac\mu2\theta(1-\theta)\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function is strongly convex with parameter mu when its Jensen inequality contains a uniform quadratic deficit proportional to the squared distance between the endpoints. The parameter depends on the ambient norm and measures uniform lower curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\theta\in[0,1])\;f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)-\frac\mu2\theta(1-\theta)\|x-y\|^2.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f-\frac\mu2\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex.
If \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, then \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|y-x\|^2\) for every \(g\in\partial f(x)\).
Under the same closed convex hypotheses, \(\partial f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone.
special_cases_latex: The quadratic \(x\mapsto\frac12\langle Ax,x\rangle+b^Tx+c\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex exactly when \(A\succeq\mu I\).
Strong convexity is uniform convexity with modulus \(t\mapsto\frac\mu2t^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper closed strongly convex function has at most one minimizer and, on the whole Hilbert space, has a unique minimizer.
At a minimizer \(x^*\), \(f(x)-f(x^*)\ge\frac\mu2\|x-x^*\|^2\).
boundary_notes: Strict convexity alone does not supply a positive strong-convexity parameter.
Changing the norm changes the admissible value of \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,\infty] be closed and convex, and let [a,b]\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f with a<b. Then there exists h:(a,b)\to\mathbb{R} such that h(t)\in\partial f(t) for every t\in(a,b) and f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^b h(t)\,dt.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a closed convex function is finite throughout a nondegenerate real interval, its increment across the interval is the integral of a subgradient selection defined at every interior point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists h:(a,b)\to\mathbb{R}\;\bigl[(\forall t\in(a,b),\ h(t)\in\partial f(t))\ \land\ f(b)-f(a)=\int_a^b h(t)\,dt\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extracted existential-subgradient formulation of strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the extract's quantifier: the subgradient may be selected for each pair \(x,y\). This should not be silently replaced by the usual universal-subgradient formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\hat f\) is called strongly convex with parameter \(\hat\sigma>0\) in the extracted formulation if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f\), there exists \(g\in\partial\hat f(x)\) such that \[\hat f(y)\ge \hat f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] If \(\hat f\) is differentiable, the extract states the equivalent condition \[\hat f(y)\ge \hat f(x)+\langle\nabla\hat f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extract defines strong convexity using, for each pair of domain points, some subgradient giving a quadratic lower bound. In the differentiable case it gives the corresponding gradient inequality. The existential subgradient quantifier is retained exactly because it is not the usual universal-subgradient wording.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f\ \exists g\in\partial\hat f(x):\ \hat f(y)\ge\hat f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\tfrac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2;\quad \hat f\text{ differentiable }\Rightarrow g=\nabla\hat f(x)\text{ in the displayed formulation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity via Quadratic Subgradient Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong convexity in Euclidean space and records its shifted-convexity and quadratic-lower-model characterizations. Complexity claims are excluded because the extract does not state their full oracle-class assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and let \(\alpha\ge 0\). A function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly convex if, for all \(x,y\in\mathcal X\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+g^\top(y-x)+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] Equivalently, \(x\mapsto f(x)-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex. Thus \(q^-_{x,g}(y)=f(x)+g^\top(y-x)+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|y-x\|^2\) is a touching quadratic lower bound for \(f\). If \(f\) is twice differentiable, strong convexity implies \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq\alpha I\) wherever the Hessian is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is alpha-strongly convex when every subgradient affine lower bound can be strengthened by an alpha-quadratic term. Equivalently, subtracting alpha times the squared norm divided by two leaves a convex function. Each subgradient therefore defines a touching quadratic lower model. For a twice-differentiable strongly convex function, every Hessian eigenvalue is at least alpha.
assumptions_latex: \text{The Hessian consequence assumes that }f\text{ is twice differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)\ge f(x)+g^\top(y-x)+\frac{\alpha}{2}\|y-x\|^2\iff f-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|\cdot\|^2\text{ is convex};\qquad f\text{ twice differentiable and strongly convex}\Rightarrow\nabla^2f(x)\succeq\alpha I.
