knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Characterizations of Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded equivalence of strong convexity, the global quadratic subgradient inequality, and strong monotonicity of the full subdifferential for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty] be proper, closed, and convex, and let \sigma>0. The following are equivalent: (i) f is \sigma-strongly convex; (ii) for every x\in\operatorname{dom}(\partial f), every y\in\operatorname{dom}f, and every g\in\partial f(x), \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2;\] (iii) for every x,y\in\operatorname{dom}(\partial f), every g_x\in\partial f(x), and every g_y\in\partial f(y), \[\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\geq\sigma\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function and a positive modulus, strong convexity is equivalent to a global quadratic subgradient lower bound and to strong monotonicity of the subdifferential. Both inequalities hold for every point and subgradient in the stated domains.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&f\text{ is }\sigma\text{-strongly convex}\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(\partial f),\ \forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall g\in\partial f(x),\quad f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\ \forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}(\partial f),\ \forall g_x\in\partial f(x),\ \forall g_y\in\partial f(y),\quad \langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\geq\sigma\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \Psi:Q\to\mathbb R is \sigma_{\Psi}\text{-strongly convex on }Q\text{, for }\sigma_{\Psi}>0,\text{ if for every }x,y\in Q\text{ and }\tau\in[0,1],\quad \Psi(\tau x+(1-\tau)y)\le \tau\Psi(x)+(1-\tau)\Psi(y)-\frac{\sigma_{\Psi}}{2}\tau(1-\tau)\lVert x-y\rVert^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity of Quadratic Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral characterization and maximal strong-convexity modulus for finite-dimensional quadratics under the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^n\) be endowed with the \(\ell_2\)-norm and let
\[
f(x)=\frac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c,
\qquad A\in\mathbb S^n,\quad b\in\mathbb R^n,\quad c\in\mathbb R.
\]
For \(\sigma>0\), \(f\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex if and only if
\[
A-\sigma I\succeq0,
\]
equivalently, if and only if \(\lambda_{\min}(A)\geq\sigma\). Consequently, \(f\) is strongly convex if and only if \(A\succ0\); when this holds, its largest possible strong-convexity parameter is \(\lambda_{\min}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic with symmetric matrix A is sigma-strongly convex exactly when A minus sigma times the identity is positive semidefinite, equivalently when the smallest eigenvalue of A is at least sigma. It is strongly convex exactly when A is positive definite, and then its largest admissible parameter is the smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }\sigma\text{-strongly convex}\iff A-\sigma I\succeq0\iff\lambda_{\min}(A)\geq\sigma;\quad f\text{ is strongly convex}\iff A\succ0,\quad \sigma_{\max}=\lambda_{\min}(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity via a Quadratic Subgradient Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition preserving the source's pairwise existential subgradient quantifier; this quantifier should not be silently replaced by the more common arbitrary-subgradient formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \hat\sigma>0. The function \hat f is strongly convex with parameter \hat\sigma if, for every x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f, there exists g\in\partial\hat f(x) such that
\[
\hat f(y)\ge \hat f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2.
\]
If \hat f is differentiable, the source states that this is equivalent to
\[
\hat f(y)\ge \hat f(x)+\langle\nabla\hat f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity with parameter hat-sigma is defined by a quadratic lower bound: for each pair of domain points, the source requires some subgradient at the first point that supports the bound. In the differentiable case, it gives the corresponding gradient inequality for every pair of points.
assumptions_latex: \hat f\text{ is defined on a normed domain}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\hat f\;\exists g\in\partial\hat f(x):\quad \hat f(y)\ge \hat f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\hat\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2,\quad\text{with the stated gradient equivalent if }\hat f\text{ is differentiable.}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(\nabla f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional characterization matching the cited optimization textbook.

source_refs.locator: 5 Smoothness and Strong Convexity p. 107

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic lower-model inequalities
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C
\]
hold if and only if
\[
\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|_2^2
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Thus the gradient operator characterizes the same strong-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable convex function on a Euclidean domain is mu-strongly convex exactly when its gradient is mu-strongly monotone.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Gradient Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function x to the fourth has a monotone gradient but no positive global strong-monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'\) is monotone but not \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for any \(\mu>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong monotonicity of a gradient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\) be a convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(f\) be differentiable on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable strong-convexity regime; the definition is stated directly as an operator inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gradient \(
abla f:D	o\mathcal H\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, for \(\mu>0\), if \[\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2\qquad( orall x,y\in D).\] For a differentiable convex function on an open convex domain, this condition is equivalent to \(\mu\)-strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient is strongly monotone when its change has a uniformly positive component along every displacement. For differentiable convex functions, this operator inequality is exactly the first-order characterization of strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x,y\in D)\;\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For differentiable convex \(f\), \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|y-x\|^2\).
For a proper closed convex function, the set-valued extension is \(\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), \(g_y\in\partial f(y)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\frac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c\) with symmetric \(A\), strong gradient monotonicity is \(A\succeq\mu I\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A \(\mu\)-strongly monotone gradient is injective.
If a zero of the gradient exists, it is unique.
boundary_notes: Ordinary monotonicity corresponds to convexity but does not imply any positive modulus.
Strong monotonicity does not by itself impose an upper Lipschitz bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The strong-convexity component of the extracted one-dimensional derivative characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and let \(\ell>0\). Then \(\psi\) is \(\ell\)-strongly convex if and only if, for every \(\tau_1>\tau_2\), \[\psi'(\tau_1)-\psi'(\tau_2)\ge \ell(\tau_1-\tau_2).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent differentiable characterizations of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convexity on an open convex domain by the global first-order support inequality, monotonicity of the gradient, and, when available, positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, suppose \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is open and convex, and suppose \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable on \(\operatorname{dom}f\). Then the following are equivalent: (i) \(f\) is convex; (ii) \( orall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(f(y)+\langle x-y,
abla f(y)angle\le f(x)\); (iii) \( orall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\langle x-y,
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)angle\ge0\). If, moreover, \(f\) is twice Gâteaux differentiable on \(\operatorname{dom}f\), these conditions are also equivalent to (iv) \( orall x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \( orall z\in\mathcal H\), \(\langle z,
abla^2f(x)zangle\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper Gâteaux-differentiable function with open convex domain, convexity is equivalent both to every tangent affine function being a global lower support and to monotonicity of the gradient. If the function is twice Gâteaux differentiable, these are also equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian at every domain point.
assumptions_latex: \text{For equivalence with the Hessian condition, }f\text{ is twice Gâteaux differentiable on }\operatorname{dom}f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(iii)},\quad\text{and under twice Gâteaux differentiability,}\quad\text{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(iii)}\Longleftrightarrow\text{(iv)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Everywhere Differentiability and Gradient Continuity of Finite Saddle Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiability regularity for finite concave-convex functions on open convex product domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\times D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, and let \(K:C\times D\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave in its first argument and convex in its second. If \(E=\{(u,v)\in C\times D:K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v)\}\), then \(E\) is dense in \(C\times D\), \((C\times D)\setminus E\) has Lebesgue measure zero, and \(\nabla K:E\to\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex product domain, a finite concave-convex function is differentiable on a dense set whose complement has measure zero, and its gradient is continuous on that differentiability set.

E=\{(u,v)\in C\times D:K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{E}=C\times D,\quad \lambda_{m+n}((C\times D)\setminus E)=0,\quad \nabla K:E\to\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\text{ is continuous}

children.title: Hessian Lower-Curvature Regimes
children.top_down_role: Twice-differentiable spectral characterizations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional twice-continuously-differentiable spectral characterization.

source_refs.locator: 5 Smoothness and Strong Convexity p. 107

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\) if and only if, for every \(x\in C\) and \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2 f(x)v\ge\mu\|v\|_2^2.
\]
Equivalently, every eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2f(x)\) is at least \(\mu\), or \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I\), throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function, mu-strong convexity is equivalent to every Hessian eigenvalue being at least mu.
knowledge_statements.title: Hessian Lower-Curvature Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Convexity Does Not Imply Uniform Hessian Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between strict convexity and a uniform positive Hessian lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^4\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb R\), but \(f''(0)=0\). Hence there is no \(\mu>0\) such that \(f''(x)\ge\mu\) for all \(x\), so \(f\) is not strongly convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strictly convex function x to the fourth is not strongly convex because its Hessian vanishes at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly convex but is not \(\mu\)-strongly convex for any \(\mu>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral lower curvature bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(f\in C^2(D)\), and let \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-continuously-differentiable finite-dimensional Euclidean characterization of strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hessian lower-curvature regime with parameter \(\mu\) is \[
abla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I\qquad( orall x\in D).\] Equivalently, \(d^T
abla^2f(x)d\ge\mu\|d\|_2^2\) for every \(x\in D\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), or \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\ge\mu\) for every \(x\). In this regime, \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(D\), and conversely every \(C^2\) \(\mu\)-strongly convex function satisfies the Hessian bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable function has lower curvature mu when every Hessian eigenvalue is at least mu throughout its convex domain. This spectral condition is equivalent to strong convexity in the Euclidean twice-differentiable setting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly convex on }D\iff(\forall x\in D)\ \nabla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I\iff(\forall x\in D)\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge\mu.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f-\frac\mu2\|\cdot\|_2^2\) has positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere and is convex.
Every directional second derivative satisfies \(D^2f(x)[d,d]\ge\mu\|d\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic with Hessian \(A\), the largest strong-convexity parameter is \(\lambda_{\min}(A)\).
Taking \(\mu=0\) recovers the Hessian criterion for ordinary convexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Hessian is positive definite at every point when \(\mu>0\).
The gradient is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone.
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness at each point without a uniform eigenvalue lower bound need not yield global strong convexity with a positive constant.
The matrix inequality is tied to the Euclidean norm.

children.title: Strong Convexity–Conjugate Smoothness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Dual exchange between lower curvature and differentiable smoothness.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(f^*\) is differentiable with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel-conjugacy correspondence with reciprocal moduli.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Smoothness and Strong Convexity Correspondence p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if its Fenchel conjugate
\[
f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}
\]
is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and satisfies
\[
\|\nabla f^*(u)-\nabla f^*(v)\|_2\le\frac{1}{\mu}\|u-v\|_2
\quad\text{for all }u,v\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The reciprocal constant \(1/\mu\) is the conjugate smoothness modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex f is mu-strongly convex exactly when its conjugate is differentiable with a 1/mu-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity–Conjugate Smoothness Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 Smoothness and Strong Convexity Correspondence p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Gradient as Unique Primal Maximizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizer representation induced by strong convexity in the conjugate correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\), then for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) the supremum defining \(f^*(u)\) has a unique maximizer and \[\nabla f^*(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\] Equivalently, \(u\in\partial f(x)\) if and only if \(x=\nabla f^*(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient of the conjugate of a strongly convex function is the unique primal maximizer and inverts the primal subdifferential relation.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f^*(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_x\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\},\quad u\in\partial f(x)\iff x=\nabla f^*(u)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Gradient as Unique Primal Maximizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Modulus Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of global conjugate differentiability when strong convexity is weakened to ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), the function is closed and convex but has no positive strong-convexity modulus. Its conjugate is \[f^*(u)=\delta_{\{0\}}(u),\] which is not finite, hence not differentiable, on all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary convexity is insufficient: the conjugate of the zero function is an indicator and is not globally differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is the zero function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\delta_{\{0\}}\) is not differentiable on \(\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: indicator function of the singleton containing zero

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel-conjugate curvature correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with dual \(\mathbb E^*\), let \(\mu>0\), and define \(f^*(u)=\sup_x\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel conjugacy with primal and dual norms; closedness is required in the strong-convexity-to-smoothness direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong-convexity–conjugate-smoothness correspondence is: if \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(f^*:\mathbb E^*\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable everywhere and \(\nabla f^*\) is \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz from the dual norm to the primal norm. Conversely, if \(g:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) is convex and \(1/\mu\)-smooth, then \(g^*\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with respect to the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugacy exchanges uniform quadratic lower curvature with an upper Lipschitz-gradient bound. A proper closed mu-strongly convex function has an everywhere finite conjugate whose gradient is Lipschitz with reciprocal constant. Conversely, a finite smooth convex function has a strongly convex conjugate.
assumptions_latex: For the forward direction, \(f\) is proper, closed, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
For the converse direction, \(g\) is finite, convex, and \(1/\mu\)-smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ proper closed and }\mu\text{-strongly convex}\Rightarrow f^*\text{ is }\mu^{-1}\text{-smooth};\quad g\text{ convex and }\mu^{-1}\text{-smooth}\Rightarrow g^*\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly convex}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the forward direction, \(\nabla f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\) is single-valued and \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz.
For closed proper convex \(f\), applying both directions to \(f\) and \(f^*\) yields the biconditional with the appropriate primal and dual norms.
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\frac12x^TAx\) with \(A\succ0\), \(f^*(u)=\frac12u^TA^{-1}u\); the lower eigenvalue bound for \(A\) becomes an upper eigenvalue bound for \(A^{-1}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Strong convexity ensures uniqueness of the maximizer defining \(f^*(u)\) for every \(u\).
The reciprocal relationship exchanges the constants \(\mu\) and \(1/\mu\).
boundary_notes: Without closedness, the forward statement is naturally applied to the closed convex representative.
Smoothness of \(f^*\) does not assert strong convexity of \(f^*\); it corresponds to strong convexity of \(f\).

notation.meaning: Dual space equipped with the dual norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent forms of conjugate strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal smoothness, inverse subgradient monotonicity, infimal-convolution, and quadratic upper-model characterizations of strong convexity of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\sigma>0\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(f^*\) is strongly convex with modulus \(\sigma\); (b) \(f\) is differentiable and \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz with constant \(1/\sigma\); (c) whenever \(v_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), \[\langle v_1-v_0,x_1-x_0\rangle\geq\sigma\|v_1-v_0\|^2;\] (d) \(f=f_0\mathbin{\oplus}\frac{1}{2\sigma}\|\cdot\|^2\) for some convex function \(f_0\); and (e) \(f\) is differentiable and \[f(x')\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),x'-x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\sigma}\|x'-x\|^2\quad\forall x,x'\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, strong convexity of its conjugate with modulus sigma is equivalent to differentiability and one-over-sigma Lipschitz continuity of the primal gradient, an inverse-strong-monotonicity inequality for the subdifferential, an infimal-convolution representation with a quadratic, and the global quadratic upper-model inequality.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b)\iff(c)\iff(d)\iff(e),\text{ with the five properties stated above.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform convexity with a modulus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued Hilbert-space uniform convexity, including nonquadratic moduli and power-type subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi\) if, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\theta\in(0,1)\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)+\theta(1-\theta)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).\] It is uniformly convex if it admits at least one such modulus. A power-type modulus has the form \(\phi(t)=c t^p\) with \(c>0\) and an admissible exponent \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity strengthens strict convexity by requiring a Jensen deficit controlled solely by the distance between the two endpoints. The controlling function is the modulus of convexity and need not be quadratic. Strong convexity is the quadratic special case.
assumptions_latex: The inequality is required for all domain points and all \(0<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\theta\in(0,1))\;f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)+\theta(1-\theta)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact modulus is the pointwise infimum of the normalized Jensen deficit over pairs at a prescribed distance and mixing parameters.
Uniform convexity holds exactly when the exact modulus vanishes only at \(0\).
special_cases_latex: Strong convexity with constant \(\mu\) corresponds to \(\phi(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\).
Functions such as \(\|\cdot\|^p\) for \(p\ge2\) provide standard nonquadratic uniformly convex examples.
immediate_consequences_latex: Uniform convexity implies strict convexity.
If \(f\) is proper and convex, uniform convexity of \(f\) with modulus \(\phi\) makes \(\partial f\) uniformly monotone with modulus \(2\phi\).
boundary_notes: Strict convexity need not be uniform on an unbounded domain.
The modulus and power-type constants depend on the norm and on whether the property is global or restricted to a subset.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi\) when, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)
\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|).
\]
Positivity of \(\phi(r)\) for every \(r>0\) makes the convexity inequality quantitatively strict at every nonzero separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity requires the Jensen gap to dominate a positive modulus depending on the distance between the two points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient Growth from the Uniform Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way consequence under the seed's Jensen-gap normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) satisfies the seed's uniform-convexity inequality, then for \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(s\in\partial f(x)\),
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|x-y\|).
\]
Consequently, if \(r\in\partial f(y)\), then
\[
\langle s-r,x-y\rangle\ge2\phi(\|x-y\|).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Jensen modulus yields a subgradient remainder bound and quantitative monotonicity of the subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the accepted seed's uniform-convexity inequality with modulus \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)-f(x)-\langle s,y-x\rangle\ge\phi(\|x-y\|)\) and \(\langle s-r,x-y\rangle\ge2\phi(\|x-y\|)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness and Uniqueness Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a minimizer is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A uniformly convex function whose modulus satisfies \(\phi(r)>0\) for \(r>0\) is strictly convex on its effective domain. It therefore has at most one minimizer on each convex subset of that domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive uniform-convexity modulus implies strict convexity and uniqueness of any minimizer over a convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the accepted seed's uniform-convexity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly convex, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\) contains at most one point for every convex \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) satisfies

f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|),

then for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(s\in\partial f(x)\),

Hence, for \(s\in\partial f(x)\) and \(r\in\partial f(y)\),

\langle s-r,x-y\rangle\ge2\phi(\|x-y\|).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-modulus criterion for uniform convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of uniform convexity by positivity of the exact modulus at every positive distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with exact modulus of convexity \(\varphi\). Then
\[
f\text{ is uniformly convex}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\varphi\text{ vanishes only at }0.
\]
In this case, \(f\) is uniformly convex with modulus \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is uniformly convex exactly when its exact modulus is positive at every positive distance. In that case, the exact modulus itself is a modulus of uniform convexity.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
\varphi\text{ is the exact modulus of convexity of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is uniformly convex}\iff\bigl(\varphi(t)=0\iff t=0\bigr),\quad\text{and then }\varphi\text{ is a modulus of }f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact modulus of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distance-indexed normalized Jensen gap for a proper convex function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Its exact modulus of convexity is the function \(\varphi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
\varphi(t)=\inf_{\substack{x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \|x-y\|=t\\ \alpha\in(0,1)}}
\frac{\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)-f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At distance t, the exact modulus of convexity is the infimum of the normalized Jensen gap over all domain points separated by t and all nontrivial convex-combination weights.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(t)=\inf_{\substack{x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \|x-y\|=t\\ \alpha\in(0,1)}}\frac{\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)-f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Midpoint-gap characterization of uniform convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison of the exact modulus with the infimal midpoint Jensen gap and the resulting uniform-convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with exact modulus of convexity \(\varphi\), and define \(\psi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) by
\[
\psi(t)=\inf_{\substack{x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\\ \|x-y\|=t}}
\left(\frac12f(x)+\frac12f(y)-f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)\right).
\]
Then, pointwise on \(\mathbb R_+\),
\[
2\psi\leq\varphi\leq4\psi.
\]
Moreover,
\[
f\text{ is uniformly convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\psi\text{ vanishes only at }0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal midpoint Jensen gap determines the exact modulus up to factors two and four. Consequently, the function is uniformly convex exactly when the midpoint-gap function vanishes only at zero.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
\varphi\text{ is the exact modulus of convexity of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall t\in\mathbb R_+)\quad2\psi(t)\leq\varphi(t)\leq4\psi(t),\qquad f\text{ is uniformly convex}\iff\bigl(\psi(t)=0\iff t=0\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Growth properties of the exact modulus of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization, monotonicity, and quadratic dilation growth of the exact modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with exact modulus of convexity \(\varphi\). Then
\[
\varphi(0)=0,
\qquad
(\forall t\in\mathbb R_+)(\forall\gamma\in[1,+\infty))\quad
\varphi(\gamma t)\geq\gamma^2\varphi(t),
\]
and \(\varphi\) is increasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact modulus is zero at zero, is increasing, and grows at least quadratically when its distance argument is multiplied by any factor γ at least one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform convexity with a modulus and strong convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global and subset-restricted definitions for proper extended-real-valued functions on a Hilbert space, including the associated convexity hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at \(0\). Then \(f\) is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi\) if, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).
\]
It is strongly convex with constant \(\beta>0\) when this inequality holds with \(\phi(t)=\frac{\beta}{2}t^2\). For a nonempty \(C\subset\operatorname{dom}f\), uniform convexity on \(C\) is defined by the same inequality restricted to \(x,y\in C\). Moreover,
\[
\text{strong convexity}\Rightarrow\text{uniform convexity}\Rightarrow\text{strict convexity}\Rightarrow\text{convexity},
\]
and none of these implications is reversible in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity requires every nontrivial convex combination to gain a distance-dependent amount of curvature. The same condition restricted to endpoints in a nonempty subset defines uniform convexity on that subset. A positive quadratic modulus gives strong convexity. Strong convexity implies uniform convexity, which implies strict convexity, which implies convexity, and none of these implications reverses in general.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\quad \phi(t)=\tfrac{\beta}{2}t^2\text{ in the strongly convex case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform convexity of powers of nonnegative uniformly convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative preservation of uniform convexity under powers with exponent at least one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R_+\) be uniformly convex with exact modulus of convexity \(\varphi\), and let \(p\in[1,+\infty)\). Then \(g^p\) is uniformly convex, and its exact modulus of convexity \(\chi\) satisfies
\[
\chi\ge 2^{1-2p}\min\{p2^{1-p},1-2^{-p}\}\,\varphi^p.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a nonnegative-valued function on a Hilbert space is uniformly convex with exact modulus φ, then its p-th power is uniformly convex for every p at least 1. The exact modulus χ has the stated lower bound in terms of φ.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R_+\) is uniformly convex with exact modulus of convexity \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g^p\) is uniformly convex, and its exact modulus \(\chi\) satisfies \(\chi\ge 2^{1-2p}\min\{p2^{1-p},1-2^{-p}\}\varphi^p\).

f((1-t)x+ty)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Power Classes Are Distinct
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that different power exponents are not interchangeable on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), a global deficit \(c\,t(1-t)|x-y|^p\) with \(c>0\) exists exactly when \(p=2\). It fails for \(1<p<2\) at arbitrarily small separations and for \(p>2\) at arbitrarily large separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the whole real line, quadratic strong convexity is not power-type uniform convexity with an exponent other than two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) admits a global positive power-type constant with exponent \(p\) if and only if \(p=2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Global Power Classes Are Distinct

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power Growth of Subgradients and Objective Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constants use the accepted seed's Jensen-gap normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is uniformly convex of power type \(p\) with constant \(c\), then
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle+c\|y-x\|^p
\quad(s\in\partial f(x)),
\]
and
\[
\langle s-r,x-y\rangle\ge2c\|x-y\|^p
\quad(s\in\partial f(x),\ r\in\partial f(y)).
\]
Every global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies
\[
f(x)-f(x_*)\ge c\|x-x_*\|^p.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-type uniform convexity yields p-order subgradient growth and a p-order objective-error bound around a global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) satisfies the accepted seed with \(\phi(r)=cr^p\), where \(c>0\) and \(p>1\).
The displayed subgradients exist at the relevant points.
\(x_*\) is a global minimizer when the objective-error assertion is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle s-r,x-y\rangle\ge2c\|x-y\|^p\), and \(f(x)-f(x_*)\ge c\|x-x_*\|^p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Power Growth of Subgradients and Objective Error

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Curvature Does Not Change Power Globally
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that different power classes are genuinely distinct on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), the Jensen gap is \(\tfrac12t(1-t)|x-y|^2\). Therefore an inequality with deficit \(c\,t(1-t)|x-y|^p\) for all \(x,y\) and some \(c>0\) can hold only for \(p=2\): for \(1<p<2\) it fails as \(|x-y|\to0\), and for \(p>2\) it fails as \(|x-y|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the whole real line, quadratic strong convexity is not power-type uniform convexity with any exponent other than two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) admits a global positive power-type constant with exponent \(p\) if and only if \(p=2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power Function Induced by a Euclidean Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a centered norm-power function in a positive-definite Euclidean metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix $x_0\in\mathbb{E}$, and let $B$ be positive definite with induced Euclidean norm
\[
\|h\|=\langle Bh,h\rangle^{1/2}.
\]
The power function of degree $p$ centered at $x_0$ is
\[
d_p(x)=\frac{1}{p}\|x-x_0\|^p,\qquad x\in\mathbb{E}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a center x_0 and the Euclidean norm induced by a positive-definite operator B, the power function of degree p is one over p times the pth power of the distance from x to x_0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb{E},\quad d_p(x)=\frac1p\|x-x_0\|^p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Uniform Monotonicity Implies Power-Type Uniform Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for power-type uniform convexity of a differentiable function on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q$ be closed and convex and let $d:Q\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable. Suppose that for some $p\ge 2$ and $\sigma>0$,
\[
\langle\nabla d(x)-\nabla d(y),x-y\rangle\ge \sigma\|x-y\|^p,\qquad \forall x,y\in Q.
\]
Then $d$ is uniformly convex on $Q$ of degree $p$ with parameter $\sigma$; that is,
\[
d(y)\ge d(x)+\langle\nabla d(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{p}\|y-x\|^p,\qquad \forall x,y\in Q.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the gradient of a differentiable function on a closed convex set is uniformly monotone with p-power modulus sigma, then the function is uniformly convex of degree p with the same parameter sigma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x,y\in Q,\quad d(y)\ge d(x)+\langle\nabla d(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{p}\|y-x\|^p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient of a Centered Euclidean Norm-Power Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability and the gradient formula for a centered power of a Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathbb{E}$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with a Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and associated norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $B:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{E}$ satisfy
\[
\langle u,v\rangle=\langle Bu,v\rangle_{\mathrm{can}},\qquad \forall u,v\in\mathbb{E}.
\]
Fix $x_0\in\mathbb{E}$ and $p\ge2$, and define
\[
d_p(x)=\frac1p\|x-x_0\|^p.
\]
Then $d_p$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{E}$ and
\[
\nabla d_p(x)=\|x-x_0\|^{p-2}B(x-x_0),\qquad \forall x\in\mathbb{E}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the centered norm-power function is differentiable for p at least two, and its gradient is the displacement transformed by the metric operator B and scaled by the displacement norm to the power p−2.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb{E}\text{ is a finite-dimensional real vector space}
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\text{ is a Euclidean inner product with associated norm }\|\cdot\|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_p\text{ is differentiable on }\mathbb{E}\quad\text{and}\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{E},\ \nabla d_p(x)=\|x-x_0\|^{p-2}B(x-x_0)

children.top_down_role: Dual relationship between generalized curvature and smoothness moduli.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space with dual \(X^*\).
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\phi\) is proper, convex, nondecreasing, supercoercive, and satisfies \(\phi(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\phi\)-curvature inequality for \(f\) is equivalent to the \(\phi^*\)-smoothness inequality for \(f^*\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional subgradient formulation using Fenchel-conjugate moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curvature condition
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|y-x\|)
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X\text{ and }s\in\partial f(x)
\]
is equivalent, under the stated hypotheses, to differentiability of \(f^*\) on \(X^*\) together with
\[
f^*(v)\le f^*(u)+\langle\nabla f^*(u),v-u\rangle
+\phi^*(\|v-u\|_*)
\quad\text{for all }u,v\in X^*.
\]
Thus primal curvature and dual smoothness exchange conjugate moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform curvature controlled by phi corresponds under Fenchel conjugacy to dual smoothness controlled by the scalar conjugate phi-star.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modulus-paired uniform convexity and dual smoothness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\), let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}\). Let \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty]\) be convex with \(\phi(0)=0\), and define \(\phi^*(s)=\sup_{t\geq0}\{st-\phi(t)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records a norm-dependent Banach-space correspondence using first-order remainder inequalities. It does not assert that every modulus yields the displayed dual relation without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((f,f^*)\) has the uniform-convexity–dual-smoothness correspondence with primal modulus \(\phi\) when, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\) and every \(u\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle+\phi(\|y-x\|),\] and, dually, for every \(u,v\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*\) and every \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\), \[f^*(v)\leq f^*(u)+\langle v-u,x\rangle+\phi^*(\|v-u\|_*).\] The first inequality defines uniform convexity through a subgradient remainder; the second defines the matched uniform smoothness of the conjugate through the scalar conjugate modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function and its Fenchel conjugate form a modulus-paired uniformly convex and dually smooth pair when every primal subgradient model underestimates the function by at least \(\phi(\|y-x\|)\), while every dual subgradient model overestimates the conjugate by at most \(\phi^*(\|v-u\|_*)\). The norm and dual norm are part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(y)-f(x)-\langle u,y-x\rangle\geq\phi(\|y-x\|),\qquad f^*(v)-f^*(u)-\langle v-u,x\rangle\leq\phi^*(\|v-u\|_*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the Bregman remainder \(D_f^u(y,x)=f(y)-f(x)-\langle u,y-x\rangle\), the primal condition is \(D_f^u(y,x)\geq\phi(\|y-x\|)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\phi(t)=\frac{\mu}{2}t^2\), the primal condition is \(\mu\)-strong convexity; its classical dual counterpart is differentiability of \(f^*\) with \((1/\mu)\)-Lipschitz gradient under the usual closedness and full-domain hypotheses.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\phi(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\), the primal inequality implies strict convexity on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
boundary_notes: The numerical modulus changes with the chosen norm.
The displayed generalized dual modulus requires an exact supporting source; the available source material only separately supports uniform convexity and quadratic strong-convexity duality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative smoothness and relative strong convexity pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(h:Q\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and put \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\cap Q\). Assume \(h\) and \(f:Q\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are differentiable on \(U\). Define \(D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable relative curvature on a specified comparison set. Nonsmooth reference geometries require subgradient-based variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(0\leq\mu\leq L<+\infty\), the pair \((f,h)\) is \((\mu,L)\)-relatively curved on \(U\) if, for all \(x,y\in U\), \[\mu D_h(y,x)\leq f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\leq L D_h(y,x).\] The upper inequality defines \(L\)-relative smoothness of \(f\) with respect to \(h\), and the lower inequality defines \(\mu\)-relative strong convexity. The ordered data \((f,h,Q,\mu,L)\), rather than \(f\) alone, constitutes the relative curvature class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective-reference pair \((f,h)\) has relative curvature parameters \((\mu,L)\) when the first-order remainder of \(f\) lies between \(\mu\) and \(L\) times the Bregman divergence generated by \(h\), for every ordered pair of points in the declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x,y\in U:\quad \mu D_h(y,x)\leq D_f(y,x)\leq L D_h(y,x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(f\) and \(h\) are differentiable convex functions on an open convex set, the condition is equivalent to convexity of \(f-\mu h\) and \(Lh-f\) on that set.

If both functions are twice differentiable, the condition is equivalently \(\mu
abla^2h(x)\preceq
abla^2f(x)\preceq L
abla^2h(x)\) for every \(x\in U\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\frac12\|x\|_2^2\), the definition reduces to ordinary \(L\)-smoothness and \(\mu\)-strong convexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\mu>0\) and \(h\) is strictly convex, then \(f\) is strictly convex on \(U\).

Boundary points at which the gradients do not exist are excluded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional upper curvature relative to a Bregman reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, let \(f,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(L\ge0\). The function \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth relative to \(h\) when \(Lh-f\) is convex on \(C\). Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\), \[D_f(y,x)\le LD_h(y,x),\] or \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+LD_h(y,x).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is }L\text{-smooth relative to }h\iff Lh-f\text{ is convex}\iff D_f\le LD_h\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of Relative Accuracy from a Surrogate Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient smoothing or approximation order converts relative accuracy for a positive surrogate into the same relative accuracy for the target objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta>0\), \(r>1\), and let \(\phi,f_p:Q\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\) satisfy \(\tfrac12\phi(y)^2\le f_p(y)\le \tfrac12 r^{1/p}\phi(y)^2\) for every \(y\in Q\). Define \(f_p^*=\inf_{y\in Q}f_p(y)\) and \(\phi_*=\inf_{y\in Q}\phi(y)\). If \(p\in\mathbb N\) satisfies \(p\ge \frac{1+\delta}{\delta}\ln r\), then every \(\bar y\in Q\) satisfying \(f_p(\bar y)\le(1+\delta)f_p^*\) also satisfies \(\phi(\bar y)\le(1+\delta)\phi_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive objectives related by the stated two-sided multiplicative bound, choosing the approximation order at least ((1+delta)/delta) log r ensures that a (1+delta)-relative solution of the surrogate is also a (1+delta)-relative solution of the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(\bar y)\le(1+\delta)\phi_*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Relative Modulus Does Not Ensure Uniqueness for a Degenerate Reference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of strict reference geometry for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{R}^2\), let \(h(x_1,x_2)=\frac12x_1^2\) and \(f=\mu h\) with \(\mu>0\). Then \(f-\mu h=0\) is convex, so \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\), but \[\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb{R}\}.\] Thus a positive relative modulus does not imply ordinary strict convexity or a unique minimizer when the reference has flat directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate quadratic reference permits positive relative strong convexity while leaving an entire affine set of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\), but its minimizer is not unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Relative Modulus Does Not Ensure Uniqueness for a Degenerate Reference

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Curvature Need Not Be Euclidean Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-adapted reference geometry versus the Euclidean quadratic reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=(0,\infty)\), set \(f=h=-\log x\). Then \(D_f=D_h\), so \(f\) is both \(1\)-smooth and \(1\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\). However, \(f'(x)=-1/x\) is not globally Lipschitz on \(C\), since \(f''(x)=x^{-2}\) is unbounded near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic barrier is perfectly conditioned relative to itself but has no globally Lipschitz Euclidean gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f=D_h\) while \(\operatorname{Lip}(f';C)=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Invariance and Positive Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator changes that preserve or uniformly rescale Bregman geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\ell\) is affine and \(c>0\), then \[D_{h+\ell}(y,x)=D_h(y,x),\qquad D_{ch}(y,x)=cD_h(y,x).\] Thus affine perturbations leave relative-curvature classes and constants unchanged, while replacing \(h\) by \(ch\) divides every relative smoothness or relative strong-convexity constant by \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine perturbations do not change a reference divergence, while positive scaling rescales relative-curvature constants reciprocally.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and convex on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{h+\ell}=D_h\) and \(D_{ch}=cD_h\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance and Positive Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer Under Comparable Reference Divergences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative change of relative-curvature constants between comparable generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \[aD_{h_1}(y,x)\le D_{h_2}(y,x)\le bD_{h_1}(y,x)\] on a common set of admissible pairs, where \(0<a\le b<\infty\). If \[\mu D_{h_1}(y,x)\le D_f(y,x)\le LD_{h_1}(y,x),\] then \[\frac\mu bD_{h_2}(y,x)\le D_f(y,x)\le\frac LaD_{h_2}(y,x).\] Without the appropriate one-sided comparison, the corresponding relative-curvature bound need not transfer; changing the reference domain may also change the admissible pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparable reference divergences transfer relative curvature bounds with rescaled constants; absent comparison or a common domain, membership need not transfer.
assumptions_latex: \(f,h_1,h_2\) are differentiable on the common interiors needed to define their Bregman divergences.
All inequalities hold on the same admissible ordered pairs \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu D_{h_1}\le D_f\le LD_{h_1}\Rightarrow (\mu/b)D_{h_2}\le D_f\le(L/a)D_{h_2}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how relative curvature constants change under comparable reference geometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) satisfies \(\mu D_{h_1}(y,x)\leq D_f(y,x)\leq L D_{h_1}(y,x)\), then comparison of the reference divergences gives \[ \frac{\mu}{b}D_{h_2}(y,x)\leq D_f(y,x)\leq\frac{L}{a}D_{h_2}(y,x). \] Thus relative strong-convexity and smoothness constants depend quantitatively on the chosen generator. Without two-sided divergence comparability, membership in either relative class need not transfer; changing the effective domain of the generator may also change the admissible pairs \((x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reference-dependent relative curvature constants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f,h\) be differentiable on a convex set \(U\subseteq Q\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\). For distinct \(x,y\in U\) with \(D_h(y,x)>0\), define \(R_{f|h}(y,x)=D_f(y,x)/D_h(y,x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates dependence on both the reference generator and the set on which curvature comparisons are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reference-geometry curvature interval of \(f\) relative to \(h\) on \(U\) is \[\mu_U(f|h)=\inf_{\substack{x,y\in U\,,\ x\ne y\\D_h(y,x)>0}}R_{f|h}(y,x),\qquad L_U(f|h)=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in U\,,\ x\ne y\\D_h(y,x)>0}}R_{f|h}(y,x).\] Reference-geometry dependence means that membership in a relative curvature class is assigned to the triple \((f,h,U)\): changing \(h\), its effective domain, or \(U\) may change either endpoint or make an endpoint infinite. Pairs satisfying \(D_h(y,x)=0\) are handled separately and require \(D_f(y,x)=0\) for a finite upper relative-smoothness constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative curvature is not an intrinsic property of the objective alone. Its best lower and upper constants are the infimum and supremum of the ratio between the Bregman remainders of the objective and reference function over the declared ordered pairs and domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mu_U(f|h)\,D_h(y,x)\leq D_f(y,x)\leq L_U(f|h)\,D_h(y,x)\quad(x,y\in U)\] whenever the zero-denominator compatibility condition holds.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite constants, \(\mu_U(f|h)\) is the largest \(\mu\) for which \(f-\mu h\) is convex on \(U\), while \(L_U(f|h)\) is the smallest \(L\) for which \(Lh-f\) is convex on \(U\).
special_cases_latex: Replacing \(h\) by \(ah+b+\langle c,\cdot\rangle\) with \(a>0\) rescales both constants by \(1/a\), because affine terms do not change Bregman divergences.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(U_1\subseteq U_2\), then \(\mu_{U_1}(f|h)\geq\mu_{U_2}(f|h)\) and \(L_{U_1}(f|h)\leq L_{U_2}(f|h)\).
boundary_notes: Degenerate references with vanishing Bregman divergence require explicit compatibility.
Constants computed on an open interior do not automatically extend to the boundary.

notation.meaning: best relative curvature endpoints on U

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Curvature Need Not Imply Euclidean Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete dependence on a singular boundary-adapted generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=(0,\infty)\), let \(h(x)=f(x)=-\log x\). Then \(D_f=D_h\), so \(f\) is both \(1\)-smooth and \(1\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\). Nevertheless \(f'(x)=-1/x\) is not globally Lipschitz on \(C\), since \(f''(x)=x^{-2}\) is unbounded near zero. Thus relative curvature membership can change when the reference geometry is replaced by the Euclidean quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic barrier is perfectly conditioned relative to itself but has no globally Lipschitz Euclidean gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f=D_h\) while \(\operatorname{Lip}(f';C)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Curvature Need Not Imply Euclidean Smoothness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate References Do Not Control Flat Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of norm-like curvature control without strict convexity of the generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a differentiable convex reference \(h\) is affine along a nonzero direction \(d\), then \(D_h(x+td,x)=0\) along every admissible segment in that direction. Consequently a bound \(D_f\ge\mu D_h\) or \(D_f\le L D_h\) supplies no positive norm-like curvature control in that direction merely from \(\mu>0\) or \(L<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference with flat directions cannot transfer relative bounds into norm-like control along those directions.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is affine on an admissible segment parallel to \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x+td,x)=0\) on that segment.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate References Do Not Control Flat Directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Invariance and Scaling of Reference Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformations of a generator that preserve or rescale its Bregman geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on a convex domain, let \(\ell(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\) be affine, and let \(c>0\). Then \[D_{h+\ell}(y,x)=D_h(y,x),\qquad D_{ch}(y,x)=cD_h(y,x).\] Therefore affine perturbations of the reference do not change relative curvature classes or constants, while replacing \(h\) by \(ch\) changes a relative smoothness or strong-convexity constant \(\kappa\) to \(\kappa/c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine changes of a reference leave its Bregman divergence unchanged, while positive scaling rescales all relative curvature constants reciprocally.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and convex on its convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{h+\ell}=D_h\) and \(D_{ch}=cD_h\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance and Scaling of Reference Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-concordant function and local Hessian geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex with nonempty interior and let \(f:\operatorname{int}C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and three times continuously differentiable. For \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), define the local seminorm \(\|h\|_x=(h^\top\nabla^2f(x)h)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional classical self-concordance. The definition is a function-class interface; barrier parameters and path-following complexity are separate refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is self-concordant with constant \(M\geq0\) if, for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\) and \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[|
abla^3f(x)[h,h,h]|\leq M\|h\|_x^3.\] It is standard self-concordant when \(M=2\). If \(
abla^2f(x)\succ0\), the associated dual local norm is \(\|u\|_{x,*}=(u^	op[
abla^2f(x)]^{-1}u)^{1/2}\), and the Newton decrement is \(\lambda_f(x)=\|
abla f(x)\|_{x,*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-times continuously differentiable convex function is self-concordant when its third directional derivative is uniformly controlled by the three-halves power of its Hessian quadratic form. Constant two gives the standard normalization. The Hessian defines the local primal and dual norms used by Newton methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in\operatorname{int}C\ \forall h\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad |\nabla^3f(x)[h,h,h]|\leq M(h^\top\nabla^2f(x)h)^{3/2}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because replacing \(h\) by \(-h\) reverses the sign of the trilinear value, the source's one-sided inequality is equivalent to the absolute-value form.
special_cases_latex: The function \(f(t)=-\log t\) on \((0,+\infty)\) is standard self-concordant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Where the Hessian is positive definite, self-concordance supplies an intrinsic local metric and the Newton decrement \(\lambda_f(x)\).
boundary_notes: Self-concordance alone is not the definition of a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier.
A singular Hessian yields only a seminorm unless an appropriate affine hull is used.

notation.meaning: third derivative applied to h in all three arguments

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with nonempty interior. Let \(F:\operatorname{int}C\to\mathbb{R}\) be standard self-concordant and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional barrier interface for minimizing a linear objective over a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(F\) is a \(
u\)-self-concordant barrier for \(C\) if it is standard self-concordant, tends to \(+\infty\) at the boundary of \(C\), and satisfies \[
abla^2F(x)\succeq rac1
u
abla F(x)
abla F(x)^	op\qquad(x\in\operatorname{int}C).\] Equivalently in the cited normalization, \(x\mapsto e^{-F(x)/
u}\) is concave. For \(t>0\), the barrier objective is \(F_t(x)=t\langle c,xangle+F(x)\), and any unique minimizer \(x^*(t)=\arg\min_{x\in\operatorname{int}C}F_t(x)\) is a point on the central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-concordant optimization interface consists of a standard self-concordant barrier with parameter \(\nu\), its local Hessian metric, and the central path obtained by minimizing the barrier plus a positive multiple of the linear objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_t(x)=t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x),\qquad x^*(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{int}C}F_t(x),\qquad \|\nabla F(x)\|_{x,*}\leq\sqrt\nu.\]

In the cited normalization, it is also equivalent to concavity of \(e^{-F/\nu}\).
special_cases_latex: The logarithmic barrier \(F(x)=-\log x\) on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}\) is a \(1\)-self-concordant barrier.
immediate_consequences_latex: The barrier parameter controls the permitted central-path parameter increase and appears in path-following iteration bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient of a Barrier-Regularized Support Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An envelope differentiability result under uniqueness of every maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \widehat P\subseteq\mathbb E be nonempty, x_0\in\widehat P, \beta>0, and F:\widehat P\to\mathbb R. Suppose that for every s\in\mathbb E^* the maximization defining U_\beta(s)=\max_{u\in\widehat P}\{\langle s,u-x_0\rangle-\beta(F(u)-F(x_0))\} has a unique maximizer u_\beta^*(s). Then U_\beta is differentiable on \mathbb E^* and \nabla U_\beta(s)=u_\beta^*(s)-x_0 for every s\in\mathbb E^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the barrier-regularized linear maximization problem has a unique maximizer for every dual vector, its value function is differentiable everywhere, and its gradient is the maximizer minus the center point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_\beta\text{ is differentiable on }\mathbb E^*,\qquad \nabla U_\beta(s)=u_\beta^*(s)-x_0\quad\forall s\in\mathbb E^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Difference Bounds for a Self-Concordant Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the local dual norm at the comparison point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a self-concordant function \(f\) on \(Q\) and all \(x,y\in Q\), letting \(t=\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|_y^*\),
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle f'(x),y-x\rangle+\omega(t).
\]
If additionally \(t<1\), then
\[
f(y)\le f(x)+\langle f'(x),y-x\rangle+\omega_*(t).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two points in the domain of a self-concordant function, the Taylor remainder is at least omega of the gradient-difference dual local norm. When that norm is below one, the remainder is also at most omega-star of the same quantity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)-f(x)-\langle f'(x),y-x\rangle\ge\omega(t),\quad t<1\Rightarrow f(y)-f(x)-\langle f'(x),y-x\rangle\le\omega_*(t)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Self-Concordant Upper Model for a Smoothed Support Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds a dual perturbation of the barrier-regularized value function in the local dual norm at its maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \beta>0, s\in\mathbb E^*, P_0\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q, and let F be standard self-concordant on \operatorname{int}Q. Suppose U_\beta(s)=\max_{y\in P_0}\{\langle s,y-x_0\rangle-\beta(F(y)-F(x_0))\} has the unique maximizer x=u_\beta^\star(s). Then U_\beta is differentiable at s, \nabla U_\beta(s)=x-x_0, and every g\in\mathbb E^* with \|g\|_x^*<\beta satisfies U_\beta(s+g)\le U_\beta(s)+\langle g,\nabla U_\beta(s)\rangle+\beta\omega_*\!\left(\|g\|_x^*/\beta\right), where \omega_*(\tau)=-\tau-\ln(1-\tau) for 0\le\tau<1 and \omega_*(\tau)\le\tau^2/[2(1-\tau)].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a uniquely attained barrier-smoothed support value, the gradient equals the maximizing point minus the center. A dual perturbation smaller than beta in the maximizer's local dual norm admits the standard self-concordant omega-star upper model, with its quadratic-over-linear bound.
assumptions_latex: x=u_\beta^\star(s)\in P_0\text{ exists and is the unique maximizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla U_\beta(s)=x-x_0,\qquad U_\beta(s+g)\le U_\beta(s)+\langle g,\nabla U_\beta(s)\rangle+\beta\omega_*\!\left(\frac{\|g\|_x^*}{\beta}\right),\qquad \omega_*(\tau)\le\frac{\tau^2}{2(1-\tau)}\ \ (0\le\tau<1).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Newton displacement \(d_x=-\nabla^2f(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) has local norm \(\lVert d_x\rVert_x=\lambda_f(x)\). Consequently, \(\lambda_f(x)<1\) places the full Newton iterate \(x^+=x+d_x\) inside the unit Dikin ellipsoid of the effective domain and therefore inside \(C\). The scalar \(\lambda_f(x)\) is affine invariant and measures the first-order residual in the dual local metric, making it both a step-size indicator and a local optimality gauge for self-concordant minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the effective domain of a closed self-concordant function, the Hessian supplies Newton's local metric, while a Newton decrement below one certifies that the full Newton step remains in the domain.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, and \(F\) is a strictly convex self-concordant barrier on \(K\).
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and for every \(t>0\) the displayed minimizer exists uniquely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla F(x(t))+tc=0\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-path formulation for linear optimization with a self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the central-path point by \[ x(t)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}\bigl\{t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\bigr\}. \] Its first-order characterization is \(\nabla F(x(t))+tc=0\). Path-following increases \(t\) and approximately minimizes each successive barrier objective using Newton steps measured in its Hessian metric. The parameter update must keep the previous point within a controlled Newton neighborhood of the new central-path point; self-concordance then supports restoration by a bounded number of correction steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path-following tracks minimizers of increasingly weighted linear objectives plus a barrier, using the self-concordant Hessian metric for Newton corrections.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Following Navigation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gap–distance–residual certificate system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper with finite attained minimum \(f_*\), and let \(S=\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\). Define \(G(x)=f(x)-f_*\), \(D(x)=d(x,S)\), and let \(R:X\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(R^{-1}(0)=S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract function-level certificate system. Particular residuals may be subgradient, proximal-gradient, KKT, or feasibility residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A growth certificate system on a set \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is the data \((G,D,R;\omega,\eta,\theta)\), where \(\omega,\eta,\theta:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty]\) vanish at zero, are positive on positive arguments in their stated ranges, and satisfy, for every \(x\in U\), \[G(x)\geq\omega(D(x)),\qquad D(x)\leq\eta(R(x)),\qquad G(x)\leq\theta(R(x)).\] Any nonempty subset of these inequalities is a partial certificate system, but its components and domain must be declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growth certificate system relates three quantities: objective gap, distance to the solution set, and a residual whose zero set equals the solutions. Comparison functions specify which quantities bound the others on a declared region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in U:\quad \omega(d(x,S))\leq f(x)-f_*\leq\theta(R(x)),\qquad d(x,S)\leq\eta(R(x)).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(\omega\) is strictly increasing, the growth inequality is equivalently \(D(x)\leq\omega^{-1}(G(x))\), using the generalized inverse.
special_cases_latex: Power comparison functions \(\omega(t)=ct^p\) produce exponent-parameterized objective growth.
Choosing \(R(x)=G(x)\) yields an objective-gap error bound.
immediate_consequences_latex: Composing valid comparison functions converts one certificate into another whenever the required inequalities have compatible directions.
boundary_notes: The zero-set condition alone does not imply any quantitative error bound.
All constants and comparison functions may be local or level-set dependent.

notation.meaning: objective gap, solution distance, and residual

review_flags: The node is a synthetic organizing concept; no inspected source states this exact three-component certificate-system definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap–distance–residual certificate system

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This synthetic three-component certificate system has no source supporting its exact data structure, comparison directions, or partial-system convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective growth relative to the minimizer set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its finite minimum \(f_*\), and let \(S=\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\). Let \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) contain \(S\), and let \(\omega:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(\omega(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General, possibly local, growth condition relative to a non-singleton solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) has \(\omega\)-objective growth on \(U\) if \[f(x)-f_*\geq\omega(d(x,S))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The condition is strict when \(\omega(t)>0\) for every positive distance attained on \(U\). A constant-modulus power growth condition is obtained by taking \(\omega(t)=ct^p\) with \(c>0\) and \(p>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective growth means that the objective gap is bounded below by a prescribed function of the distance from the point to the entire minimizer set. The domain on which the inequality is required is part of the condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in U:\quad f(x)-\inf f\geq\omega\bigl(d(x,\operatorname{argmin}f)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\omega\) is strictly increasing, the condition is equivalently \(d(x,S)\leq\omega^{-1}(f(x)-f_*)\) on \(U\), with generalized inverse if necessary.
special_cases_latex: The choices \(\omega(t)=\alpha t\) and \(\omega(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\) give sharp and quadratic growth, respectively.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\omega(t)>0\) for \(t>0\), every point in \(U\) having zero objective gap belongs to \(S\).
boundary_notes: Growth relative to \(S\) does not imply that the minimizer is unique.
A local growth condition need not extend to the full domain.

notation.meaning: infimum of d(x,s) over s in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Minimum Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global linear objective growth at a minimizer, together with the unconstrained smooth-function failure boundary stated by the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x^*\) is a sharp minimum point of \(f\) if there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that \[f(x)\geq f(x^*)+\alpha\|x-x^*\|\qquad\text{for every }x.\] At an unconstrained minimum that is an interior accumulation point of the domain, this condition cannot hold when \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sharp minimum is separated from every other point by a uniform positive linear objective-growth bound. Such growth is incompatible with differentiability at an unconstrained interior minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\geq f(x^*)+\alpha\|x-x^*\|\quad\forall x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Local-to-Global Principle and Strict-Convexity Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States globality of local minimizers for convex objectives and uniqueness, conditional on existence, for strictly convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex. If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is convex, every local minimum of \(f\) over \(X\) is a global minimum. If \(f\) is strictly convex on \(X\), then \(f\) has at most one global minimum over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function on a convex feasible set, every local minimizer is global. If the function is strictly convex, two distinct global minimizers cannot exist; the theorem does not assert that a minimizer exists.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the uniqueness clause, }f\text{ is strictly convex on }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ local minimizer}\Rightarrow x^*\text{ global minimizer},\qquad f\text{ strictly convex}\Rightarrow |\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)|\le 1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global minimizers, argmin sets, and nested minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines attainment and characterizes product-space minimizers through partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \bar f:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x). A point \bar x\in X is a global minimizer of f on X precisely when f(\bar x)=\bar f\le f(x) for every x\in X; in this case the infimum is attained and is the minimal value. The set of all such points is \operatorname{Argmin}_{x\in X}f(x), with \operatorname{argmin} used when it is a singleton. Moreover, for \varphi(x):=\inf_{y\in Y}g(x,y),
\[(\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}g(x,y)\iff \bar x\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{x\in X}\varphi(x)\ \text{and}\ \bar y\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}g(\bar x,y).\]
The symmetric characterization follows by interchanging x and y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimizer attains the infimum of a function over its domain, and Argmin denotes the set of all global minimizers. For a function on a product set, a pair is globally minimizing exactly when its first component minimizes the partial-infimum function and its second component minimizes the remaining slice; the analogous statement holds with the variables interchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\iff \bar x\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{X\times Y}g\iff \bar x\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{X}\varphi\ \land\ \bar y\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{Y}g(\bar x,\cdot).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Variational-Inequality Optimality Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity uses convexity of the feasible set and differentiability at the local minimizer; convexity of the objective makes the condition sufficient for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(x^*\in X\), and suppose \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\). If \(x^*\) is a local minimum of \(f\) over \(X\), then \[\nabla f(x^*)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^*)\ge 0\qquad\forall x\in X.\] If, in addition, \(f\) is convex on \(X\), this inequality is sufficient for \(x^*\) to be a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a differentiable local minimizer over a convex feasible set, the gradient has a nonnegative inner product with every displacement from the minimizer to another feasible point. When the objective is convex, this condition also guarantees global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ local minimizer}\Rightarrow \nabla f(x^*)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^*)\ge0\ \forall x\in X;\qquad f\text{ convex and the inequality holds}\Rightarrow x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local, Global, and Strict Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the principal minimizer classes over a feasible set and records the corresponding maximizer definition and convex local-to-global implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(x^*\in X\). The point \(x^*\) is a local minimum of \(f\) over \(X\) if \(\exists\varepsilon>0\) such that \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) satisfying \(\|x-x^*\|<\varepsilon\). It is a global minimum if \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Either minimum is strict when the corresponding inequality is strict for every admissible \(x\ne x^*\). Local and global maxima are the corresponding local and global minima of \(-f\). If \(X\) is convex and \(f\) is convex on \(X\), every local minimum is global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is locally minimizing when no sufficiently close feasible point has a smaller value, and globally minimizing when no feasible point anywhere has a smaller value. Strict minima require strict inequality at every distinct point in the relevant comparison set. Maxima are minima of the negative objective. For a convex function on a convex feasible set, every local minimum is global.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the local-to-global clause, }X\text{ and }f\text{ are convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}x^*\text{ local min}&\iff \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall x\in X:\ \|x-x^*\|<\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(x^*)\le f(x),\\x^*\text{ global min}&\iff \forall x\in X:\ f(x^*)\le f(x),\\X,f\text{ convex and }x^*\text{ local min}&\Rightarrow x^*\text{ global min}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Unique and Nonsingular Minimum Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two local notions for smooth unconstrained minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A minimum point x^* is locally unique if there exists a neighborhood U of x^* containing no other minimum point. A local minimum point x^* is nonsingular if the sufficient second-order conditions hold at x^*, namely \nabla f(x^*)=0 and \nabla^2 f(x^*)\succ0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum is locally unique when it is the only minimum in some neighborhood. A smooth local minimum is nonsingular when its gradient vanishes and its Hessian is positive definite.
