children.title: Set-Relative Growth Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometries requiring set-relative rather than pointwise growth.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of point-relative growth with valid set-relative growth
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have a nonempty minimizer set \(S\), let \(\bar x\in S\), and let \(\psi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) be positive away from zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry with nonisolated minimizers, where distance to the solution set is the appropriate growth variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set-relative growth regime on \(U\) is specified by a constant \(c>0\) such that \[f(x)-\min f\geq c\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,S))\qquad(x\in U).\] It is a point-relative growth failure regime at \(\bar x\in S\) if no \(c'>0\) satisfies \[f(x)-f(\bar x)\geq c'\psi(\|x-\bar x\|)\qquad(x\in U).\] In particular, if \(U\cap(S\setminus\{\bar x\})\neq\varnothing\), the point-relative inequality fails automatically while the set-relative inequality may remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-relative growth measures displacement normal to the entire minimizer set. A point-relative certificate can fail simply because other minimizers lie near the reference minimizer, even though objective growth away from the solution set is quantitatively strong.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set-relative growth holds on \(U\), but no positive point-relative growth constant at \(\bar x\) is admissible.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Point-relative failure is \(\inf_{x\in U\setminus\{\bar x\}}(f(x)-f(\bar x))/\psi(\|x-\bar x\|)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a manifold of minimizers, quadratic growth may hold in normal directions through \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) while pointwise quadratic growth fails.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convergence of objective values can control distance to \(S\) without selecting a unique minimizer.
boundary_notes: When \(S=\{\bar x\}\), set-relative and point-relative distances coincide.
The definition does not impose smoothness or manifold structure on \(S\).
review_flags: No precise source locator for this named failure regime was found.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of point-relative growth with valid set-relative growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between set-relative and point-relative growth is mathematically coherent, but the proposed named regime lacks independent source support.

children.title: Nonisolated Solution Sets
children.top_down_role: Solution geometries containing continua of minimizers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonuniqueness Implies Nonisolation for Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity turns any pair of distinct minimizers into a minimizing segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex on a real normed space and let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Then \(S\) is convex. If \(x_0,x_1\in S\) are distinct, every point \((1-t)x_0+tx_1\), \(0\leq t\leq1\), belongs to \(S\), and every point of that segment is nonisolated in \(S\). Consequently, \(S\) contains an isolated minimizer if and only if \(S\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective, two minimizers generate an entire minimizing segment; therefore a nonsingleton minimizer set has no isolated points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|S|>1\), then no point of \(S\) is isolated; equivalently, \(S\) contains an isolated minimizer exactly when it is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Implies Nonisolation for Convex Objectives

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set is nonisolated when some \(\bar x\in S\) is an accumulation point of \(S\setminus\{\bar x\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard topological definition applied to an optimization solution set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological nonisolation of at least one minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a metric space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum, with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). The solution set is nonisolated at \(\bar x\in S\) if every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a point of \(S\setminus\{\bar x\}\); equivalently, there exists a sequence \((x^k)\subset S\setminus\{\bar x\}\) such that \(x^k\to\bar x\). The problem has a nonisolated solution set if this condition holds at at least one minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is nonisolated when distinct minimizers approach it arbitrarily closely; a solution set is nonisolated if it contains such a point.

children.title: Degenerate Solution Geometry

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set-relative quadratic growth holds exactly, while pointwise quadratic growth about any fixed minimizer fails because of the tangent solution direction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular curvature along a nonisolated solution direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x,y)=x^2\). Its solution set is \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\), and
\[
f(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^2,
\]
so set-relative quadratic growth holds globally. However, for any fixed \(\bar z=(0,\bar y)\in S\) and any \(\mu>0\), the point \(z=(0,y)\in S\) with \(y\neq\bar y\) satisfies \(f(z)-f(\bar z)=0\) while \(\|z-\bar z\|>0\). Thus pointwise quadratic growth about \(\bar z\) fails because the solution geometry contains an unpenalized tangent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat solution direction can destroy pointwise growth even when exact quadratic growth relative to the whole solution set holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Solution Geometry

children.title: Set-Relative Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth measured relative to an entire solution set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Comparison of Set-Relative Growth Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent monotonicity on bounded-distance regions and its global limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that for some \(p>0\), \(\mu>0\), and set \(U\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu\,\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f),
\]
and that \(0<\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq R\) for all \(x\in(U\cap\operatorname{dom}f)\setminus S\), where \(R>0\). Then for every \(q\geq p\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu R^{p-q}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
Thus order-\(p\) growth implies every higher-order bound on a bounded-distance region, but this implication is not automatic globally when distances from \(S\) are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded-distance region, order-p growth implies every higher order q with a rescaled modulus; this need not extend to an unbounded global region.
assumptions_latex: Order-\(p\) set-relative growth holds on U.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(q\geq p\), order-\(q\) growth holds on U with modulus \(\mu R^{p-q}\).

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and has nonempty minimizer set \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local or global Hölder growth measured from the complete minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). For a set \(U\subset X\), \(f\) has set-relative growth of order \(p\) on \(U\) if there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu\,\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p
\]
for every \(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), where \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{s\in S}\|x-s\|\). The condition is local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(S\), and global when \(U=X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-relative growth lower-bounds objective suboptimality by a positive power of the distance to the entire minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Relative Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise and locally appropriate, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Pointwise Growth Forces Local Isolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General obstruction to every positive-order growth inequality centered at one minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum \(f^*\), let \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and suppose that for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(\mu>0\), and \(p>0\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu\,d(x,\bar x)^p
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
Then \(U\cap\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\). Consequently, if \(\bar x\) is a nonisolated minimizer, no positive-modulus pointwise growth inequality of any order \(p>0\) can hold near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any positive point-centered growth bound makes its center locally unique, so a nonisolated minimizer defeats every such bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and f attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise growth implies \(U\cap\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\); nonisolation implies failure of every positive pointwise growth modulus.

notation.meaning: selected minimizer serving as the pointwise center

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Pointwise Growth Forces Local Isolation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise growth about any chosen minimizer fails, although quadratic growth relative to \(S\) holds exactly.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonisolated minimizers invalidate growth measured from one selected solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(u,v)=u^2\), the minimum value is \(f^*=0\) and \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\). For every \(\bar x=(0,\bar v)\in S\), \(p>0\), \(\mu>0\), and neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), there exists \(v\neq\bar v\) such that \((0,v)\in U\) and
\[
f(0,v)-f^*=0<\mu\|(0,v)-\bar x\|^p.
\]
Thus no positive pointwise growth bound about \(\bar x\) holds, whereas
\[
f(u,v)-f^*=\operatorname{dist}((u,v),S)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat line of minimizers defeats every positive growth bound from one chosen minimizer, while quadratic growth relative to the full solution set remains valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Growth Failure

children.title: Local–Global Error-Bound Gap
children.top_down_role: Failure of neighborhood regularity to extend over the full domain.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is the stated convex continuously differentiable function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A quadratic error bound valid near \(S\) need not extend globally with any positive constant.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex example separating neighborhood quadratic growth from global quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&|x|\leq 1,\\2|x|-1,&|x|>1.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable, with \(f^*=0\) and \(S=\{0\}\). On \([-1,1]\),
\[
f(x)-f^*=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.
\]
For every \(\mu>0\), there exists \(x>1\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*=2x-1<\mu x^2=\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.
\]
Hence the local quadratic error bound has no global extension with a positive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can grow quadratically near its minimizer but only linearly at infinity, so its local quadratic error bound has no global extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Error-Bound Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman geometry generated by a Legendre function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(h\) is differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional non-Euclidean geometry; the second Bregman argument must lie in the differentiability domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bregman divergence generated by \(h\) is \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle,\qquad x\in\operatorname{dom}h,\ y\in C.\] If \(h\) is Legendre, then \(h^*\) is Legendre, \(
abla h:C	o C^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\) is bijective with inverse \(
abla h^*\), and the associated Bregman–Legendre geometry consists of the primal divergence together with these dual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman–Legendre geometry is generated by the first-order deviation of a convex Legendre function from its supporting affine function. Legendre duality supplies one-to-one gradient coordinates between the interiors of the primal and conjugate domains.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and Legendre.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)\) is defined as above, and \(\nabla h:C\to C^*\) has inverse \(\nabla h^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x,y\in C\), \(D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(\nabla h(y),\nabla h(x))\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity gives \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\).
Strict convexity on \(C\) gives \(D_h(x,y)=0\) only when \(x=y\) for \(x,y\in C\).
boundary_notes: A Bregman divergence is generally asymmetric and need not satisfy the triangle inequality.
Boundary points at which \(h\) is not differentiable cannot serve as the second argument.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Univariate Fenchel conjugacy and inverse-derivative identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy identities for a strictly convex differentiable function on the nonnegative half-line whose derivative increases from zero toward one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and strictly convex, with \(\omega'(0)=0\) and \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\omega'(t)=1\). For \(\tau\in[0,1)\), define
\[
\omega_*(\tau):=\sup_{s\ge0}\{\tau s-\omega(s)\},\qquad \omega_*'(\tau):=(\omega')^{-1}(\tau).
\]
Then, for every \(t\ge0\) and \(\tau\in[0,1)\),
\[
\omega'(\omega_*'(\tau))=\tau,\qquad \omega_*'(\omega'(t))=t,
\]
\[
\omega(t)=\max_{0\le\xi<1}\{\xi t-\omega_*(\xi)\},\qquad
\omega_*(\tau)=\max_{\xi\ge0}\{\tau\xi-\omega(\xi)\},
\]
\[
\omega(t)+\omega_*(\tau)\ge \tau t,
\]
and
\[
\omega_*(\tau)=\tau\omega_*'(\tau)-\omega(\omega_*'(\tau)),\qquad
\omega(t)=t\omega'(t)-\omega_*(\omega'(t)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable strictly convex function on the nonnegative half-line whose derivative is zero at the origin and tends to one at infinity, the derivative and the designated conjugate derivative are inverse coordinates. The function and its Fenchel conjugate have the stated maximum representations, satisfy the Fenchel–Young inequality, and satisfy the corresponding gradient equality identities.
assumptions_latex: \omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable and strictly convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall t\ge0,\ \forall\tau\in[0,1):\ \omega'(\omega_*'(\tau))=\tau,\ \omega_*'(\omega'(t))=t,\ \omega(t)=\max_{0\le\xi<1}\{\xi t-\omega_*(\xi)\},\ \omega_*(\tau)=\max_{\xi\ge0}\{\tau\xi-\omega(\xi)\},\ \omega(t)+\omega_*(\tau)\ge\tau t,\ \omega_*(\tau)=\tau\omega_*'(\tau)-\omega(\omega_*'(\tau)),\ \omega(t)=t\omega'(t)-\omega_*(\omega'(t))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict convexity implies interior differentiability of the conjugate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional strictly convex functions and interior points of the conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly convex, then \(f^*\) is differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\). For every \(s\) in this interior, \[Df^*(s)=x(s),\] where \(x(s)\) is the unique point satisfying \[s\in\partial f(x(s)),\qquad sx(s)-f(x(s))=f^*(s),\] equivalently \[x(s)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\bigl(f(x)-sx\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly convex function, the conjugate is differentiable in the interior of its domain, and its derivative is the unique primal point attaining the conjugate supremum, equivalently solving the subgradient relation or the tilted minimization problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Minimum Characterization by Stationarity and Convex-Envelope Contact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gâteaux differentiable functions on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), without an asserted convexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be G\hat{a}teaux differentiable on \mathbb{R}^n. A point x is a global minimizer of f on \mathbb{R}^n if and only if \nabla f(x)=0\ \text{and}\ (\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)(x)=f(x). In that case, \overline{\operatorname{co}}f is differentiable at x and \nabla(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)(x)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point globally minimizes a Gâteaux differentiable function exactly when it is stationary and the function agrees there with its closed convex hull. Then the closed convex hull is differentiable there with zero gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman distance-generating function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Set \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generator class suitable for Bregman divergences; strong convexity is included when quantitative distance domination is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Bregman generator on a nonempty convex reference domain \(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\) is a proper, closed, strictly convex function \(h\) that is differentiable on \(C
eq\varnothing\), with \(Q\cap C
eq\varnothing\). It generates \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle\quad(x\in Q,\ y\in Q\cap C).\] It is a \(\sigma\)-strong distance generator relative to \(\|\cdot\|\) if \[h(x)\geq h(y)+\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle+ rac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\] for all admissible \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman generator is a proper closed convex reference function, differentiable on the interior of its domain, whose first-order remainder defines a nonnegative divergence. Strong convexity makes that divergence dominate squared norm distance.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, strictly convex, and differentiable on \(C\neq\varnothing\).
\(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\) is nonempty and convex, with \(Q\cap C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) is defined on \(Q\times(Q\cap C)\), and strong generation yields \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The strong-generator inequality is exactly the lower bound \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: The Euclidean generator is \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\).
Negative entropy is a generator on the positive orthant or simplex interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity implies positive definiteness of \(D_h\) on the differentiability domain.
boundary_notes: Differentiability is required at the second argument only.
A generator need not produce a metric because symmetry and the triangle inequality may fail.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) is a distance-generating function with modulus \(\sigma>0\) relative to \(\|\cdot\|\) if it is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, differentiable on \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and
\[
h(y)\geq h(x)+\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2
\]
for all \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(y\in C\). Its associated Bregman divergence is \(D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\), hence \(D_h(y,x)\geq(\sigma/2)\|y-x\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance-generating function is a differentiable strongly convex reference function whose Bregman divergence controls squared displacement in a chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Legendre convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, with \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional Rockafellar definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is essentially smooth if it is differentiable throughout \(C\) and \(\|\nabla h(x_k)\|\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in C\) converges to a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}h\). It is essentially strictly convex if it is strictly convex on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h\). A Legendre function is a proper closed convex function that is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre function is a closed proper convex function combining interior differentiability and gradient blow-up at the domain boundary with strict convexity on convex subsets where subgradients exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is Legendre exactly when it is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, essential smoothness gives \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h=C\), while essential strict convexity is dual to essential smoothness of \(h^*\).
special_cases_latex: Every differentiable strictly convex cofinite function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is of Legendre type.
The negative entropy on the strictly positive orthant is a standard boundary-steep Legendre generator.
immediate_consequences_latex: The conjugate \(h^*\) is also Legendre.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(h\) is essentially smooth if: \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\); \(h\) is differentiable throughout \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\); and whenever \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) converges to a point of \(\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), one has
\[

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity restricted to convex subsets where subgradients exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(h\) is essentially strictly convex if its restriction to every nonempty convex subset \(K\subset\operatorname{dom}\partial h\) is strictly convex. Equivalently, for every such \(K\), all distinct \(x,y\in K\), and every \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[
h((1-t)x+ty)<(1-t)h(x)+t h(y).
\]
The definition does not require strict convexity on portions of \(\operatorname{dom}h\) lying outside \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre, let \(h^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate, and set \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), \(C^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre conjugacy on the interiors of the effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Legendre duality is the bijective coordinate correspondence \[y=
abla h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=
abla h^*(y),\qquad x\in C,\ y\in C^*,\] together with the Fenchel equality \[h(x)+h^*(y)=\langle x,yangle.\] Thus \(
abla h:C	o C^*\) and \(
abla h^*:C^*	o C\) are mutually inverse continuous maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Legendre duality identifies every interior primal point with a unique interior dual point through the gradient. The conjugate gradient returns the primal point, and the pair satisfies Fenchel equality.

abla f)^{-1}(x^*),x^*ightangle-f\!\left((

Canonical reference geometries are generated by
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{domain}&h(x)\\ \hline

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional vector space and let \(h\) be a convex function differentiable on \(Q^\circ=Q\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reference-domain geometry on \(Q\) is the pair \((Q,h)\) equipped with \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle,\qquad x\in Q,\ y\in Q^\circ,\] where \(h\) is proper, closed, strictly convex on \(Q^\circ\), and its effective domain and boundary behavior are compatible with \(Q\). A quantitative geometry additionally requires \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\) for a specified norm and \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference-domain geometry chooses a convex generator whose domain and boundary behavior match the feasible domain. Its Bregman divergence supplies the local notion of displacement, while optional strong convexity compares that displacement with a norm.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, strictly convex, and differentiable on \(Q^\circ\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((Q,h)\) defines \(D_h\) on \(Q\times Q^\circ\), with norm domination when \(h\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong convexity relative to the chosen norm is equivalent to \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: Euclidean space: \(Q=\mathbb R^n\), \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\).
Simplex: \(Q=\Delta_n\), \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\), with second argument in \(\Delta_n^{++}\).

For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(y\in U\), the Bregman divergence generated by \(h\) is
\[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle.\]

otin\operatorname{dom}h\) or \(y
otin U\). Thus \(D_h(x,y)\) is the error between \(h(x)\) and the affine first-order model of \(h\) based at \(y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman Function and Full-Range Bregman Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the generator class on a solid closed convex zone and the additional full-range condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be solid, closed, and convex. A function f:K\to\mathbb{R} is a Bregman function with zone K if: (i) f is strictly convex and continuous on K; (ii) f\in C^1(\operatorname{int}K); (iii) for every x\in K and \eta\in\mathbb{R}, the set \{y\in\operatorname{int}K:D_f(x,y)\le\eta\} is bounded; and (iv) whenever x^k\in\operatorname{int}K and x^k\to x\in K, D_f(x,x^k)\to0. Its divergence D_f is called a Bregman distance. If additionally \nabla f(\operatorname{int}K)=\mathbb{R}^n, then f is a full-range Bregman function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman function is a strictly convex continuous generator, differentiable on the interior of its solid closed convex zone, whose right-oriented divergence sublevel sets are bounded and whose divergence vanishes when the second argument approaches the first. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implications characterizing full-range Bregman generators, with equivalence under a nonsingular-Hessian hypothesis.

abla f(y^k)^T(y^k-x)	o+\infty. Then (a)\Rightarrow(b)\Rightarrow(c). If f\in C^2(\operatorname{int}K) and

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Point Identity and Convergence Detection for Bregman Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two intrinsic properties of the primal Bregman divergence on its asymmetric domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f be a Bregman function with zone K. For every x\in K and y,z\in\operatorname{int}K,
\[
D_f(x,y)=D_f(x,z)+D_f(z,y)+(\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(z))^T(z-x).
\]
Moreover, let x^k\in K and y^k\in\operatorname{int}K. If D_f(x^k,y^k)\to0 and either \{x^k\} or \{y^k\} converges, then the other sequence also converges and has the same limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal Bregman divergence satisfies a three-point identity. If the divergence between two admissible sequences tends to zero, convergence of either sequence forces the other to converge to the same limit.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a Bregman function with zone }K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_f(x,y)=D_f(x,z)+D_f(z,y)+(\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(z))^T(z-x),\quad\text{and }x^k,y^k\text{ converge to the same limit whenever either sequence converges.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bregman divergence formed in conjugate gradient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual Bregman divergence generated by the conjugate \(h^*\) is
\[
D_{h^*}(p,q)=h^*(p)-h^*(q)-\langle\nabla h^*(q),p-q\rangle.
\]
It is nonnegative by convexity of \(h^*\). When \(p=\nabla h(x)\) and \(q=\nabla h(y)\) for \(x,y\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), Legendre duality gives
\[
D_{h^*}(p,q)=D_h(y,x),
\]
so passage to dual coordinates reverses the primal arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual Bregman divergence applies the usual construction to the Fenchel conjugate; under gradient coordinates it equals the primal divergence with reversed arguments.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(p=\nabla h(x)\) and \(q=\nabla h(y)\). Legendre duality yields \(x=\nabla h^*(p)\), \(y=\nabla h^*(q)\), and the Fenchel equalities \(h(x)+h^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\) and \(h(y)+h^*(q)=\langle q,y\rangle\). Consequently,
\[
D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(q,p).
\]
Thus the gradient bijection identifies the ordered primal pair \((x,y)\) with the reversed ordered dual pair \((q,p)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the convention \(D_h(a,b)=h(a)-h(b)-\langle\nabla h(b),a-b\rangle\), the three-point identity is
\[
D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z)
=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle
=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).
\]
The identity requires only differentiability at the base points \(y\) and \(z\); convexity additionally ensures that all displayed divergences are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point identity expresses a gradient pairing as the difference of three Bregman divergences and underlies projection and mirror-descent calculations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-point Bregman defect and identity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(D_h\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional geometry. All three points lie in the differentiability region so every displayed divergence and gradient is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y,z\in U\), define the three-point Bregman defect by
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The three-point geometry is the identity
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle,\]
or equivalently
\[D_h(x,z)=D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)+\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point Bregman defect compares the direct divergence from z to x with the two-stage divergences through y. It equals the pairing of the dual-coordinate displacement ∇h(y)−∇h(z) with the primal displacement x−y.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and is differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)-D_h(x,z)=\langle\nabla h(z)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
\(D_h(x,z)-D_h(y,z)=D_h(x,y)+\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), the identity becomes \(\tfrac12\|x-z\|^2=\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2+\tfrac12\|y-z\|^2+\langle y-z,x-y\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\geq0\), then \(D_h(x,z)\geq D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)\).
If the pairing term vanishes, the three divergences satisfy an exact Pythagorean equality.
boundary_notes: This identity is algebraic and does not itself assert that any point is a projection.
The three-point defect need not have a fixed sign without an additional variational or orthogonality condition.
review_flags: No inspected source locator supplied direct support for the three-point Bregman identity with this sign and orientation convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-point Bregman defect and identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed three-point identity has a consistent sign and orientation, but the record supplies no independently verifiable source.

children.title: Bregman Metric-Axiom Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating Bregman divergences from metric distances.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-axiom profile of a Bregman divergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on a nonempty open convex set \(U\subseteq E\), and let \(D_h:U\times U\to[0,+\infty)\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records exactly where a Bregman divergence agrees with or departs from the axioms of a metric; it does not classify all generators producing metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the symmetry and triangle defects by
\[S_h(x,y)=D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,x),\qquad T_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The Bregman metric-axiom profile consists of nonnegativity \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\), reflexivity \(D_h(x,x)=0\), separation when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), symmetry when \(S_h\equiv0\), and the triangle inequality when \(T_h\leq0\) for every ordered triple. A Bregman divergence is metric-valued on \(U\) precisely when separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality all hold in addition to nonnegativity and reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric boundary is described by two defects. The symmetry defect compares the two orientations, while the triangle defect compares a direct divergence with a two-leg route. Every convex differentiable generator gives nonnegativity and zero diagonal; strict convexity gives point separation, but symmetry and the triangle inequality are additional properties and generally fail.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq E\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) has the metric axioms on \(U\) exactly when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), \(S_h(x,y)=0\), and \(T_h(x,y,z)\leq0\) for all \(x,y,z\in U\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S_h(x,y)=2(h(x)-h(y))-\langle\nabla h(x)+\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
\(T_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a positive-definite quadratic generator, \(D_h\) is a squared norm: it is symmetric and separating, but \(D_h\) itself generally fails the triangle inequality; \(\sqrt{2D_h}\) is the associated metric.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity supplies separation but does not supply symmetry or a triangle inequality.
The term “divergence” does not imply that \(D_h\) is a distance metric.
boundary_notes: A squared norm is not itself a metric except in degenerate restrictions, despite being symmetric and nonnegative.
This profile concerns \(D_h\), not transformations such as \(\sqrt{D_h}\) or symmetrizations such as \(D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)\).

notation.meaning: Symmetry defect of the directed divergence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional negative-entropy counterexample to symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=t\log t\) on \((0,\infty)\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=x\log(x/y)-x+y.\] At \(x=1\) and \(y=2\), one has \[D_f(1,2)=1-\log 2,\qquad D_f(2,1)=2\log 2-1.\] These values are unequal, so a Bregman divergence need not satisfy \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\), even when its generator is smooth and strictly convex.

children.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure
children.top_down_role: Geometric obstruction to metric triangle behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Triangle Inequality Forces Affinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp smooth boundary for the triangle inequality applied to the divergence itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(h\in C^2(C)\) be convex. If \[D_h(x,z)\le D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)\quad\text{for all }x,y,z\in C,\] then \(h\) is affine on \(C\) and \(D_h\equiv0\). Conversely, an affine generator produces the zero divergence, which satisfies the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable Bregman divergence satisfies the global triangle inequality only in the trivial affine, zero-divergence case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h\equiv0\quad\text{and}\quad h\text{ is affine on }C.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle Inequality Forces Affinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure concerns the divergence itself, not its square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the smooth strictly convex generator \(f(t)=\tfrac12t^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^2.\] Taking \(x=0\), \(y=1\), and \(z=2\) gives \[D_f(0,2)=2>1=D_f(0,1)+D_f(1,2).\] Thus even a symmetric Bregman divergence need not obey the triangle inequality and therefore need not itself be a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared Euclidean distance is a Bregman divergence, but at 0, 1, and 2 it violates the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The squared-Euclidean calculation correctly demonstrates failure of the triangle inequality for the divergence itself, and counterexample fits the leaf. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Metric-Compatible Special Cases
children.top_down_role: Restricted generator regimes exhibiting metric-like features.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Quadratics Give a Quotient Metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic metric-compatible cases and their exact point-separation boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) with symmetric \(Q\succeq0\), \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y),\qquad \sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2.\] The square root is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\) exactly when \(Q\succ0\). If \(Q\) is singular, it is a pseudometric on \(\mathbb R^n\) and induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\). The affine part of \(f\) does not affect the divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic yields a Mahalanobis pseudometric; it is a genuine metric exactly for positive-definite curvature, and otherwise becomes one on the quotient by the null space.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_f}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\iff Q\succ0\); for singular \(Q\), it induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left Bregman projection onto a feasible set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(C\subseteq E\) satisfy \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued left projection with the feasible point in the first divergence argument. Existence and uniqueness are not built into the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a base point \(y\in U\), the left Bregman projection of \(y\) onto \(C\) is
\[P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y).\]
Its projection value is
\[d^{h,L}_C(y)=\inf_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y).\]
The projection is defined as a set of minimizers; it may be empty, contain one point, or contain several points unless further hypotheses are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The left Bregman projection of y onto C is the set of feasible points x minimizing the divergence D_h(x,y), where the variable occupies the first argument and y is the fixed base point. The associated projection value is the corresponding infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\{p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h:D_h(p,y)=d^{h,L}_C(y)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in E}\{\iota_C(x)+h(x)-\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\}\), where constants independent of \(x\) are omitted.
\(p\in P^{h,L}_C(y)\) exactly when \(p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(D_h(p,y)\leq D_h(x,y)\) for every \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), \(P^{h,L}_C\) is the ordinary Euclidean projector.
If \(C=\{c\}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\), then \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\{c\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\) is convex and \(h\) is strictly convex on \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), then the projection contains at most one point.
Attainment of the infimum is a separate requirement from finiteness of the projection value.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(C\) alone need not ensure attainment when the generator domain is open or the objective is not level-bounded.
The right projection minimizes \(D_h(y,x)\) and is a distinct orientation.
review_flags: The supplied Euclidean-projection locators do not directly support this Bregman projection definition and its orientation/domain conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Left Bregman projection onto a feasible set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-valued left-projection definition is plausible and distinguishes attainment from definition, but no cited source supports its domain and orientation conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left- and right-oriented Bregman projections
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\). Let \(C\subseteq E\) and fix \(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, set-valued formulation distinguishing the two minimization problems created by the directed argument order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The orientation-dual projection pair is
\[P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y),\qquad
P^{h,R}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap U}D_h(y,x).\]
The left orientation varies the evaluation point of the first-order-model error. The right orientation varies its base point, so differentiability requires the variable \(x\) to lie in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are two directed Bregman projections. The left projection minimizes D_h(x,y) over feasible x, while the right projection minimizes D_h(y,x). These are different optimization objects because a Bregman divergence is generally asymmetric and because the variable in the right problem must lie where the generator is differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
The left feasible domain is \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), while the right feasible domain is \(C\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordered pair \((P^{h,L}_C(y),P^{h,R}_C(y))\) is defined by the two orientation-specific argmin sets above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{h(x)-\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\}\), with extended-value conventions.
\(P^{h,R}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap U}\{h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D_h\) is symmetric on \(C\cup\{y\}\), then \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=P^{h,R}_C(y)\).
For a positive-definite quadratic generator, both orientations reduce to the same weighted Euclidean projection.
immediate_consequences_latex: Existence or uniqueness of one orientation does not by definition imply existence or uniqueness of the other.
The two projection values can differ whenever the divergence is asymmetric.
boundary_notes: The right projection objective need not be convex in its variable, even when \(h\) is convex.
Points in \(C\cap(\operatorname{dom}h\setminus U)\) may be eligible for the left problem but not for the right problem.
review_flags: No inspected authoritative locator was available for both orientation-specific projection definitions and their distinct feasible domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Left- and right-oriented Bregman projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two orientation-specific argmin definitions are mathematically distinct and plausible, but they have no independently inspectable support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropic Optimal Transport by Iterative Proportional Fitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL-projection representation, alternating marginal rescaling, convergence, and the finite-dimensional zero-regularization limit for discrete entropic transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i>0\), \(b_j>0\), \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\), \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). Set \(\eta_{ij}=e^{-c_{ij}/\varepsilon}>0\). The problem \[\min\left\{\sum_{i,j}\bigl(c_{ij}\gamma_{ij}+\varepsilon\gamma_{ij}\log\gamma_{ij}\bigr):\gamma_{ij}\geq0,\ \sum_j\gamma_{ij}=a_i,\ \sum_i\gamma_{ij}=b_j\right\}\] is equivalently the left KL projection \(\min_{\gamma\in C^x\cap C^y}\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\gamma\mid\eta)\). Starting from \(\gamma^0=\eta\), alternately rescale rows and columns by \[\gamma_{ij}^{2k+1}=\frac{a_i}{\sum_\ell\gamma_{i\ell}^{2k}}\gamma_{ij}^{2k},\qquad \gamma_{ij}^{2k+2}=\frac{b_j}{\sum_\ell\gamma_{\ell j}^{2k+1}}\gamma_{ij}^{2k+1}.\] These IPFP iterates converge to the regularized minimizer and have the diagonal-scaling form \(\gamma_{ij}^k=\eta_{ij}p_i^kq_j^k\). In the finite-dimensional topology, the entropy-regularized objectives, extended by \(+\infty\) outside the nonnegative transport constraints, \(\Gamma\)-converge to the unregularized discrete transport objective as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropic discrete optimal transport is a left KL projection of the Gibbs kernel exp(-c/epsilon) onto the prescribed row- and column-marginal constraints. Alternating exact row and column rescalings form IPFP and converge to the regularized optimizer while retaining a diagonal-scaling representation. In finite dimensions, the regularized objectives Gamma-converge to the unregularized transport objective as epsilon tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma^k\to\gamma_\varepsilon^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\gamma\in C^x\cap C^y}\operatorname{KL}(\gamma\mid\eta),\qquad F_\varepsilon\xrightarrow{\Gamma}F_0\ \text{as }\varepsilon\downarrow0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the quadratic-metric projection point and its equivalent support-function condition.

Let $S$ be a nonempty compact convex set and let $Q$ be symmetric positive definite. There exists a unique $s^\star\in S$ such that

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness, Conjugacy, and Cocoercivity of the Metric Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core analytic properties of a Moreau envelope formed with a positive-definite quadratic metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be closed and convex, let $M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0$, and set $W=M^{-1}$. Then $f_M$ is finite everywhere, convex, and differentiable, with
\[
\nabla f_M(x)=s_M(x)=M\bigl(x-p_M(x)\bigr).
\]
Its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
f_M^*(s)=f^*(s)+\frac12\langle s,Ws\rangle.
\]
Moreover, for every $x,x'\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
\langle s_M(x)-s_M(x'),W(s_M(x)-s_M(x'))\rangle
\le \langle s_M(x)-s_M(x'),x-x'\rangle,
\]
and, in the Euclidean norm,
\[
\|\nabla f_M(x)-\nabla f_M(x')\|\le\lambda_{\max}(M)\|x-x'\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric Moreau envelope is finite, convex, and differentiable everywhere. Its gradient is the distinguished proximal subgradient, its conjugate adds the quadratic form induced by M inverse to f conjugate, its gradient is metric-cocoercive, and it is Euclidean Lipschitz with constant lambda_max(M).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_M\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n),\quad \nabla f_M(x)=M(x-p_M(x)),\quad f_M^*(s)=f^*(s)+\frac12\langle s,Ws\rangle,\quad \langle\Delta s,W\Delta s\rangle\le\langle\Delta s,\Delta x\rangle,\quad \|\Delta\nabla f_M\|\le\lambda_{\max}(M)\|\Delta x\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Moreau–Yosida Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a closed convex function using a fixed positive-definite quadratic metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be closed and convex, and let $M$ be symmetric positive definite. The Moreau--Yosida regularization of $f$ associated with $M$ is
\[
f_M(x):=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, its defining joint objective is $g(x,y):=f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function f and a symmetric positive-definite metric M, the metric Moreau–Yosida regularization at x is the minimum over y of f(y) plus one half of the M-quadratic distance from y to x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Proximal Point and Distinguished Proximal Subgradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Notation and identities associated with the unique minimizer of the metric Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f$ be closed and convex, let $M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0$, and set $W:=M^{-1}$. For $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, define the proximal point
\[
p_M(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\},
\]
with $x$ called the proximal center. Define the distinguished proximal subgradient
\[
s_M(x):=M\bigl(x-p_M(x)\bigr)\in\partial f\bigl(p_M(x)\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
p_M(x)=x-Ws_M(x).
\]
The vector $s_M(x)$ is the subgradient selected by the proximal minimization and need not equal an arbitrary oracle subgradient at $p_M(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric proximal point p_M(x) is the unique minimizer of the regularized problem. Its distinguished proximal subgradient is s_M(x)=M(x−p_M(x)), which lies in the subdifferential at p_M(x), and p_M(x)=x−M^{-1}s_M(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_M(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\},\quad s_M(x):=M(x-p_M(x))\in\partial f(p_M(x)),\quad p_M(x)=x-Ws_M(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Softmax formula for entropy-regularized simplex maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The entropy convention extends continuously to the boundary of the simplex by setting \(0\ln0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(\Delta_m=\{u\in\mathbb R^m:u^{(j)}\ge0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}=1\}\), and \(d_2(u)=\ln m+\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\ln u^{(j)}\), with \(0\ln0=0\). Fix \(\mu_2>0\), and define \(s^{(j)}=f_j+\langle g_j,\bar x-x_j\rangle\). Then \[\max_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}\] has a unique maximizer \(\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\), whose components are \[\nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{\exp(s^{(j)}/\mu_2)}{\sum_{l=1}^m\exp(s^{(l)}/\mu_2)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective regularized by scaled negative entropy over the probability simplex has a unique optimizer, and that optimizer is the softmax of the coefficient vector divided by the regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}=\{\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\},\quad \nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{e^{s^{(j)}/\mu_2}}{\sum_{l=1}^m e^{s^{(l)}/\mu_2}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gâteaux Gradient Supporting Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order global lower bound for a convex function at a point of Gâteaux differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, and let \(x\in\mathcal H\). If \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\), then \[\forall y\in\mathcal H,\qquad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle y-x,\nabla f(x)\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex extended-real-valued function that is Gâteaux differentiable at x, the affine function determined by its value and gradient at x is a global lower bound: for every y, f(y) is at least f(x) plus the inner product of y−x with the gradient at x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, Uniqueness, and Optimality of the Metric Proximal Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of the minimizer defining the metric Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be closed and convex, let $M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0$, and fix $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then
\[
\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac12\langle M(y-x),y-x\rangle\right\}
\]
has a unique solution $y$, characterized equivalently as the unique point satisfying
\[
M(x-y)\in\partial f(y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strongly convex problem defining the metric Moreau envelope has a unique minimizer. It is exactly the unique point y for which M(x−y) is a subgradient of f at y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z}\left\{f(z)+\frac12\langle M(z-x),z-x\rangle\right\}\iff M(x-y)\in\partial f(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Softmax Solution of Entropy-Regularized Simplex Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded closed-form characterization of the unique entropy-regularized maximizer over a finite simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\Delta_m=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^m:u^{(j)}\ge0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}=1\right\},
\qquad
d_2(u)=\ln m+\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\ln u^{(j)},
\]
where \(0\ln0=0\). Fix \(\mu_2>0\), \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), and data \(f_j\in\mathbb R\), \(g_j,x_j\in\mathbb R^n\), and set \(s^{(j)}=f_j+\langle g_j,\bar x-x_j\rangle\). Then
\[
\max_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}
\]
has a unique maximizer \(\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\), with
\[
\nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{\exp(s^{(j)}/\mu_2)}{\sum_{l=1}^m\exp(s^{(l)}/\mu_2)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive regularization, maximizing a linear function minus normalized negative entropy over the probability simplex has a unique solution. Its components are the softmax of the scores divided by the regularization parameter.
assumptions_latex: \bar x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad f_j\in\mathbb R,\quad g_j,x_j\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\langle s,u\rangle-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}=\left\{\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\right\},\qquad \nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{e^{s^{(j)}/\mu_2}}{\sum_{l=1}^m e^{s^{(l)}/\mu_2}}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing-Regularization Limit for Increasing Metric Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise limiting behavior as the smallest eigenvalue of the quadratic metric diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be closed and convex, and let $M$ range over symmetric positive-definite operators such that $\lambda_{\min}(M)\to+\infty$. Then
\[
f_M(x)\to f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
and
\[
p_M(x)\to x\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Moreau Envelope Value Identity and Upper Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation among the envelope value, proximal point, distinguished subgradient, and original function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be closed and convex, let $M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0$, and set $W=M^{-1}$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
f_M(x)+\frac12\langle s_M(x),Ws_M(x)\rangle
=f\bigl(p_M(x)\bigr)+\langle s_M(x),Ws_M(x)\rangle
\le f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every center x, adding one half of the squared dual metric norm of the proximal subgradient to the envelope value equals f at the proximal point plus the full squared dual metric norm, and this quantity is at most f(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_M(x)+\frac12\langle s_M(x),Ws_M(x)\rangle=f(p_M(x))+\langle s_M(x),Ws_M(x)\rangle\le f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tikhonov Selection of the Minimum-Norm Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical quadratic vanishing regularization for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) with \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathcal H} f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\|x\|^2\) has a unique solution \(x_\varepsilon\), characterized by \(0\in\partial f(x_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon x_\varepsilon\). If \(x_0\) is the unique minimum-norm point of \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\), then \(x_\varepsilon\to x_0\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function with at least one minimizer, adding a positive quadratic penalty produces a unique minimizer satisfying the corresponding subdifferential inclusion. As the penalty weight decreases to zero, these minimizers converge strongly to the minimum-norm minimizer of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!x_\varepsilon\in\mathcal H:\;0\in\partial f(x_\varepsilon)+\varepsilon x_\varepsilon,\qquad x_\varepsilon\to x_0\quad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential and Jacobian of a vector-valued map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator, componentwise, and coordinate-matrix descriptions of finite-dimensional differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y=\mathbb R^m$ be Euclidean spaces, $\Omega\subset X$, and $F:\Omega\to Y$. The map $F$ is differentiable at $x\in\Omega$ if there is a linear operator $L:X\to Y$ such that $F(x+h)=F(x)+Lh+o(\|h\|)$ as $h\to0$. This operator is $F'(x)=DF(x)=JF(x)$. For component functions $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$, differentiability of $F$ at $x$ is equivalent to differentiability of every $f_j$ there, and $JF(x)h=(f_1'(x)h,\ldots,f_m'(x)h)$ for all $h\in X$. If $\dim X=n$, its matrix in chosen bases is the $m\times n$ matrix with entries $\partial f_i/\partial\xi^j(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued map is differentiable when it has a linear first-order approximation. Its differential is the Jacobian operator. Differentiability is equivalent to componentwise differentiability, and the Jacobian matrix consists of the component partial derivatives.
assumptions_latex: $X$ and $Y=\mathbb R^m$ are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The limit is taken through increments for which $x+h\in\Omega$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $F$ is differentiable at $x$ iff all component functions $f_j$ are differentiable at $x$; then $JF(x)h=(f_1'(x)h,\ldots,f_m'(x)h)$, and its coordinate matrix has entries $(JF(x))_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial\xi^j(x)$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fermat Rule for a Bounded Linear Equality Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality, multiplier, and differentiable stationarity conditions for an affine-constrained convex problem in Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal K\) be Hilbert spaces, \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), and \(r\in\operatorname{sri}L(\operatorname{dom}f)\). For every \(\bar x\in\mathcal H\), \(\bar x\) solves \(\min\{f(x):Lx=r\}\) if and only if \(L\bar x=r\) and there exists \(\bar v\in\mathcal K\) such that \(-L^*\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\). In that case \(\bar v\) is a Lagrange multiplier and \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f(x)+\langle x,L^*\bar v\rangle\bigr)\). If \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(\bar x\), the subgradient condition is equivalent to \(\nabla f(\bar x)=-L^*\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and a bounded linear equality constraint satisfying the stated strong-relative-interior qualification, a point is optimal exactly when it is feasible and its subdifferential contains the negative adjoint image of some multiplier. That multiplier also makes the point minimize the corresponding unconstrained Lagrangian; at a Gâteaux differentiability point, stationarity is the gradient equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Lx=r}f(x)\iff\bigl[L\bar x=r\ \land\ (\exists\bar v\in\mathcal K)\,-L^*\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\bigr]\); such \(\bar v\) is a multiplier and \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal H}(f(x)+\langle x,L^*\bar v\rangle)\). If \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(\bar x\), stationarity becomes \(\nabla f(\bar x)=-L^*\bar v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameterized intersection of two balls admits a smaller enclosing ball
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\mathrm B(x,r)\) denotes the Euclidean ball centered at \(x\) with radius \(r\). The center \(c\) is independent of \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and \(g\in\mathbb R_+\), with \(\lVert a\rVert\ge g\). Then there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) such that, for every \(\delta\ge0\), \[\mathrm B\!\left(0,1-\varepsilon g^2-\delta\right)\cap\mathrm B\!\left(a,g^2(1-\varepsilon)-\delta\right)\subseteq\mathrm B\!\left(c,1-\sqrt{\varepsilon}-\delta\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a has norm at least the nonnegative parameter g and epsilon lies strictly between zero and one, then one can choose a center c such that, for every nonnegative delta, the intersection of the two specified Euclidean balls lies in the ball centered at c with radius 1 minus the square root of epsilon minus delta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity, Growth, and Differential Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong convexity on a closed convex set and records its principal consequences and smooth equivalent conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) be closed and convex, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuous on \(C\), and let \(\sigma>0\). The function \(f\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex on \(C\) when, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \[f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)+ rac{\sigma}{2}\alpha(1-\alpha)\|x-y\|^2\le \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).\] Such an \(f\) is strictly convex, has a unique minimizer \(x^*\in C\), and satisfies \[f(x)\ge f(x^*)+ rac{\sigma}{2}\|x-x^*\|^2\qquad orall x\in C.\] If \(\operatorname{int}C
e\varnothing\) and \(f\in C^1(\operatorname{int}C)\), strong convexity is equivalent to each of \[(
abla f(x)-
abla f(y))^	op(x-y)\ge\sigma\|x-y\|^2\] and \[f(y)\ge f(x)+
abla f(x)^	op(y-x)+ rac{\sigma}{2}\|x-y\|^2\] for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{int}C\). If additionally \(f\in C^2(\operatorname{int}C)\), these are equivalent to \(
abla^2f(x)-\sigma I\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity means that every chord dominates the function by a uniform quadratic amount. It implies strict convexity, a unique minimizer, and quadratic growth from that minimizer. On a set with nonempty interior, smooth strong convexity is equivalently strong monotonicity of the gradient or a quadratic supporting inequality; in the twice-smooth case it is equivalently a uniform Hessian lower bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jensen's inequality and characterization of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers finite convex combinations and probability measures; integral and expectation forms require the relevant quantities to exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex. For every \(k\ge 2\), \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^k\theta_i=1\), \[f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\theta_i x_i\right)\le \sum_{i=1}^k\theta_i f(x_i).\] More generally, if a random variable \(X\) lies in \(\operatorname{dom}f\) almost surely and the expectations exist, then \[f(\mathbf E X)\le \mathbf E f(X).\] Equivalently, if \(p\ge0\) on \(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\int_Sp(x)\,dx=1\), and the integrals exist, then \[f\!\left(\int_Sp(x)x\,dx\right)\le\int_Sf(x)p(x)\,dx.\] The expectation inequality for all finitely supported \(X\) characterizes convexity: if \(f\) is not convex, some such \(X\) satisfies \(f(\mathbf E X)>\mathbf E f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, its value at any finite convex combination is at most the same convex combination of its values. The analogous inequality holds for normalized integrals and expectations whenever the relevant integrals or expectations exist and the measure is supported in the function's domain. Conversely, validity of the expectation inequality for every finitely supported random variable characterizes convexity; a nonconvex function admits a finitely supported counterexample with the strict reverse inequality.
assumptions_latex: X\in\operatorname{dom}f\ \text{almost surely, with the relevant expectations existing}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\!\left(\sum_i\theta_i x_i\right)\le\sum_i\theta_i f(x_i),\qquad f(\mathbf E X)\le\mathbf E f(X),\qquad f\!\left(\int_Sp(x)x\,dx\right)\le\int_Sf(x)p(x)\,dx;\ \text{moreover, the expectation inequality for all finitely supported }X\text{ is equivalent to convexity.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Strong Convexity versus Primal Quadratic Upper Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded equivalence for finite continuous convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, let \(\gamma>0\), and set \(q=\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2\). Then
\[
f^*-\gamma^{-1}q\text{ is convex}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma q-f\text{ is convex}.
\]
Equivalently, \(f^*\) is \(\gamma^{-1}\)-strongly convex if and only if \(\gamma q-f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite continuous convex function f on a Hilbert space and positive gamma, the conjugate of f is reciprocal-gamma strongly convex exactly when gamma times the half-squared norm minus f is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Güler objective-gap inequality for a proximity step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-step reciprocal-gap improvement bound for the proximity operator of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(x\in\mathcal H\), and \(z\in\operatorname{Argmin}f\). If \(p=\operatorname{Prox}_f x\notin\operatorname{Argmin}f\), then
\[
\frac{f(p)-f(z)}{f(x)-f(z)}\le 1-\frac{2}{3}\frac{f(p)-f(z)}{\lVert x-z\rVert^2}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{2}{3\lVert x-z\rVert^2}\le \frac{1}{f(p)-f(z)}-\frac{1}{f(x)-f(z)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space, if z minimizes f and the proximal point p of x is not itself a minimizer, then the post-proximal objective gap satisfies the stated relative-decrease inequality; equivalently, the reciprocal objective gap increases by at least 2 divided by 3 times the squared distance from x to z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{f(p)-f(z)}{f(x)-f(z)}\le 1-\frac{2\bigl(f(p)-f(z)\bigr)}{3\lVert x-z\rVert^2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{2}{3\lVert x-z\rVert^2}\le \frac{1}{f(p)-f(z)}-\frac{1}{f(x)-f(z)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-step accelerated scheme for simple sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The recurrence uses \(q=\mu/L\), an exact projected-gradient step at each extrapolated point, and the specified momentum parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha_0\in(0,1)\), set \(y_0=x_0\) and \(q=\mu/L\). For each \(k\ge0\), compute
\[
x_{k+1}=x_Q(y_k;L),
\]
choose \(\alpha_{k+1}\in(0,1)\) satisfying
\[
\alpha_{k+1}^2=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\alpha_k^2+q\alpha_{k+1},
\]
set
\[
\beta_k=\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)}{\alpha_k^2+\alpha_{k+1}},
\qquad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, take a projected-gradient step from the extrapolated point, update the acceleration parameter using the strong-convexity ratio, and extrapolate with the resulting momentum coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=x_Q(y_k;L),\quad \beta_k=\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)}{\alpha_k^2+\alpha_{k+1}},\quad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential characterization, calculus, and optimality for finite convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded collection of equivalent characterizations and calculus rules for a finite-valued convex function on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex and x\in\mathbb{R}^n. Then: (a) d\in\partial f(x) iff f'(x;y)\ge y^\top d for every y\in\mathbb{R}^n. (b) \partial f(x) is nonempty, convex, and compact, and \[f'(x;y)=\max_{d\in\partial f(x)}y^\top d\quad(\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Hence f is differentiable at x iff \partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}; moreover, \bigcup_{u\in X}\partial f(u) is bounded whenever X is bounded. (c) If x_k\to x and d_k\in\partial f(x_k), then (d_k) is bounded and every limit point belongs to \partial f(x). (d) If f=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j with each f_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} convex, then \partial f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\partial f_j(x). (e) If f(x)=h(Ax), where h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R} is convex and A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, then \partial f(x)=A^\top\partial h(Ax). (f) For every convex X\subset\mathbb{R}^n, x minimizes f over X iff there exists d\in\partial f(x) such that d^\top(z-x)\ge0 for all z\in X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite convex function, subgradients are exactly the vectors dominated by every directional derivative, and the directional derivative is the support function of the nonempty compact convex subdifferential. A singleton subdifferential characterizes differentiability; subgradients are uniformly bounded over bounded sets and have a closed-graph limit property. Subdifferentials obey exact finite-sum and linear-composition rules, and constrained minimizers over convex sets are characterized by a subgradient having nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the sum rule: }f=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j,\quad f_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ convex}
\text{For the composition rule: }f(x)=h(Ax),\quad h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\text{ convex},\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}
\text{For the optimality condition: }X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is convex and }x\in X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in\partial f(x)\iff[\forall y,\ f'(x;y)\ge y^\top d];\quad \partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\text{ is convex and compact};\quad f'(x;y)=\max_{d\in\partial f(x)}y^\top d;\quad f\text{ differentiable at }x\iff\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\};\quad \bigcup_{u\in X}\partial f(u)\text{ is bounded for bounded }X;\quad [x_k\to x,\ d_k\in\partial f(x_k)]\implies[(d_k)\text{ bounded and }\operatorname{Lims}(d_k)\subset\partial f(x)];\quad \partial(\sum_j f_j)(x)=\sum_j\partial f_j(x);\quad \partial(h\circ A)(x)=A^\top\partial h(Ax);\quad x\in\arg\min_{z\in X}f(z)\iff\exists d\in\partial f(x)\ \forall z\in X,\ d^\top(z-x)\ge0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercive and supercoercive functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the zero-dimensional convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The function \(f\) is coercive if \(\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}f(x)=+\infty\), and it is supercoercive if \(\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}f(x)/\|x\|=+\infty\). By convention, when \(\mathcal H=\{0\}\), every such \(f\) is both coercive and supercoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is coercive when its values tend to positive infinity as the norm of its argument tends to infinity, and supercoercive when its value divided by that norm tends to positive infinity. On the zero space it is, by convention, both coercive and supercoercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ coercive}\iff\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}f(x)=+\infty\), and \(f\text{ supercoercive}\iff\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}\frac{f(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty\), with both properties imposed by convention if \(\mathcal H=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex–concave minimax equality on compact convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality permitting interchange of minimization and maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be convex compact sets, and let \(f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. If \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(\mathcal X\) for every \(y\in\mathcal Y\), and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(\mathcal Y\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), then \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}f(x,y)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous function on compact convex sets that is convex in its first variable and concave in its second, the minimum of the pointwise maximum equals the maximum of the pointwise minimum, so the two optimization orders may be interchanged.

f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous}
\forall y\in\mathcal Y,\;f(\cdot,y)\text{ is convex on }\mathcal X
\forall x\in\mathcal X,\;f(x,\cdot)\text{ is concave on }\mathcal Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\mathcal X}\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}f(x,y)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x,y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attained support representation of a vectorial-norm directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents each directional derivative as the cone-order maximum of evaluations by supporting continuous linear maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real reflexive Banach spaces, let $C_Y\subseteq Y$ be a closed convex Daniell cone with a weakly compact base, and let $\|\cdot\|:X\to Y$ be a vectorial norm continuous at $\bar x\in X$. Define $$\mathcal S(\bar x):=\{T\in B(X,Y):T(\bar x)=\|\bar x\|,\ \|x\|-T(x)\in C_Y\ \forall x\in X\}.$$ Then, for every $h\in X$, $$\|\bar x\|'(h)=\max_{T\in\mathcal S(\bar x)}T(h).$$ The maximum is attained: for each $h$ there is $\bar T\in\mathcal S(\bar x)$ such that $\|\bar x\|'(h)=\bar T(h)$, and $\|\bar x\|'(h)\in T(h)+C_Y$ for every $T\in\mathcal S(\bar x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a continuity point, the directional derivative of a vectorial norm is the attained cone-order maximum of the directional evaluations of all continuous linear maps that support the norm globally and agree with it at the reference point.
assumptions_latex: $X$ and $Y$ are real reflexive Banach spaces.
$C_Y\subseteq Y$ is closed, convex, Daniell, and has a weakly compact base.
$\|\cdot\|:X\to Y$ is a vectorial norm continuous at $\bar x\in X$.
$\mathcal S(\bar x)=\{T\in B(X,Y):T(\bar x)=\|\bar x\|,\ \forall x\in X,\ \|x\|-T(x)\in C_Y\}$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall h\in X,\quad \|\bar x\|'(h)=\max_{T\in\mathcal S(\bar x)}T(h),\quad \exists \bar T\in\mathcal S(\bar x):\|\bar x\|'(h)=\bar T(h),\quad \forall T\in\mathcal S(\bar x),\ \|\bar x\|'(h)\in T(h)+C_Y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower bound from the projected-gradient mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inequality holds for every comparison point in Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal S^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), \(\gamma\ge L\), and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\). Then, for every \(x\in Q\),
\[
f(x)\ge f\bigl(x_Q(\bar x;\gamma)\bigr)+\langle g_Q(\bar x;\gamma),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|g_Q(\bar x;\gamma)\|^2+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mu-strongly convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient and gamma at least L, the function value at any feasible comparison point is bounded below by the value at the projected-gradient point, a gradient-mapping linear term, the squared mapping residual, and the strong-convexity term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\ge f(x_Q(\bar x;\gamma))+\langle g_Q(\bar x;\gamma),x-\bar x\rangle+\frac{\|g_Q(\bar x;\gamma)\|^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Openness of Uniform Symmetric-Difference Loci
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes openness of the set where a convex function satisfies a fixed-tolerance uniform symmetric-difference bound at some positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(\varepsilon>0\), and define
\[
S_\varepsilon=\bigcup_{\eta>0}\left\{x\in\operatorname{cont}f\ \middle|\ \sup_{\substack{y\in\mathcal H\\\|y\|=1}}\frac{f(x+\eta y)+f(x-\eta y)-2f(x)}{\eta}<\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Then \(S_\varepsilon\) is open in \(\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function and any positive epsilon, consider the continuity points at which some positive step gives a unit-direction symmetric second-difference quotient uniformly below epsilon. The union of these points over all positive steps is open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\varepsilon\text{ is open in }\mathcal H.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Directional Minorization and Majorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directionally quadratic second-order support models and records their trivial boundary cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\operatorname{Conv}(\mathbb R^n), x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f, s\in\partial f(x_0), and let \varphi_s be directionally quadratic. It defines a second-order minorization of f at x_0 associated with s when, as h\to0,\n\[f(x_0+h)\ge f(x_0)+\langle s,h\rangle+\varphi_s(h)+o(\|h\|^2),\]\nand a second-order majorization when the reverse inequality holds. If x_0\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f, then \varphi_s\equiv0 and \varphi_s=\delta_{\{0\}} give, respectively, trivial minorizations and majorizations for every s\in\partial f(x_0).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directionally quadratic function is a second-order minorant or majorant when adding it to the affine subgradient model bounds the function locally up to a term negligible relative to the squared displacement. The zero function and the indicator of the origin give the respective trivial models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_0+h)\gtreqless f(x_0)+\langle s,h\rangle+\varphi_s(h)+o(\|h\|^2)\quad(h\to0),\text{ with }\ge\text{ for minorization and }\le\text{ for majorization}.
